16029-the-great-round-world-and-what-is-:
Number forty-eight of The Great Round World, dated October 7, 1897, opens with peace news from the Near East. After a three-hour conference on September 18, ambassadors and Tewfik Pasha signed a treaty. The Sultan then accepted it. It ended the war between Greece and Turkey on terms set by Lord Salisbury and the Powers. Troops were to leave Thessaly within a month, while the Powers held Greek income until a war indemnity was paid.

The paper retells such diplomacy in short sentences for young readers, who could follow kings, sultans, and treaties without a textbook. Its mix of foreign news and plain explanation made world affairs feel near at hand. The number keeps a child's-eye record of peacemaking in 1897.
23627-messenger-no-48:
James Otis, author of Toby Tyler and The Boy Captain, wrote this eighteen ninety nine boys' book of Messenger Number Forty Eight, printed by Saalfield. Jet, whose full name is Jethro Lewis, opens the tale, answering questions on his name and age with a boy's plain honesty, and running messages through city streets.

Trouble, kidnappers, an engagement, a battle, a bold attempt, an arrest, a detective, a prisoner, close quarters, a snare, a capture, and a stern chase follow. Chapters on the Adirondacks, a small guide, a visit, and a final success also follow. Otis writes for boys who love action and pluck, with a messenger hero who earns his place by speed, sense, and nerve. Young readers will enjoy Jet's run from errand boy to hero.
25066-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
October 1844 brought volume 56, number 348 of Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine, issued in Edinburgh and London by William Blackwood and Sons. Like other numbers of the long-running Tory monthly, it mixes reviews, fiction, poetry, and topical essays in a single thick issue for general readers.

Its contents open with a memoir of a diplomatist drawn from family papers, followed by a second set of Goethe poems and ballads in translation. Other pieces cover a great drought, a tale called A Tender Conscience, Thierry's history of the Gauls, the closing part of The Witchfinder, a Louisiana courtship story, and Greece under Roman rule.
29187-graham-s-magazine-vol-xxxii-no-1-j:
George R. Graham and Robert T. Conrad edited this January 1848 number of Graham's American Monthly Magazine of Literature and Art, published in Philadelphia. The magazine boasted leading contributors, from William Cullen Bryant and James Fenimore Cooper to Henry Wadsworth Longfellow and Lydia Sigourney, with mezzotint and steel engravings and music.

This number opens with Theodore Fay's Lace and Diamonds, or Take Care What You Do. Other contents range across biography, battle history, and scenery, including a sketch of General William Butler and an account of the Battle of Fort Moultrie. Readers get a month of a leading American literary magazine, rich in names that still anchor the period.
29218-graham-s-magazine-vol-xxxii-no-2-f:
Graham's Magazine for February 1848, volume 32, number 2, opens with R. Balmann's piece on Stoke Church and Park. Stoke, near Windsor, was the scene of Thomas Gray's Elegy and the residence of the Penns of Pennsylvania. A monument to Gray, erected in 1799, stands among the scenes his poem celebrated.

Balmann describes the manor, its park, and the churchyard where Gray lies, with Slough and Herschel's home nearby and Eton across the Thames. The issue continues the magazine's mix of travel, biography, and literature. Readers get a mid-century magazine number that pairs English scenery with American literary interests, in the illustrated style Graham's readers expected.
29236-graham-s-magazine-vol-xxxii-no-3-m:
Graham's Magazine for March 1848, volume 32, number 3, opens with Frank Byrne's The Cruise of the Gentile. On the evening of March 25, 1839, the ship Gentile of Boston lies at anchor in the harbor of Valetta, Malta. She is a handsome craft of six or seven hundred tons, high out of the water in ballast trim. Byrne introduces ship and crew in turn, as a yarn about them unfolds.

Other contents include Alfred Street's White Creek and Thomas Buchanan Read's The Alchemist's Daughter, a dramatic sketch set in Ferrara. Readers get a month of Graham's magazine at its mid-century height, mixing sea yarns, poems, and drama for a literate American audience.
29239-graham-s-magazine-vol-xxxii-no-4-a:
Graham's Magazine for April 1848, volume 32, number 4, opens with T. S. Arthur's Jacob Jones, or The Man Who Couldn't Get Along in the World. Jacob, a clerk earning five hundred dollars a year at twenty-two, saves nothing and owes his tailors fifty to one hundred dollars. His careful employer asks what he has laid by, and Jacob must admit the answer.

Other contents include Blanche Bennairde's The Darling, Henry Hirst's The Poet's Love, Anna Blackwell's Song of the Elves, and Henry Wadsworth Longfellow's The Fire of Drift-Wood. Readers get a month of a leading American literary magazine, mixing moral tales, poems, and songs in the illustrated style of the 1840s.
29262-graham-s-magazine-vol-xxxii-no-5-m:
Graham's Magazine for May 1848, volume 32, number 5, opens with G. G. Foster's Clara Harland, engraved expressly for the magazine. The narrator insists he is no visionary, yet his life has been a struggle between everyday care and shadowy phantoms that haunt him in city, hills, prairie, and sea. Men and women move mechanically around him while he floats along their current.

Other contents include Lyman Long's The Ancient and the Modern Muse, Jane Taylor Worthington's Theresa, or Genius and Womanhood, a tale of domestic life, and John Neal's prediction. Readers get a month of Graham's magazine mixing fiction, poetry, and domestic tales, with the engraved portraiture its readers prized.
29344-graham-s-magazine-vol-xxxii-no-6-j:
Graham's Magazine for June 1848, volume 32, number 6, opens with Fayette Robinson's life of Captain Samuel Walker, with an engraving. Walker was born in Prince George's County, Maryland, in 1815, to a respectable family without fortune or influence to advance him. Thrown on the world young, dependent on his own exertions, he still attracted more attention than any man of his grade since the Mexican war began.

Other contents include Lamartine to Madame Jorelle, translated from the French, Caroline Butler's Phantoms All, a fantasy, and E. Curtiss Hine's Homeward Bound. Oliver Buckley's Poor Penn, a real reminiscence, and Lydia Jane Peirson's Enchanted Isle complete the number. Readers get a month of Graham's magazine, mixing biography, verse, and tale.
arxiv-2509-00148:
David J. Setton leads a team of fifteen authors who test why carbon monoxide glow fades fast in post-starburst galaxies in 2025. Post-starburst galaxies have just stopped a burst of star birth, yet many still glow brightly in CO, a tracer of cold gas. That glow hints at more gas than the standard story expects.

Deep ALMA views of fifty massive galaxies at a redshift near zero point seven detect CO in twenty-seven of them. Glow strength tracks the age of the last burst, which implies gas leaves in under one hundred forty million years. New fits with mid- and far-infrared data test if dust-hidden star birth can explain the trend. The title states the verdict: buried star formation cannot explain it.
arxiv-2509-00348:
Shixiao Liang leads a team of six authors who build the theory behind Physics-Enhanced Residual Learning in 2025. The method, PERL, uses a neural network to estimate the residual, the gap between a physics model's prediction and the truth. Numeric tests hinted at three gains: fewer network parameters, faster convergence, and fewer training samples for the same precision.

Those gains lacked theoretical backing. The team studies a general class of problems with Lipschitz continuity, a bound on how fast outputs can change with inputs. Their analysis explains all three gains from that structure. A firm theory could guide when to trust physics-plus-learning hybrids in engineering design.
arxiv-2509-00948:
Denghang Hu leads five authors in total, with Taolue Chen, Philipp Rummer, Fu Song, and Zhilin Wu, in giving a decision procedure for a theory of string sequences. SMT solvers support sequences for modeling arrays and lists, and strings are intimately related, yet operations such as regex matching, splitting, and joining are typically not directly supported.

Hu and his co-authors propose a theory of string sequences and study its satisfiability. The theory is undecidable in general, but decidability returns for the straight-line fragment. They encode each string sequence as a string and each operation as a string operation, computing pre-images with automata inside the OSTRICH framework. Their tool performs well on benchmarks from JavaScript programs and templates.
arxiv-2509-01448:
Antennas shaped to wrap curved surfaces, called conformal antennas, are hard to make with flat printing methods. Ivan Revenga Riesco, Borut Lampret, Connor Myant, and David Boyle use a low-cost five-axis, multi-material desktop printer to build them directly. The custom open-source machine prints with conductive filaments, so the antenna itself is part of the printed object.

The team fabricated an S-band patch antenna and an ultra-wideband antenna in conformal form. Both were compared against planar-printed versions and against electromagnetic simulations. The conformal builds showed better impedance matching, a key measure of how well an antenna transfers power, along with shorter build times and lower cost. Revenga Riesco and the co-authors present the result as evidence that multi-axis, multi-material prototyping suits antennas with complex shapes.
arxiv-2509-01548:
Model merging combines several fine-tuned expert models into one multi-task model at low cost, but public models can be merged without their makers' consent. Zihao Wang, with four co-authors, warns that unauthorized merging may infringe developers' rights and leak private information held in a model. Past defenses mostly detected merging after the fact instead of preventing it.

Their mechanism, MergeLock, actively disrupts a model's parameters so it can no longer be merged, while leaving its own output unchanged. The trick uses a symmetry inside transformer attention: pairs of invertible matrices are applied to two attention branches, pushing the model away from the shared parameter space of other fine-tuned models. Experiments across tasks support the protection. Wang and the team offer MergeLock for secure model sharing.
arxiv-2509-01948:
Ruijun Wang proves results about kernels in directed graphs under Borel measurability rules. A directed graph has edges with direction, and a quasi-kernel is a set that reaches all outside points in at most two steps. Borel means the sets involved stay tame in the descriptive set theory sense. His graphs are locally countable, so each point touches only countably many edges.

He shows a Borel quasi-kernel exists whenever the Borel coloring number is finite. For graphs with bounded out-degree, he bounds that coloring number by a clean quadratic formula or shows it is infinite. The bound gives an alternative proof of a theorem by Palamourdas. Such results matter where infinite graphs model logic and computation tasks.
arxiv-2509-02048:
Yi Yin, Guangquan Zhang, Hua Zuo, and Jie Lu balance privacy against utility when publishing data for model training. Sharing raw data risks membership inference attacks, which test whether a person record was in the training set. Common defenses blur or synthesize data but often damage accuracy and diversity. Their framework splits the problem into two linked optimization levels.

The upper level guards sample quality with a discriminator that steers generation toward faithful outputs. The lower level measures each sample exposure through local curvature of the data manifold, a geometric risk score. Perturbing samples toward low curvature zones hides distinctive feature mixes. Alternating optimization lifts both goals together. Tests beat prior methods on attack resistance, quality, and diversity.
arxiv-2509-02148:
Rutvik Ashish Mahajan leads three co-authors in improving detection of ionized regions during the epoch of reionization. That epoch marks when early stars ionized the cosmic gas, ending the dark ages. Twenty-one centimeter observations can map the ionized bubbles, but finding the largest ones is hard. A matched filter search within a Bayesian framework anchors their method.

Replacing a spherical filter with an eight parameter spheroidal filter adds shape flexibility. Detectability and orientation recovery both improve markedly. For a representative scenario at a set redshift, the largest region reaches strong detection with about an hour on a planned low frequency array. Flagged regions become prime targets for deeper follow-up. The method also constrains bubble properties and their source populations.
arxiv-2509-02248:
Shweta Patil tests code based reads of palm traits as a data led swap for the gut feel of palmistry. A sight pipeline pulls main line forms, grain, and shape marks from palm shots. Those marks train forecast models on a fresh set built from marked palm shots. Traits or states checked by third party means give the aims for the forecasts.

Models find rich patterns in palm data in the tests the author runs. The frame counts links from palm form to the checked aims in hard terms. Uses in body measure work and user stats are pitched, with phone use in view. The work recasts a folk craft through code based study of palms. Feasibility is the claim the author stakes, not claims of fate.
arxiv-2509-02548:
L. Elesin and sixteen co-authors wrote a 2025 nanophysics paper on turning heat into electrical signals at terahertz frequencies using moiré superlattices, patterns formed by stacking two atom-thin sheets at a slight angle. Such detection could be quiet and need no applied bias.

Thermoelectric response grows near van Hove singularities, points where electron states pile up, but those points are hard to reach in normal materials. Moiré band engineering makes them tunable in graphene superlattices. Tuning the Fermi level onto a singularity raised the terahertz photothermoelectric response strongly. A modest magnetic field boosted it further through the Nernst effect, a sideways current from a heat gradient. The results promote engineered band structures for terahertz sensors.
arxiv-2509-03248:
Igor Rogachevskii and Nathan Kleeorin derived how stratified turbulence with shear can build large-scale magnetic fields in a 2025 paper. In astrophysical fluids, turbulence plus a smooth shearing flow can act as a dynamo, amplifying weak seed fields into strong ones. The alpha effect names one key part of that amplification.

Their analysis allows the gas to be compressible at any Mach number, the ratio of flow speed to sound speed. Compressibility, they find, does not change the alpha contributions coming from uneven turbulence combined with shear. The main alpha part also ignores the shape of the turbulence energy spectrum. A further effect pumps the large-scale field, driven by density gradients alongside overall expansion or collapse. Applications include discs forming planets and collapsing clouds that birth stars and galaxies.
arxiv-2509-03348:
Yewen Li and 9 co-authors proposed a generative auto-bidding method for online advertising auctions in 2025. Advertisers let algorithms set bids under budget and cost constraints, in fast, crowded auctions against many rivals. Generative diffusion models are attractive because they plan whole trajectories of future states, which helps when rewards are sparse.

Diffusion outputs, however, can drift into sequences that break dynamic logic between neighboring states, producing poor bids. The proposed completer-aligner design trains the model to finish partial histories, improving that legitimacy. A second model scores whole trajectories by return and refines them toward advertiser goals. On large benchmarks the method improved conversion value strongly in sparse-reward settings. On a major live platform it also raised target-cost performance.
arxiv-2509-03448:
Anweshika Pattanayak and three co-authors wrote a 2025 research paper on chiral active matter. Their subject is tiny self-moving particles that also turn, held inside a harmonic trap, a bowl-like confining potential. They compare flat, two-dimensional motion with three-dimensional motion driven by torque.

Working from an exact mathematical framework, checked against simulations, they derive formulas for how far particles spread and how their distributions depart from a bell curve. Three kinds of steady behaviour appear, including active states peaked away from the centre. Turning suppresses activity in two dimensions, yet preserves it along the twist axis in three. Simple length-scale arguments map where each regime begins, giving experiments clear signals to look for.
arxiv-2509-03648:
Apurba Das introduces a new algebraic structure in a 2025 mathematics paper: associative-Yamaguti algebras. The structure is the associative counterpart of Lie-Yamaguti algebras, a known family with both binary and ternary operations. Several known families sit inside the new one as special cases, including plain associative algebras and certain triple systems.

Das first shows every such algebra can be wrapped by an associative algebra, meaning it arises from a reductive associative algebra. A suitable skew-symmetrisation, which forces an operation to flip sign under swapping inputs, produces a Lie-Yamaguti algebra from it. Cohomology groups for the new structure are then defined to study how it deforms and extends. The paper closes with relative Rota-Baxter maps, linking the new algebras to dendriform-Yamaguti algebras, which split their operations into parts.
arxiv-2509-03948:
Formally verifying the local robustness of a neural classifier built for a satellite fault-detection system occupies a 2025 research paper by Delphine Longuet and three co-authors. Component failures in orbit are costly and hard to fix, so an onboard hybrid artificial intelligence system promises earlier detection with less ground effort. Such a system must be extremely reliable before anyone trusts it in space.

The team uses Marabou, a formal verification tool for neural networks, on the models inside their classification algorithm. Formal verification proves properties over all inputs in a region, rather than testing samples one by one. Here the property is local robustness: how far an input can be perturbed before the model's output turns unstable. Quantifying that margin improves trust under uncertainty, a real concern when sensor readings drift in orbit. The spatial use case grounds the study in an actual satellite scenario, not a toy benchmark.
arxiv-2509-04248:
Daniel Ferreira Lopes, writing alone, offers a short guided tour of Hamiltonian systems for readers of ergodic theory in a 2025 exposition paper. Ergodic theory studies how systems evolve over long times and what they preserve along the way. A measure, a way of assigning sizes to sets, that stays unchanged under the motion is called invariant. Lopes first introduces the needed measure theory briefly, then proves the Poincaré recurrence theorem, which says systems keep returning near their starting states under the right conditions.

With those tools in place, Hamiltonian differential equations enter as the leading example. Their vector fields and flows preserve the key measure, marking the systems as conservative. Students gain a compact route from basics to a classic result.
arxiv-2509-04348:
The LIGO Scientific Collaboration, together with the Virgo and KAGRA collaborations, uses gravitational-wave catalog data to measure the universe's expansion rate in a 2025 research paper. Their catalog, GWTC-4.0, lists 218 wave sources from merging black holes and neutron stars. Distances come straight from the waves, while redshifts must be inferred statistically, either from features in the mass pattern of merging objects or from likely host galaxies inside each event's sky region.

Of the catalog, 142 sources feed the joint estimate. The Hubble constant lands near seventy-five kilometers per second per megaparsec, with wide uncertainty bands. The team also tests modified wave propagation, where distance behavior deviates from Einstein's general relativity. Their deviation measure stays consistent with relativity within errors.
arxiv-2509-04748:
A clean reputation can encourage cooperation, while stigma can follow a person into later life. David Li and one co-author model that dynamic in a 2025 game theory paper with overlapping generations. In each round, a young agent deals with an old one. The young agent then grows old carrying a simple two-value record from that meeting.

Honest agents cooperate when a partner's record is clear. Strategic agents, by contrast, weigh a private loss they would suffer if a partner exploits them. The authors build beliefs that stay consistent with how records form. With evenly spread losses, the equilibrium reduces to a simple equation. They show cases with coexisting low and high cooperation outcomes, and find record clearing weakens cooperation incentives.
arxiv-2509-05148:
Dark matter brushing against radiation in the early universe could leave a viscous fingerprint on cosmic expansion. Hermano Velten and one co-author explore that mechanism against new survey data in a 2025 cosmology paper. If the two components share a temperature, their interaction creates bulk viscous pressure for a range of light dark matter masses.

That pressure changes the expansion rate near matter-radiation equality and can raise the inferred Hubble constant. Because the mechanism also affects the sound speed of the early fluid, the authors use recent baryon acoustic oscillation measurements to bound the model's thermalisation timescale. Their bound constrains how strong the effect can be.
arxiv-2509-05248:
Programs that can grow or shrink while running need fast ways to move their data, a problem Iker Martín-Álvarez and two co-authors examine in a 2025 computing paper. Their focus is MPI, a standard system that lets many processors work on one job and pass data between them.

The team adds one-sided remote memory access methods, where one processor reads or writes another's memory directly, to a library for resizing applications. They compare this with older group-based transfers and extend a waiting strategy so resizing can happen in the background. Performance is similar overall, though high start-up costs for the new methods currently limit their advantage.
arxiv-2509-05448:
Scientific discovery by machines should reason from axioms rather than only spot patterns, Pingchuan Ma and six co-authors argue in a 2025 position paper. Ordinary machine learning works inside fixed assumptions, so it struggles to invent genuinely new theory.

Their proposal recasts inquiry as game design: agents act in worlds governed by stated rules and may rewrite those rules when observations do not fit. Early experiments with logic-based games show agents evolving axioms that solve problems previously out of reach. The authors offer the framework as a base for systems that discover in a creative, readable, theory-driven way. The title gestures from Newton's rules toward Einstein's deeper rewrite.
arxiv-2509-05548:
Groups defined by pictures rather than finite lists of relations are studied through their actions at infinity by Chris Karpinski, Damian Osajda, and Koichi Oyakawa in a 2025 group theory paper. Graphical small cancellation groups allow infinitely many defining relations, encoded in labelled graphs with cancellation rules.

The authors examine how such a group acts on the Gromov boundary of its coned-off Cayley graph, a boundary that captures the group's large-scale shape. They show that for a broad class, including classical small cancellation groups with infinite presentations, the orbit equivalence relation of that action is hyperfinite. Hyperfiniteness means the relation can be built from finite pieces, a strong regularity property in measured group theory.
arxiv-2509-05648:
Five-quark particles containing hidden charm are sorted into a predicted mass spectrum by Zhi-Gang Wang in a solo 2025 particle physics paper. The work uses QCD sum rules, a method that links quark-level calculations to hadron properties. The states are built from two diquarks and an antiquark, with isospin fixed unambiguously this time.

Wang studies the two-light-quark, charm, anti-charm family systematically and obtains masses for several spin and parity combinations. Possible assignments are proposed for five observed candidate states in the proton plus J/psi mass spectrum. The lightest predicted hidden-charm pentaquark sits just above the threshold for a charmed baryon and an anti-charmed meson. The work offers targets and identities for experiments.
arxiv-2509-06148:
A universe that bounces instead of beginning in a singularity is modeled with two fields in a 2025 paper by Emmanuel Frion and two co-authors. Loop quantum cosmology supplies the bounce, replacing the classical big bang. The challenge is matching the observed pattern of early fluctuations while keeping anisotropies from exploding during contraction.

One field acts as quasi-dust, matter with a slightly negative equation of state that also plays the role of a small positive cosmological constant, generating scale-invariant perturbations with a slight red tilt. A second field with an ekpyrotic potential tames anisotropy growth. The perturbation equations couple the two fields in a rich way, yielding fuller behavior than either alone. Checks against current data show the scenario viable as a base for further work.
arxiv-2509-06448:
Two black holes in a tight spiral are replaced by one effective body in a 2025 paper by Jiliang Jing and three co-authors. The effective one-body theory rewrites binary dynamics around an effective metric, and this team builds a full version for spinless binaries. Scattering-angle information from the metric guides the build of the Hamiltonian.

A separated Teukolsky-like equation then yields the energy flux, the radiation-reaction force, and the plus and cross waveforms. Numerical results track numerical relativity data from the SXS group closely. The binding energy against angular momentum relation differs by well under a percent up to the innermost stable orbit, with a better match at larger mass ratio. The framework sharpens waveform modeling for gravitational wave astronomy.
arxiv-2509-06748:
Curved spaces rebuilt without manifolds are presented by Dan Jonsson in a solo 2025 geometry paper. Jonsson defines pointwise affine spaces as a replacement for the manifold concept at the heart of differential geometry. Familiar notions then need fresh definitions inside the new setting.

Connections, torsion, the Riemann curvature tensor, vector fields, and ways to differentiate vector fields are all reintroduced in the pointwise affine framework. Examples show the resulting machinery at work. Jonsson reports that the notions and results generally take simpler and more transparent forms than in conventional treatments. Frameworks of this kind are judged over time: if the simpler forms help prove new results or clarify old ones, the reformulation earns its place beside the standard manifold language of geometry.
arxiv-2509-06848:
Sunquakes, ripples racing across the Sun after a flare, are modeled with an atmosphere included by John Stefan and one co-author in a 2025 solar physics paper. A leading idea says flare-accelerated particles stream down from the corona and slam into lower layers, depositing energy that launches acoustic waves. Earlier models cut the domain off too low to capture that top-down path.

The authors extend a three-dimensional acoustic model of the whole Sun tens of megameters above the surface, resolving the transition region and lower corona. Heating rates from flare radiative hydrodynamic simulations, stretched into three dimensions, excite the quakes realistically. Besides the usual sunquake wavefronts, waves also travel through the chromosphere and corona, resembling known Moreton-Ramsey waves and large-scale coronal fronts. Studying those waves may constrain how sunquakes are excited.
arxiv-2509-07048: Why no planet grows much larger than Jupiter is explained with a simple energy argument by David Garfinkle and one co-author in a 2025 planetary science paper. Adding mass to a planet strengthens gravity, and past a point gravity squeezes the planet so hard that its radius shrinks instead of growing. That competition creates a maximum size near Jupiter's. The authors show the effect quantitatively using a variational principle, the same style of argument used to compute the size of the hydrogen atom.
arxiv-2509-07148: Yury A. Neretin, writing alone in a 2025 mathematics paper, studies an algebra built from the symmetric group, the group of all permutations of a finite set. He looks at one part of its group algebra: the functions whose values stay unchanged across conjugacy classes, taken relative to a Young subgroup, a subgroup that fixes blocks of elements. For that algebra he writes a formula for the structure constants. His formula follows the spirit of Hurwitz numbers, which count certain factorizations in symmetric groups.
arxiv-2509-07348:
The LIGO Scientific Collaboration reports a detailed study in 2025 of GW230814, the loudest gravitational wave signal in its latest catalog. Gravitational waves are ripples in spacetime from colliding massive objects. This signal was caught by a single detector, the LIGO Livingston observatory, with a signal-to-noise ratio of 42.4, high enough to study in unusual depth.

The source fits a merger of two black holes of roughly 34 and 30 solar masses with almost no net spin. The loud signal let the team detect a higher vibration mode of the merger for the first time. Most checks agree with theory, and small wobbles in the fading ringdown phase also appear in realistic simulations, so they do not count as evidence against general relativity. The case also shows the limits of drawing deep conclusions from one detector alone.
arxiv-2509-07448:
Frank Zimmermann, writing alone in 2025, reviews what the SuperKEKB collider teaches the builders of FCC-ee, a planned future collider. SuperKEKB in Japan has reached much higher specific luminosity than its predecessor KEKB. Luminosity measures how many collisions a machine delivers. The machine has also proved more robust to run. It has shown several key design elements planned for FCC-ee can work.

SuperKEKB has not yet reached its design luminosity. Zimmermann notes that this fact is often used, in his view wrongly, to doubt the FCC-ee design goals. The note reviews what SuperKEKB has achieved, and the problems it has faced. It then compares each point with the FCC-ee design. The aim is a fair reading of the proof so far: which lessons back the future machine, and which problems still need work.
arxiv-2509-07548:
Weize Kong and 3 co-authors propose FlexSAN in 2025, a flexible architecture for regenerative satellite access networks. In a regenerative network, the satellite carries mobile network equipment, either a full base station, called gNB, or a partial unit, gNB-DU. Prototype measurements show the full unit gives lower latency while the partial unit costs less, so operators face a quality-versus-cost trade-off that static deployments cannot adjust.

FlexSAN reconfigures the payload dynamically with real-time user demand. When all demands can be met, it picks the cheapest configuration that satisfies them; otherwise it admits as many users as possible while protecting quality for those connected. An adaptive greedy heuristic, a stepwise choice rule, keeps the selection problem computationally manageable. The design aims to cut waste and poor experiences that rigid satellite payloads cause.
arxiv-2509-07648:
Lachlan Simpson leads a 5-author team in 2025 adapting Integrated Gradients to explain graph neural networks. Integrated Gradients is a method that credits a network's output to its inputs. It fights the black-box problem of neural networks. It assumes continuous data, though. Graphs are discrete structures of nodes and edges. That makes the standard method a poor fit for graph models.

Their extension is called graph-based Integrated Gradients. On four synthetic datasets, it picks out the structural parts the classifier truly used. On three widely used real-world graph datasets, it beats standard Integrated Gradients. It highlights the key features for node classification tasks more sharply. Better explanations matter where graph models screen molecules, transactions, or networks. In such fields, users must be able to trust or contest the answer.
arxiv-2509-07748:
Alexander Dorsey and 3 co-authors augment a missile autopilot with online learning in a 2025 paper. The classical autopilot uses a three-loop topology. Nested control loops each carry tunable gains. Fixed gains can lag when flight conditions depart from design assumptions. The missile model here is planar. It includes nonlinear dynamics and nonlinear air-flow forces and moments.

An adaptive version adds a learning-based controller on top of the fixed-gain loops. Retrospective cost optimization tunes the learner step by step, from past performance errors. The authors frame the design as a swarm-tuned add-on. Simulations test both nominal interception scenarios and off-nominal ones, where conditions stray from the plan. Online learning improves tracking performance in both kinds of case. The design keeps the proven classical autopilot while gaining flexibility in flight.
arxiv-2509-07848:
Felipe Avila and 6 co-authors test a basic rule of cosmology in a 2025 paper. The cosmic distance duality relation links two ways of measuring distance to faraway objects. If the rule fails, something in standard assumptions about light and space must be wrong. The team checks it at high redshift, meaning very large distances.

Angular distances come from baryon acoustic oscillations and galaxy clusters. Light-based distances come from exploding stars in the Pantheon+ sample and from quasars, with noisy quasar data cleaned by selection and binning. Gaussian processes rebuild the relation without assuming a fixed cosmic model. A clean test like this helps confirm that distance measures used across astronomy agree with each other.
arxiv-2509-07948:
Regularity structures gave mathematicians a way to solve singular stochastic equations, but the theory assumes ordinary variables that commute. Ajay Chandra, Martin Hairer, and Martin Peev extend it in a 2025 research paper. Their version allows processes valued in algebras where the order of multiplying matters. Such settings arise in equations with fermions and in some random motions in high dimensions.

The hard part is renormalization, the careful removal of infinite terms, in one family of random objects called q-Gaussians. Free insertions of operators make the estimates delicate. The authors give a new Banach algebra norm on these operators that controls the insertions. They believe the norm itself may interest other researchers on its own. The extension widens the class of singular equations that strict theory can now handle.
arxiv-2509-08248:
Arin Upadhyay designs a messaging protocol that hides who is talking, not just what is said, in a solo 2025 paper on privacy technology. EFPIX floods encrypted messages across relay nodes, so no single path or server reveals the route. Metadata stays hidden from the relays themselves, and messages are end-to-end encrypted by default.

Spam and replay attacks are deterred without accounts or trusted authorities: proof-of-work makes junk costly, deduplication drops repeats, and aging clears stale traffic. The design ignores network topology and survives infrastructure failures, with no central server to seize or shut down. It suits asynchronous, privacy-critical communication where anonymity and resilience matter far more than raw speed.
arxiv-2509-08348:
Yanqing Wang and 2 co-authors widen the rules for when a fluid flow keeps its energy in a 2025 maths paper. Rough flows may leak energy in ways smooth flows cannot. A famed 2008 result set a sharp class where inviscid flow still conserves energy. The new class is anisotropic: it treats one direction more loosely than the rest.

The trick leans on the flow's divergence-free trait. For thick, viscous flows, the team extends the classic Lions rules as well. Sideways parts and the upright part of the flow may now have different strength demands. Real flows in seas and skies do treat directions differently. Sharp rules split true physical loss from mere roughness, a split that turbulence models rely on.
arxiv-2509-08548:
Dementia care tools count symptoms and scores, but patients are people with histories, preferences, and feelings. Rhiannon Owen and Jonathan C. Roberts present a visualization framework built around empathy in a 2025 research paper. Current digital tools, they note, favor hard metrics over personal understanding. Their framework joins person-centred care ideas with empathy mapping methods from design practice.

The methodology also addresses a subtle problem: designing for indirect users: patients shaped by tools they never touch. The authors validated the framework with healthcare professionals. Testing a working prototype with users, plus a survey study, suggested the approach is feasible. Participants saw scope for warmer, more personal staff-patient ties. The work is an early step toward clinical displays that treat emotional understanding as data worth designing for.
arxiv-2509-08748:
Prototype-guided learning is the defense Wei Guo and 3 co-authors propose against backdoor attacks in a 2025 paper. A backdoor makes a model act normally on clean inputs but give an attacker's label when a trigger appears. Defenders often have very little verified clean data.

Their method, PGRL, needs only a small set of trusted samples. One part checks label consistency to find and remove suspect training items. Another part measures feature distance to unlearn backdoor patterns during fine-tuning. Tests against eight defenses show stronger robustness across models, datasets, and attack styles. The approach aims for practical use.
arxiv-2509-08948:
The deuteron, a proton bound to a neutron, is the simplest nucleus and a natural first target for quantum computing in nuclear physics. Sreelekshmi Pillai and 3 co-authors compute its binding energy on a quantum simulator in a 2025 research paper. They use the variational quantum eigensolver, an algorithm that searches for a system's lowest energy. Their nuclear forces come from two realistic interaction models, including tensor forces.

A renormalization group method softens the interactions to lower resolution before the quantum run. Softer interactions need fewer basis states, hence fewer qubits, to reach one percent of the experimental energy. The team included noise models from real IBM hardware and extrapolated to the zero-noise limit. They also tracked entanglement between modes, which shrank as the interaction softened. The study maps what near-term quantum devices must handle for real nuclear calculations.
arxiv-2509-09048:
Diana Vieira Fernandes and 2 co-authors propose decentralized local voltage control for active distribution networks in a 2025 paper. More distributed energy resources and two-way power flows strain local grids. Voltage must stay within limits without a central supervisor.

A saddle-point reformulation drives consensus plus innovation updates at each controllable bus. Each agent sets its own points using only neighbor communication. Passive buses are embedded directly, and a linearized model preserves network physics. Simulations on a modified CIGRE low voltage network improve voltage stability within operational limits. The authors present the scheme as a viable fully decentralized, edge based control solution.
arxiv-2509-09148:
Nannan Ma and 2 co-authors advocate a penalty-free quantum algorithm to find energy eigenstates in a 2025 paper. Finding eigenstates of a many-body Hamiltonian, the energy operator of a system, is a long standing hard problem. Quantum computers naturally hold the huge state spaces involved.

Their fully quantum algorithm finds ground and excited states without penalty functions. It also avoids variational steps and hybrid quantum-classical loops used by many current methods. The authors present it as an important addition to the quantum toolbox. Such methods could tackle problems intractable on classical machines. Details of the algorithm's construction form the core of the paper.
arxiv-2509-09248:
Lingyun Wan and 2 co-authors calculate Green's functions on near-term quantum computers via Cartan decomposition in a 2025 paper. The Green's function connects experimental observations to underlying quantum states. Simulating time evolution for strongly correlated systems is exponentially hard classically.

Deep circuits needed for time evolution exceed what near-term devices with limited coherence can do. Cartan decomposition yields an algorithm needing only fixed depth circuits for arbitrarily long times. Analytical gradients speed the decomposition using a factorized unitary form. The method simulates long time Green's functions for the Fermi-Hubbard and transverse field Ising models. Fourier transforms then extract spectral functions.
arxiv-2509-09448:
Minhyuk Kim and 2 co-authors introduce TORSO in 2025, a prompting approach that asks large language models to reason from templates rather than from hand-built examples. Few-shot prompts can steer step-by-step answers, yet they lean heavily on the examples given. Writing a fresh set for each new task also costs time and can produce uneven behaviour across tasks.

TORSO instead orients the model toward its own internal reasoning, so proper replies can be formed for general tasks with no manually crafted examples. The authors report strong scores across varied language model benchmarks. The replies also came with rationales they judge reasonable, a point that matters for users who need to inspect the path taken.
arxiv-2509-10248:
Janis Keuper, writing alone, tests whether hidden instructions can rig AI-written peer reviews in this 2025 paper. As journals debate using language models to review science, reports have appeared of authors planting prompt injections in their papers to push scores up. Keuper asks whether such tricks actually work when tested systematically.

He generated a thousand reviews of 2024 conference papers across many language models, with injections planted in the texts. Simple injections proved highly effective, in some setups driving acceptance scores to the maximum. The reviews were also lenient on their own, favoring acceptance in the great majority of cases. Both findings bear directly on whether model-written reviews can be trusted in real editorial work.
arxiv-2509-10648:
Nibuna Siranjeevi Madam Subashchandar and 8 co-authors measure how energetic particles spread through the near-Sun solar wind in this 2025 paper. Data came from the Parker Solar Probe, which sampled the inner solar system closer to the Sun than earlier craft. The team computed how fast particles diffuse along the magnetic field and across it, using two levels of transport theory.

Measured turbulence spectra fed the calculations across a range of particle energies. Spread along the field changed strongly with energy and distance, while cross-field spread stayed much smaller except in rough patches. The team cross-checked their numbers against the rise pattern of a real solar particle event. The higher-order theory matched that event better than the classic model.
arxiv-2509-11048:
Mengfan Tan and three co-authors wrote this 2025 mathematical biology paper. It models how a tumor and the immune system push against each other. The model tracks four interacting groups. It includes two effects that are often left out. Antigens pile up over time. Tumor cells also mutate to escape attack.

The system can settle into one of two stable outcomes. One is immune control. The other is immune escape. This helps explain why similar cancers can end so differently. Random noise in nearby tissue can tip the system between outcomes. The authors estimate how strong that noise must be. They also estimate how long tipping takes. Oddly, stronger immune pressure can sometimes help a tumor escape.
arxiv-2509-11348:
Viet-Hoang Tran and three co-authors test a geometric property in mixture-of-experts models. This 2025 machine learning paper concerns linear mode connectivity. Two separately trained networks may join by a straight line in weight space. Loss stays low along the line once inner symmetries line up.

The team first pins down the symmetries of mixture-of-experts models in full. They act by permuting the expert networks. They also permute the gating function that routes inputs. With that in hand, the team built a matching algorithm. It aligns two trained models so the joining path can be found. Tests spanned dense, sparse, and shared-expert variants. Data of many scales and types were used. Connectivity held across the board.
arxiv-2509-11648:
Sai Kartheek Reddy Kasu presents a pilot benchmark for ethical reasoning by AI in mental health settings, in a 2025 paper called EthicsMH. Language models entering therapy and psychiatry contexts face dilemmas where privacy, autonomy, benefit, and bias intersect. Past moral benchmarks capture those cases poorly.

The dataset holds over one hundred scenarios of ethically charged cases in therapy and psychiatry practice. Each scenario carries structured fields: several decision options, expert-aligned reasoning, expected model behavior, real-world impact, and views from several stakeholders. That structure lets raters score the quality of explanations and fit with professional norms, not just final choices. Kasu releases it as a seed resource, modest and partly model-made, for joint expert growth.
arxiv-2509-11748:
Marius Mignard and three co-authors lint machine learning notebooks like ordinary code. This 2025 software engineering paper notes a quality gap. Notebook code is often sloppier than production software. Its flaws live on three levels at once. Plain Python style is one. The notebook's own layout is another. Machine learning specifics, like reproducibility, form the third.

Their tool is Vespucci Linter. It is built on the Moose analysis platform. Notebook structure and Python code merge in one metamodel. Checks can then use context from every level. Twenty-two rules from past work were implemented. Five thousand Kaggle notebooks were scanned. Violations turned up at all three levels. The case for multi-level checks is confirmed.
arxiv-2509-11948:
Watching a 360-degree video, where do people actually look? Mahmoud Z. A. Wahba and 2 co-authors address that question in a 2025 paper introducing Sphere-GAN. Knowing the salient areas, the parts that draw the eye, helps systems process and send immersive video more efficiently.

Sphere-GAN uses a generative adversarial network, a pair of competing models that improve by challenging each other. It adds spherical convolutions, operations shaped for wrapped-around images rather than flat ones. The authors tested the model on a public dataset of 360-degree video saliency, where viewers' attention had been recorded. They report that Sphere-GAN predicted saliency maps more accurately than leading earlier models, a step toward better handling of immersive content.
arxiv-2509-12148:
Siegel modular forms are highly symmetric functions that generalize the classical modular forms of number theory, and their Fourier coefficients carry deep arithmetic information. Pramath Anamby and one co-author prove in 2025 that nice coefficients of these forms are never a fluke: they must recur infinitely often.

Given one nonzero coefficient whose corner entry avoids the level, the theorem produces infinitely many fundamental integers realized as discriminants of matrices with nonzero coefficients. For odd degree the integers can even be taken prime, and quantitative versions count how many arise. One payoff settles a gap in earlier work on special values of spinor L-functions.
arxiv-2509-12248:
Yuriel Ryan and 3 co-authors test whether large multimodal models understand humor in comics, in a 2025 paper. Humor is a core part of social intelligence, yet models that handle both images and text still struggle with it. The authors introduce PixelHumor, a benchmark of twenty-eight hundred annotated multi-panel comics.

The dataset evaluates whether a model can interpret a joke and recognize the order of panels in a narrative sequence. Top models reached only about three fifths accuracy on panel sequencing, far below human performance in the authors' comparison. That gap points to weak integration of visual and textual cues. PixelHumor is offered as a rigorous framework to push models toward more socially aware interaction.
arxiv-2509-12348:
Reflected signals usually wreck indoor positioning. They smear a device's location across every wall bounce. Hua Chen and seven co-authors turn that nuisance into the signal in 2025. They pair a fluid antenna with an active intelligent reflecting surface. The pair pins down a user in three dimensions, with no timing data.

Clever pilot signals and surface settings separate the paths. The direct path is split from the reflected ones. One algorithm reads the arrival angle off the direct path. Another recovers the bounced channel. Geometry then combines them into a position. Theory sets accuracy bounds. Simulations show near-optimal fixes that hold up in rich multipath rooms.
arxiv-2509-12448:
Clinical trials that steer patients toward the better-looking treatment can gain power, but they can also fake significance if the error rate slips. Stef Baas and three co-authors build computational safeguards in 2025 for response-adaptive randomization schemes that chase maximum power.

They first test classic power-chasing designs under exact tests, including a generalized Boschloo test, then evaluate designs posed as constrained decision processes that cap error rates on average. The winning combination pairs an unconditional exact test with the constrained design that protects assignment to the superior arm. It gains real power over equal allocation while sending more patients, on average, to the better treatment.
arxiv-2509-12948:
Chao Xiong, Xianwen Yu and four co-authors propose FIT in 2025, a pre-ranking model that lets user and item sides talk early. Pre-ranking picks a short list fast in large shop systems. Classic twin towers score each side alone, which is fast but misses cross links.

FIT adds a learned item store for early cross talk. A light scorer then adds late cross talk between the towers. Speed at test time stays high. Trials on public sets beat top prior pre-rankers by clear gaps. The design shows early talk need not break fast service.
arxiv-2509-13248:
Juanita Duque-Rosero, Christopher Keyes and three co-authors characterize in 2025 the integral Hasse principle for stacky curves from generalized Fermat equations. Spherical curves with genus in a set band form an infinite family. Darmon and Granville gave a prior result that this work extends.

Methods from that extension sort which curves obey the principle. Local solvability versus global integral points is the core test. A positive share of curves in the family passes the test. That share is proved, not just sampled. Stacky curves thus give a tractable infinite lab for Hasse failures and successes in number theory.
arxiv-2509-13448:
Danila Valko, Rohan Paranjpe, and Jorge Marx Gómez empirically evaluate two shortest-path methods for the Lightning Network in a 2025 paper. Efficient routing is critical for payment channel networks such as Lightning, where shortest-path computations commonly use Dijkstra-based methods. A recent theoretical method, Bounded Multi-Source Shortest Path, reaches an asymptotically faster running time on sparse directed graphs.

The authors compare that method against a standard Dijkstra implementation written in Rust, across five Lightning Network topology snapshots and one hundred randomized source-node trials per snapshot. The newer method consistently exhibited higher runtimes, with statistically notable differences in all evaluated data sets. For current network graph sizes and the implementations studied, it gives no practical runtime advantage despite stronger asymptotic guarantees, a cautionary result for routing optimization.
arxiv-2509-13548:
Manan Mittal and 6 co-authors propose a mixture-of-experts system for binaural audio of moving talkers in a 2025 paper. Good spatial audio should follow that motion as it happens. It should let a listener turn sounds up or down by direction, choosing what to hear. All the while it must keep the natural clues that two ears give us, the small differences that tell us where a sound sits.

Some first estimate the direction a sound arrives from, out in the open. Others work inside the Ambisonics domain. This system does neither. It is signal-dependent, and it blends many binaural filters together on the fly, locating sources implicitly as it goes. Moving sources can then be tracked and lifted out in real time. The method also does not care how the microphones are arranged. That makes it a flexible fit for consumer devices.
arxiv-2509-13948:
Benedict Barrow and Roger K. Moore ask what makes a robot face look trustworthy in a 2025 human-robot interaction paper. First impressions steer how people treat social robots, just as they do with humans, and the authors test the babyface hypothesis: that rounded, infant-like features invite trust.

They manipulated the back-projected face of a Furhat robot, varying its facial features across study conditions, and measured how trustworthy participants judged the robot to be. Eye shape and eye size had a significant impact on perceived trustworthiness, confirming the hypothesis in part. The result feeds directly into design practice: small choices about a social robot's eyes can measurably change whether people are willing to rely on it.
arxiv-2509-14048:
M. Muñoz-Echeverría and a large international team map hot gas in a distant galaxy cluster in a 2025 astronomy paper. The thermal Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect, the shadow hot cluster gas casts on the cosmic microwave background, reveals the gas pressure. Their target, CL J1226.9+3332 at high redshift, had never been mapped in detail at its core.

Observations with the NOEMA millimeter interferometer gave the first detailed maps for such a distant cluster, and careful removal of contaminating millimeter sources isolated the gas signal. Combined with earlier single-dish data, the team reconstructed the pressure profile from the core out to the outskirts. The core profile is flat, confirming a disturbed, unsettled cluster, and the maps trace the thermal gas around the central galaxy at arcsecond resolution for the first time.
arxiv-2509-14848:
Houssem Sifaou and Osvaldo Simeone study reinforcement learning when several simulators of different quality are available, in a 2025 machine learning paper. Training a policy usually needs many runs in an expensive high-fidelity simulator. Offline learning from stored data helps, but it is limited by the size and quality of that data.

Their algorithm, MF-HRL-IGM, mixes offline data with online runs and chooses which simulator to use at each step. The choice is driven by information gain, estimated through a bootstrapping approach, under a fixed total cost budget. Theory shows the method has a no-regret property, meaning its performance catches up with the best fixed choice over time. Experiments show it beating existing benchmarks, making better use of cheap simulators without wasting money on costly ones.
arxiv-2509-14948:
Katja Fahrion leads a team of ten authors measuring the distance to the Sombrero galaxy from its globular clusters, in a 2025 astronomy paper. Globular clusters are dense star clusters around massive galaxies, and their internal velocity spread follows a tight relation with luminosity. That relation turns clusters into distance markers.

The team measured velocity dispersions for eighty-five clusters around the Sombrero galaxy using a high-resolution spectrograph on the Very Large Telescope. For the seventy-seven clusters with reliable data, the luminosity-dispersion relation gives a distance of about nine megaparsecs, with small statistical and systematic uncertainties. The clusters follow the same relation traced by Milky Way and Andromeda clusters. The result validates the method on a new galaxy and refines the Sombrero's place in the local cosmic map.
arxiv-2509-15048:
Sumit Yadav and five co-authors build maiBERT, a language model for Maithili, in a 2025 natural language processing paper. Maithili is spoken by millions yet lacks the data and models that digital tools require. Low-resource languages like it are routinely left out of AI-driven services.

The team assembled a new Maithili text corpus and pre-trained a BERT-style model on it with masked language modeling, where the model learns by filling in hidden words. Evaluation used a news classification task. The model reached accuracy above that of existing regional models for Nepali and Hindi, with the clearest gains on several individual news classes. Releasing maiBERT openly on Hugging Face lets others fine-tune it for sentiment analysis, named entity recognition, and further Maithili applications.
arxiv-2509-15248:
Zitong Yang and six co-authors pre-train language models partly on text the models' own family synthesized in a 2025 machine learning paper. Standard pre-training learns correlations among tokens inside single documents. Relations between documents, which papers cite or resemble which, carry extra signal that ordinary training uses poorly.

Synthetic Bootstrapped Pretraining first learns a model of those inter-document relations from the corpus itself. That relation model then synthesizes a vast new corpus designed for joint training with the real one. In compute-matched tests, models of a few billion parameters trained on up to a trillion tokens consistently beat a strong repetition baseline. The method captures a large share of the gain an oracle with far more unique data would get. Analysis of the synthetic text shows what relations the synthesizer chose to amplify.
arxiv-2509-15348:
Guillermo Matera studies how well entropy can stand in for rank in a branch of algebra. His objects are algebraic matroids, which track which sets of items depend on each other. For each such object over a finite field, random sampling gives entropy values that form a shape of their own. Earlier work showed that shape nears the true rank as the field grows.

Matera makes that claim exact. He gives clear error bounds that depend on the size of the field, the set, and the shape's degree. His proof joins tools from geometry with facts about entropy and shared information. The result ties two ideas of independence, one from algebra and one from information theory, with firm numbers.
arxiv-2509-15448:
Saeed Amizadeh leads a team that extends the attention step used in transformer models. Attention lets a model weigh which inputs matter most. It works well for text, images, and graphs taken one scale at a time. Data that mixes scales and kinds at once, though, does not fit the standard form. Past fixes leaned on ad hoc tricks.

The team first build a math object that can hold mixed scale, mixed kind data. They then derive a new attention rule from a basic principle: keep doubt as low as the setup allows. Their rule stays as close as can be to the standard one while honoring the data's shape. They also give a fast method to compute it.
arxiv-2509-15548:
Deming Li leads a team that rebuilds three dimensional scenes from few photos taken in the wild. Such photo sets vary in light, time of day, and season. Past methods tend to smooth detail or fit the few views too tightly. The team build on a method that splats soft blobs to form a scene.

Their system, MS-GS, starts from depth guesses made from single photos. A step anchored on known scene points pulls out local meaning regions for firm alignment. They then add checks at fake views, at both pixel and trait levels, to keep the scene true from many angles. They also release a new data set and test setup. Results look photo real across hard cases.
arxiv-2509-16048:
Placing a hot emitter very close to a solar cell can yield huge power, yet much of that power is often wasted. Kartika N. Nimje and four co-authors show that the layer under the cell plays a key role in this trade-off. With computer-guided design, they test thin metal films whose traits are tuned to match the emitter.

The tuned films focus heat transfer into a narrow color band just above the cell's working threshold. The result is more than ten times the useful power flow of noble metal designs, at high efficiency. Careful choice of the base layer may lift a basic limit of these devices.
arxiv-2509-16148:
Tent spaces are tools in harmonic analysis that bundle functions over a half-space so their size can be measured at once. Liliana Forzani, Roberto Scotto, and Wilfredo Urbina carry that theory into the Gaussian setting, where the bell curve sets the weight. They define a Gaussian area function and matching tent spaces for this weighted world.

For these spaces they prove a split into simple atom pieces and a full account of the dual space. Some uses of the new theory are also sketched. The work extends a classic scheme built by Coifman, Meyer, and Stein to a setting used in probability and heat flow.
arxiv-2509-16248:
PyTorch 2 speeds up neural code by capturing it as one graph, but some code patterns break that graph and force a slow fallback. Savini Kashmira and five co-authors present GraphMend, a compiler tool that fixes such breaks on its own. It reads the program's structure, spots break patterns, and rewrites code only when the change is provably safe.

In a study of nearly two hundred public models, about one in seven had breaks. GraphMend removed most breaks and fully fixed most affected models. Cold starts sped up by five times on average in tests, with steady gains as well.
arxiv-2509-16548:
Yuyang Ding and co-authors address a costly step in training language models in a 2025 paper. Process reward models grade each step of a solution, which helps with hard tasks like math. Yet human labels for each step are slow and costly to gather. The team builds a way to make those labels with far less human work.

Their method, called SCAN, uses repeated sampling to label steps and clean its own noise. Even with a small set of made-up data, their models beat strong rivals. Some rivals used large human-labeled sets. Adding more made-up data kept raising scores. The result suggests a cheaper path to step-level training.
arxiv-2509-16648:
Debarpan Bhattacharya, Apoorva Kulkarni, and Sriram Ganapathy tackle trust in multimodal models in a 2025 paper. Such models take in images, sound, and text at once. Users need a sign of when a prediction may be wrong. That sign would let the model hold back on shaky cases. The team propose a sampling method to build that sign.

Their method feeds the model varied but equal inputs. Shifts in the answers reveal doubt. The doubt score improved detection of wrong predictions by about a third for vision models. Gains for audio models were close behind. Code is shared in public, so others can test the idea.
arxiv-2509-16748:
Heyuan Li and co-authors build better fake heads in three dimensions in a 2025 vision paper. A common trick stores a head on three flat planes of features. Looking up features by plain grid points can tangle them. That tangling shows up as mirrored flaws on the face.

Their design uses a new plane layout that avoids the tangle. A single shared feature map replaces several split maps. That change stops features from leaking through the head. With these fixes, their system earns top scores for full-head synthesis. More faithful heads help film, games, and virtual meeting tools.
arxiv-2509-17248:
Leandro Lyra Braga Dognini, writing alone, rethinks how markets grope toward balance in a 2025 arXiv paper. Classic economics often assumes a trial process that adjusts prices before any trade happens. Real trade, though, happens along the way, at prices that may not clear the market. Dognini argues that such non-tâtonnement processes, with a random twist, arise naturally from general equilibrium theory.

He revisits demand theory to define two reshaping maps, one for normalized Walrasian demand and one that flattens indifference surfaces. With those maps he derives an attraction principle from how swap rates move on the flat domain. That principle grounds his stochastic processes and yields a random version of the First Welfare Theorem. For a friendly class of utility functions, the processes suit Monte Carlo simulation. They can map trade outcomes along the contract curve and model sticky prices.
arxiv-2509-17548:
Hugo Villamizar, Jannik Fischbach, Alexander Korn, Andreas Vogelsang, and Daniel Mendez ask whether prompts deserve the care given to code. Their 2025 arXiv paper notes that developers now use language models across software tasks every day. If prompts steer that work, they may count as software artifacts that need sound development, records, and upkeep.

The authors lay out a research programme in three parts. It maps current prompt practice and its pain points. It studies prompts as artifacts with a life cycle of their own. It then builds tested guidelines for prompt management. A first survey of software professionals in six countries shows practice is largely ad hoc. Prompts are written on the fly, rarely tracked, and seldom reused with care. The agenda asks when systematic management pays for its own effort, a question the field has barely posed.
arxiv-2509-17648:
Hui Li, writing alone, derives an exact identity for strongly interacting quantum matter. His 2025 arXiv paper works in Keldysh-Schwinger field theory and targets many-body systems with generic bilinear interactions. A core puzzle in this field is which excitations really govern how such systems behave and correlate.

From the Dyson-Schwinger equations, Li establishes a universal identity that holds exactly, not as an approximation. It shows composite particles emerging as the elementary excitations of the system. Their Green's functions then determine the original single-particle Green's function in full. The relation also ties the composite spectra to the observable single-particle spectrum in a rigorous way. Li offers the identity as a new pathway toward a paradigm for correlated matter, where the right building blocks are pairs and clusters rather than lone particles.
arxiv-2509-17748:
Siyi Liu, Kazi Injamamul Haque, and Zerrin Yumak ask people how they feel about their own digital doubles. Their 2025 arXiv paper notes that avatars of real people are now easy to make on consumer gear. The team tested how avatar style and familiarity shape the bond: realistic or cartoon, and a face that is one's own, an acquaintance's, or a stranger's.

They built both styles, realistic MetaHumans and cartoon ReadyPlayerMe figures, with facial animation from performance capture. In a controlled study, more realistic looks raised identification, perceived realism, and social presence. Familiar faces cut the other way, above all when realistic: people liked their own double least of all. Participants still knew the double was theirs. They judged their own avatar harshly yet forgave the doubles of acquaintances and strangers. The title quotes the mood: I don't like my avatar.
arxiv-2509-17848:
L Staveley-Smith leads a large survey team that maps gas torn between two dwarf galaxies. Their 2025 paper comes from the WALLABY pilot survey, which scans the sky in hydrogen radio light. The pair, NGC 4532 and DDO 137, lies near the Virgo cluster.

Radio maps show a wide gas bridge between the pair and long tails past them. Models point to two forces at work: wind-like push as the pair falls through hot gas, and tidal pull from the pair itself. Both forces lifted gas from the pair's shared cloud. The case mirrors the Magellanic gas near our own galaxy.
arxiv-2509-18048:
Antonino Ficarra and Somayeh Moradi build the Rees algebra of ideals tied to graph complements. Their 2025 paper works with squarefree monomial ideals made in a set high degree. Each such ideal comes from the complement of a finite simple graph.

They spell the algebra's defining equations from the graph's own traits. For trees and for graphs with one short cycle, the algebra proves to be Koszul, a strong tidy trait. They also pin how depth grows for powers of the ideal, in the long run. That limit counts the graph's bipartite parts, and the depth settles by a bounded step.
arxiv-2509-18248:
James Walkling, Antonio Strkalj, and F Nur Unal study a twisted twin-lattice system that keeps turning. Their 2025 paper extends a classic model where two square lattices lie at a twist angle. Here one lattice turns in a steady way with respect to the other, so the drive shifts with place and time.

That twist gives a multi-tone drive whose rate grows with range from the turn axis. Tunnelling is best read as a local trapping effect that changes in space. Ring-shaped trapped states form in the bulk, with rich topological marks. Mixed ring states drive much of that zoo of marks.
arxiv-2509-18448:
Intense laser shots destroy the mirror that reflects them, so some labs use films that can be remade after each shot. A. Vazquez and 18 co-authors study films of a liquid crystal called 8CB for such plasma mirrors. Their 2025 paper tests a windmill device that forms fresh films over an opening. The goal is a steady rate of shots with stable aim.

The team measured film quality with low-power light and tracked how steady the films were from shot to shot. At slow forming speeds, over 97 percent of films formed well. At four times that speed, success fell to 45 percent. In the best zones, the added surface error stayed very small. In the ideal temperature band, aim wobble stayed at or below a tight bound. The best forming rate reached about one film every four seconds. The results guide the next design round.
arxiv-2509-18648:
A robot policy trained in simulation can act unsafely when the real world differs. Yarden As and eight co-authors present SPiDR, a method for safe transfer from simulation to reality, in this 2025 paper. Strict safety methods carry proofs but scale poorly. A common practical trick, domain randomization, trains across varied simulations but can still act unsafely.

SPiDR folds the unknown sim-to-real gap into its safety limits through a pessimistic form of domain randomization. That design stays compatible with existing training pipelines. The method carries provable safety guarantees, which the practical tricks lack. Tests covered simulation benchmarks and two distinct real robot platforms. Across them, SPiDR kept behavior safe despite the reality gap. It also held strong task performance. The authors offer it as a scalable middle path between proof-bound and purely practical methods.
arxiv-2509-19248:
József Balogh and three co-authors count maximal sum-free sets in abelian groups, finite number systems where addition commutes. A sum-free set contains no two members that add to a third member, and a maximal one cannot grow without breaking that rule. Earlier work predicted how the count should scale with the size of the largest sum-free set. The team confirms part of that picture and breaks the rest.

For most even-order groups, such sets are exponentially rarer than in the special group built from order-two pieces. Yet the authors construct infinitely many groups whose counts grow at an intermediate rate, disproving a conjecture. They also settle the count for a stricter distinct-sum version, with exactly one exceptional group. A side result bounds maximal independent sets in graphs with a perfect matching, resolving another open conjecture.
arxiv-2509-19348:
Markus Gabl, writing alone, turns a tool around: he uses optimization theory to prove a new matrix completion result. Completion asks when a partly filled symmetric matrix can be finished into a matrix of a desired type. Classic results serve positive semidefinite and completely positive matrices. Gabl treats a broader class, set-completely positive matrices, and a pattern the classic results miss: arrow-head patterns of width one, where only a border strip is given.

His conditions come from copositive optimization, a field that works with matrices that stay safe on positive inputs. The result adds to the known literature on both axes, the matrix class and the pattern. The theory is then applied to a class of quadratic problems, where answers are scored by a squared-cost rule. Completion results of this kind matter because they can slash the number of variables in large optimization problems.
arxiv-2509-19448:
Quantum computers often make their largest errors when a qubit is set up and when it is read out. Muhammad Qasim Khan, Leigh M. Norris, and Lorenza Viola show how to measure those two error kinds apart. Their method uses only single-qubit gates and repeated readouts, with no reset step. The circuit depth stays fixed no matter how many qubits are tested.

The team ran the method on IBM quantum machines and measured setup and readout errors on many qubits at once. Readout errors reached about one fifth of shots on some qubits. Tests also show that fixing readout errors while ignoring setup errors skews the final results. Careful fixes must treat both error kinds together.
arxiv-2509-20148:
Sanish Suwal and four co-authors wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on trust in vehicle artificial intelligence. Self-driving and connected vehicles lean on models whose decisions are hard to inspect. After-the-fact explanations, such as saliency maps, aim to show what a model used. Their quality is often doubted, since they can shift or mislead.

The team compared three training styles for traffic sign classifiers: natural training, adversarial training, and pruning. They measured how each style affected the clarity and faithfulness of the explanations. Pruning, which removes unneeded connections, clearly improved both. It also made models smaller and their internal patterns sparser. The authors argue pruning is a strong strategy for transparent models in vehicles with limited computing power.
arxiv-2509-20648:
Teams of learning agents can stall when rewards are rare and the world is noisy. Yiyuan Pan, Zhe Liu, and Hesheng Wang propose a curiosity-based method for that problem in a 2025 paper on multi-agent reinforcement learning. Their framework is called CERMIC, and it needs no communication between agents.

Random surprises in a noisy world can mislead curiosity-driven agents. CERMIC filters those noisy surprise signals so agents chase real novelty instead. It also pays attention to the novelty of peer behavior, which hints at the hidden structure of a task. The idea borrows from how children adjust their exploring by watching other children. Tests in sparse-reward settings show stronger exploration, the authors report.
arxiv-2509-20848:
Learning which side of a boundary each point lies on can be done with surprisingly few questions, if you may invent your own test points. Hadley Black and four co-authors remove that luxury in a 2025 paper published in COLT 2026. The task is actively learning halfspaces without synthetic data.

A classic result needs only about d log n queries when arbitrary points may be queried. Without synthesis, an older lower bound says learning every label could take as many queries as there are points. The authors design algorithms that work within the given dataset alone. They use structural assumptions to get around the worst case. The work matters wherever queries must be real examples, such as labeled medical or survey data.
arxiv-2509-21148:
A slight modification of Einstein's gravity creates a new field, the scalaron, which might itself be the dark matter. Shibendu Gupta Choudhury, Koushik Dutta, and Deep Ghosh study that candidate in a 2025 paper published in the Journal of Cosmology and Astroparticle Physics. The scalaron's interactions with ordinary matter are heavily suppressed.

For the scalaron to behave as cold dark matter, it needs a three-way interaction with the Higgs boson, induced by the Higgs's own self-coupling. The authors add a non-minimal coupling of the Higgs to gravity, which contributes a competing piece to that interaction. They trace how the enlarged coupling changes the scalaron's cosmic dynamics. The scenario would explain why dark matter has shown no interactions beyond gravity in any experiment so far.
arxiv-2509-21348:
Spherical dynamos that settle into a MAC force balance behave in ways modellers must extrapolate with care. The 2025 paper is by Justin Nicoski and 3 co-authors. A dynamo is a flow of conductive fluid that sustains a magnetic field. Models must be extrapolated to real core conditions, which differ from simulations. The authors study dynamos that reach a MAC balance at the convective scale. MAC balances magnetic, buoyancy, and rotation forces.

They examine how physical quantities depend on the Ekman number, which measures viscosity against rotation. Velocity scalings matched quasi geostrophic theory in both magnetic and non magnetic cases. The key difference was temperature fluctuation size in dynamos. That made buoyancy scale with the Coriolis force. The MAC state gave flow speed scaling equal to a known CIA scaling.
arxiv-2509-21448:
Preprojective algebras encode the representation theory of hereditary algebras in a doubled quiver structure. Andrew Hubery studies their global dimension and Koszul property in a 2025 paper. Settings include finite dimensional hereditary algebras and locally finite hereditary tensor algebras. Non Dynkin type is the main case, where the underlying graph is not a finite Dynkin diagram. Dynkin type receives separate treatment at the end.

Hubery shows these preprojective algebras have global dimension two in non Dynkin type. Starting from a locally finite tensor algebra of non Dynkin type, the preprojective algebra is Koszul. Its Hilbert polynomial and Koszul dual are computed. For Dynkin type, properties of the Weyl group appear in the algebra structure. The results tie homological invariants to classical Lie theory objects.
arxiv-2509-21648:
Maps separating the cosmic microwave background from galactic dust are presented by the BICEP/Keck Collaboration in a 2025 paper. Data come from BICEP and Keck records through the 2018 season, plus Planck. A maximum likelihood method using observing matrices produces unbiased component maps. Polarized background and thermal dust signals are separated. Computational challenges of the estimator are outlined with a fast implementation.

Power spectra of the maps can be computed and described, opening an alternative route to the tensor to scalar ratio. That ratio constrains early universe inflation models. The map based separation is matched with the standard BICEP/Keck analysis. Consistency between the two methods is demonstrated, with a high correlation between workflows.
