The paper is the twentieth in the collaboration series. Two ways to split the sky signal agree, and that cross check builds trust in both.
arxiv-2509-21748:
Picking a small training sample from a big data set should save effort, yet most methods first need costly training on the full data. Brian B. Moser and six co-authors remove that step with SubZeroCore, presented in this 2025 paper. A coreset is a small, well-chosen sample meant to stand in for the whole set. Their method picks one with no training at all.

SubZeroCore balances two goals inside a single score. One goal is covering the whole data set, and the other is matching its dense regions. A closed-form rule sets the balance between them. Tests show the method matches rivals that do train first. It pulls ahead when most of the data is cut, and it stays robust when some labels are wrong.
arxiv-2509-21848:
A single language model can only read so much text at once, but a team of models can split a long document between them. Taejong Joo and six co-authors ask how such a team should be organized. In this 2025 paper they note that most multi-agent setups rely on hand-made teamwork plans and careful prompting, which do not travel well to new tasks.

The authors recast the whole problem as compression, which gives a clear score for how well a team squeezes a document down. Their system, Graph of Agents, builds a fresh teamwork graph for each input, shaped to raise that score. Two mid-size models using the system beat both retrieval-based answering and a fixed-structure team across six document benchmarks. Even with a tiny reading window, the system outscored a model reading the full long text on a standard long-document test.
arxiv-2509-22148:
Speech can flag suicide risk in teenagers, but it also carries the speaker's identity, a serious privacy risk for such a vulnerable group. Ziyun Cui and eight co-authors present the first systematic study of speaker anonymization for this task in this 2025 paper, accepted at ICASSP 2026. If recordings leak or are misused, the voices themselves can identify the young speakers. The study asks whether identity can be hidden without losing the risk signal.

The team investigated a broad range of anonymization methods: classic signal processing, neural voice conversion, and speech synthesis. They built an evaluation frame that scores both sides of the trade: how well identity is protected, and how much risk-relevant information survives. Combining methods that retain complementary information worked best. The combined approach matched the detection performance of the original speech while protecting speaker identity, a hopeful result for safe screening tools.
arxiv-2509-22948:
Christoph Pitzal and co-authors, with the ASDEX Upgrade Team, simulate bursts at the edge of a fusion plasma. These bursts, called pedestal relaxation events, eject energy in I-mode discharges. They look like a better known burst type but seem to work in a distinct way. The team ran global fluid simulations with the GRILLIX code.

The runs produced bursts that matched many traits seen in the real device. Close study of mode traits pointed to micro-tearing modes as the trigger. Paths in gradient space matched growth rates from simple linear theory. The authors sketch a full burst cycle from these clues. They also note hard parts of modeling low-collision plasmas.
arxiv-2509-23548:
Data that mix sound, images, and text carry both shared facts and facts private to each channel. Yijie Zhang and 2 co-authors build IDMVAE, a generative model that tries to keep those two kinds apart. Older models split them into two variables, but the split often stays muddy when the data are hard. Their fix leans on mutual information, a measure of how much one variable reveals about another.

One term pulls shared variables toward capturing what views agree on. A cycle-style loss, fed by generated augmentations, strips out redundancy. Diffusion models strengthen the latent priors. On hard data sets, the model showed a cleaner split, with better generation quality and semantic coherence than rivals.
arxiv-2509-23648:
General relativity's core action term might be born, not assumed, in a mechanism built from ghosts. Ichiro Oda, the sole author, starts from nothing but a cosmological constant in curved space-time. Fixing Weyl symmetry with a gauge condition through the BRST formalism, he finds that the Faddeev-Popov ghosts condense, with a nonzero vacuum value. That condensation generates the Einstein-Hilbert term of general relativity.

Oda calls the mechanism new: shrinking fermionic degrees of freedom effectively creates bosonic ones. He also views it as a bound-state problem. The asymptotic fields of those bound states turn out to be confined to the unphysical part of the Hilbert space.
arxiv-2509-24248:
Reasoning models often think far longer than a problem needs, and the delay hurts real use. Rubing Yang and 9 co-authors built SpecExit, a way to stop reasoning early without the cost of probing the model mid-stream. Earlier exits relied on probes that ate the time they saved. SpecExit instead reads hidden states through a light draft model.

The draft model predicts both coming tokens and an exit signal, with no probe overhead. Average output length fell by about two thirds, and end-to-end latency beat a speculative decoding baseline by a wide factor. Accuracy held steady. The team suggests hidden states carry more useful control signals worth mining.
arxiv-2509-24548:
Gilberto Colangelo introduces dispersive methods in a set of lectures aimed at low-energy phenomenology of the Standard Model. The approach leans on analyticity of Green functions and scattering amplitudes, often joined with unitarity constraints. Keeping the vast subject coherent takes a chain: start with the two-point function, which needs the three-point function as input.

That function in turn needs the four-point function, and the chain stops there, since the four-point function relates only to itself once inelastic effects are set aside. Colangelo treats toy scalar models first, then the case that matters most in practice, quantum chromodynamics. The lectures serve as a basic entry to a classic toolkit.
arxiv-2510-00048:
Mostafa and colleagues build a full hybrid deep learning ensemble to separate Alzheimer's disease from mild cognitive impairment. Its subtle prodromal stage, in structural brain MRI scans of the brain. Gray and white matter slices feed three pretrained convolutional networks, ResNet50, NASNet, and MobileNet, each carefully fine-tuned end to end. And a three-way stacked ensemble with a meta-learner and weighted averaging combines their judgments into one decision in the study.

On the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative dataset the framework reaches reported 99.21 percent accuracy distinguishing Alzheimer's from mild impairment and 91.02 percent for impairment versus normal controls, beating conventional transfer learning and baseline ensembles in their comparisons. Gradient-weighted class activation maps also add explainability, producing heatmaps over the gray and white matter slices that reveal the key structural regions driving each decision for clinical users in practice.
arxiv-2510-00248:
N. Fraija and a team of co-authors published this 2025 astrophysics paper on the late afterglow of gamma-ray bursts. A burst's narrow jet can push a broad, nearly spherical outflow into the space around it. That outflow glows later, once it has dumped enough energy into its surroundings. The authors built an analytical model for that late synchrotron glow.

Their model handles surroundings whose density falls off with distance in a stratified way. It also includes self-absorption and the chance that only some electrons get accelerated. They fit seven low-luminosity bursts that showed a late glow component. A constant-density environment fit those bursts better than a stellar wind profile did. The team further checked upper limits for short bursts in the Swift satellite database. The model gives observers a ready tool for reading late afterglow light curves.
arxiv-2510-00348:
Alperen Tercan and Necmiye Ozay published this 2025 theory paper on constrained decision problems whose starting conditions shift. A constrained Markov decision process balances rewards against limits on cost, energy, or risk. Unlike ordinary versions, no single policy stays optimal for every starting distribution. Re-solving the whole problem each time the start changes is expensive and slow.

The authors bound how much the best achievable value can move when the initial distribution changes. They develop three bounding methods drawn from duality, linear programming perturbation, and concavity. The duality-based bound proved tightest in their comparisons across the board. The perturbation method gave both upper and lower bounds with moderate accuracy. With these bounds, a user can map where a fixed policy stays near-optimal. They also define a regret measure for policies facing an unknown starting mix.
arxiv-2510-00548:
Tatsuya Numajiri and five colleagues published this 2025 physics paper on how entangled quantum states weather noise. Graph states encode entanglement along a network's edges and power measurement-based quantum computing. Checking their quality exactly explodes in cost as systems grow. The team maps that fidelity onto the partition function of a classical spin system.

Statistical mechanics tools, from transfer matrices to Monte Carlo sampling, then do the heavy lifting. Under random Pauli noise, fidelity shows a sharp phase transition on regular graphs. In two dimensions, transitions need degree six or more; in three, degree five suffices. Sparse, low-dimensional graphs instead cross over smoothly and prove more robust. Oddly, the fully connected graph loses its transition entirely and regains robustness. Connectivity and dimension together dictate fragility, the authors conclude.
arxiv-2510-00948:
Zhang and seven co-authors present InfVSR in this 2025 arXiv paper on video super-resolution, the task of rebuilding sharp high-resolution video from blurry low-resolution input. Real videos can run to thousands of frames, and diffusion-based enhancers handle such length badly. Running many denoising steps over a full sequence is slow, while chopping the video into chunks creates visible seams and flicker.

InfVSR reframes the task as one-step autoregressive diffusion, so frames stream through the model in order. The authors reshape a pretrained video diffusion model into a causal form with a rolling memory cache, then distill its multi-step process into a single step. They also built a new benchmark for long videos with semantic consistency metrics. In their tests the method matched leading quality while running up to fifty-eight times faster than a strong rival.
arxiv-2510-01048:
Feldhus and Kopf survey a young research field in this 2025 arXiv paper: using language models to write plain-language descriptions of what parts of a neural network do. Mechanistic interpretability tries to reverse-engineer the computations inside large models, neuron by neuron and head by head. Assigning human meaning to those parts is the hard step. Newer work asks strong generator models to describe components in open vocabulary, rather than testing a fixed list of guesses.

The survey maps how such descriptions are generated for neurons, attention heads, sparse autoencoder features, and larger circuits. It also reviews the metrics used to judge them, from predictive correlation to causal faithfulness tests and human ratings. The authors see a clear trend toward higher-level abstractions and stricter evaluation. They close with open challenges, including heavy computing costs and doubts about description faithfulness.
arxiv-2510-01148:
Atazadeh and Golsanamlou test hybrid metric-Palatini gravity against energy conditions and gravitational baryogenesis in this 2025 arXiv paper on cosmology. The f(R,R-calligraphic) theory mixes two ways of computing curvature, the metric and Palatini versions, which gives it more freedom to explain cosmic acceleration without dark energy. Freedom needs discipline, so the authors derive the standard energy conditions for their chosen model, where the action adds a power of the Palatini scalar to the usual term.

For some values of that power, the strong energy condition fails, which is exactly what an accelerating universe requires in this framework. Over wide parameter ranges the other conditions hold, and plots confirm accelerated expansion phases. The authors then study gravitational baryogenesis, where gravity itself may have tipped the early universe toward matter over antimatter. The hybrid model supports that mechanism in the radiation era.
arxiv-2510-01248:
Liu and co-authors teach graph models to transfer across datasets by letting text serve as the common language. Graphs differ in features and structure from domain to domain, which traps trained models at home. Labels are also scarce exactly where graphs are biggest.

Their method, SSTAG, pre-trains with self-supervision on text-attributed graphs. A dual distillation squeezes both a language model and a graph network into lean perceptrons. The distilled student keeps semantic and structural knowledge in a compact form. Structure-aware training aims to give graph learning the cross-domain portability that text and vision already enjoy. Text attributes give every node a description the language model can read. Multilayer perceptrons deploy cheaply once the teachers retire. Heterogeneity across graphs is the core obstacle named throughout. Co-distillation forces the two teachers to agree on one student. Pretraining finally gets a graph recipe.
arxiv-2510-01348:
Werner and co-authors win a national challenge by flying a drone nine kilometers with no satellite navigation at all. Odometry drifts, new terrain offers no landmarks to close loops, and onboard computers are weak. The competition demanded low, waypoint-guided flight without prior dense maps.

The system matches laser-scanned local height maps against public terrain data by their gradients. A clustered particle filter fuses those matches with odometry to cancel drift. Flights crossed city, forest, and open field while running entirely on ordinary processors. Final position error stayed near eleven meters over the whole course. Twenty-five meters of altitude capped the challenge flights. Gradient templates resist the lighting and season changes that fool photographs. CPU-only real-time operation keeps the hardware cheap and light. Field lessons, not just architecture, fill the report's later pages. Drift correction is the invention on trial.
arxiv-2510-01548:
Fan, Xiong, and Yang extend a classic comparison tool to complex manifolds with a blended notion of curvature. Comparison theorems translate curvature bounds into concrete control over distance and volume. Kähler manifolds, the stage for much of complex geometry, mix two curvature ideas that older theorems treat separately.

New curvature quantities interpolate between Ricci curvature and holomorphic bisectional curvature. Under these, the authors prove fresh controls on how the distance function spreads. Rigidity results then pin down the shape completely when the bounds are met exactly. Such tools feed later work on classification and on geometric flows. Distance controls feed estimates for eigenvalues, volumes, and heat flow. Interpolating curvatures widens the family of spaces the theorems cover. Equality cases are the fingerprints of perfectly symmetric spaces. Complex geometry gains a ruler that respects its special structure. Rigidity turns estimates into identifications.
arxiv-2510-01748:
Zayyani and three co-authors add a third dimension to noise modulation in this 2025 communications paper. Noise modulation encodes data in the statistical shape of a random signal rather than in a clean carrier. Earlier schemes used two features of a Gaussian distribution, its mean and its variance. Each symbol in the new scheme carries three bits, one per feature.

The third feature is the mixture probability of a mixture-of-Gaussians distribution. Different detectors read the three bits at the receiver side. A threshold detector reads the mean bit, and a maximum-likelihood detector reads the variance bit. Kurtosis-based and Bayesian detectors read the new probability bit by telling Gaussian shapes from non-Gaussian ones. The authors derive error probabilities for these detectors in closed form. Simulations showed the third bit achieves error rates comparable with the established two-dimensional schemes.
arxiv-2510-01948:
Montello, Güldenring, and Nalpantidis slim down vision transformers for pixel-level labeling in this 2025 paper. Transformers label every pixel accurately, but their attention cost grows quadratically with image size. Robots with tight power budgets struggle to run them in real time. Token merging helps classification, yet dense prediction needs the detail that merging discards.

Their model, ClustViT, merges tokens by clustering them inside the transformer backbone. A trainable cluster module groups similar tokens, guided by pseudo-clusters drawn from segmentation masks. A regenerator module then restores the fine detail that downstream heads require. The savings are largest where scenes hold few objects and large background areas, a common robotics setting. Across three datasets, ClustViT cut computation to under half the original cost. Inference ran notably faster as well. Segmentation accuracy stayed comparable to the uncompressed backbone throughout.
arxiv-2510-02148:
Qi, Tang, and Zhu borrow diffusion guidance to steer reinforcement learning policies at test time in this 2025 paper. Classifier-free guidance lets image models trade fidelity against prompt strength with one knob. Classic policy gradient methods lack any such dial after training. Their method, policy gradient guidance, adds an unconditional branch beside the conditional policy.

Interpolating the two branches creates a control knob that modulates behavior without retraining. Theory shows the extra normalization term vanishes under advantage estimation, leaving a clean guided update. Experiments covered discrete and continuous control benchmarks. Conditioning dropout helped simple discrete tasks and low-sample regimes, but it destabilized continuous control. Training with slightly amplified guidance improved stability, sample efficiency, and controllability across the board. The results move guidance beyond diffusion policies into standard on-policy learning. Controllable online reinforcement learning gains a simple, general tool.
arxiv-2510-02248:
Miao and five co-authors refine drone flight policies inside an editable photorealistic simulator in this 2025 robotics paper. Visual navigation policies overfit the single track they train on and stumble when geometry changes. FalconGym 2.0 rebuilds the training world with Gaussian splatting, plus an edit API. New static and dynamic tracks generate programmatically in milliseconds.

Their performance-guided refinement algorithm exploits that editability. Training concentrates on the tracks where the current policy struggles, then iterates. Two case studies cover fixed-wing drones and quadrotors with distinct dynamics and scenery. A single policy trained this way beat state-of-the-art baselines on generalization. The loop turns failure data into curriculum automatically. Editable simulation collapses the cost of diverse training environments. Policies meet varied geometry before ever leaving the ground. The approach suits any robot skill where one frozen scene invites overfitting.
arxiv-2510-02348:
Dar simplifies a method that aligns word embedding spaces without any paired examples. His 2025 paper presents mini-vec2vec. Embedding spaces from different models use different coordinates. Aligning them lets tools share knowledge across models. The earlier vec2vec method aligned spaces almost perfectly. It was also costly and unstable to run. mini-vec2vec replaces that machinery with a linear map. The method first guesses rough matches between vectors. It then fits a transformation and refines the matches in rounds.

The linear version proved far cheaper to compute. It also ran with much greater stability. Accuracy matched or beat the original method. The steps stay simple enough to inspect and explain. Results support a bold hypothesis behind the work. Embedding spaces may share one universal geometry. Cheaper alignment opens the trick to smaller labs.
arxiv-2510-02448:
Majumder, Barre, and Gupta build a general theory for fluctuations in finite oscillator crowds. Their 2025 physics paper studies synchronization transitions. Coupled oscillators famously fall into step together. Infinite systems switch sharply at the transition. Finite systems smear that switch through large random wobbles. The authors reduce a stochastic equation for the whole crowd. Their method follows the slow center directions of the dynamics. The result is one Langevin equation for the order parameter. It yields the first closed form steady distribution for that parameter. No special ansatz or integrability is assumed anywhere.

Simulations matched the theory across many coupling choices. Varied frequency distributions also agreed well. Near the critical point the theory beat recent rivals. It also won inside the incoherent phase, where fluctuations rule. Fireflies, power grids, and neural rhythms all synchronize. Finite size honesty matters for every real crowd.
arxiv-2510-02848:
Huynh-Nguyen and co-authors present Flamed-TTS, a fast system that clones a voice from a short sample. Such zero-shot speech tools can copy a speaker's tone without long recordings. Many rival systems are slow and costly to run. Some also repeat words or borrow the wrong content. Their rhythm often sounds flat and fixed. The team rebuilt the training recipe around flow matching. Their model drops attention, a main source of delay.

A rich prior gives the model a strong starting point. The core network then acts as a pure denoiser of sound. Two extra samplers add timing variety. One varies how long each sound lasts. The other inserts pauses with natural odds. Tests showed the best word error rate among leading rivals. Speech stayed clear, natural, and close to the target voice. Pauses and pace varied in a human-like way.
arxiv-2510-03048:
Hughes and Kusmartsev recast a variant of Einstein gravity in algebraic form. Unimodular gravity keeps only the trace-free part of the field equations. In that theory, the cosmic constant returns as a constant of motion. Four-dimensional space-time has a special duality for two-forms. That duality splits the curvature into clean blocks. Their condition equates two commutators built from those blocks.

One side pairs the Riemann tensor with the Hodge dual. The other pairs the dual with a product of the Maxwell tensor. The condition matches the trace-free equations exactly. Its right side vanishes just when the energy flow does. That case recovers plain Einstein space-times as it should. Solving the condition for a round, charged mass gave one answer. It was the Reissner-Nordström-de Sitter solution, with no rivals. Each view stresses different pieces of the same curvature.
arxiv-2510-03348:
Yugay and colleagues at the University of Amsterdam present a 2025 arXiv paper on visual odometry, the task of tracking a camera's motion from video alone. Classic systems chain many hand built steps and need careful camera calibration. Their system, VoT, takes a simpler path. A transformer reads a run of single camera frames and predicts the motion directly. It skips depth maps, feature matching, and test time tuning altogether.

Training used only camera poses as the teaching signal. Tests on indoor and outdoor data sets showed VoT beating classic pipelines and large 3D models. It also ran more than three times faster than those rivals in the study. The system held up under camera settings it had never seen in training. Stronger pre-trained image encoders lifted its scores further. Simple, fast tracking like this could help robots, drones, and phone based reality tools move through new spaces.
arxiv-2510-03448:
Shah and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper on saving energy in industrial refrigeration by cooling ahead of demand. Big cold stores burn large amounts of power, yet product inside acts like a thermal battery. Cooling extra during cheap hours lets compressors rest when demand and prices peak. The authors recast the cooling problem as an inventory control problem with convex ordering costs. That lens imports a rich theory from operations research into plant control rooms.

Three results anchor the study. An optimal algorithm covers the case of known demand, and its best cooling paths never rise over time. Bounds price the value of load shifting from cost shape, demand swings, and timing patterns. A practical heuristic then handles uncertain demand with provable near optimal performance. Simulations backed the theory, and a case study on real plant data showed room for better shifting than current practice achieves.
arxiv-2510-04148:
Liu, Lu, and Liu present this 2025 arXiv paper on superfluidity in an open quantum system where particles are lost in pairs. Ultracold atom experiments see two-body loss from inelastic scattering, which theorists model with complex-valued interactions. The resulting system is non-Hermitian, and the standard biorthogonal mean-field treatment misbehaves. Under moderate dissipation it yields no nontrivial solutions and abrupt discontinuities.

The authors develop a mean-field theory based on right eigenstates alone. That framework produces smooth, continuous solutions where the biorthogonal one breaks down. Its lower condensation energy further suggests it describes the system better. They then add backscattering, an unavoidable feature of realistic setups. Even moderate backscattering destabilizes the superfluid when two-body loss is present. Strong backscattering destroys the superfluid state completely. The work identifies a concrete fragility mechanism for this non-Hermitian phase.
arxiv-2510-04348:
Hou and Li present this 2025 arXiv paper on how instantons change the electromagnetic behavior of a strongly coupled plasma, studied through holography. Instantons are topological excitations of the quantum chromodynamics vacuum tied to chiral symmetry breaking. Gauge-gravity duality models them as D-instanton branes inside a higher-dimensional geometry. Flavor quarks enter as probe D7-branes, whose action gives the electromagnetic theory of the plasma.

The authors numerically evaluate the vacuum decay rate, the critical electric field, and the current-voltage curve for various field strengths. Their results show particles in the plasma acquiring an effective mass in the presence of instantons, as field theory expects. Below the critical field, the plasma trends toward insulating behavior rather than conducting. A magnetic field alone, with no electric field, produces no vacuum decay in their analysis. The work links instantonic structure of the vacuum to measurable electromagnetic response.
arxiv-2510-04448:
Tomoyuki Morimae, Yuki Shirakawa, and Takashi Yamakawa wrote this 2025 paper on the foundations of quantum cryptography. Some quantum security tools may exist even where classic one way functions do not. A young primitive called a one way puzzle sits near the base of that hoped for world. The team asked what hardness assumption could support such puzzles. Their answer rests on measurements that do not collapse quantum states.

Such measurements are magical: real physics says a measurement always disturbs the state it reads. The team defines a sampling class built around a single query to that magical oracle. They prove that if the class is hard on average for quantum machines, then one way puzzles exist. They also build a bridge from the other side, using a new collision resistant puzzle. Two known tools, hiding commitments and one shot authentication codes, feed into that bridge.
arxiv-2510-04848:
Yuto Nishida, Masaru Isonuma, and Yusuke Oda wrote this 2025 paper on a wobble that haunts language model training. Teams judge training runs by task scores and keep the checkpoint that scores best. The authors show those scores jump around wildly during pretraining. A checkpoint crowned as best may just be a lucky spike. They studied a model trained on diverse web scale data and tracked scores over time.

Fluctuations appeared in total scores and in answers to single examples alike. The team then tested two ways to smooth the ride without changing training. Averaging neighboring checkpoints blends their weights into one model. Ensembling keeps several checkpoints and pools their answers. Both methods steadied downstream performance in experiments. Theory backed the effect, explaining why aggregation cancels part of the noise. Steadier scores mean fairer comparisons between runs and models. They also mean the chosen checkpoint is more likely to be good.
arxiv-2510-04948:
Wentao Fan and Boris Hasselblatt study a classic setup from dynamical systems in this 2025 arXiv paper. A billiard table here is a region where a point moves in straight lines and bounces off the walls. Their table, called a lemon billiard, is the overlap of two circles of different sizes. One circle holds the centers of both.

The authors prove that motion on this table is ergodic. In plain terms, a bouncing point eventually explores the whole table in an even, predictable pattern. Earlier tests for this kind of chaos did not apply to lemon tables. Fan and Hasselblatt instead show steady expansion of direction vectors and control the curves where the motion breaks. The result settles a conjecture about these tables and extends the tools used for dispersing billiards.
arxiv-2510-05048: Ondřej Kubíček and Viliam Lisý work on planning in games of hidden information in this 2025 arXiv paper. Strong game agents plan ahead by searching with a model of the game. Real settings rarely provide such a model, and learned models exist mainly for games with full information. The authors introduce an algorithm that pairs look-ahead search with a learned model for the hidden-information case, where many states matter for each single decision.
arxiv-2510-05148:
Qi Li, Runpeng Yu, Haiquan Lu, and Xinchao Wang fingerprint a new kind of language model in this 2025 arXiv paper. Discrete diffusion models generate text by refining many tokens at once, not left to right. That decoding process leaves a trajectory behind each answer. The authors ask whether the trajectory betrays which model wrote the text.

Raw confidence scores per step performed poorly as fingerprints. Bidirectional decoding makes those scores redundant and washes out structural signals. Their Directed Decoding Map instead captures relationships between decoding steps. A Gaussian model then scores how likely a trajectory is under each candidate model. Experiments across settings, including different checkpoints of one model, validated the approach. Reliable attribution helps police misuse of these fast new generators.
arxiv-2510-05248:
Daniel Loughran and Ross Paterson settle a counting problem about exotic number fields in this 2025 arXiv paper. Malle's conjecture predicts how many number fields exist below a discriminant bound, grouped by Galois symmetry. The quartic case with alternating group A4 resisted proof for decades. The best lower bound had stood since 1980.

The authors prove a lower bound that finally matches Malle's predicted growth. Their count grows like the square root of the bound times its logarithm. The proof fixes a cyclic cubic field and counts quartic fields sharing it as resolvent. A key step bounds those fields with an effective error term. Summing over resolvent fields then delivers the sharp total.
arxiv-2510-05348:
George Stavisskii and Leonid Fedichkin describe quantum measurement through the current in a tiny device in this 2025 arXiv paper. A quantum point contact watches a quantum dot by letting electrons flow past it. Standard theory traces out the surroundings to get irreversible dynamics. That machinery often becomes too complex for clean answers.

The authors build an alternative on the many-particle wave function. They derive master equations for the coupled dot and contact system. The framework generalizes to arbitrary dot-contact measurement setups and related quantum graphs. It yields the tunnel current's noise spectrum with first-order corrections. In the coherent regime it predicts an asymmetry in the noise spectra that earlier approaches had missed.
arxiv-2510-05448:
Zhou continues a study of the generalized Fermat equation in number theory. The equation asks when a power plus another power can equal a third power. Only ten solutions are known in the hard range of exponents. The 2025 paper is part two of the author's work on this problem.

Zhou applies inter-universal Teichmüller theory, with a small change for curves over the rationals. He argues that no further solutions exist outside a list of unsettled exponent patterns. As a result, the search for solutions with all exponents at least four shrinks to 244 patterns. The related Beal conjecture search shrinks to a few thousand patterns. Mathematicians still debate the foundations of the theory that the argument rests on. Readers should weigh the claims with that debate in mind. The paper thus turns an endless search into a finite, if large, checklist.
arxiv-2510-05748:
Madmoun and Lahlou test two ways to make language-model agents cooperate. Multi-agent systems face social dilemmas where selfish play hurts everyone. The authors compare direct communication against a teaching curriculum of games. Their 2025 experiments pit both ideas against classic game setups.

In a four-player Stag Hunt, a one-word cheap talk channel transformed behavior. Cooperation rose from zero to about forty-eight percent of plays. The Stag Hunt result held in a hard heterogeneous group of diverse models. A curriculum of progressively harder games fared far worse. It cut agent payoffs by about twenty-seven percent in a public goods game. Games favoring defection taught a learned pessimism that spilled into cooperative settings. Simple communication looks more reliable than experience-based training for coordination. For alignment work, the lesson favors cheap protocols over clever curricula. Curriculum designers must watch which strategic lessons their sequences embed.
arxiv-2510-05848:
Civino and Fedele sort small binary bibraces through linear algebra. Bibraces link to set-based solutions of the Yang-Baxter equation. Binary bibraces match alternating algebras over the two-element field. Their 2025 paper sorts those algebras up to size eight.

Each algebra becomes a subspace of skew-symmetric matrices over that field. Sorting then means listing orbits under congruence by the general linear group. Rank lists and other markers separate the classes from each other. Primitive algebras sort the harder cases. Magma software handles the counting at larger sizes. Their products vanish at class two, which keeps the counting tractable. Other group laws can replace XOR in how differences spread through a cipher. The sorting also counts certain subgroups of affine groups. The counts also tally other operations used in differential cryptanalysis.
arxiv-2510-06148:
Ferreira and three co-authors study how light diffracts through aperiodic slit arrays in a 2025 optics paper. Fraunhofer diffraction links a scattering object to its far-field pattern through the Fourier transform. Physicists use those patterns to characterize materials, trap particles, and sense tiny changes. Periodic arrays are routine, but aperiodic scatterers remain much less studied.

The authors analyze which interference maxima appear when light passes through aperiodic arrangements. They derive general conditions for experimentally observing peaks in these patterns. Surprisingly, the patterns can display periodic structures at several different distance scales at once. Thorough laboratory demonstrations back the theory, confirming the predicted peak structure. The work matters because aperiodic arrays show up in modern photonics, from engineered metasurfaces to quasicrystal-like structures. Knowing when their diffraction peaks are observable helps researchers design experiments and read material properties from scattered light with more confidence.
arxiv-2510-06348:
Quigg surveys the open questions of particle physics in a wide-ranging 2025 essay. The 2012 Higgs boson discovery at CERN crowned the standard model. That triumph validated a long chain of theory joining electroweak gauge symmetry to spontaneous symmetry breaking. Some claim the subject is finished, while others fear an impasse without fresh clues.

Quigg rejects both satisfaction and discouragement. The essay assembles the many questions still unanswered across the field. Together they form an expansive agenda for deepening our understanding of the physical world. The standard model's keystone is set, but the structure around it stays incomplete. Much of nature still points beyond the current paradigm, even without a named successor. Quigg writes as an insider taking stock after a generational triumph. His message is simple: the absence of easy wonders is not the absence of wonders.
arxiv-2510-06448:
Singh, Hess, and Vanschoren argue the benchmarks for transferability estimation metrics are fundamentally flawed in a 2025 machine learning paper. These metrics predict which pretrained model suits a target task best. They promise model selection without fine-tuning or source data. The benchmarks grading them had gone largely unexamined.

The standard setups mislead in two compounding ways. Their model spaces are unrealistic versus real selection problems. Their hierarchies are static, freezing rankings reality keeps reshuffling. Together they artificially inflate how good existing metrics appear. The inflation is severe. Simple dataset-agnostic heuristics can outperform sophisticated published methods here. Real selection involves shifting candidate pools and task mixtures that static leaderboards never capture. The paper closes with concrete recommendations for robust, realistic evaluations. The warning is direct: leaderboard scores for these metrics say little about real-world usefulness.
arxiv-2510-06548:
Seng Pei Liew and Takuya Kato study a cost-saving idea for training large language models. Their 2025 paper examines bootstrapped pretraining, where builders keep training an existing model instead of starting over. The approach covers continual pretraining and growing a model to a larger size. It promises lower costs, but its limits were unclear, especially for models already trained for a long time.

The authors run experiments to measure how the gains from a second training stage change. They find that the benefit shrinks in a predictable way. The scaling exponent for the second stage falls logarithmically as the first stage uses more data. A simple scaling law captures how both stages interact. The lesson is a clear trade-off for builders. The more a base model has already been trained, the less extra value further training adds.
arxiv-2510-06848:
Jonathan Allcock, Joao Doriguello, Gábor Ivanyos, and Miklos Santha revive a quantum measurement trick for systems beyond qubits. Their 2025 paper develops Bell sampling, which measures two copies of a quantum state together. The method helps identify stabilizer states and gauge a resource called magic. Extending it to qudits, systems with more than two levels, had resisted all useful attempts.

Earlier work by the same authors showed the natural extension fails to reveal anything meaningful. Their new primitive rests on a unitary built using Lagrange's four-square theorem. It converts four copies of any stabilizer state into four copies of its mirror image. Built on that step, Bell difference sampling works in every dimension. The team improves sample counts for several tasks over recent rivals. One result cuts the needed samples from order n times d down to order n. Stabilizer learning, testing, and randomness bounds all benefit.
arxiv-2510-06948:
Lorenzo Copparoni, Rohit Chandramouli, and Enrico Barausse propose a self-consistency check for gravitational-wave signals from extreme mass ratio inspirals. Their 2025 paper targets LISA, the future space-based wave detector. Such inspirals pair a small black hole with a huge one. They likely form partly in dense places like galactic nuclei or dark matter spikes.

Astronomers usually analyze the signals assuming empty space around the pair. Gas or dark matter nearby would quietly distort the waveform and bias the results. Modeling those effects directly is hard, because the physics is uncertain. Their test instead splits the signal into portions and fits each part separately. If the inferred parameters disagree systematically, the vacuum assumption has failed. Injected signals with disk migration torques triggered the test clearly. Observations longer than two years revealed the effect robustly, whatever the noise did. The method can even flag departures from general relativity itself.
arxiv-2510-07248:
Lee, Song, Han, Pyun, and Jo argue that small language models fail at tool use because tool names fight their training. Their 2025 paper names the failure schema misalignment. A small model invents plausible tool names that the real toolkit does not contain. Rather than retrain the model, the authors rename the tools to match what the model already expects. Their method, PA-Tool, needs no training at all.

PA-Tool tries several candidate names for each tool part. It keeps the names that make the model's outputs most concentrated and consistent. That concentration signals familiarity from pretraining. On two tool-use benchmarks, scores rose by up to seventeen points. Schema misalignment errors fell by about four fifths. Small models approached the performance of far larger systems while staying cheap to run. The trick is a practical fix for compact models with changing toolkits.
arxiv-2510-07348:
Jin, Yu, and Nanayakkara build an artificial whisker that feels turbulence underwater. Their 2025 paper mimics the flow sensors of seals and fish. The whisker is a tapered nylon spring with motion sensors embedded along it. Its taper spreads different vibration frequencies along its length, separating them spatially. Physical reservoir computing then reads flow patterns from those vibrations with minimal processing. Towing-tank experiments and flow simulations checked the design against fins set at varied angles.

The whisker told vortex regimes apart across those angles. Vibration strength grew with flow speed while dominant frequencies held steady, following the classic Strouhal law. Frequency analysis found vortex shedding rates within ten percent of truth. A simple classifier named the flow regime with accuracy near ninety percent, answering in milliseconds. Cheap whisker sensing could give underwater robots a feel for wakes cameras cannot provide.
arxiv-2510-07448:
Kristof-Tessier proves the Parallel Wall Theorem for a broad family of non-positively curved two-dimensional complexes. The 2025 paper works with CAT(0) complexes built from regular polygons with an even number of sides. Such complexes underlie Coxeter groups, whose geometry is governed by walls, the fixed mirrors of reflections. Distance between points equals the number of walls separating them, making walls the atoms of the geometry. The Parallel Wall Theorem says that a wall not cut off from a vertex by another wall must stay within a uniform distance of that vertex.

The new proof extends combined work by Janzen and Wise and by Hruska and Wise. Uniform wall control feeds directly into automatic structures for Coxeter groups, which make their word problems computationally tractable. It also supports the study of when such groups act nicely on cube-like spaces.
arxiv-2510-07648:
Amin and Alam wrote this 2025 machine learning paper on continual learning for adaptive AI systems. Neural networks learn new tasks well but often erase older skills. That failure is called catastrophic forgetting. The authors propose a framework named Cluster-Aware Replay, or CAR. It aims to let a network add tasks in sequence while keeping earlier performance.

CAR stores a small, class-balanced set of past examples for replay during training. It adds a penalty that pushes new and old tasks apart in feature space. That separation reduces interference between tasks. On a five-task version of the CIFAR-10 image benchmark, CAR preserved earlier tasks better than plain fine-tuning. The authors call their results preliminary, since performance still fades as tasks pile up. They suggest stronger spacing rules and larger benchmarks as next steps. Robots and personal assistants face the same demand in daily use.
arxiv-2510-08548:
Bo Yang, Elham Kashefi, and Harold Ollivier design a verified way to estimate observables on untrusted quantum servers in a 2025 arXiv paper. Near-term quantum hardware may soon run tasks classical machines cannot check, on remote servers users cannot trust. Existing verifiable blind quantum computation covers only problems whose answers can be amplified by majority voting. Many near-term applications instead estimate observables, like average energies, without such amplification.

Their protocol, Secure Delegated Observable Estimation, guarantees the estimate lands within a chosen error of the true expectation value, or aborts. Security is composable, covering both confidentiality and integrity of the delegated task. Overhead is modest: added test rounds are no more complex than the unprotected computation itself. The security error shrinks negligibly as the total number of rounds grows. This extends rigorous verification to a broad class of estimation tasks.
arxiv-2510-08748:
Yeh, Christianson, Wierman, and Yue work on a trust problem for deep learning in this 2025 arXiv paper. A trained model can be accurate on average yet offer no proof that its risk stays within a set limit. Conformal risk control is a method that adds such a guarantee after training, for almost any model. The catch is that it guards only average loss, while many users fear rare but severe losses most.

The authors extend the method to a broad family of risk measures that includes tail risks, meaning the worst outcomes rather than the typical ones. They also fold the control step into training itself, so the model learns with the guarantee in place instead of being patched afterward. In tests on image classification and battery storage trading, the approach kept its guarantees and beat the after-the-fact version on everyday performance.
arxiv-2510-08848:
Conroy and colleagues find a new way to read the spin of matter swirling around a black hole, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The Event Horizon Telescope, a planet-wide array, is preparing to make movies of black holes rather than single stills. Earlier work measured how bright patterns on the glowing ring appear to rotate. This team moves that measurement into the visibility domain, the raw data the telescopes record, skipping image making.

Using a large library of simulated black hole sources, they show the new speed measure depends on viewing angle, mass, spin, magnetic state, and telescope separation. For strongly magnetized models it reacts sharply to separation, and the slope of that reaction can pin down the black hole's spin. In all models the speed sits well below the local orbital speed, which suggests it tracks waves crossing the glowing gas. A future space telescope would sharpen the test.
arxiv-2510-08948:
Lu and colleagues build an AI assistant for fraud investigators at a giant online retailer, in this 2025 arXiv paper. E-commerce platforms fight a running battle with shadow-economy operators whose tricks keep evolving. Human analysts must dig through suspicious cases to spot new fraud patterns, but each case demands deep experience and scrutiny across many risk dimensions. Volume is enormous, and standards vary between analysts.

Their framework, SHERLOCK, extracts hard-won knowledge from mixed data sources into a domain knowledge base. A platform built on a data flywheel, where daily work steadily improves the system, folds in expert annotations and model evaluations, with repeated fine-tuning to match expert preferences. A reflect-and-refine module then reacts quickly when risk patterns shift. On real JD.com transaction data, it improved precision of factual alignment and risk pinpointing, and deployment sped up case work.
arxiv-2510-09048:
Tupayachi and co-authors forecast where and when electric vehicle drivers will plug in across Tennessee, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Charging demand is patchy in space and jumpy in time, which strains power grids and misleads investors deciding where to build stations. Their model treats the station network as a graph, so each station's forecast learns from its neighbors, and layers time-aware components on top. Real traffic flows, weather records, and data from a major charging company feed the system.

Experiments varied the forecast horizon, the grouping of stations, and the length of history used. Three-hour forecasts hit the sweet spot between responsiveness and stability. Among the time components tried, simple one-dimensional convolutional networks, which scan for local patterns, consistently won. Accuracy differed by region, with east, middle, and west Tennessee behaving differently. They tie those gaps to station density, nearby attractions, and local demand swings.
arxiv-2510-09248:
Chatterjee, Soh, and Eichenfield work out the quantum theory of a sound amplifier built from electrons drifting across a piezoelectric chip, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The device stacks a two-dimensional electron gas, a thin sheet where electrons move freely, on a material converting between electricity and vibration. A drift voltage pumps electrons into excited momentum states, like a laser's population inversion. The pumped electrons then release phonons, sound quanta, amplifying a sound wave.

The authors show dimensionality is the trick. A one-dimensional gas amplifies well only when the sound wavelength roughly equals the electron spacing. The two-dimensional version amplifies any longer wavelength. They derive the gain per unit length and the quantum noise, and show the gain matches the classical formula for short-lived carriers. Pump depletion clamps the gain and caps the intensity. The results frame designs for a sound-based quantum laser.
arxiv-2510-09748:
Michelle Ntampaka and six co-authors test whether models trained on simulated galaxies survive contact with different simulations, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Simulation-based inference trains networks on synthetic data and applies them to real observations. The catch is domain shift: test data can differ subtly from training data in ways that quietly wreck the estimates.

Their test case is the estimation of galaxy cluster masses from X-ray profiles. Training data come from the Magneticum simulation, while the test set derives from IllustrisTNG. A plain neural network gained seventeen percent on its training distribution yet scored forty percent worse on the test set from the other domain. The authors apply two remedies: training on scatter-augmented catalogues, and a semi-supervised deep reconstruction-regression network built for domain shift. The study shows how easily out-of-domain test data hides, and why adaptability must be tested, not assumed.
arxiv-2510-10048:
Meng and co-authors evaluate generative AI guidance for Type 2 diabetes in this 2025 arXiv study of health information. Patients increasingly ask AI systems for everyday health advice, yet the reliability and clinical fit of the answers remain uncertain. Diabetes is a chronic condition where bad guidance can do real harm.

The study has two parts and mixes methods. It examines how patients and physicians in China judge the quality and usability of AI-generated information for intrauterine insemination decisions in diabetes care, as framed by the authors. Comparing the two groups' views shows where patient trust and clinical judgment diverge. The findings speak to how AI health tools should be checked before patients rely on them.
arxiv-2510-10348:
Zhang, Shaleen Deep, Jignesh M. Patel, and Karthikeyan Sankaralingam index logs for pattern searches in this 2025 arXiv paper on data systems. Log analysis hunts regular expressions, text patterns, inside huge log files. Without an index, every query scans everything, which is slow.

Their system, REI, builds an n-gram index, cataloging short character sequences so queries can skip most of the data. With an efficient storage design, they report speedups of up to fourteen times over state-of-the-art regex engines that do not index, at a cost of only about two percent extra space. Fast log search speeds up debugging and security investigations that depend on finding rare patterns quickly.
arxiv-2510-10448:
Zhichao Xu and six co-authors tackle a cost problem in retrieval-augmented generation in this 2025 arXiv paper. Such systems fetch documents and feed them to a language model so it can reason over them. Long, noisy documents raise costs and hurt answers. The team's framework, RECON, adds a trained summarizer that squeezes the evidence down inside the reasoning loop itself.

The summarizer is trained in two stages. It first learns relevance from question-answering data, then it is distilled from large proprietary models to keep it factual and clear. Plugged into the Search-R1 pipeline, RECON cut total context length by 35 percent while speeding up both training and answering. It also raised answer quality: the average exact-match score rose by 14.5 percent for the smaller model and by 3.0 percent for the larger one. Gains were strongest on multi-hop questions, which need several linked facts.
arxiv-2510-10548:
Katsunori Kusakabe, Yoshiyuki Inoue, and Daisuke Toyouchi check whether known black hole populations can explain a recently detected hum of gravitational waves, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Pulsar timing arrays have found a stochastic background at nanohertz frequencies, a sea of faint waves from many distant sources. The leading suspects are binaries of supermassive black holes. The team builds an estimate of that background from observed dual active galactic nuclei and X-ray luminosity functions.

Dual active nuclei are galaxy pairs with two feeding black holes. Their observed fractions depend in a clear way on luminosity, which the team compiles from recent datasets, and that pattern constrains the binary population. Their model reproduces the current background measurements within the timing uncertainties. They conclude that supermassive black hole binaries dominate the nanohertz signal, so light based and wave based observations tell a consistent story.
arxiv-2510-10748:
Alexander Smirnov and Vladimir Smirnov review two decades of algorithms for reducing Feynman integrals, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Feynman integrals are the workhorse quantities of particle physics calculations. A key step in evaluating them is solving integration by parts relations, which express whole families of integrals as combinations of a smaller set of master integrals. Software that automates this reduction has become essential as calculations grow in complexity.

The review is historiographical: it traces how the algorithms and computer codes developed over twenty years. The authors restrict attention to general algorithms, ones that in principle apply to any family of Feynman integrals rather than special cases. They recount the lineage from early Laporta style approaches to modern finite field methods used by current codes. The paper serves as a map for researchers who rely on these tools.
arxiv-2510-10848:
Huub de Jong classifies which orbit lengths can occur in certain symbolic dynamical systems, in this 2025 arXiv paper. A periodic point returns to itself after some number of steps, and the set of achievable least periods is a basic fingerprint of a system. Interest traces back to Sharkovskii's theorem for interval maps, and the question feeds checkable conditions for Krieger's embedding theorem. De Jong works with systems whose zeta function has a rational logarithmic derivative.

Using the Skolem-Mahler-Lech theorem, he classifies for which natural numbers such a system has a periodic point of a given period. Building on work on finitely presented systems and their ties to symbolic dynamics, he then classifies the sets of least periods for arbitrary finitely presented systems. This extends a known classification for shifts of finite type. He also gives constructions realizing any such least period set, showing the classification is complete.
arxiv-2510-11048:
Onyedikachi J Okeke and nine co-authors map how location shapes household wealth across one New Mexico county, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The study covers Bernalillo County, home to Albuquerque. Instead of one global regression, the team uses multiscale geographically weighted regression, which lets each factor's influence vary across space and operate at its own scale. Inputs include income, home value, elevation, fine particle pollution, and distances to schools, markets, hospitals, and other services.

The model explained about 63 percent of the variation in household wealth. Proximity to markets, schools, and parks raised wealth in over 40 percent of neighborhoods. Closeness to hospitals and bus stops, by contrast, was linked to lower wealth, suggesting nearby disamenities can drag down desirability. A Moran's I statistic of 0.53 confirmed that wealthy households cluster strongly. The headline lesson is that locational suitability has no single countywide effect: its payoff changes from neighborhood to neighborhood.
arxiv-2510-11148:
Simulating molecules at coarse-grained resolution lets researchers reach larger systems and longer times, but training the machine learning potentials behind such models is data-hungry. Weilong Chen, Franz Görlich, Paul Fuchs, and Julija Zavadlav propose a better training data strategy in this 2025 arXiv paper. Standard training relies on long atomistic trajectories drawn from the unbiased equilibrium distribution, which leaves transition regions poorly sampled.

Their approach uses enhanced sampling to bias data generation along the coarse-grained degrees of freedom, then recomputes the forces against the unbiased potential. This shortens the simulation time needed for equilibrated data and enriches sampling in transition regions while preserving the correct potential of mean force. They demonstrate the method on the Müller-Brown potential and on capped alanine, finding notable improvements. The results support enhanced sampling as a promising direction for more accurate coarse-grained machine learning potentials.
arxiv-2510-11448:
Self-driving stacks pass sensor data between modules through middleware, and that plumbing can eat most of the time budget between seeing and braking. Yuankai He and Weisong Shi present a faster transport in this 2025 arXiv systems paper. Their Sensor-in-Memory middleware runs beside the ROS 2 framework and moves data through shared memory.

Sensor-in-Memory keeps data in native layouts, uses lock-free double buffers that overwrite stale readings to favor freshness, and needs four lines of code to integrate into a ROS 2 node. Sequence numbers, a writer heartbeat, and optional checksums preserve ordering, liveness, and integrity. On a Jetson Orin Nano it cut transport latency by up to 98 percent against zero-copy DDS transports. On a level-4 vehicle running Autoware, perception-to-decision latency fell from 521.91 to 290.26 milliseconds on average, shortening emergency braking distance by about four meters at 40 miles per hour.
arxiv-2510-11748:
Huw Day and Nina C. Snaith connect random matrix theory with the biology of DNA copying. When a cell copies its DNA, the work starts at many points called origins of replication. In simple organisms such as some yeasts, the spacing between origins follows a curious pattern. It matches the spacing of eigenvalues, the special numbers of random matrices from a family called the Circular Orthogonal Ensemble. The authors' 2025 arXiv paper explores that match.

The match breaks down for more complex organisms, whose origins look less rigidly spaced. Day and Snaith therefore thin the matrix model: they delete a uniform fraction of the eigenvalues. Thinning slides the statistics smoothly from the rigid ensemble pattern toward fully random, uncorrelated spacing. That gives one flexible model spanning both extremes. With it, they compare origin patterns across species and probe what spacing says about replication.
arxiv-2510-11848:
Efstratios Reppas, Ali Wadi, Brendan Gould, and Kyriakos G. Vamvoudakis ask how deception works when a game is played with quantum rules. Their 2025 arXiv paper extends the Honey-X paradigm, a classical framework where one player manipulates another's view of the payoffs. In the quantum version, payoffs live in a Hamiltonian, the operator that encodes a system's energy and rewards. Deception becomes a controlled tampering with that Hamiltonian, limited by a deception budget.

A surprise anchors the theory. When victims know deception is possible, their best responses match those of naive victims who trust the fake payoffs completely. Awareness, in equilibrium, buys no protection. That equivalence lets the authors recast the problem as a two-level optimization, solvable as a bilinear semidefinite program. Simulations of the Penny Flip game, played with quantum rules, show quantum strategies and non-classical payoffs can amplify deception beyond the classical case.
arxiv-2510-12148:
Yuki Yasuda and Ryo Onishi sharpen city-scale temperature maps at a fifth of the usual computing price. Urban micrometeorology needs street-level detail, but physics simulations at that resolution are costly. Their 2025 arXiv paper performs super-resolution of two-meter temperature fields using a Schrödinger bridge, a diffusion-based transformation between two data distributions rather than from pure noise.

Training pairs came from physics-based simulations at low and high resolution under identical conditions. Against a standard denoising diffusion model, the bridge model matches accuracy while needing only ten neural evaluations per field instead of fifty. Its high-resolution samples also show larger variance, implying better uncertainty quantification, an ensemble's spread being its honesty about ignorance. Cheap sampling changes what is operationally possible: the authors argue real-time ensemble micrometeorological prediction becomes feasible.
arxiv-2510-12248:
Tireli and co-authors show how collider searches could probe heavy neutral leptons that couple mainly to the tau neutrino, in a 2025 arXiv particle physics paper. Heavy neutral leptons are heavier cousins of the known neutrinos and could explain why neutrinos have mass. Long lived ones travel some distance before decaying, leaving a displaced vertex, a decay point away from the collision.

Current searches usually demand a prompt lepton next to the displaced vertex, which misses events where the tau decays into hadrons. The authors simulate the full production and decay chain for lepton pair final states, with selection rules modeled on the ATLAS experiment. Cuts on lepton pair mass and vertex position greatly improve signal visibility. They estimate that existing Run 2 data could improve current bounds by more than a factor of ten. Future high luminosity running could gain up to three orders of magnitude.
arxiv-2510-12348:
Panayiotou and co-authors introduce MOUFLON, a community detection method that balances group quality against fairness across demographic groups, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Community detection splits a network into clusters of tightly connected members. Standard modularity based methods can quietly align communities with demographic groups, baking structural bias into the result.

MOUFLON lets users adjust how much weight modularity, the quality score for a partition, receives relative to fairness outcomes. Its proportional balance fairness metric gives consistent and comparable fairness scores even when groups are several and uneven in size. The authors evaluate the method on synthetic and real networks, examining the trade off between modularity and fairness. They vary network size, density, and group distribution, and include scenarios where homogeneous groups cluster strongly, which stresses fairness the most. Their findings map how fairness constraints reshape detected communities and offer guidance for designing and benchmarking fair network analysis methods.
arxiv-2510-12648:
Arous, Haif, Farhang, and Arslan propose a unified framework that lets wireless systems switch their signal representation to whichever domain suits the channel, in a 2025 arXiv telecommunications paper. Beyond the classic time and frequency domains, newer domains based on delay and Doppler shift, or on chirps, offer channel descriptions with extra degrees of freedom. These matter for next generation networks facing difficult propagation environments.

The article analyzes channel characteristics, delay, Doppler shifts, and coefficients, across domains, emphasizing how the domains relate and where they genuinely differ. It evaluates which domain wins under which channel conditions. Building on that analysis, the authors propose an adaptive transform domain framework. It rests on pre and post processing around the discrete Fourier transform, enabling dynamic transitions between domains as conditions and requirements change. Representative use cases show the cross domain processing in diverse scenarios, and future directions and open challenges are discussed.
arxiv-2510-13048:
Guo and colleagues assemble functional articulated objects from spare parts in this 2025 arXiv paper on computer graphics. Their framework, kinematic kitbashing, takes a tree describing how joints connect. It also takes a library of jointed parts from existing models. From these it synthesizes new objects that move correctly. The optimizer places every part at once.

Placement must keep attachments sound through the whole range of motion. It must also meet user goals such as reachability, collision-free actuation, or path following. The core is an attachment energy built around how parts move. It aligns features sampled from existing articulations. This sits inside a Langevin sampling framework that treats functional goals as extra energies and tolerates their non-smoothness. Examples range from a multi-head lamp to a workstation that can be rearranged. On standard metrics the method beat leading baselines by strong margins.
arxiv-2510-13148:
Kikuchi develops a flexible way to find where a treatment's effect fades with distance in this 2025 arXiv economics paper, then applies it to bank branches. Parametric models force spatial effects into fixed shapes and can invent boundaries that are not there. His nonparametric framework uses local linear regression with data-driven bandwidth choice to estimate spatial decay patterns and detect boundaries without imposing a functional form.

Simulations showed lower bias than parametric rivals and correct detection of absent boundaries. Applying the method, Kikuchi matched several thousand new branches opened between 2015 and 2020 to millions of mortgage applications across census tracts. Branch proximity raised application volume but not approval rates, suggesting branches stimulate demand while credit decisions stay centralized. Branch survival fell in high-income areas, a pattern explained by consolidation of redundant branches in over-banked wealthy districts rather than discrimination.
arxiv-2510-13348:
Anastos and colleagues solve two long-standing problems about the giant component of the percolated hypercube. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies a cube-like network in many dimensions, with each edge kept at random. Above a threshold chance, one huge connected piece, the giant component, holds most vertices. The work sits in random graph theory.

They prove the typical diameter of this giant piece grows in proportion to the dimension. They also prove the typical mixing time of a lazy random walk grows with the square of the dimension. These results close questions open since 1994 and 2003. Their proof uses a sharp estimate on the giant piece's size, built from new ideas about its spread and stability. The same tools yield optimal bounds on how well the giant piece expands.
arxiv-2510-13448:
Rønne, Vegge, and Bhowmik introduce GO-Diff, a diffusion method that searches for low-energy atomic structures. Their 2025 arXiv paper tackles global structure optimization, a core task in materials science and catalysis. Finding the most stable arrangement of atoms is hard because the energy landscape is vast and rugged. Traditional search methods need many costly energy evaluations to explore it. Stable structures underpin the design of new catalysts and materials.

GO-Diff learns to sample low-energy arrangements directly, with no prior dataset to learn from. Training uses only the known energy function, weighted toward favourable regions. A two-stage loop of sampling and refinement steadily sharpens the model's aim. The method matches traditional pipelines while using far fewer energy evaluations. Pretrained models can also transfer to related systems, speeding new searches without retraining. This reuse, called amortized optimization, cuts the cost of each fresh problem.
arxiv-2510-13548:
Ben and Zhang hunt for strange pentaquark molecules using QCD sum rules. Their 2025 arXiv paper builds candidate states in the hadronic molecular picture, where two hadrons bind loosely. The targets are partners of known pentaquark multiplets in the sector containing strange quarks. Such exotic states stretch the traditional quark model of hadrons.

The authors construct twenty-one distinct currents with two sets of spin-parity values. No bound state emerges from the first set of currents. Three currents in the second set do yield bound-state solutions. Those three match known resonances and read as molecules pairing a baryon with a meson. Two of them appear to be multiplet partners of each other. Other constructions align with excited states or resonances already listed by the Particle Data Group.
arxiv-2510-13648:
D'Alimonte and Manolescu extend Ornstein-Zernike theory to the random-cluster model near its critical point. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies a planar percolation model, where random connections form clusters on a lattice. The classic theory describes how the two-point connection chance decays far apart. It was proved only away from the critical regime, where behaviour changes character.

Their formula holds uniformly below the critical point and blends both regimes smoothly. The proof explores a subcritical cluster step by step, in slices as thick as the correlation length. That exploration behaves like a killed Markov renewal process, which wanders much like Brownian motion. Further results follow: a scaling limit for the rescaled cluster and strict convexity of the inverse correlation length. Their dynamic exploration differs from the static diamond constructions of earlier work. The model covers the range where its cluster weight stays between one and four.
arxiv-2510-13748:
Van Vuren, Sloothaak, Wolf, and Sanders prove an asymptotically optimal regret bound for reinforcement learning in block-structured worlds. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies Block Markov Decision Processes, where huge observation spaces hide few true states. Dynamics depend only on the latent state behind each observation. Clustering methods can recover that hidden structure, but their effect on learning speed was unquantified.

Their algorithm runs in two phases. Random exploration first uncovers the latent blocks through clustering. Then an optimism-guided strategy exploits the recovered structure for the remaining time. The regret grows like the square root of the time horizon plus the observation count, up to small factors. That beats the best prior bound, which carried a squared observation term. A matching lower bound shows no algorithm can do better on this class. Accurate latent estimates, the analysis confirms, genuinely accelerate learning.
arxiv-2510-13948:
Yang Bai, Keping Xie, and Bei Zhou propose turning giant neutrino telescopes into colliders for exploring physics beyond the Standard Model, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Cosmic neutrinos with extreme energies slam into atomic nuclei inside detectors such as IceCube. The collision energy can exceed what the Large Hadron Collider can reach. That machine is currently the world's most powerful accelerator.

Using predicted and measured high-energy neutrino fluxes from IceCube and the KM3NeT telescope, the authors estimate how sensitive detectors of one to thirty cubic kilometers would be to representative new particles. Their results show these 'Large Neutrino Colliders' could probe multi-TeV particles, meaning particles thousands of times heavier than a proton, with sensitivity comparable to, and sometimes better than, the LHC's. The appeal is a new search avenue that uses instruments already being built for astronomy, rather than waiting decades for a bigger accelerator.
arxiv-2510-14048:
Shashi B. Mishra and co-authors compute how well electricity flows through the TaAs family of Weyl semimetals when phonons, vibrations of the crystal lattice, are the main obstacle, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Weyl semimetals are exotic crystals whose electrons behave like massless particles, and understanding what limits their conductivity matters for future electronics.

Using first-principles calculations feeding the Boltzmann transport equation, the team studied all four family members: TaAs, TaP, NbAs, and NbP. Their calculated conductivities matched experiments on high-quality samples well, confirming phonon scattering dominates. Niobium phosphide conducted best, because its carriers move fastest, offsetting stronger scattering. Tantalum arsenide conducted worst, with smaller carrier pockets and slower velocities. Small doping barely changed NbP's conductivity, while TaAs responded one way to electron doping and another to hole doping. The other two compounds fell in between, their behavior set by Fermi surface shape and scattering opportunities.
arxiv-2510-14148:
Mikhail Alfimov and Andrey Kurakin continue a study of how the beta function of supersymmetric sigma models depends on the renormalization scheme, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The scheme is the bookkeeping choices theorists make when removing infinities. Sigma models describe fields taking values on a target space, and their beta function governs how the space's geometry flows as the energy scale changes.

Earlier work computed the beta function to four loops, the fourth order of quantum corrections. Here they extend the result to five loops. They find a renormalization scheme where the fifth-loop contribution vanishes. The fourth-loop contribution reduces to a single invariant quantity, independent of coordinates, for certain models. These include families of deformed sphere-like spaces, whose metrics they show solve the flow equation up to fifth-loop order. They also discuss the Kähler structure, a geometric property, of two deformed cases.
arxiv-2510-14548:
Nachkov, Wang, and Van Gool ask, in a 2025 arXiv paper, whether a language model agent can be more than a handy tool. Today's agents reason step by step and call functions to finish set tasks. The authors wonder if such software could act as an entity in its own right. Could it plan, invent its own tasks, and work toward broad, fuzzy goals?

To test this, they gave a pretrained agent extra powers. It could generate its own tasks, store knowledge, and interact with its environment over long stretches. They studied the result qualitatively, meaning by observing and judging its behavior rather than scoring it. The agent followed complex multi-step instructions reliably and reused stored information across runs. It also proposed and solved tasks of its own. Still, it stayed sensitive to prompt wording, generated repetitive tasks, and showed no sign of representing itself.
arxiv-2510-14648:
Liao and co-authors tackle, in a 2025 arXiv paper, instruction-based video editing, where a user asks for changes such as adding or removing an object in a clip. Image editing by instruction works well, but video lags behind. The main obstacle is data: building large sets of before-and-after video pairs is slow and expensive, so editors cannot learn from examples at scale.

The authors pretrain a video generation model on unpaired clips instead, letting it pick up basic editing ideas from context, with about one million real clips. A short fine-tuning stage on fewer than 150,000 curated editing pairs then sharpens the skill. In comparisons, their method beat existing instruction-based video editors on both following the instruction and visual quality. The reported gains were a twelve percent improvement in instruction following and a fifteen percent improvement in editing quality.
arxiv-2510-14748:
Hu and a large team of co-authors report, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a new kind of fast wave in the Sun's corona, found in three-dimensional simulations of a solar eruption. During magnetic reconnection, plasma jets shoot out of a vertical current sheet. Above and below the sheet sit termination shocks, where the jets slam to a halt. The simulations show waves born at both ends of the sheet.

The jets partly reflect off the shocks and strike the fork-shaped walls at the sheet's ends, which ring like a tuning fork. The resulting waves race away at about 1,400 kilometers per second with a two-second period, matching oscillations inside the fork. Some oscillation energy turns into heat at the sheet's center. This is the first report of such waves from a tuning-fork effect.
arxiv-2510-14948:
Reimann and a large collaboration report, in a 2025 arXiv paper, on the commissioning path of FAIR, the Facility for Antiproton and Ion Research rising beside the GSI Helmholtz Centre in Darmstadt. Its first stage centers on SIS100, a superconducting heavy-ion synchrotron, together with the Super Fragment Separator and new beam transport lines. Two existing GSI machines, UNILAC and SIS18, will feed it as injectors.

Installation inside the tunnels and supply buildings has run since early 2024. The paper lays out status, strategy, and timeline as the project pivots from construction to turning systems on. Commissioning begins in 2025 with the cryogenic plant, the refrigeration that keeps the superconducting magnets cold. The transport line follows at the end of 2025. Beam commissioning, the first particles circulating through the new complex, is scheduled for the second half of 2027. The authors frame the sequence as the road toward first science at the facility.
arxiv-2510-15048:
Ursell, Hoy, Harry, and Nuttall identify, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a way that gravitational-wave astronomy can fool itself about the heaviest black hole mergers. Reading source properties from a signal needs waveform models, used correctly. Time-domain models must start at some frequency. Start too late and the model omits low-frequency power carried by higher-order multipoles, the signal's harmonics.
