Focusing on binaries of at least two hundred solar masses, the authors show current detectors are sensitive to that missing power, and biased properties follow. For systems up to about three hundred solar masses, with mass ratios above roughly a third and signal-to-noise above twenty, templates starting at twenty hertz already recover biased properties. Heavier and more lopsided systems are biased even from thirteen hertz. Only when the signal is quieter does starting at twenty hertz become safe, because statistical uncertainty then swamps the modeling error.
arxiv-2510-15148:
Xingrui Wang and nine colleagues probe whether AI models that read text, images, and sound truly reason the same way across all three. Their 2025 arXiv paper introduces XModBench, a benchmark of about sixty-one thousand multiple-choice questions spanning five task families. Each question and answer can arrive in any mix of text, vision, and audio, giving six combinations that expose whether a model favors one channel over another.

Even the strongest system tested, Gemini 2.5 Pro, scored under 60 percent on spatial and temporal reasoning tasks. The same content delivered as audio instead of text caused sharp performance drops across models. Models also stayed less consistent when an image, rather than text, supplied the context for a question. Wang and colleagues conclude that current omni-modal models are far from treating all channels equally, and they offer XModBench as a diagnostic tool for closing that gap.
arxiv-2510-15448:
Nengbo Zhang and Hann Woei Ho teach computers to recognize what a small drone is doing from video, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Spotting the maneuvers of micro aerial vehicles matters when drone swarms must perceive and coordinate with each other. Models that read only ordinary color video miss the fine motion patterns that separate one action from another.

Their network, MAVR-Net, reads three views of the same footage at once. It combines raw frames, optical flow showing pixel motion, and segmentation masks outlining the drone. Separate encoders extract features from each view at several scales, preserving motion detail. A cross-view attention module lets the views inform each other, and an alignment loss keeps their meanings consistent. On three benchmark datasets covering short, medium, and long actions, the system scored about ninety-eight, ninety-six, and ninety-three percent accuracy.
arxiv-2510-15848:
Xiran Bai and the HAYSTAC Collaboration report a particle search in a 2025 paper. They hunted dark photons. These hypothetical particles could make up dark matter. The search covered a narrow mass band. It sits around nineteen micro-electronvolts. The team reused data from the HAYSTAC detector's axion hunts. They added an unpublished data set too. Another experiment had claimed a possible signal in that region.

HAYSTAC was sensitive enough to test the claim. The claimed signal should have stood out clearly. It would have been a towering excess above the noise. No such signal appeared. The team thus excludes stronger coupling values across the region. The exclusion holds at ninety percent confidence. The claimed reading is effectively ruled out.
arxiv-2510-16448:
Yongxiang Hua leads six co-authors in a 2025 study on routing inputs inside large image-and-text models. These models use expert parts, where each input goes to a few experts. Old routers pick experts by score match, which blurs who should own what. Their design, Input Domain Aware MoE, routes by input zone instead.

A chance-based mix model splits the input space into clear zones. Each expert then owns a zone and trains apart from the main task. That split keeps training stable and picks crisp, not vague. Tests on image-and-text tasks beat older expert models on score and balance. Balanced expert use means less waste and faster runs.
arxiv-2510-16748:
Jiaogen Zhang works on a family of hard equations in a 2025 mathematics paper. The equations involve Hessian operators, which are built from second derivatives of a function. The problem is an eigenvalue problem, asking for special numbers and matching solutions. The solution must also vanish at the edge of its region.

Zhang proves early estimates that any solution must obey. He then shows a first nonzero eigenvalue exists, with a smooth matching solution. The class covered includes several famous operators used in geometry. As a bonus, every operator of one broad invariant family gets a unique first eigenvalue. A theory of splitting solution branches completes the work.
arxiv-2510-16848: Michael Kapovich proves one estimate about shapes in four dimensions in a 2025 mathematics paper. The shapes are hyperbolic 4-manifolds, curved spaces with constant negative bending. He bounds their intersection pairing, a count of how two surfaces inside must cross. The bound uses Thurston norms, which measure the simplest surface carrying a given class. The result ties crossing numbers to surface complexity inside these spaces.
arxiv-2510-16948:
Ruiming Guo and Ayush Bhandari attack a signal recovery problem in a 2025 paper. The task is finding sharp spikes hidden inside filtered measurements. Spikes sit at exact real-valued times, not on a neat grid. Strong and weak spikes together break ordinary digital recording.

Strong spikes clip, while weak ones sink below recording noise. The authors use a recording method called unlimited sensing. It folds oversized signals instead of clipping them outright. That folding preserves detail that ordinary recording would destroy. New theory then recovers spike times and sizes together. The results extend to common non-ideal filter shapes as well. Better spike recovery helps radar, imaging, and communications systems alike.
arxiv-2510-17148:
Yu Gao and nine co-authors blend two styles of self-driving control in this 2025 paper. One style plans safe paths well but fails on rare road scenes. The other uses broad world sense but can plan paths cars cannot drive. The team wants the strengths of both in one system.

Their system builds sense-based paths and a dense set of safe path picks. A score tool then lines up the two sets by road measures. The blend keeps world sense while paths stay fit to drive. In a 2025 grand challenge test, the system scored well on the board. The work shows sense and safe planning can aid each other.
arxiv-2510-17348:
Picking the best option from several uncertain ones, while keeping each person data private, is the tension at the heart of a study by Marc Jourdan and Achraf Azize. Their setting is best arm identification, used in sensitive trials and user studies, under a global differential privacy rule that limits what the full data set can reveal about anyone. Known methods in the private setting sat far from the proven lower limits on how many samples any method must use.

Jourdan and Azize close most of that gap for outcomes that follow a coin flip style distribution. They prove a sharper lower bound built on a new cost measure, then design a stopping rule and a top two sampling rule to match it. Their method stays within a small constant factor of the bound and beats existing private methods across privacy budgets.
arxiv-2510-17548:
When people disagree about whether a text is offensive, a single accuracy score hides what the model has actually learned. Nisrine Rair, Alban Goupil, Valeriu Vrabie, and Emmanuel Chochoy turn to Mapper, a tool from topological data analysis that maps the shape of a model inner representation space. They apply it to a large RoBERTa model fine tuned on an offence data set where human annotators often disagreed.

Fine tuning, they find, reshapes the space into separate, curved regions that match the model own predictions, even on the most ambiguous texts. Nearly all regions were highly pure in prediction, yet agreement with the human labels dropped exactly where annotators had disagreed. Rair and her co-authors argue that Mapper exposes overconfident clusters and collapsing boundaries that standard plots miss.
arxiv-2510-17648:
Kyuseong Choi and Gabriella Ciolek build a resampling method for dependent data in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their data come from Markov chains, which are random processes where each step depends on the last one. They focus on Harris recurrent chains, a broad class that returns to states in a stable way. The goal is approximating the spread of a worst case statistic over many test functions.

A splitting trick breaks the chain into blocks that are independent or nearly so. That yields a Gaussian approximation with error rates matching much simpler settings. On top of the splitting, they design a multiplier bootstrap, which reweights blocks to mimic new samples. They prove finite sample guarantees for the method. One use is a confidence band for a diffusion process's steady density.
arxiv-2510-17948:
Christopher A McClurg and Alan R Wagner test, in virtual reality, whether a robot could slow a school shooter. One hundred fifty university players took the shooter's role inside a simulation. A self-driving robot predicted their path and moved to block and distract them, either head-on or from a distance.

Distraction levels ran from plain presence to siren and lights, then smoke as well. A bold robot with the strongest distraction cut the victim count sharply against the no-robot case in the study. The authors stress the safety promise and the hard ethical questions such use would raise in real schools.
arxiv-2510-18248:
Akiyoshi Tsujita, with Seiji Fujimoto and forty co-authors, measures dust dimming in distant galaxies in a 2025 study. The galaxies formed stars when the universe was young, at redshifts near four to six. Dust dims starlight and gas glow by different amounts, which can distort readings of galaxy properties.

The team studied eighteen galaxies with the James Webb Space Telescope and fitted their light in detail. They found starlight suffers about half the dimming that glowing gas suffers. Assuming equal dimming, as many studies do, understates some galaxy outputs by large margins. Their ratio helps astronomers correct early galaxy measurements more honestly.
arxiv-2510-18348:
Alexandros Ntagkas, working with Chairi Kiourt and Konstantinos Chatzilygeroudis, presents a method for teaching legged robots to walk over rough ground. Their approach, called Phase-Guided Terrain Traversal, uses reinforcement learning, where a controller improves through trial and error. Earlier controllers either forced a fixed walking rhythm on the robot or gave it no view of the ground ahead.

Phase-Guided Terrain Traversal instead builds the walking rhythm into the rewards the learner receives, and it adjusts step height to match the ground nearby. Training took place in a simulated world with stair-like ground, random changes, and pushes meant to knock the robot off balance. The method beat the compared systems there, and the team also tested it on a real four-legged robot using laser scans of the ground.
arxiv-2510-18948:
Robert Penna describes a semiclassical route by which a cosmic string can decay into a burst of gravitational waves. Cosmic strings are thin, dense lines that some early universe theories predict, and how they can vanish is a basic question for those theories.

Penna finds the tunneling solution, called an instanton, and computes the decay rate. Locally the solution matches an analytic extension of the Kerr metric, though no black hole is present. A striking point is that a cone-like flaw in the starting state is gone in the final state, showing flaws can vanish in quantum gravity.
arxiv-2510-19248:
Juntang Wang and four co-authors present Configuration-Mixed Prediction. It uses clustering features at many resolutions at once. Most methods force one global choice of resolution. Recent work shows only finitely many stable splits arise. Each stable split is called a configuration.

Their module is called MixConfig. It pulls configurations from any frozen embedding. For each sample, it learns how to weight them. The weights use context, cluster assignment, and stability scores. Tests span tabular, molecular, vision, and text data. The mixed features help prediction. The base model needs no retraining.
arxiv-2510-19348:
Paul Strang and five co-authors formulate variable selection in branch and bound as a standard Markov decision process, giving reinforcement learning a clean footing in integer programming solvers. Branch and bound solves hard combinatorial problems, and which variable it branches on strongly shapes how fast the search finishes.

Earlier learning approaches used custom formulations and one-off convergence results. The new BBMDP model is deliberately plain, so a broad range of reinforcement learning algorithms can be applied to learn branching policies. Experiments validate the model, opening solver tuning to the standard toolbox of sequential decision research.
arxiv-2510-19548:
Jie Song and three co-authors present a control strategy that sends fleets of drones out to map flooding whose extent is not known in advance. Their method builds on centroidal Voronoi tessellation, which divides a region among drones so each covers its own cell. The key change is modeling flood density with a mixture of Gaussian functions rather than simple axis-aligned shapes.

The mixture model follows the irregular outlines of real inundation more closely. In ROS and Gazebo simulations with fleets of sixteen, twenty, and twenty-four drones, the new density model consistently reached higher coverage rates than the conventional one. Better spatial spread of the drones means faster, fuller estimates of flooded area during emergencies.
arxiv-2510-19748:
Yi Liu proves a test that links a knot's Alexander polynomial to how its group maps into SL(2,R). The test says this: if the polynomial has a zero of odd order on the complex unit circle, then one special map can be approached by a whole family of irreducible maps. That special map is abelian and of noncentral elliptic type. The statement bridges a classical knot invariant with modern representation theory.

As a use case, Liu shows the Alexander polynomial of every nontrivial L-space knot passes the test. It follows that the group of any nontrivial L-space knot complement admits an irreducible map into SL(2,R). Such maps are tied to deep questions about orderability and foliations of three-manifolds.
arxiv-2510-20048:
Ian Berry and five co-authors report the discovery of seventy-nine pulsating delta Scuti stars in the open cluster NGC 3532 using data from the TESS mission. Open clusters are useful here because their stars share one age and one chemical makeup. At three hundred million years old, the cluster holds the largest such group found in a single cluster so far.

About half of the eligible stars in the cluster pulsate, a share well below that in younger populations such as the Pleiades. After correcting for missed stars, the true share is higher but still points to a decline with age. The pulsating stars also spin much faster, which suggests rapid rotation helps keep the pulsations alive.
arxiv-2510-20148:
Tingting Dan and four co-authors model how harmful tau protein spreads through the brain in Alzheimer disease using both structural and functional connectivity. Imaging evidence shows tau builds up along brain networks, but how the wiring diagram and the activity-based links interact has been unclear. Their multi-layer graph diffusion model uses a large volume of longitudinal imaging data.

Functional connectivity drives tau spread mainly in subcortical areas, the insula, and frontal and temporal cortex, while structural connectivity matters more in occipital, parietal, and limbic regions. The balance shifts with disease stage, with functional routes ahead early and structural routes later. The regional patterns also align with expression of Alzheimer-related genes, and results held in an independent cohort.
arxiv-2510-20748:
Brandon Gary Kaplowitz, writing alone, uses reinforcement learning to explain two odd patterns in how households spend and save during downturns. Standard models assume people form sharp forecasts of future income, yet real spending after job loss and stimulus payments does not fit that neat picture.

In his model, agents learn spending rules from trial and feedback, guided by a neural value estimate whose errors shift with experience. Households with low liquid savings before job loss spend a far larger share of stimulus cash than richer ones, even without borrowing limits. People with more past job loss spells also keep spending lower for longer, a scarring pattern seen in recent studies, and both effects flow from the same learning flaw.
arxiv-2510-21048:
Jiabo Shi leads two co-authors on xMem, a CPU based method to estimate GPU memory needs of deep learning training jobs before they run. Shared clusters waste scarce graphics processors and suffer out of memory crashes when job memory is guessed badly.

Static analysis and history based learning miss runtime dynamics, while probing the GPU directly burns the resource being saved, and some tools demand intrusive code changes. xMem aims for accurate estimates from the CPU side alone, with no scarce hardware consumed and no code surgery. Better estimates enable smarter scheduling and safe GPU sharing across tenants.
arxiv-2510-21148:
Yang Zhao leads two co-authors on EGO-Prompt, an evolving framework that auto tunes prompts and reasoning steps for domain tasks with language models. Hand crafting prompts for niche fields is slow, and weaving in domain knowledge well is an open craft.

Starting from a general prompt with fault tolerant initialization, evolving graph optimization refines wording, reasoning steps, and causal knowledge integration together. The system can even return refined knowledge hints to domain experts. Automated prompt design at this level could standardize how professional applications, from medicine to engineering, get reliable model behavior.
arxiv-2510-22048:
Ana K. Rivera, Anvita Bhagavathula, Alvaro Carbonero, and Priya Donti release a benchmark for one of the power grid's core computations. Power flow calculations, which solve where electricity actually travels through the network, sit inside security checks and control room decisions. Running them fast enough across huge scenario spaces is a standing bottleneck.

Machine learning promises shortcuts, yet its solvers had not been tested systematically against the variability real grids face. The dataset, named with a delta for change, varies load, generation, and network topology together, mirroring the spread created by renewable growth and extreme weather. It gives learning-based solvers a common, demanding proving ground, so speed claims can be weighed against accuracy under the conditions operators actually meet.
arxiv-2510-22148:
W. S. Oliveira, J. Pimentel de Lima, F. A. Pinheiro, and R. R. dos Santos model quantum percolation in two dimensions. Electrons hop through a lattice with blocked sites placed at random. The question is how states pass from trapped to free as the open share grows.

The team studies level statistics and an entropy measure of spread. Two transitions appear, not one. A critical phase sits between them. Its wave functions are multifractal, textured at every scale. The first transition is of BKT type. It sits at the classical percolation threshold. A second, power-law transition then frees the states fully, at a higher open share. The results also separate this model from the Anderson impurity model. In two dimensions, the two fall in different universality classes.
arxiv-2510-22348:
Aryan Ranjan builds a trading system that first forecasts danger, then trades on the forecast. The framework predicts five-day drawdowns in the main United States stock index fund using features drawn from across equities, bonds, currencies, commodities. Volatility markets, and it pairs neural networks with tree-based voting models in a hybrid ensemble so different pattern types get a vote.

Interpretability tools then name the macroeconomic and market-microstructure factors that separate crash weeks from calm ones, turning the risk signal into an explanation. Over a twenty-year backtest ending in twenty twenty-five, Ranjan reports a Sharpe ratio above two and a half and a strongly positive market-adjusted return with roughly half the market's directional exposure. The paper presents the ensemble design, causal and predictive together, as the reason short-horizon risk can be forecast systematically at all.
arxiv-2510-22548:
Long documents are easy to claim and hard to truly use, even for models with huge context windows. Ziyuan He, Yuxuan Wang, Jiaqi Li, Kexin Liang, and Muhan Zhang introduce LooGLE v2 in 2025, a benchmark built from real long texts in law, finance, games, and code.

Texts run from sixteen thousand to two million tokens, with ten task types that need links across distant parts. The set holds nearly two thousand questions made by a scalable pipeline. Ten models were tested, and the best scored under sixty percent overall. The gap shows usable context stays far shorter than advertised context.
arxiv-2510-22748:
Waves on water change shape when plates or films float on top. Travis Askham leads a team with four co-authors. In 2025 they study linearized surface waves. The water has infinite depth. Cover may have one hole or many holes. At each hole edge, the surface rules jump.

The team builds a boundary integral method. It turns the wave problem into equations on the boundary. They analyze two key cases in depth. One is a partial membrane. The other is a polynya, an open water patch. They prove the equations are of Fredholm second kind. Fast solvers then resolve wave patterns in tests.
arxiv-2510-22948:
Zhaoming Hu, with Ruikang Zhong, Xidong Mu, Dengao Li, and Yuanwei Liu, studies how a new antenna design could speed up edge computing over wireless links. Pinching antennas sit on waveguides and can shift position to form short direct links. That helps cut signal loss and blockage at high frequencies.

The team jointly chooses where tasks should run and how the uplink beams should form, aiming to cut total delay. They frame the choice as a learning problem and solve it with a load-aware policy method. Their results suggest the design could make offloaded phone and device tasks finish faster.
arxiv-2510-23048:
Y Alipour Fakhri develops a geometric framework for vortices in superconductors whose properties depend on direction. Standard Ginzburg-Landau theory treats the material as the same in all directions, which misses real anisotropic cases. A Finsler structure, which lets length depend on direction, encodes that uneven response in the energy.

Within the new frame, Fakhri derives a renormalized energy that governs where vortices rest and how they move. He proves its limit and stability, and shows vortex motion follows a Finsler gradient flow with uneven damping and drift. The model gives a unified view for designing and reading anisotropic superconducting devices.
arxiv-2510-23148:
Aryan Mathur and Asaduddin Ahmed adapt an interleaved encoder with PPO training for language-guided tasks in the BabyAI world. Agents often split seeing and deciding into separate modules, so the policy cannot teach perception what matters. The PDiT design alternates perception and decision layers inside one transformer, which the authors implement here.

They train the interleaved model with proximal policy optimization on tasks that pair vision with language instructions. Tight coupling lets decision errors shape perception directly. The study tests whether that shared learning helps small agents follow spoken goals in grid worlds more reliably.
arxiv-2510-23248:
Diego Pavon applies the generalized second law of thermodynamics to the apparent horizon of a smooth, isotropic universe. He requires that the equation of state stays no less than minus one, ruling out phantom energy. Combined with the dominant energy condition, the law sorts universes by their spatial shape.

Flat and closed cosmos models pass both the law and the dominant energy condition together. Open models with hyperbolic space, he finds, do not. The argument uses only broad thermodynamic and energy principles, not a named gravity model. It gives cosmologists a simple check on the global shape the cosmos can take.
arxiv-2510-23348:
Zhong-Lv Huang, Xin-Yu Du, Xiao-Gang He, Chia-Wei Liu, and Zi-Yue Zou study the electric dipole moment of the tau lepton, the least constrained among charged leptons. A nonzero dipole moment would signal new physics and a source of CP violation. The imaginary part, they show, imposes strong limits that had not been discussed.

Motivated by the planned Super Tau-Charm Facility, they track how the moment depends on momentum transfer and compare projected reach with Belle II. An axion-like coupling of the tau could create sizable real and imaginary parts. Future tau factories may thus probe GeV-scale new physics sharply.
arxiv-2510-23448:
Xingtu Liu analyzes out-of-distribution generalization in meta-reinforcement learning through information theory. He first establishes generalization bounds for meta-supervised learning under two shift scenarios: standard distribution mismatch, and a broad-to-narrow training setting. Those results ground the harder reinforcement learning case.

He then formalizes generalization for meta-reinforcement learning and proves fine-grained bounds that exploit the structure of Markov decision processes. Finally he analyzes a specific gradient-based method. The bounds explain when a meta-trained agent should adapt to new tasks and when distribution shift will break it, guiding safer deployment. Readers can follow the full argument and data in the paper itself.
arxiv-2510-23548:
Eun-jin Shin and four co-authors run detailed simulations of how stars help or hinder the growth of black holes at the centers of dwarf galaxies. These mid-size black holes sit inside dense nuclear star clusters, fed by gas discs smaller than a hundredth of a parsec across. The team resolves the gas flow all the way from the galaxy's interstellar gas down to the black hole.

Without stellar feedback, the galactic disc breaks apart too much and builds a massive ring around the center. Light from young stars calms that breakup, while supernova blasts heat the gas and starve the black hole most. With both effects together, the central disc forms, gets destroyed, and rebuilds over tens of millions of years, yet the black hole still grows and spins up. The results bode well for spotting such black holes with future telescopes and gravity-wave detectors.
arxiv-2510-23948:
Qianfeng Wen and two co-authors present ChessQA, a benchmark that tests how deeply language models understand chess, beyond merely picking decent moves. Chess suits evaluation well: its rules are crisp, truth is objective, and skill spans a wide range. Earlier tests were ad hoc and narrow, so they could not show how understanding varies with model size, training recipe, or architecture.

ChessQA sorts its questions into five categories that climb the ladder of player mastery: structure, motifs, short tactics, position judgment, and semantics. That spread separates knowing the rules from calculating tactics and describing high-level ideas. The benchmark is built to evolve, with prompts, answer keys, and construction scripts that refresh as models improve. Across a range of current models, the authors find persistent weaknesses in every category, with error analyses per category. Code, refreshed data, and a public leaderboard will be released to support comparisons.
arxiv-2510-24048:
C. Tyler Diggans and two co-authors propose a new way to find the bottleneck that stops a network from synchronizing. Engineers care about complete synchronization — every node settling onto the same behavior — in systems from power grids to distributed databases. The classic measures, conductance and the isoperimetric number, bound the coupling needed for bulk synchrony. But they often miss the cut that actually limits it, and both are NP-hard to compute.

The authors define a bottleneck ratio for every two-way cut; its minimum better identifies the true limiting cut for a class of coupled dynamics. The global minimum is still NP-hard, but the ratio uses only local information. That locality pays off: local heuristics built on the ratio can steer each node toward synchrony without a map of the whole network. The Fiedler vector fails on exactly the small-set bottlenecks their measure catches.
arxiv-2510-24448:
Pablo Acuaviva and six co-authors investigate video pretraining as a route to broader visual intelligence. Large scale pretraining let language models adapt quickly to new problems, but visual models still struggle with compositional understanding, sample efficiency, and general problem solving. Video diffusion models, trained on data that unfolds over time, may carry strong biases for structure and dynamics.

The team designs a controlled evaluation comparing a video pretrained model against alternatives on downstream tasks. They test whether spatiotemporal pretraining supports broad task adaptability with little supervision, as language pretraining does for text. The study offers insights into what visual pretraining must provide for general purpose visual systems.
arxiv-2510-24548:
Jonathan Gratus, Spyridon Talaganis, and Willow Sparks, three authors, model dust in relativity. Dust here means matter that flows without pressure or self-force. They squeeze an extended dust cloud down to one moving point. The path of that point through spacetime is its worldline. Its stress-energy is written with delta functions along the worldline.

A delta function is a spike that is zero except at one point. Derivatives of the spike build a multipole, a layered point model. The model can be prescribed to any order the user wants. For plain dust, the stress-energy has zero divergence, as physics demands. For charged dust, the divergence matches current and the outside field. Both forms come from squeezing a smooth dust tensor down.
arxiv-2510-24748:
Dong-Hyeon Kang, Ju-Hyeon Nam, and Sang-Chul Lee built a lean net to sort long twelve lead heart traces. Hand reads of such traces can err, and past nets had to pick a fixed view width that may not fit all trace lengths. A past all scale net fixed that by trying many widths, but at huge cost.

Their net, EcoScaleNet, caps the width at each stage to what is still needed after the trace shrinks. Tight squeeze steps keep the channel count in check and join traits across scales. On a large trace set, it cut weights by most of the past net's count and cost by far more, while its score rose.
arxiv-2510-25248: Li He gives an internal description of constructible objects in an infinity-topos. His 2025 paper works in pure mathematics. An infinity-topos is a very general kind of space. A poset is a set where some pairs have an order. He shows that P-constructible objects are locally constant objects. They sit inside a related function setting. This holds for any noetherian poset P. The result is short, dense, and highly abstract. It speaks to readers who already know this field.
arxiv-2510-25348:
Jie Peng led six co-authors on cascade prediction benchmarks. Rui Wang, Qiang Wang, and Zhewei Wei helped. Bin Tong, Guan Wang, and Bo Zheng followed. Their 2025 paper questions temporal cascade prediction evaluation. Cascades describe how information or purchases spread over time. Existing benchmarks often split data randomly across time. That mixes past and future signals together.

Random splits can leak information into test results. Reported gains may then reflect leakage, not skill. The team propose a fidelity-aware benchmarking standard. It centers on a Full Temporal protocol. Overlap diagnostics measure leakage between data parts. Analyses track performance inflation and temporal drift. They also present Taoke, an e-commerce cascade dataset. It has promoter and product features included. Observed purchase conversions support two forecasting stages. CasTemp serves as a lightweight reference method.
arxiv-2510-25448:
Wentao Hu and Zhengce Zhang study weak answers to MHD formulas. Their 2025 paper concerns 3D incompressible magnetohydrodynamics. Suitable weak answers are the answer class considered. Their starting point is a direct iteration scheme. Scaled energy quantities from Caffarelli-Kohn-Nirenberg theory are used.

Velocity field smallness and magnetic field boundedness are assumed. Scaling-invariant quantities for each field are chosen independently. Finiteness of one quantity allows only Type I blowup. That claim is proved as an intermediate step. It extends Seregin Type I criteria for Navier-Stokes. Magnetohydrodynamic formulas add magnetic coupling to fluid motion. Interpolation and embedding give further criteria in mixed norms. General scaled mixed Lebesgue norms describe both fields. Their formulation offers a unified, direct route. It naturally fits the Type I blowup approach.
arxiv-2510-25848:
Soumavo Ghosh and Elena D'Onghia use a high resolution cosmic simulation to ask why spiral galaxies show such varied arms. The simulation, called TNG50, follows galaxies much like the Milky Way and Andromeda from early times. Earlier work had not mapped spiral formation, visible traits, and physical drivers together in a systematic way inside such a realistic setting.

Ghosh and D'Onghia find that most of their sample galaxies grow two armed spirals in both stars and gas, while gas discs often show stronger, tighter, multi armed patterns. Gas content and disc coldness, meaning low random motion, jointly control how strong the spirals become. Bars, inflows, and feedback add scatter to simple predictions.
arxiv-2510-25948:
Quentin Labriet, Lucia Morey, and Luc Vinet give an algebraic account of discrete families of matrix valued orthogonal polynomials. Orthogonal polynomials are families where distinct members integrate to zero against each other under a weight, and matrix valued versions replace numbers with matrices. Such families appear in probability, physics, and special function theory.

Labriet and his co-authors build the families from representations of a Lie algebra, a structure that encodes symmetry, acting on a module over matrices. Cases tied to the algebras su two and su one one, plus a q deformed algebra at a root of unity, yield matrix analogues of the Krawtchouk, Meixner, and discrete Chebyshev polynomials. The view unifies known families under one construction.
arxiv-2510-26248:
Remi Jaoui and Jonathan Kirby mix differential algebra with model theory. They study when a function counts as exponentially algebraic. Such a function can be defined from restricted elementary functions. That is a tame class built from basic steps and raising to powers. The questions go back to Abel and Liouville. They asked when an integral can be written in finite terms.

Jaoui and Kirby ask two things. Does a given equation have a solution of this tame kind? Do solutions of several equations share a nontrivial relation of this kind? Their methods yield transcendence results for classic functions. The list includes the error function and the Bessel functions. It also includes integrals with the Lambert W function and the pendulum equation.
arxiv-2510-26448:
Dong Xie and Chunling Xu chase measurement precision beyond a famous limit in quantum metrology, the science of exact measurement. The Heisenberg limit sets how error should shrink as more particles or more time are used. Beating it, called super-Heisenberg scaling, was known to need many-body forces or a changing drive.

Xie and Xu show that nonlinear quantum scrambling, a fast spreading of quantum information, can do the job even with a fixed drive. In open systems that lose energy, the effect survives in a friction model. In an optical cavity, pairing squeezed light from outside with squeezing inside the cavity gives an exponential gain in precision over time, in their account. The work offers a route to sharper sensors that use nonlinear effects as a resource.
arxiv-2510-26648:
Timothy De Deyn, Pat Lank, Kabeer Manali-Rahul, and Sridhar Venkatesh work in algebraic geometry on a categorical way to judge singularities, the bad points of a shape. Their focus is birational derived splinters, a notion that extends rational singularities beyond the classical setting of characteristic zero. The team asks whether a single number can measure how far such a singularity is from being good.

De Deyn and his three co-authors use an invariant called level, taken from the associated derived category. They show that level measures exactly the failure of these singularities to behave as hoped. The result gives researchers a concrete dial to read when sorting singular spaces by this newer test.
arxiv-2510-26848:
The LIGO Scientific Collaboration, together with the Virgo and KAGRA collaborations, searches decades of gravitational-wave data for a background hum from the early universe. Many violent early processes, from phase transitions to cosmic strings, should have left a faint background of gravitational waves. The teams analyse the fourth LIGO observing run together with the three earlier runs.

No detectable background signal was found. That absence sets upper limits on the background's energy density. Those limits constrain many early-universe scenarios: first-order phase transitions, cosmic strings, domain walls, a stiff equation of state, and axion inflation. They also constrain second-order perturbations, primordial black hole binaries, and parity violation. An astrophysical background from merging black holes and neutron stars is accounted for throughout. The authors conclude the data already rule out parts of numerous models.
arxiv-2510-27248:
Ronja Ronnback leads five co-authors in a large study of how search engines shape exposure to polarizing content on LGBTIQ+ issues. Search engines are trusted daily by hundreds of millions, yet their ranking algorithms necessarily elevate some views over others. Prior polarization research focused on social media, leaving search largely unexamined.

The team analyzes one and a half million results for neutral and negative queries across the United Kingdom, Germany, and France. Choice of search engine proves the strongest determinant of exposure to polarizing content, ahead of query polarity, while location and language matter comparatively little. The findings give quantitative evidence that differences between search technologies, more than user opinions or language, drive what people encounter on contested topics in Europe.
arxiv-2510-27348:
Hernán A. González and Jakob Salzer study energy counters at the edge of space-time in this 2025 paper. The edge is null infinity, the far zone where light rays end up. Their counters tally energy raised to a chosen power as particles fly out. Such counters give a clean basis for describing energy flow in crashes and scatters.

The pair work out how two counters combine when their rays nearly align. One case stands out: the counter with power two counts particles outright. They show this counter is just the square of a soft current in gravity, a gentle flow tied to a known symmetry. In force theories of the Yang-Mills kind, it is a product of two soft currents. The link ties lab-style counters to the soft side of space-time theory.
arxiv-2510-27448:
Yuhao Zhang, Dingxin Hu, and three other co-authors make fresh geometry problems for AI training in this 2025 paper. Models that see images and text still stumble on geometry, mostly for lack of good practice data. Older ways to fake data reword old problems or follow fixed templates. The results are narrow, noisy, or unlike real diagrams.

Their method, GeoFM, writes problems in a formal language, a strict notation the computer can check. It mixes and matches conditions in metric space, the space of lengths and angles. A symbolic engine, a rule-based checker, verifies each new problem as it is made. Models trained on this data did far better than those trained on older fakes. On one geometry test, their model beat the commercial GPT-4o by a wide margin.
arxiv-2510-27648:
Francesco Moretti, Martin Gorbahn, and Sebastian Jaeger compute a refined weak-force term in 2025 that tests the unity of the quark mixing matrix. The term, called g_V, sets the strength of a vector part in decays where a lepton is emitted. Small light-based fixes to that term must be known with great care to judge if row sums match the rule of unitarity.

Their work is the first at this log depth to join light fixes with strong-force fixes at a mixed order. It blends three-loop and two-loop parts with a clean split of short-range effects. The updated fix lands near two and a half percent, with a small stated doubt. Sharper values tighten a key check of the standard model of particles.
arxiv-2511-00248:
Shurui Gui, Deep Anil Patel, Xiner Li, and Martin Renqiang Min want generated videos of people to obey basic physics. Current video models often warp bodies, break object rules, or ignore how people interact with things around them. Their framework builds motion in a 3D scene first, using ready-made 3D humans and objects as anchors.

A method they call MSDI refines the motion with guidance from trained motion models and language model knowledge about space and meaning. No new training on interaction data is needed, so the approach transfers to new objects and scenes. Tests show natural, physically plausible motion that respects the 3D layout, a step toward reliable 4D content creation.
arxiv-2511-00348:
Michael Hasselbeck describes a listening device that spots leaks from pressurized plumbing without touching the pipes. The design borrows ideas from glass-break and smoke detectors, raising an alert when leak sounds appear. In tests, a simulated water leak at a slow flow was detected reliably from more than ten meters away, even through walls, doors, floors, and ceilings.

The unit is built as a battery-powered wireless node that processes sound on the spot, sending only a few status bytes when asked. Power draw stays extremely low, in the tens to hundreds of microwatts, depending on noise and response speed. It listens above the range of human speech, so it cannot eavesdrop. Though developed for water, the concept also fits gas leaks.
arxiv-2511-00448:
Thomas Chalopin, Igor Ferrier-Barbut, Thierry Lahaye, Antoine Browaeys, and David Clément explain why connected correlations matter in cold atom experiments. New probes that resolve single atoms give full counting statistics: the complete distribution of measurement outcomes, not just averages. From high-order moments of that distribution, researchers extract cumulants, also called connected correlations, with high precision.

Two uses stand out. A nonzero connected correlation beyond second order proves a quantum state is non-Gaussian, beyond the simplest class. And a connected correlation of a given order identifies genuine clusters of that many particles, clusters whose behavior cannot be reduced to smaller groups. Through recent experiments, the article shows how these measures expose microscopic structure in strongly correlated quantum matter that averages alone would hide.
arxiv-2511-00648:
C Díaz-Faloh and R Mulet prune restricted Boltzmann machines to the bone and watch what survives. Modern AI leans on ever-larger networks, with rising computing and environmental costs, so leaner models matter. Inspired by the lottery ticket hypothesis, which says big networks hide small trainable sub-networks, the authors prune connections before training and ask how much generative quality remains.

Even with up to eighty percent of connections removed before training, the machines generated high-quality samples, confirming that viable sub-networks exist inside. The catch came later: prune a trained network further and retraining cannot fully restore lost quality. A sharp transition appears once pruning breaks a minimal core of essential connections. Retrained sparse networks also lag fresh ones of the same sparsity, so the practical lesson is to prune early.
arxiv-2511-00748:
Yi Yang, Jian Pei, Jun Yang, and Jichun Xie study Simpson's paradox, the effect where a trend seen in pooled data reverses when the data are split into subgroups. Hunting for such reversals in large multidimensional data turns up many copies of the same pattern, which waste time and hide what matters.

They define three kinds of redundancy between paradoxes and show the relation between them is an equivalence, so copies can be grouped and summarized. Their algorithms combine depth first table building with redundancy aware search. On real and synthetic data, over forty percent of paradoxes on some sets were redundant, run times fell by up to sixty percent, and the search scaled to millions of records.
arxiv-2511-01148:
Kazushige Machida proposes a new mechanism that can suppress the upper critical field of a spin triplet superconductor, the magnetic field strength at which superconductivity dies. In equal spin pairing, he shows theoretically, that field can be pushed down from the usual orbital limit to arbitrarily small values while the transition stays second order.

That behavior differs sharply from the known Pauli limit for ordinary singlet superconductors, where the reduction is capped and the transition turns first order. Machida applies the mechanism to UTe2, a leading spin triplet candidate, fitting critical field data for several crystal orientations at ambient and applied pressure. He concludes the material realizes a non-unitary equal spin triplet state, and the analysis identifies its pairing symmetry.
arxiv-2511-01248:
Hanxiu Zhu, Ruijia Chen, and Yuhang Zhao design FocusView, an interface that lets viewers with ADHD reshape informational videos to hold their attention. Videos now deliver much educational and professional content, but their moving, multimodal elements can distract viewers who already struggle with attention.

FocusView lets users customize several aspects of a video. In a study with twelve participants with ADHD, it greatly improved viewability by reducing distractions. The study also surfaced surprises: background music counted as a distraction for some and a helpful stimulant for others, and the customization controls themselves could distract if too many options were offered. The authors derive design considerations for future video tools built for the ADHD community.
arxiv-2511-01348:
Robin Gropler and colleagues, writing for the European GENIUS project, set out a shared industry and academic vision for generative artificial intelligence in software engineering. The technology already generates code, finds bugs, suggests fixes, and supports quality assurance. Using it across the whole software development life cycle is largely unexplored. Questions of reliability, accountability, security, and privacy remain open.

The vision paper has four parts. One is an overview of today's adoption challenges. Another is a five year outlook for advances in tools and method. A third covers how software professionals' roles and skills will shift. A fourth describes the contribution the GENIUS consortium, over thirty European partners, aims to make in response.
arxiv-2511-01548:
Ludmila Carone and four colleagues build a forecast tool for reading exoplanet climates from transit light. As a planet crosses its star, the morning and evening edges of its atmosphere filter starlight differently. Measuring that asymmetry across wavelengths can reveal clouds and temperature structure on tidally locked gas giants.

The team combined a grid of three-dimensional climate models for 50 planets around varied stars with a detailed kinetic cloud formation model. The output is a library of synthetic transit spectra and limb asymmetries from the optical to the infrared, spanning warm, hot, and ultra-hot regimes. Clouds generally enlarge the limb differences; for ultra-hot Jupiters the morning cloud can dominate, even flipping the sign of the asymmetry between wavelength bands.
arxiv-2511-01648:
Dinesh Kumar Keshari, Shubhankar Mandal, and Avijit Pal work in multivariable operator theory, on two naturally occurring domains associated with 3-by-3 matrix problems. A rich structure is a package that links four natural objects of analysis for such domains. Joined with the classical realization formula and Agler-style Hilbert space models, it lets one build analytic maps into the domain effectively.

The authors describe several maps inside this structure for the two domains named in the title. They define an SE map between two Schur-type classes. They relate one class to analytic kernels on the tridisc. Then they construct Upper W, Upper E, Right S, and SE maps through a UW procedure. A payoff is that interpolation problems for these domains reduce to a standard matricial Nevanlinna-Pick problem, with direct use for solvability criteria in mu-synthesis.
arxiv-2511-01848:
Po-Yan Tseng and Yu-Min Yeh look for primordial black holes that should have evaporated away but, under the memory-burden effect, might linger as dark matter. Memory burden stabilizes an evaporating black hole and suppresses its emission, reopening a mass window below a quadrillion grams for black hole dark matter that older constraints had closed.

The authors probe an earlier, unsuppressed phase instead. In their first scenario, gravitons emitted while the holes were still young cross the recombination era. They convert into photons in filament magnetic fields, through the Gertsenshtein effect. The resulting photon spectrum is compared with gamma-ray sensitivities. It excludes a window of masses, from hundreds of thousands to tens of millions of grams, for holes making up the dark matter. A second scenario, mergers today recreating young holes, is noted as highly model-dependent.
arxiv-2511-02348:
Yusaku Nishimiya and Masaya Taniguchi connect the complexity of languages to the rules of a logical system. The Lambek calculus, a fragment of non-commutative linear logic where the order of assumptions matters, comes with direction-sensitive implication connectives and has long been used to model grammar. The authors ask which fragments of this logic correspond exactly to familiar language classes: regular languages, linear context-free languages, and context-free languages.

By restricting the inference rules, formula sizes, and permitted connectives, they obtain characterisations of all three classes, with the identifications for regular and linear context-free complexity being the first of their kind. Even one of the weakest possible variants, allowing a single inference rule, still captures context-free complexity. Their proofs translate directly between the logic and formal grammars, using cut elimination to expose the analogue of a classical normal form.
arxiv-2511-02448:
Francesco Rosa and eleven co-authors compare the magnetic and orbital behaviour of two layered oxides that look alike but behave differently. PrNiO2, a nickelate, superconducts without any chemical doping; CaCuO2, a cuprate, is an insulator. Both share the infinite-layer crystal structure, and the nickelates are advertised as cousins of the cuprates. Using resonant inelastic X-ray scattering, the team measured spin and orbital excitations in the nickelate against the cuprate reference.

In the nickelate the in-plane magnetic exchange is weaker, while the out-of-plane coupling matches, so both support three-dimensional antiferromagnetic order. Orbital excitations look similar and fit a single-ion model. One nickel orbital peak, though, sits much lower in energy and disperses the opposite way, which the authors attribute to orbital superexchange between neighbouring sites. The verdict: the two families share most spin and orbital properties despite distinct charge-transfer energies.
arxiv-2511-02548:
Michel Gaglioni Rocha and Emiliano Rezende Martins untangle how surface texture helps and hurts the most promising design in solar energy. Perovskite-on-silicon tandem cells stack two absorbers to catch more of the spectrum, and texturing the surfaces traps light better, but texturing the perovskite layer itself tends to raise electrical losses. Using optical simulations, the authors separate the jobs done by the texture at the front of the device from the texture at the rear.

That separation suggests a new architecture: keep the useful textures and leave the perovskite flat. The proposed structure matched the light management of fully textured devices in simulation, while its planar perovskite should cut electrical losses. If the texture-related voltage loss can be held near fifty millivolts, roughly six times lower than in fully textured cells, the simpler design wins on efficiency as well.
arxiv-2511-03048:
Anthony Hevia and six colleagues built ROBoto2, a web platform that helps reviewers judge bias in clinical trials with language model support. Risk of bias checks are slow hand work, yet they anchor systematic reviews of medical evidence. Their 2025 system parses trial PDFs, retrieves passages, and prompts a model to draft answers to the standard RoB 2 signaling questions, with evidence attached.

Reviewers see the drafts, correct them, and feed the fixes back in real time. The team also released a data set of 521 pediatric trial reports, with nearly nine thousand questions and over a thousand evidence passages, annotated by hand and with model help. They benchmarked four language models on it and chart the remaining hurdles for automation.
arxiv-2511-03148:
Paria Mehrbod, Pedro Vianna, Geraldin Nanfack, Guy Wolf, and Eugene Belilovsky adapt vision models at test time, when the incoming data no longer matches training. Models trained on clean photos stumble on corrupted or shifted ones, and retraining is often impossible on the spot. Their 2025 method, Adaptive Quantile Recalibration, adjusts a model's internal activations as it runs, with no labels and no retraining.

The method aligns the quantiles of each channel's activation distribution with source statistics saved from training. A robust tail strategy keeps the estimates steady when batches are small. It works across batch, group, and layer normalization designs. On corrupted CIFAR and ImageNet test sets, it beat existing test-time methods across several architectures.
arxiv-2511-03348:
Changxi Zhu, Mehdi Dastani, and Shihan Wang teach teams of learning agents to share skills for talking across many tasks at once. In multi-agent learning, agents gain by messaging, and tasks gain from each other when lessons carry over. Their method, called MCS, maps each task's view into a shared message space with a transformer encoder.

A prediction part links each message to what its sender does next, which tightens teamwork. Three standard test worlds were reshaped into multi-task versions with changing team sizes. Agents using the shared skill setup learned faster and handled new mixes better than rivals. The work suggests one learned language of coordination can serve many jobs at once.
arxiv-2511-03448:
Dhaval Pujara and Ankur Sinha review bilevel optimization, where one decision maker must plan around another's response. A leader's problem wraps a follower's problem inside it as a constraint, matching real hierarchies from pricing to policy. Forms covered include linear, mixed-integer, single-goal, and multi-goal versions.

Solving routes split into classic methods and evolutionary search, each with strengths the review weighs. Application areas run wide, and recent advances get their own survey. Readers new to the field gain a map of which solver fits which problem shape. The review also flags open gaps where nested problems still defeat current tools.
arxiv-2511-03648:
Qiling Liu constructs knotted surfaces of every genus inside the four-dimensional sphere with tightly limited self-symmetries. A knotted surface is a membrane embedded in four-space, far wilder than a knotted loop in three-space. Liu asks how the surface's looping structure, its first homology, constrains motions that extend over the whole surface.

A norm defined on that homology, proved to add cleanly across pieces, does the constraining. Only finitely many extendable self-motions survive the norm's restrictions for the built surfaces. Such rigidity results help classify four-dimensional embeddings, a frontier where intuition from three dimensions often fails. The norm tool may serve other extendability questions in topology.
arxiv-2511-04048:
Ayaan Bedi and Karoliina Lehtinen study explorability, a measure of nondeterminism in pushdown automata that extends history-determinism. An automaton counts as k-explorable when following k runs at once, built only from input seen so far, is enough to find a winning run when one exists.

Explorable automata sit strictly between history-deterministic and fully nondeterministic ones in expressiveness and size. Each higher level forms a strictly stronger class, yet the whole family stays below general nondeterminism. A scaled version where run count may grow with input length captures exactly the context-free languages at exponential level. Size gaps can be doubly exponential, and one gap cannot be listed by any program.
arxiv-2511-04248:
Salma Mekaoui is the lead author among seven authors proposing a graph-based method to label topics extracted from text, as a lightweight alternative to deep models. Topic modelling finds themes as word distributions, which are statistically useful but often hard for a person to interpret without a clear label.

Topic words are enriched with semantically related terms, and relationships among them are explored as a graph. Labels derived from that structure aim to capture each topic's meaning accurately. In comparisons on two datasets against several benchmarks, including a commercial chat model, the graph method achieved consistently better labelling. The pitch is practical: good labels without heavy computation as text collections keep growing.
arxiv-2511-04748:
Derek Perera leads eight authors using lensed arc asymmetry to probe dark matter clumps. Tiny subhalos in galaxy clusters should dent the smooth arcs of background galaxies. Those astrometric shifts appear near the critical curve where lensing is strongest.

Their statistical method turns the induced asymmetry into a bound on the average subhalo mass fraction. A semi-analytic model of subhalo tidal evolution is extended for realistic cluster hosts. Simulated arc populations then show what the signal should look like. Cold dark matter predicts many low-mass subhalos, so arc dents offer a fresh test of that picture.
arxiv-2511-05148:
Moto Togawa and co-authors show how fine-structure effects boost a two-photon ionization path in highly charged ions. X-ray free-electron lasers fire intense pulses that can strip many electrons in femtoseconds, through paths too tangled to match with theory.

The team first made highly charged ions in an electron beam trap, then hit them with the pulses. That clean start let them trace each step. Relativistic fine structure shifts energy levels and mostly cancels core screening, which lets two near-tuned X-ray photons be taken up in a row, a resonant path now shown in full.
arxiv-2511-05448:
Alexander Imre and co-authors improve the reliability factor used in quantitative low-energy electron diffraction, a method that reads surface structure from how electron beams bounce off a crystal face. The method fits computed beam strengths to measured ones and grades the fit.

The standard Pendry R factor is noisy as a fit target and jumps at small shifts in strength, which can mislead the search for the true surface. Their improved factor aims to smooth those flaws. A steadier grade should make surface calls from diffraction data more firm and less prone to false best fits.
arxiv-2511-06448:
Qibing Ren and co-authors test whether language model agents can team up to commit financial fraud online. Multi-agent systems raise a fresh worry: agents might coordinate scams rather than act alone. The team built MultiAgentFraudBench, a benchmark simulating realistic online interactions across twenty-eight common fraud scenarios and the full fraud life cycle.

Experiments measured how conversation depth, activity levels, and patterns of collaboration shape fraud success, including where teamwork breaks down. Defenses tested include content warnings, monitor models that block malicious agents, and group information sharing. Malicious agents adapted to some defenses, underlining real-world risk while pointing to practical countermeasures.
arxiv-2511-06748:
Ji Li and Chao Wang present a method for restoring damaged images, such as blurry, noisy, or partly missing pictures. Their approach plugs a modern flow-based generative model into a classic optimization system as the denoising step. The generative model supplies a strong learned prior about what clean images look like.

Older plug-and-play methods mostly assume smooth Gaussian noise. The new algorithm, built on the primal-dual hybrid gradient method, also handles rougher noise such as Poisson and impulse noise by allowing different measures of fit to the observed image. Tests on denoising, super-resolution, deblurring, and inpainting show it is efficient, light on memory, and more accurate under non-Gaussian noise.
arxiv-2511-07448:
Fatemeh Shahhosseini and co-authors survey how large language models are used to invent scientific ideas. Good ideas must be both new and sound, a double demand that makes automation hard. Recent models can draft plausible proposals, yet the limits of their creativity stay unclear.

The survey groups methods into five families, from adding outside knowledge to multi-agent teamwork and direct model tuning. Each family trades novelty against validity in a different way. The authors also review how researchers judge idea quality. Readers get a structured map of a fast-growing field and the open questions that decide whether machine ideas can aid discovery.
arxiv-2511-07748:
Yuezhe Yang, Yiyue Guo, and Wenjie Cai built an agent that diagnoses from ultrasound video clips. Static image models miss the motion clinicians watch, and past video work used narrow datasets with weak clinical reach. Their system pairs video classification with language model reasoning over findings.

A new dataset gathers four hundred ninety five videos across five categories and three organs from open sources. Their CTU-Net classifier reaches leading accuracy on that benchmark. The agent then turns classifications into diagnostic text a clinician can review. Video-aware assistance could shorten ultrasound reading queues, especially where specialists are scarce.
arxiv-2511-08048:
Jer Pelhan, Alan Lukezic, and Matej Kristan present GECO2, a few shot counter that finds objects given only a few example images. Counting across very different object sizes is hard, and pipelines often upscale and tile images to catch tiny items in crowds. Those fixes raise memory cost and still struggle when sizes vary widely within one picture.

GECO2 uses a dense query representation that gradually gathers exemplar features across scales. The result is a high resolution query set able to detect both large and small objects in one pass. It improves counting and detection accuracy by about ten percent over leading few shot counters while running three times faster.
arxiv-2511-08248:
Kunal Mahatha, Jose Dolz, and Christian Desrosiers present NERVE, a training free method for open vocabulary semantic segmentation, labeling image regions for categories named in text. Existing training free methods often need costly affinity refinement or smooth attention maps with fixed kernels that ignore object shape. NERVE instead uses the neighbourhood structure inside a stable diffusion model self attention layer.

A stochastic random walk refines affinities, spreading labels across connected, related areas of any shape. Entropy based uncertainty selects which attention maps from different heads and layers deserve weight, instead of treating all equally. The method needs no standard post processing and reaches top zero shot results on seven benchmarks.
arxiv-2511-08348:
Arpan Phukan and co-authors introduce VideoChain, a transformer framework that generates multi hop questions about videos. Question generation tests reasoning, but video versions usually ask simple questions about a single segment. Multi hop questions force a viewer to connect facts across separated parts of a video, a harder and more realistic reasoning challenge for education and evaluation alike.

A modified BART backbone enriched with video embeddings captures text and visual links across time. From the TVQA plus data set, the team automatically builds MVQ-60, a large set of merged multi hop questions. Scores on standard generation metrics and semantic similarity show coherent, context grounded questions that demand genuine cross segment reasoning.
arxiv-2511-08548:
Shubhra Mishra and eleven co-authors ask what makes a math problem interesting, and whether language models judge that quality the way people do. Their study compares model ratings with judgments from two human groups: adults with college math experience and International Math Olympiad competitors.

Many models broadly agree with people about which problems seem interesting, yet they miss the spread of human ratings. They also match poorly with the reasons people give for their choices. When asked to create problems, the models do produce engaging ones once invalid items are filtered out. The authors argue for teams that pair people with several models, stressing both the promise and the limits of such help.
arxiv-2511-08648:
Stanislav Selitskiy asks whether small neural networks, trainable on ordinary university hardware, can predict where proteins bind RNA. Big models do this job well but demand heavy computing and large datasets, which many life-science labs do not have, and their binding data is often scarce and lopsided.

Shallow feed-forward networks with two hidden layers read sequence context through a sliding window instead of explicit structure. Only three of seven common activation functions produced converging models. Standard rebalancing tricks failed, while more training data and model ensembles helped greatly. A context window near thirty residues and bases balanced the two error types best. The study concludes that accurate protein-RNA binding prediction is within reach of modest hardware.
arxiv-2511-08748:
Estefania Talavera and seven co-authors report on the Women in Computer Vision workshop held with CVPR 2025 in Nashville, Tennessee. Now in its sixteenth edition, the workshop works to raise the visibility and professional growth of women and underrepresented minorities in computer vision.

Fourteen papers appear in the proceedings from thirty-two full submissions, five of them given as talks, alongside thirty-six extended abstract posters. The mentoring program paired eighty mentees with thirty-seven mentors from universities and industry. More than one hundred participants attended in person, backed by ten sponsors and roughly forty-four thousand dollars in travel grants and diversity awards. The report also traces trends across earlier editions, offering a reference for future organizers of similar efforts.
arxiv-2511-08948:
Jay Tharwani and two co-authors benchmark high-performance computing style processor work across the four biggest cloud providers, asking what speed costs in rented virtual machines. OpenMP workloads from the SPEC ACCEL suite run on Intel, AMD, and ARM general-purpose instances at both on-demand and one-year discounted prices.

Amazon Web Services finishes fastest on every processor family but charges a premium, steepest for on-demand use. Oracle's cloud is the cheapest everywhere yet generally slower than AWS. Microsoft Azure sits in the middle on both axes. Google Cloud improves markedly from Intel to AMD. But its ARM instance runs at less than half its own AMD speed, for more money. Inside AWS, the ARM instance beats its Intel and AMD siblings by up to forty-nine percent. Priorities, the authors conclude, should pick the instance.
arxiv-2511-09048:
Anthony Baez and five co-authors bolt a hard guarantee onto physics-informed neural networks, the models that learn solutions of differential equations by penalizing law-breaking softly. Soft penalties bend during training, so a trained network can quietly violate conservation laws even while fitting the equation well.

A projection step, derived by solving constrained nonlinear optimization problems, forces the network's solution to conserve linear and quadratic integral quantities exactly, separately or jointly. The projected network cuts conservation error by three to four orders of magnitude compared with the soft constraint and slightly improves the solution error itself. Evidence suggests the projection also smooths the loss landscape, helping training converge. The authors frame the method as a general recipe for guaranteeing any conserved integral in these networks whenever a tractable projection exists.
arxiv-2511-09248:
Tim Wittenborg, Niklas Stehr, Oliver Karras, and Sören Auer design a shared library for science communication media such as videos and podcasts. These formats now carry civic information widely, but also misinformation, and the knowledge infrastructure curating them is fragmented. The team wants a central, collaborative platform to represent such media properly.

They surveyed 53 stakeholders, refined the findings in 11 interviews, and built an open-source system centered on Wikibase. The goal is media records that are findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable, following the FAIR principles. A prototype evaluation with 14 more participants found the approach suitable, while exposing how underdeveloped collaborative curation tools remain. The authors compare the vision to a Wikidata-style hub for science media.
arxiv-2511-09348:
Yanpeng Gong and six co-authors pair two kinds of models to analyze heat and stress in electronic packaging. Finite elements handle regular shapes well, while virtual elements tolerate complex geometry with flexible meshes. Packaging structures mix both kinds of regions, plus several materials, making them a natural test case.

Their coupled method splits the domain by design, assigning each region the better-suited method. Coincident nodes at the interfaces keep the solution continuous across the boundary and simplify meshing. Packaging case studies agree well with reference solutions and converge cleanly as meshes refine. Thermal patterns and stress hot spots in multi-material systems come out clearly, and the source code is public.
arxiv-2511-09748:
Muskaan Chopra, Lorenz Sparrenberg, Sarthak Khanna, and Rafet Sifa ask how small a language model can be while still catching meaning-changing errors in machine translation. Large models judge translation quality well but are costly and awkward for private, on-device use. The study centers on English to German critical error detection, where a mistake alters what a sentence actually says.

The team benchmarks five models under two billion parameters across three test sets, using standard prompts, light calibration, and majority voting. Models near one billion parameters hit the sweet spot: a fine-tuned Gemma model scored strongly while answering in about 400 milliseconds on a laptop. The smallest models stayed usable with few-shot calibration but missed more entity and number errors.
arxiv-2511-10048:
Yanjiao Yang, Daniel Suen, and Yen-Chi Chen study how to choose a good imputation model for filling in missing data. The common masking-one-out procedure hides an observed value, imputes it, and scores the match, but the authors show that this measures prediction accuracy, not imputation quality. A model can predict well yet misrepresent the randomness that proper imputation must preserve.

They present three modified criteria based on rank transformation, energy distance, and likelihood principles, each designed to reward models that respect the data's stochastic nature. The likelihood version also yields an approach for learning an imputation model from data, with theory for its statistics, computation, and model selection consistency. A prediction-imputation diagram plots both utilities side by side for visual comparison.
arxiv-2511-10348:
Alex J. Vernon and Konstantin Y. Bliokh propose a new kind of geometric phase for light, one that lives in the relationship between its electric and magnetic fields. Known geometric phases track how polarization moves on the Poincaré sphere, or how spin direction moves on its own sphere. This electric-magnetic phase appears only in nonparaxial light, the tightly focused or strongly structured kind, when the relative amplitude and phase between the two fields cycle around.

The phase is represented naturally on a recently introduced electric-magnetic sphere, a companion to the familiar polarization sphere. The paper is a compact theoretical proposal: it defines the effect, places it in the geometric phase family, and points to the nonparaxial regime as the only place it can occur.
arxiv-2511-10548:
Jack Allsop, Daniel Kotlar, and Ian Wanless work on a combinatorics question about Young diagrams, the left-justified rows of boxes used across algebra and combinatorics. A diagram is called Latin if its cells can be filled so each row contains the numbers one up to its length, with no repeats in any column.

Chow and co-authors conjectured in 2003 that every wide diagram, one whose row subsets dominate their conjugates, is Latin. Allsop's team introduces allocations, a coarser attempt at a Latin filling, and uses a theorem of Hilton to prove a diagram has an allocation exactly when it is Latin. That equivalence lets them prove the conjecture for all diagrams with three distinct row lengths.
arxiv-2511-10748:
Alptuğ Ulugöl, Frank Smallenburg, and Laura Filion fix a flaw in a popular tool for analyzing local structure in materials. Knowing each particle's nearest neighbors is central to studying condensed matter, and the solid-angle-based nearest-neighbor algorithm, SANN, is prized for being parameter-free and fast.

In systems where particles have few neighbors, however, SANN systematically counts particles outside the true neighbor shell. The authors propose an inscribed circle modification that corrects the overcounting without adding any free parameters. Benchmarked against Voronoi analysis and the original algorithm across crystalline, quasicrystalline, and heterogeneous systems, the modified method, called mSANN, gave robust and cheap neighbor identification in both two and three dimensions.
arxiv-2511-10848:
Brad Shook and six co-authors test whether a general-purpose time series foundation model can read brain waves as well as models built specially for EEG. No head-to-head comparison of the two families on EEG tasks had been done. So they built STAMP, a lightweight adapter that lets a general model exploit the spatial structure of multi-channel recordings.

STAMP takes the univariate embeddings a general foundation model produces for each channel and pools them with a multi-head mechanism that implicitly captures spatial and temporal patterns. Across eight clinical EEG classification benchmarks, with ablation studies, the adapted general model performed comparably to state-of-the-art EEG-specific foundation models. The adapter is light in trainable parameters and flexible about inputs, which the authors pitch as an easier modeling path.
arxiv-2511-11148:
Yanze Zhu, Qingqing Wu, and their colleagues study how to boost a wireless system that sends both data and power through the air at once. Such systems could keep small Internet-of-Things devices charged and connected, but power fades badly over distance. Smart reflecting surfaces and movable antennas are two new levers that can reshape the signal path.

The team jointly tunes the base station's beams, the surface's reflections, and the antenna positions to raise data rates while meeting each energy receiver's needs. A layered algorithm mixes several known optimization frames to handle the non-convex problem. A feasibility check method rounds out the work.
arxiv-2511-11648:
Shunyu Wu and six co-authors tackle data valuation for time series foundation models: judging which training series actually help, so poor data can be dropped and good data credited. Classic influence methods collapse under the size of these models and ignore the time structure of the data.

Their lightweight method, LTSV, uses in-context finetuning, which theory suggests approximates the influence function at a fraction of the cost. A sample's value is estimated from how the model responds when it is included in context. Efficient, time-aware valuation matters because foundation models are only as good as the vast, uneven corpora they absorb during pretraining.
arxiv-2511-11948:
Zachary Couvillon and Anwesh Ray count elliptic curves whose division fields overlap in prescribed, unexplained ways, a phenomenon called entanglement. Such overlaps change the Galois groups that control a curve's arithmetic, and knowing how common they are shapes conjectures across number theory.

Curves are drawn from one-parameter families coming from genus zero modular curves, and techniques from the geometry of numbers and sieve methods produce asymptotic lower bounds ordered by naive height. For entanglements between the two- and three-division fields, and between the two- and five-division fields, the counts grow at least like explicit powers of the height bound. Entanglement, once an exotic exception, gets a population estimate.
arxiv-2511-12348:
Mostafa Nozari and three co-authors work on small subnetworks that must both communicate and sense where a target is, a pairing known as integrated sensing and communication. Sensing and data traffic compete for the same limited resources, so picking which subnetworks should sense at each step matters.

Their low-complexity algorithm selects sensing nodes in rounds, using the spatial spread of the deployment to refine the set and raise localization accuracy. Simulations reach very fine accuracy in a few rounds under simple noise, with a large gain over the best benchmark at the same sensing budget. They also measure the trade-off: fewer sensing rounds raise throughput but lower precision.
arxiv-2511-12548:
Wenzhang Du proposes CAO, an optimizer that adapts to curvature only where curvature matters most, to speed training in sharp, uneven regions of a loss landscape. First-order methods are reliable but slow in such regions. CAO periodically sketches a low-rank picture of the Hessian, the matrix of second derivatives, using products that avoid forming it in full.

Gradients are then corrected inside that sketched subspace, while all other directions keep the plain first-order step. Theory restores the standard convergence guarantee for smooth non-convex losses, with a wider stable step range, and faster contraction under an added growth condition. On image benchmarks with residual networks, the method reaches a set loss level far earlier than Adam, with final accuracy matched.
arxiv-2511-12948:
Jinwoo Park works out the theory for borrowing statistical strength across time series that keep changing. Locally stationary series drift slowly, so a regression fitted in one period may mislead in another. Locally linear smoothing handles the drift better than the classical local constant estimator.
