Fully supervised medical segmentation is accurate but demands large annotated datasets, and expert annotation is slow and expensive. Their semi supervised framework, SSL-MedSAM2, pairs two branches that improve each other in turn.

One branch adapts the pretrained Segment Anything Model 2 with a training free few shot method to generate pseudo labels for unlabelled scans. The other branch trains a standard medical segmentation network on those labels, and its refined output feeds back to improve the pseudo labels further. Entered in a liver segmentation challenge, the system achieved outstanding overlap scores on two MRI contrasts and competitive boundary distances. The code is publicly released. The work shows how foundation models can stretch scarce clinical annotation much further.
arxiv-2512-11648:
Gabriele Di Luzio and Giacomo Morelli introduce Dynamic Conditional SKEPTIC, a tool for tracking how market assets move together over time. Links between stocks shift with moods and crises, and traders need those links to build safe mixes. Classic models can leave messy, biased leftovers.

Their method is semi parametric and leans on rank based stats, Spearman rho and Kendall tau, which resist outliers. They prove the model settles into steady behavior under clear mixing rules. On S&P 100 and S&P 500 stocks from 2013 to 2025, it passed checks that classic models failed. Lowest risk mixes built with it traded less often and earned better risk adjusted returns.
arxiv-2512-11748:
Mohammed El Fallaki Idrissi and co-authors present Generative Parametric Design, a framework that creates both a part shape and its performance answer at once. Engineers often need to test many shapes under many settings, and full simulations are slow. The framework learns a compact code for shapes and a second code for solutions.

Two special autoencoders do the work. One encodes shapes, the other encodes solution modes from a sparse decomposition method. A regression link joins the two code spaces, so a new shape instantly yields its solution modes. Tests on two phase micro materials, with two varying traits, show fast design search. The idea feeds digital twin tools that must react in real time.
arxiv-2512-12048:
Muddsair Sharif and Huseyin Seker present CAMAC-DRA, a multi agent system for smart electric vehicle charging through the Smart2Charge app. Charging networks must juggle drivers, grid limits, prices, weather, and traffic at once. Single goal optimizers serve one master and slight the rest.

Their agents coordinate 250 vehicles and 45 stations with deep Q networks joined to graph networks and attention. Twenty context signals feed the choices, and five stakeholder weights balance the outcome. On 441,077 real charging records the system hit a 92 percent coordination rate, cut energy waste 15 percent, and lowered cost 10 percent. Grid strain fell 20 percent, with convergence 2.3 times faster than rivals.
arxiv-2512-13148:
Fabio Coppini and Wioletta Ruszel review and extend central limit theorems for nonlinear functions of Gaussian fields on a lattice. Such theorems say when a complicated random quantity settles into a bell curve. Their main result follows the spirit of the classic Breuer-Major theorem.

They apply the theory to powers of the Gaussian Free Field, a basic random surface in probability. Even powers converge to Gaussian white noise, a fully uncorrelated field. Odd powers instead converge to a continuous Gaussian Free Field with an explicit covariance. The proofs use the Wiener chaos decomposition and the fourth moment theorem, plus a tightness result.
arxiv-2512-13348:
Yucheng Wang derives the eigenstate thermalization hypothesis, a cornerstone claim about how isolated quantum systems settle into thermal behavior. The hypothesis says single energy states already look thermal for local measurements. A clear derivation from basic principles had been missing.

Wang starts from an eigenstate typicality principle: in quantum chaotic systems, energy states look, to local probes, like random states drawn from a narrow energy shell. Diagonal parts of the hypothesis then follow from concentration of measure. Off-diagonal parts are fixed by entropy scaling and finite-time dynamics of local observables. Random matrix assumptions are never invoked. The result clarifies where thermalization from unitary dynamics holds.
arxiv-2512-13648:
Antonio Junior Iovino, Gabriele Perna, and Hardi Veermäe reassess what the LISA space mission can say about primordial black holes. LISA will listen for millihertz gravitational wave backgrounds from the early universe. A non-detection could, in standard stories, rule out asteroid-mass black holes as dark matter.

The authors show that verdict weakens a lot with astrophysical foregrounds and strongly non-Gaussian early density changes. Those factors blur the link between scalar-induced waves and black hole counts. Uncertainty in the non-Gaussianity measure f_NL leads to large uncertainty in black hole abundance. That caps how fully LISA can probe the asteroid-mass window, even though the mission still tests the link itself.
arxiv-2512-13848:
Mufhumudzi Muthivhi, Terence L. van Zyl, and Hairong Wang present BiCoRec, a recommendation model that tackles popularity bias. Sequential recommenders learn from a user's evolving tastes, but top models favor popular items too strongly. That hurts users who prefer niche items, whose signals get drowned out.

BiCoRec uses a co-attention mechanism to build a popularity-weighted view of each user's sequence, adapting to how tastes shift between popular and niche goods. A new training scheme learns from future preferences through a consistency loss. For niche-preferring users, BiCoRec improved NDCG@10 by 26.00% on average over top baselines. The authors also report full-collection NDCG@10 scores for Movies, Fashion, Games, and Music data sets.
arxiv-2512-14448:
Xingfu Zhou and Pengfei Wang introduce reasoning style poisoning in a 2025 paper on large language model agents. Agents that use external retrieval now work in high stakes settings. Most known attacks fake content or inject instructions, but the authors target how an agent reasons instead.

Their attack, Generative Style Injection, rewrites retrieved documents into pathological tones like analysis paralysis or cognitive haste, without changing facts or adding triggers. A Reasoning Style Vector tracks verification depth, self confidence, and attention focus. On HotpotQA and FEVER, the attack raised reasoning steps by up to 4.4 times or caused early errors, and it bypassed leading content filters. A light runtime monitor, RSP M, flags unsafe style shifts in real time.
arxiv-2512-14848:
Claudio Lopez, Emilio Donoso, and Mariano Javier de L. Dominguez Romero present Skykatana, a tool that builds masks for wide sky surveys. Masks mark the bad parts of sky images: halos of bright stars, bleed trails, and poor regions that science must skip. New surveys like the Vera Rubin Observatory make such masks at huge scale.

Skykatana builds and merges maps in the HEALPix format while using little memory. It can draw coverage maps and scatter random test points across half the sky on modest hardware. The team shows two uses: a mask joining Subaru and WISE data, and star masks for Rubin made on demand from Gaia data. Full bright star masks for parts of the Rubin footprint are released with the study, along with the open source code.
arxiv-2512-15248:
Maria Becker and four coauthors build the Moralization Corpus, a dataset for studying how speakers use moral values to push demands. Moralizations are arguments that dress a position in moral terms, and they are often implicit, which makes them hard for people and machines alike to pin down. The corpus spans German political debates, news articles, and online discussions.

A frame based annotation scheme marks each moralization's parts: the moral values invoked, the demand made, and the protagonists involved. The team then tests large language models on finding moralizations and extracting their parts, under several prompting styles. Detailed prompt instructions helped more than few shot examples or explanations. Even so, the task stayed highly subjective and context sensitive. All data, guidelines, and code are released for future work on moral discourse.
arxiv-2512-15348:
M. V. Kondrin and two coauthors derive melting criteria for the simplest possible crystal: a plane of hard disks. Hard sphere and hard disk models are the zero order picture of fluids and solids, yet few exact results exist for them. The authors study melting by tracking how extended defects of one type accumulate in the crystal, and how the disk packing jams.

Their analysis bounds the volume ratio at the melting transition between 25/21 and 5/4. In line with the celebrated BKTHNY theory, the two dimensional crystal melts first into an anisotropic liquid. A second transition, from that anisotropic liquid to a normal isotropic one, is bounded between volume ratios 5/4 and 13/9. The work adds rare analytic anchors to the theory of two dimensional melting.
arxiv-2512-15448:
Sinan Emre and co authors present a load based variable transmission for robot joints in a 2025 paper. Robot legs need high torque at some moments and speed at others, yet most gear systems keep one fixed ratio. Systems that change ratio usually need an extra motor just for that task.

Their design uses a pre tensioned spring and a four bar linkage to shift ratio on its own when load rises. Simulations show the ratio grows by up to 40 percent once a set torque level is reached. Torque boost kicks in when applied force passes 18 newtons. The result points to lighter, simpler joints for legged robots.
arxiv-2512-15848:
Michal Zimmerman and co authors map quadrupolar and dipolar phases of excitons in trilayer stacks in a 2025 paper. Excitons, bound electron hole pairs, in three layer transition metal dichalcogenide stacks can carry dipole moments whose direction flips as charge tunnels between outer layers. Recent tests revealed rich group behavior in these systems.

Large scale quantum Monte Carlo runs chart the low temperature phase chart against tunable settings. Under strong dipole flips, a quadrupolar superfluid emerges. Suppressing tunneling nucleates a droplet state, and high densities bring a partly split condensate. At large effective mass, a staggered dipolar crystal appears. Field based energy shifts offer guidance for reading current experiments.
arxiv-2512-15948:
Samuel Gershman asks where objective functions come from in a 2025 paper on subjective functions. Human intelligence invents new goals on the fly, not just pursues given ones. A subjective function is a higher order objective defined relative to the agent's own features rather than an external task.

Expected prediction error serves as the concrete example: an agent can value states by how much they would reduce its own forecasting error. Gershman develops that example and traces connections to ideas in psychology, neuroscience, and machine learning. The proposal aims to explain how artificial systems might synthesize their own objectives the way people appear to do.
arxiv-2512-16048:
Yu P Lyakhno examines how atomic nuclei hold together in an arXiv paper uploaded in 2025. Recent high-precision calculations describe the lightest nuclei using realistic forces between protons and neutrons. Lyakhno uses those results to reason about heavier nuclei, focusing on tensor forces, the part of the nuclear force that depends on spin and direction.

Including tensor forces, he argues, makes four groups of slow-moving nucleons each settle mainly into a paired cluster state. Groups with orbital motion also cluster where the potential energy is lowest. He shows the picture can explain the lifetime of beryllium-8, the famous Hoyle state in carbon, and features of reactions that emit alpha particles. The approach also suggests nucleons orbit a power center inside the nucleus.
arxiv-2512-16148:
Zhisheng Hu, Jiacheng Shen, and Ming-Chang Yang present a data store design in a paper uploaded to arXiv in 2025. Disaggregated memory splits processors and memory into separate pools in a data center. Key-value stores on that layout manage remote data, but slow down because index lookups lean on one-sided atomic network operations and compute-side caches work poorly.

Their store, FlexKV, moves the index onto the compute nodes, whose strong processors speed up lookups and caching. Three fixes keep it efficient: a hotness detector balances index load across nodes, a two-level memory scheme stretches limited compute memory, and batched remote calls cut cache coherence costs. FlexKV improved throughput by up to 2.94 times and cut latency by up to 85.2 percent versus leading disaggregated stores.
arxiv-2512-16748:
Derek Long studies how to pick stock portfolios that keep tail risk in check when markets shift. The task uses a CVaR limit, a cap on losses in the worst cases. A robust method guards the cap. It hedges against a ball of nearby chance models.

Picking the ball size is the snag. Too big is timid. Too small can break under regime change. Long gives a two-phase check. It first solves the robust task over a grid of sizes. It then reweights a later data fold to mimic the target market. It also builds a confidence band that respects time links. Any portfolio that passes meets the risk cap with set odds. Tests show better return-risk trade-offs than a naive baseline.
arxiv-2512-16848:
Yulun Jiang and coauthors present LaMer, a meta-learning frame that teaches language model agents to explore. Agents trained by reward learning often fail at tasks needing active probing, and they adapt poorly from trial and error at test time.

LaMer trains across episodes to reward exploration and long-term gains, then adapts at test time by reflection in context, with no weight updates. Across varied settings it beat reward-trained baselines by 11 percent on Sokoban, 14 percent on MineSweeper, and 19 percent on WebShop. It also held up better on harder and unseen tasks, showing that meta-learning can build exploration habits that carry to new ground.
arxiv-2512-17348:
Yuki Horii, Tomoaki Murata, and Tsutomu Kobayashi ask whether a field shaped like a two-index grid can break the universe's left-right symmetry without breaking physics. Such 2-form fields might drive cosmic expansion, but careless versions spawn ghost modes with negative energy, which ruin a theory. The team hunts for versions that stay ghost-free while treating left and right unequally.

Starting from the most general allowed terms, they find a two-parameter family that stays healthy. Most of the left-right bias, though, washes away under a change of variables. Only the field's potential can keep it. In an expanding universe model, that leftover bias can produce chiral gravitational waves, ripples stronger in one twist than the other. Telescopes could one day test that signal.
arxiv-2512-17648:
Marco Gaido and four co-authors release simulstream, an open toolkit for judging live speech translation fairly. Translating speech as it arrives is a race: wait too long and the translation lags uselessly behind; rush and errors pile up. Research groups grade their systems with mismatched tools, so scores across papers rarely line up.

The most used older tool only handles one decoding style and short pre-cut clips. Simulstream handles both styles, incremental and full re-translation, on long uncut speech. It logs quality and delay in fine detail and ships a web page where rival systems can be watched translating side by side in real time. Shared yardsticks like this are how a field learns which ideas truly work.
arxiv-2512-17748:
Aurelia Kusumastuti and four co-authors map how to keep secrets safe on a quantum cloud, where customers rent time on quantum machines they do not own. Sending a quantum program or its data to a stranger's hardware invites snooping, and ordinary encryption fails when the cloud must compute on the very data it should not see.

The team tests homomorphic encryption, which lets a server compute on locked data, inside the Qrisp programming framework. Three post-quantum schemes went in successfully. A quantum one-time pad proved cheapest, while two heavier schemes traded speed and memory for their security style. Their closing guidance covers encrypted storage and processing, quantum key distribution, and strict access control. Cloud builders get a tested menu, not just theory.
arxiv-2512-18148:
Mohammed Alghadeer and seven colleagues at Oxford and Chalmers study crosstalk, the unwanted interaction between qubits that limits how large quantum processors can grow. Their 2025 paper builds a combined theory and experiment framework for fixed frequency transmon lattices. It captures residual coupling between neighboring qubits and between distant ones. The model joins three effects: sharp falloff in banded capacitance matrices, the muting of virtual couplings through detuning, and the fading of below cutoff fields.

Measurements on a 4 by 4 superconducting qubit lattice with inductive shunt pillars confirm the predicted patterns. Coupling falls off sharply with distance and weakens with frequency separation. The model matches every nearest neighbor coupling across the 4 to 6 gigahertz working range. The usual simple approach, by contrast, tends to overstate long range coupling. The framework gives design guidance for cutting crosstalk in larger processors built under real world fabrication limits.
arxiv-2512-18248:
Siqiao Mu and Diego Klabjan give LoRA, the popular cheap way to fine tune large AI models, its first firm speed promise. LoRA trains two small adapter matrices instead of the whole model, yet its training lacked a proof of how fast it settles. The usual proofs need a smoothness trait that LoRA lacks, so past work leaned on heavy extra assumptions.

The pair recast the problem around the product of the stacked adapters and prove a fresh step down rule for that view. With care on step size, they show the training loss nears a flat point at a rate of one over the log of the step count. Bench tests back the slow but sure pace.
arxiv-2512-18648:
Sungwoo Kang, at Korea University, studies how traders' buy and sell flows should be scaled before they are used as trading signals. In this 2025 finance paper he argues that the right scaling depends on who is trading. Big institutions size positions by firm value, so dividing their flow by market capitalization acts as a matched filter. Volume-targeting traders, such as VWAP algorithms, are best scaled by trading value instead.

Monte Carlo tests confirm the principle both ways, with matched filters giving up to 1.99 times higher signal correlation. On 2.7 million Korean stock-days from 2020 to 2024, domestic institutional flow predicts next-day returns under market cap scaling, while foreign flow predicts better under trading value scaling. Kang reads this as informed investors hiding in volume-based execution.
arxiv-2512-18748:
Recep Kaan Karaman and Meftun Akarsu argue that teaching AI to write code documentation starts with cleaner lessons. Most training sets are scraped from public repositories with little quality control, so they carry noisy docs, duplicates, and growing amounts of AI-generated text. Their dataset, Code2Doc, posted to arXiv in December 2025, takes the opposite approach: quality first.

A four-stage pipeline checks documentation completeness and clarity, filters functions by structure and complexity, removes duplicates, and flags likely AI-written docs. From 52,069 candidates, only 25.6 percent survive, leaving 13,358 function-documentation pairs across Python, Java, TypeScript, JavaScript, and C++. The set averages a quality score of 6.93 out of 10. Fine-tuning a model on it improves BLEU by 29.47 percent over zero-shot use, despite the modest size.
arxiv-2512-18848: Nurgül Gökgöz works on speeding up iterative methods for solving large linear systems. Generalized Chebyshev acceleration can turbocharge a basic iteration, but only when the iteration matrix's eigenvalues meet a strict inclusion condition, which limits its use. Her paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, relaxes that requirement with an alternative iterative scheme that converges to the same solution. She tests the approach on a large-scale sparse normal matrix to show it works in practice.
arxiv-2512-18948: Wojciech Bielas answers a question in set-theoretic topology from a recent arXiv paper, its Problem 1. Can the real line contain a dense plastic subset smaller than the continuum? His short paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, works under one assumption: the continuum is at least omega-2. Under it, he constructs exactly such a set. The set X is dense and plastic, and its cardinality is strictly less than c. The example settles the existence problem in the affirmative.
arxiv-2512-19348:
Shubhankar Sahai works in prismatic geometry, a modern framework that unifies several cohomology theories in arithmetic geometry. His object is the Nygaard-filtered prismatization of a ring in positive characteristic, a stack built from prismatic data. The note proves that stack is simpler than it looks.

Sahai shows the prismatization is naturally the relative spectrum, over a base stack, of the Rees algebra of Nygaard-filtered prismatic cohomology. He names the pattern de Rham affineness, after the classic de Rham stack, and uses it as an organizing tool for coming work on Frobenius-liftable schemes. A structural result ties such functors to ring stacks by transmutation.
arxiv-2512-19548:
Michał Maj, Sandra Musiał, and Marcin Nowak measure how a magnesium alloy splits plastic work between heat and stored energy. Extruded AZ31B can deform by slip or by twinning, depending on how it is loaded. The two modes, the team shows, handle the energy budget very differently.

Under slip, flow stays stable and about half the plastic work leaves as heat. Under twinning, most work is stored at first, which delays heating and drives rapid hardening plus early strain localization. Microstructure tracking ties those responses to the active mechanism. In this alloy family, stored energy is a property of the deformation mode, not just the metal.
arxiv-2512-19648:
Arnold Caleb Asiimwe and Carl Vondrick reframe a popular way of animating three-dimensional scenes. Four-dimensional Gaussian splatting normally deforms a cloud of Gaussian blobs frame by frame. Their version, EvoGS, instead treats the scene as a physical system whose state flows continuously under a learned motion law, integrated over time like a dynamical system.

That single change buys three abilities deformation methods lack. Motion can be learned from sparse time samples, because the underlying law fills the gaps. Scenes can be extrapolated forward and backward beyond the observed window. And local dynamics can be injected into one region for controllable editing. On dynamic scene benchmarks, EvoGS shows more coherent motion and better temporal consistency than deformation-field rivals, while still rendering in real time.
arxiv-2512-19848:
Hira Ali and Naeem Shahid compare the click-by-click records of a quantum system and a classical one, hunting for a fingerprint that separates them. Their quantum case is a driven, dissipative two-qubit system emitting jump trajectories; the classical rival is a telegraph model tuned to matched rates. Both are scored with Lempel-Ziv complexity, mutual information, and temporal correlations.

As coupling grows, both systems pass from independent to synchronized behavior. Only the quantum trajectories, though, develop enhanced complexity and durable information sharing when the drive strongly outweighs decay, while classical correlations fade quickly under strong drive. A tight correlation between complexity and information appears uniquely in the quantum data. The authors offer trajectory-level measures as an efficient diagnostic of quantumness in open systems.
arxiv-2512-19948:
Kai Xu decomposes spaces of bundles on a curve into simpler building blocks. The objects are moduli of principal bundles, the stack of all bundles for a group G over a curve and the coarse moduli space of semistable ones. Semiorthogonal decomposition is a way of splitting a triangulated category into ordered pieces, and Xu constructs such splittings whose pieces are the curve's symmetric powers.

The proof assembles heavy machinery: Borel-Weil-Bott theory for loop groups, the highest-weight structure of current-group representations, derived theta-stratification, and local-global compatibility of Kac-Moody localization. Both the stack and the semistable space receive decompositions, unifying their derived categories with concrete geometric ingredients. Results of this kind feed into broader programs relating moduli spaces, representation theory, and the geometric Langlands circle of ideas.
arxiv-2512-20148:
Robert van de Ven leads a six-author team using 3D reconstruction to slash annotation work in orchards. Judging an apple's pose is hard. The calyx, a key mark, hides under leaves and fruit. Labels for the same apple can clash or vanish across views. Their pipeline rebuilds the orchard scene with 3D Gaussian Splatting. It then projects simplified labels into each image on its own.

Just 105 hand labels yielded 28,191 training labels. That is a cut of over ninety-nine percent. Training on fruit occluded up to ninety-five percent gave the best pose calls. Position accuracy was best for the least hidden fruit. Orientation defeated the tested method outright. Dataset size shifts mattered little next to occlusion handling.
arxiv-2512-20648:
Sami Lakka rebuilds fluid flow as geometry on a landscape of heat and disorder. One metric comes from the second derivatives of a heat potential and makes entropy act like time, with pressure as space. A second metric, built from the Onsager loss matrix, rules how fluxes move. The shortest paths of this joined geometry become the laws of motion.

For a simple fluid with fixed viscosity, those paths give back the Navier-Stokes laws for an unsqueezable fluid, with no closure rule pasted in. Turbulence scaling then reads as a contest between the bending of this space and the stiffness of the loss metric, and the Kolmogorov length is where the two balance. Points where the old laws blow up become places of wild bending whose own clock runs forever, hinting blow-up is held back in single-phase fluids. Heat flow and diffusion fit the same mould.
arxiv-2512-20848:
NVIDIA's large team presents Nemotron 3 Nano, an open language model built for agent-style reasoning. The design mixes two architectures, Mamba and Transformer, and a mixture-of-experts layout that wakes only part of the network per pass. Training used twenty-five trillion text tokens, then fine-tuning and reinforcement learning across many task settings.

The model beats its predecessor, Nemotron 2 Nano, on accuracy while activating under half the parameters each step. Throughput runs more than three times higher than similar open rivals, and context can stretch to a million tokens. Both base and post-trained versions are released openly on Hugging Face for others to use and study.
arxiv-2512-21248:
Richard Derbyshire shows how an intruder inside a factory network can walk from controller to controller using nothing but the controllers' own features. Lateral movement is routine in office IT, but operational technology offers few paths between programmable logic controllers, the rugged computers running industrial processes. Known paths chain exploits that are noisy and patchable. The technique here is the first PLC-centric one relying exclusively on native functionality. It is an industrial variant of living off the land, which the author names living off the plant.

Dual-homed controllers even let the attacker slip off IP networks onto legacy serial segments defenders forget exist. Because the movement rides on ordinary network communication functions, it stays covert and hard to flag. The message is uncomfortable: defenses built around patching and malware scanning miss an adversary who introduces nothing foreign, so OT security practice needs rethinking from the ground up.
arxiv-2512-21348:
Fairness in machine learning is usually argued on ethical grounds, but Ying Xiao, Shangwen Wang, and five co-authors reframe it as software quality: unequal performance across user groups is a defect. Their fix, Correlation Tuning, works before training by adjusting the data itself. It measures how strongly sensitive attributes track the labels and retunes those correlations under multi-objective optimization.

The payoff is practical, not just principled. True positive rates for unprivileged groups rose by an average of seventeen and a half percent, and three standard bias metrics fell by more than half. Correlation Tuning beat leading methods on both single and multiple sensitive attributes. It also claims better out-of-distribution generalization and geographic transfer as quality dividends.
arxiv-2512-21448:
Paúl Risco Iturralde writes a short note in descriptive computational complexity, the field that describes computing problems with logical formulas instead of machines. The note concerns PARTITION, a classic decision problem, and whether it is NP-hard under very weak reductions, meaning changes too simple to do much work.

Work by Murray and Williams had suggested that PARTITION was not known to be NP-hard under small AC0 reductions. Risco Iturralde shows it is NP-hard under first-order projections, an even more restricted reduction built purely from logic. He adapts the standard reductions from 3SAT to SUBSET-SUM and from SUBSET-SUM to PARTITION, rewriting each step as a first-order definition. Since first-order reductions are a special case of the AC0 kind, the hardness result follows. The note closes a gap in how little machinery such a hardness proof needs.
arxiv-2512-22248:
Rohit Pandey and Rohan Pandey teach a neural network to estimate model rocket aerodynamics without any real flight training data. Predicting a rocket's peak altitude needs drag and thrust parameters that are hard to measure directly. Simulators can generate unlimited synthetic flights, though. Their network trains on ten thousand simulated flights, learning to invert the physics: from one measured apogee plus motor and design features, it predicts the drag coefficient and a thrust correction factor.

Tested on eight real flights, the model predicted apogee with a mean absolute error of 12.3 metres and no fine-tuning on real data. Its predictions ran systematically high, which usefully measures the gap between idealized physics and real conditions. It also beat OpenRocket baseline predictions, and the code is public for the amateur rocketry community.
arxiv-2512-22348:
Aleksandar Tomašević, Ana Vranić, Aleksandra Alorić, and Marija Mitrović Dankulov trace what happened on Voat after Reddit banned whole communities in four waves between 2015 and 2020. Deplatforming is a standard removal tool, yet research usually watches the banned groups or the source platform, not the rival sites absorbing the displaced users. The team combined network analysis, toxicity spotting, and reputation modeling on Voat's generalist groups.

Two regimes emerged. Early waves brought hostile takeovers, where arrival cohorts built parallel forms that bypassed current cores by sheer volume. Later waves settled into a toxic equilibrium as flattened rank orders let arrivals join the dominant toxic community. Under five percent of arrivals reached central positions in most months, yet toxicity doubled, driven from the periphery.
arxiv-2512-22448:
Peleg Shefi, Amir Ayali, and Gal A. Kaminka borrow tricks from locusts to make robot swarms that move together without falling apart. Artificial swarms are usually brittle, mainly when members navigate by vision, which loses information and creates ambiguity. Natural collective motion, by contrast, survives constant sensory mess. The authors build two methods inspired by locust studies for perceptually limited individuals with no central control.

First, a distance estimate combines the horizontal and vertical apparent sizes of neighbors, which is more robust than either alone. Second, intermittent locomotion, pausing and moving in turns, lets robots reliably spot peers that fail to keep up. The swarm then avoids those faulty members, in a way tolerant of classification errors. Physics-based simulations showed dramatic resilience gains across both avoid-attract and alignment-based swarm models.
arxiv-2512-22648:
Michele Arzano, Alessandra D'Alise, Simone del Rosso, and Domenico Frattulillo re-derive the Unruh effect, the warmth an accelerating observer feels in empty space, from pure symmetry. A massless field in 2D splits into left- and right-moving sectors on the light cone. Quantum mechanically, those sectors carry an action of the affine group. Shifts come from light-cone momenta. Scalings come from mixes of boost and dilation generators.

Inertial observers' particles are eigenstates of the shift generators. Rindler observers' particles are eigenfunctions of the scaling generator. The authors show that simple steps connecting the two pictures, through the Mellin transform, produce the thermal spectrum the accelerated observer sees. The group-theory route suggests similar vacuum thermal effects may appear in any quantum system with shift and scaling eigenstates.
arxiv-2512-23048:
Giuseppe Rossi re-examines whether black holes can trigger the decay of a false vacuum, a process in which a bubble of true vacuum nucleates and expands to convert space itself. Earlier discussions often used eternal black holes. Rossi studies the more physical case of a black hole formed by gravitational collapse, within the semiclassical approximation, with a bubble growing outside the horizon.

The calculation shows the dominant configuration corresponds to a single energy state, and memory of the collapsing star's interior fades exponentially fast at late times. Rossi also gives prescriptions for carrying the boundary conditions over to the eternal black hole geometry. The conclusion tempers earlier excitement. A black hole can only weakly catalyze vacuum decay, because the suppression exponent reaches its minimum at a finite black hole mass. As that mass shrinks, the result smoothly returns to the flat-space rate.
arxiv-2512-23148:
Aliaksandr Hancharuk and Ruben Louis construct differential Z-graded varieties, objects used to encode constrained systems and their symmetries. Their starting data are a commutative algebra, an ideal inside it, and a graded differential variety over the quotient algebra. The goal is to extend that one-sided object into a full two-sided graded variety.

The negative half of the extension is an arborescent Koszul-Tate resolution of the quotient, a tree-shaped resolution of the constraint surface. An algorithm produces the extension by reusing the resolution's homotopy retract data, cutting computation sharply. When the positive half preserves the ideal, the whole extension admits a clean account in terms of decorated trees. As a by-product, every Lie-Rinehart algebra over an affine variety yields an explicit graded variety whose negative side resolves the coordinate ring. Concrete examples are worked out.
arxiv-2512-23248:
Shuang-Quan Ma, Jing-Yi-Ran Jin, and Qing Ai show that an optical computing platform can double as a lab for quantum phase transitions. Coherent Ising machines, networks of degenerate optical parametric oscillators built to solve hard search problems, turn out to mirror spin systems. The authors map the XY spin chain onto such an oscillator network and show the oscillator spectrum faithfully encodes its critical behavior.

In a strongly anisotropic regime the setup realizes a near transverse-field Ising chain, with the energy gap closing exactly at the critical point. Ground-state energy density is tracked, and the singularities appearing in magnetic susceptibility pinpoint the quantum critical points of the spin model. The reach extends beyond optimization. Coherent Ising machines can probe universal quantum critical events. Physicists gain a photonic tool for questions born in quantum magnetism, and the machines gain a second career in science.
arxiv-2512-23348:
Selçuk Kayacan builds a data analysis framework on filtrations of finite topological spaces, an alternative to simplicial complexes. Starting from points with distances, the method lays a sequence of ever-coarser topologies over them. These yield persistence modules and barcodes as usual. They also keep information homology discards, like which points are topologically indistinguishable.

The author develops the theory, proves stability results, and gives constructions starting from a distance matrix. On synthetic clusters of varying shape, size, and density, the finite topologies reveal how regions form and merge as the topology coarsens. Paths inside the structure locate the cycles behind one-dimensional homology. Two real datasets test the ideas. One is single-cell data, where fine cellular states assemble into larger groups. The other is the COIL20 image collection, where rotating objects show a cyclic organization in the evolving topology.
arxiv-2512-23548:
Jonathan Lozano-Mayo derives a family of virial identities, the balance relations that any stable, localized field configuration must obey. Solitons, instantons, and bounces are such configurations, and virial arguments are often used to prove some of them cannot exist or to check numerical solutions. His family is continuous, indexed by an exponent that sets how strongly different radii are weighted.

Splitting the global balance into radially resolved pieces lets each special choice of the exponent isolate a different mechanism. For BPS configurations the identity holds automatically at every valid exponent, and the author verifies the formalism on the Fubini-Lipatov and BPST instantons and the BPS monopole. Numerical tests on the Coleman bounce and the Nielsen-Olesen vortex show that errors at different exponents pinpoint whether inaccuracies sit in the core or the tail. In this way one tool can probe one part of a system at a time.
arxiv-2512-23648:
Simone Minniti and four co-authors present a solver for steady water flows whose upper surface is free to move, as in flow over a riverbed bump or under a submerged wing. The surface profile is part of the answer, not given in advance, which makes such problems harder than fixed-domain ones. Their method is a high-order spectral element scheme, built in the open-source Firedrake framework.

A pseudo-time iteration driven by the surface's kinematic condition gradually determines the unknown profile. Curved elements, obtained by transfinite blending, represent the surface and submerged bodies accurately while preserving high-order convergence. Benchmarks move from fixed-domain cases, a lid-driven cavity and flow past a cylinder and an airfoil, . It then moves to free-surface cases with a bathymetry bump and a submerged airfoil, where the solver clearly outpaced low-order schemes.
arxiv-2512-23948:
Kacem Khaled, Felipe Gohring de Magalhães, and Gabriela Nicolescu defend small neural networks against thieves who copy them by querying them. Model extraction attacks reconstruct a victim model's behavior from its answers, stealing the model itself. Quantized networks, compressed for edge devices, are widely deployed yet their extraction safety is barely studied, and existing defenses bolt noise onto predictions after training, often expensively and with rosy assumptions.

DivQAT builds the defense into training itself. It modifies quantization-aware training, the process that teaches a network to survive low-precision arithmetic, so the quantization process hardens the model against extraction at the same time. The authors say it is a first. On benchmark vision data sets, models trained this way resisted extraction attacks without losing accuracy. Combining the technique with established defenses made those defenses stronger than pairing them with ordinary quantization-aware training.
arxiv-2512-24248:
Partha Rana and Sriparna Bandopadhyay study consistency in sign patterns. A sign pattern is a matrix filled with plus, minus, and zero. A pattern is consistent when every real matrix matching it has the same count of real eigenvalues. Earlier authors set a necessary condition for a special family. The family was irreducible, tridiagonal, with zero diagonal. They proposed the condition was also sufficient.

That proposal fails, the authors show. They characterize the consistent patterns in that family up to order five. Useful necessary conditions follow for a broader class. Those patterns are irreducible and combinatorially symmetric. A new class is also introduced. It collects all 2-consistent sign patterns. Several necessary conditions for membership are provided. The paper corrects the record and maps a niche of qualitative matrix theory.
arxiv-2512-24348:
Palle Jorgensen, Jay Jorgenson, and Lejla Smajlovic construct heat kernels and Green's functions in measure spaces. Heat kernels describe how heat spreads from a point source. Green's functions solve the associated steady problems. The setting is broad: a locally compact Hausdorff space with Borel structure and extra measure data. Function spaces over it include the Lebesgue and Hilbert cases.

The construction is explicit. A Neumann series builds the kernel term by term. The input is a parametrix, a small-time approximation to the kernel. The method adapts classical work of Minakshisundaram and Pleijel. New instances follow from the general machine. Normalized Laplacians on finite and infinite graphs are covered. Hilbert spaces with reproducing kernels are covered as well. Analysts gain a uniform route to kernels on spaces far from smooth manifolds.
arxiv-2512-24548:
Samuel Dentan extends Poincare duality, a pairing between homology groups, to singular tropical hypersurfaces built from non-primitive triangulations. Tropical geometry replaces curves from algebra with piece-by-piece linear objects tied to lattice polytopes. He defines a level of primitivity for a triangulation, measured against a chosen integral domain, that is weaker than the standard notion.

Duality then holds in part, with the level setting how much, and in full when the triangulation is primitive over that domain. A corollary covers hypersurfaces built by patchworking from simple polytopes over the rationals. Readers get a broader duality result and a converse to an earlier patchworking theorem.
arxiv-2512-24848:
Srija Mukhopadhyay, Sathwik Reddy, Shruthi Muthukumar, and colleagues introduce PrivacyBench, a conversational benchmark testing whether personalized AI assistants keep user secrets. Such agents read private email, chats, and purchases, yet may leak sensitive facts when social context calls for discretion. Their datasets embed secrets in socially grounded material and probe them over multiple turns.

Retrieval-augmented assistants leaked secrets in up to about a quarter of interactions in their tests. A privacy-aware prompting approach is also examined. Readers building personal agents get a measurable warning and a test harness. Keeping secrets across a conversation is shown to be a distinct skill from answering questions well.
arxiv-2512-24948:
Xinran Gong, Gorkem Durak, Halil Ertugrul Aktas, and colleagues present ProDM, a diffusion model that corrects heart motion artifacts in coronary calcium scoring from ordinary chest scans. Calcium scoring guides cardiovascular risk, but cardiac and respiratory motion blur calcified lesions in non-gated scans. Gated cardiac scans reduce artifacts yet are limited by requirements and coverage in routine screening.

Their synthetic reality-driven, property-aware progressive diffusion approach aims to recover accurate calcium measures from non-gated images. Medical imaging readers get a method to use scans already taken for other reasons. Reliable incidental calcium scoring could widen risk screening without extra radiation or appointments.
arxiv-2601-00448:
Dimitris Vartziotis uses large language models as a testing ground for old debates about how language carries meaning. One side, linked to language games, treats meaning as built through social use. The other, which he calls Semantic Field Theory, treats language as mathematical structure. He formalizes ideas of lexical fields and linguistic fields as interacting structures in a continuous space of meaning.

Vartziotis then compares those ideas with how Transformer models actually work, including distributed word representations, attention, and geometric patterns in embedding spaces. He argues that model success at capturing regularities supports the structural view, while model weakness at context and practical reasoning supports the social view. His conclusion is that both structure and social grounding are needed.
arxiv-2601-00648:
Minghui Bi and Yixian Gao study an inverse problem for biharmonic wave equations, the fourth-order equations that describe vibrations of plates and beams. Their goal is to recover a material's density and its initial displacement from measurements taken only at the boundary, for a clamped plate with known damping. Such recovery questions are useful wherever internal properties must be inferred from surface data.

For smooth, finite-dimensional profiles, they prove the observation map is strongly differentiable and establish local Lipschitz stability, meaning small measurement errors cause only small recovery errors, under an injectivity condition. For a simpler one-mode case they prove a global estimate from a single curvature trace. Repeated-noise numerical experiments support the theory, including on a square-plate configuration beyond the proved class.
arxiv-2601-00848:
Ron Del Rosario documents an open framework for training language models to spot attack patterns that unfold over time inside multi-agent AI systems. Security analysts increasingly read OpenTelemetry traces, the structured logs of system activity, to find such attacks, and models could help if trained on the right data. Del Rosario curated about eighty-one thousand examples from eighteen public cybersecurity sources plus about thirty-five thousand synthetic traces.

Fine-tuning used an efficient low-rank method on a single ARM-based machine, over three iterations with targeted augmentation. Accuracy on a custom benchmark climbed from about forty-three percent to about seventy-four percent, a statistically significant gain. Examples aimed at specific knowledge gaps beat indiscriminate scaling, and the full methodology is released openly.
arxiv-2601-00948:
Federico Escudero, Zhen Zhan, Pierre Pantaleón, and Francisco Guinea study how disturbances settle in moiré materials, the patterned systems made by stacking two slightly rotated atomic sheets. Twisted bilayer graphene is the famous example, and in real experiments substrates or strain always perturb it, shifting its electronic behavior. The authors show those perturbations do not simply stay where they land.

Instead, disturbances tend to transfer between the two coupled Dirac cones of the twisted layers, eventually reaching an equilibrium, especially near the magic angle where the most exotic physics lives. The equilibrium behavior survives even when the moiré potential itself is perturbed. Their findings extend the very notion of the magic angle into a broader regime governed by this balancing process, with direct links to experiments.
arxiv-2601-01348:
Huaying Wei and Michel Zinsmeister study function spaces defined on rough curves. Start with a Jordan curve, a closed loop that does not cross itself. On each side of it sit harmonic functions, and a weighted energy decides which ones belong to the space. On a perfect circle, the two sides match a known fractional smoothness space on the boundary.

The question is which rough curves keep that match. For curves that are radial-Lipschitz, the authors prove the boundary traces from inside and outside agree with the fractional space, across stated ranges of the parameters. For the wider class of chord-arc curves, the same holds under a stricter range. A side result gives a near-Dirichlet principle for the plain energy in some ranges, and a counterexample shows one range's upper limit cannot be raised. The work maps where smooth theory survives rough geometry.
arxiv-2601-02048:
A material that is simultaneously polar, antiferromagnetic, and metallic sounds contradictory, since each property tends to exclude the others. Yang Shen and four co-authors propose a route to that combination. The host is the layered perovskite Sr3Co2O7. The driver is charge disproportionation. In that process, identical cobalt sites split into unequal charge states.

The evidence comes from molecular orbital analysis of first-principles calculations. Density matrix renormalization group results back it up. Localized molecular orbitals form within each bilayer. They order antiferromagnetically. The charge imbalance breaks inversion symmetry. It also creates polar metallicity. The same physics couples carriers to local spins, producing in-plane ferromagnetism by double exchange. The framework should extend across the bilayer Ruddlesden-Popper oxide family.
arxiv-2601-02348:
Mackenzie Ticoras and a large team study the gas halo around galaxies, the circumgalactic medium, using the FOGGIE simulation suite of Milky Way like galaxies. Two ions serve as tracers, magnesium two for cooler, lower ion gas and oxygen six for hotter, higher ion gas. Knowing where each kind sits, and whether they move together, is central to tracing how galaxies gain and lose fuel.

In the simulations the oxygen bearing gas forms a diffuse halo around the disk, while magnesium bearing gas sits closer in. The team builds mock sightlines through the simulated halos in two ways and compares covering fractions and line of sight motions. The two ions often share motions when seen along the same direction, a pattern observers can test against real absorption data.
arxiv-2601-02548:
Joseph J. Soliz and William F. Welsh ask whether complex life could arise on planets around the dimmest red dwarf stars. On Earth, oxygen built up about two point three billion years ago, long after oxygen making photosynthesis began. If that lag scales with oxygen production rate, starlight level sets a planet's biological timetable. A planet in the habitable zone of TRAPPIST-1, a very cool late M star. Gets less than one percent of the photosynthetically useful light Earth receives, since most of its light falls outside the wavelengths plants use.

On a naive linear scaling, an oxygen buildup there would take tens of billions of years, far longer than the star stays suitable. The authors then examine why the linear guess misleads, since photosynthesis saturates and declines as light rises. Their conclusion is that the shortage of useful light argues against complex life on such worlds.
arxiv-2601-02648:
Mehdi Fatemi improves the reinforcement learning stage that fine tunes a large language model after its main training, by choosing which practice problems deserve the most attempts. The idea borrows from prioritized replay in deep reinforcement learning, joined with the observation that problems a. Model solves about half the time produce the strongest learning signal under group based methods such as GRPO. Problems always solved or always failed teach almost nothing.

A simple priority score from the model's own success statistics ranks the problem pool, and training naturally concentrates on the informative middle. No preset difficulty tiers, extra predictors, or outside labels are needed, and the ranking updates continuously as the model improves. Lightweight machinery, including heap based prioritized sampling, makes the scheme practical to deploy at scale.
arxiv-2601-03048:
Siyi Lyu, Quan Liu, and Feng Yan argue that vision transformers hit a wall in spatial reasoning for reasons built into the architecture itself. These models excel at recognizing what is in an image but fail at tasks such as mental rotation, and the usual explanation blames limited training data. The authors instead frame spatial understanding as preserving the algebra of physical transformations inside the model's embeddings.

Formalized that way, the problem for non-solvable groups, such as rotations in three dimensions, is at least as hard as a known complete problem. That problem belongs to a circuit class beyond what constant-depth transformers can compute. Their Latent Space Algebra benchmark backs the theory: transformer representations degrade sharply as the compositional depth of transformations grows. The gap, they argue, is one of logical depth, not data scale.
arxiv-2601-03148:
Alireza Maleki, Ebrahim Bedeer, and Robert Barton propose a more spectral-efficient version of LoRa. LoRa is the long-range radio modulation used by low-power Internet of Things devices. Their SE-LoRa scheme packs more data into the same bandwidth. The optimal joint detector for it is too complex to use. So they design a successive interference cancellation detector. It exploits the frequency-domain shape of the dechirped signal, and costs about as much as ordinary LoRa detection.

In simulations over Rician fading channels, the scheme raises spectral efficiency a lot. Gains run to several hundred percent at low spreading factors, and over a thousand percent at the highest one tested. At the same time, error performance stays within three decibels of conventional LoRa, at a reference error rate. The trade-off makes much denser use of scarce spectrum practical for LoRa networks.
arxiv-2601-03248:
Juntong Ni and four co-authors teach language models to reason about time series that live on networks, where what happens at each node depends on its neighbors. Such spatio-temporal reasoning supports high-stakes choices in traffic systems, power grids, and disease spread, yet most prior work chased prediction accuracy rather than reasoning. The team builds ST-Bench, a benchmark with four task types, from cause analysis to in-context forecasting, synthesized through a network-based multi-agent pipeline.

Their model, STReasoner, fuses time series, graph structure, and text for explicit reasoning. A new reinforcement learning algorithm rewards exactly the gains that come from using spatial information. Experiments show accuracy gains from seventeen to one hundred thirty-five percent over baselines, at a tiny fraction of the cost of proprietary models, with robust generalization to new settings.
arxiv-2601-03348:
Constantin Schrade, Sujit Manna, and Mathias S. Scheurer explain an experimentally observed superconducting diode effect, where current flows more easily one way than the other, in a device built from the altermagnet Mn3Pt. Altermagnets split electronic bands by spin while keeping zero net magnetization, a combination that suits time-reversal-breaking superconducting effects. The authors build a theory for the effect seen in a Mn3Pt-superconductor heterostructure.

Through symmetry analysis and model calculations on a breathing kagome lattice, they show how the material's spin textures split the bands without any magnetization, even with spin-orbit coupling included. Proximity coupling across the interface then turns that splitting into a diode effect. The angular dependence of the critical current, they note, can serve as a probe of the magnetic order itself.
arxiv-2601-03748:
Dario Maio and Stefano Rizzi argue that huge retrieval-augmented systems should split their corpora using ideas from data warehousing. Large systems hold millions of documents and tens of millions of chunks, and they scale through sharding and approximate search. Those tricks are fast but organize collections bottom-up by similarity, with no conceptual plan for where retrieval should happen.

The authors propose combining semantic grouping with multidimensional splitting, a borrowing from online analytic processing. Dimensions like time and firm context would govern which part of the corpus a query searches, while embeddings handle local likeness inside each part. The dimensions already exist implicitly in most systems, they note. Making them open could improve both speed and the relevance of what workplace search returns.
arxiv-2601-03848:
Jens Otten and Torsten Schaub present automated theorem provers for the first-order logic of here and there, a logic used as the foundation of answer set programming semantics. They build provers two ways: a native sequent calculus designed for this logic, and an embedding of it into intuitionistic logic that reuses existing calculi. The native proof search is optimized with free variables and skolemization.

Combining the embedding with sequent, tableau, and connection methods for intuitionistic logic gives several prover variants. All are evaluated on a large benchmark set of first-order formulas. The comparison lays a foundation for building more efficient provers for this logic, which matters because here-and-there reasoning sits underneath tools that verify and explain answer set programs.
arxiv-2601-04348:
Diego Revilla and three co-authors build a better compressor for 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes in a 2026 arXiv paper. Splatting renders new views of a scene in real time from millions of soft three-dimensional blobs, but the files are large, which hurts cloud storage and streaming. Recent progressive codecs shrink them with masking and simple quantization, yet treating each feature number separately wastes the correlations inside high-dimensional feature vectors.

Their codec, SCAR-GS, replaces that step with residual vector quantization, which compresses features as vectors in successive coarse and refinement layers. An autoregressive entropy model, guided by a multi-resolution hash grid, predicts how likely each next index is, so the transmitted layers squeeze down efficiently. The design aims at high fidelity per bit while keeping the progressive, stream-friendly structure.
arxiv-2601-04748:
Xiaoxiao Li asks whether a team of agents can be folded into one agent carrying a toolbox of skills, and where that bargain breaks, in a 2026 arXiv technical report. Multi-agent systems buy modularity with heavy communication overhead. Viewing skills as internalized agent behaviours, a multi-agent setup can in principle be compiled into a single agent that selects skills instead of messaging colleagues. Preliminary experiments suggest the compiled version slashes token usage and latency while holding accuracy on reasoning benchmarks.

The scaling question is the catch. Drawing on cognitive science, Li proposes that skill selection has a bounded capacity like human choice. Accuracy holds steady as the library grows, then falls off a cliff past a critical size — a phase transition, not a slope. The driver seems to be semantic confusability among similar skills rather than raw count, and hierarchical routing, the trick human organizations use, partially restores performance.
arxiv-2601-04848:
Mariagrazia Iuliano and 5 co-authors demonstrate a quantum gate between two separate devices in a 2026 paper. Quantum networks link processing nodes by light, enabling modular computation, and gates between remote qubits can be performed by teleportation protocols. Those protocols need remote entanglement, local logic in each processor, and classical messages carrying measurement results between the nodes.

The team demonstrates an unconditional controlled-NOT gate linking two far-apart diamond qubit devices. Carbon-13 nuclear spins serve as the control and target qubits, while nitrogen-vacancy electron spins enable the photonic link. A working remote gate is a core building block for distributed quantum computers, where many small processors act as one larger machine.
arxiv-2601-04948:
Junchi Gu and 8 co-authors teach a humanoid robot to roller skate in a 2026 paper. Walking and running make humanoids strike the ground repeatedly, causing high impact forces, joint wear, and poor energy use. Skating instead slides continuously, exploiting body inertia with minimal kinetic energy loss, so the authors fit each robot foot with a row of four passive wheels.

Their system, SKATER, synthesizes skating kinematics built around the swizzle, the scissoring leg motion skaters use for propulsion. Deep reinforcement learning helps turn those motions into stable control. Efficient gliding locomotion could extend humanoid range and battery life, and it shows how human sports techniques can inspire robot movement beyond stepping and running.
arxiv-2601-05048:
Relativistic jets blast from black holes across the universe, yet analytic models of how individual particles launch remain scarce. Jibril Ben Achour, Ileyk El Mellah, and Eric Gourgoulhon develop such a model for a rotating Kerr black hole in a 2026 paper. Simulations reproduce jets well, but they do not directly explain the trajectories of the accelerated charged particles that build the jet and emit its radiation.

The authors take an electrogeodesic approach, tracking charged particle paths shaped by both gravity and the black hole's magnetosphere. Their framework aims to describe jet launching analytically rather than only numerically. A clear particle-level picture would help interpret observations of jets from active galaxies and X-ray binaries with simpler, testable theory.
arxiv-2601-05248:
Zhuoyang Liu and 13 co-authors give robot world models a hushed form of step-by-step thought in a 2026 paper. Such models tie what a robot sees and is told to what it does next. Spelled-out thought can help them. So can a guess at the next view. But words and shots both cost time ere a move, and robot work can not spare that time. Words also fail to catch facts of the touch-and-push world that are hard to say.

Their frame, LaST0, thinks in the model's own code space, in a chain that tracks both place and time. The chain does its work with no words to write and no shots to draw. That cuts the lag, and it frees thought from the word trap. Swift, rich thought of this kind could let robots work through mess and change at the pace real tasks demand.
arxiv-2601-05448:
Xingchi Yan and 2 co-authors describe, in a 2026 imaging paper, a photoacoustic tomography method that uses no ultrasound sensors at all. Photoacoustic imaging shines pulsed light into tissue and listens for the sound waves that light creates. Normally, arrays of pressure transducers record those waves.

Here, an array of light beams records the waves by being deflected by them. The measured signal equals the Radon transform of pressure gradients, a mathematical summary taken along lines. An optimization step rebuilds the pressure gradient field, and a Galerkin method then recovers pressure itself. The all-optical design promises higher sensitivity and less signal distortion than transducer-based systems.
arxiv-2601-05548:
Jeonghyun Kang and 2 co-authors introduce KEEM, a 2026 dataset for keeping long-term conversation memory accurate and emotionally aware. Chat systems that remember users often just accumulate facts, which creates conflicts and stale pictures of a person's state. KEEM instead generates fresh, integrated memories at update time.

Each memory preserves essential facts while adding emotional context and causal links between events. That richer record should help a system track how a user is doing now, not just what was said earlier. The authors argue that combining emotional and essential information supports deeper empathy in open-domain conversation. The dataset offers a generation-based alternative to simple accumulation or rule-based memory edits.
arxiv-2601-05648:
Haoran Wang and 7 co-authors present OKR-CELL, a 2026 foundation model that joins single-cell gene data with written cell descriptions. Single-cell RNA sequencing reveals how cells differ, but models trained on it often ignore rich individual profiles and suffer from noisy multi-modal data.

Two ideas drive the design. A retrieval-augmented workflow uses large language models to enrich each cell's text description with open-world knowledge. A robust alignment objective then weighs sample reliability, orders training from easier to harder, and uses momentum contrastive learning to resist noise. Pretrained on millions of cell-text pairs, the model reportedly led on six tasks, including clustering, cell-type annotation, and cell-text retrieval.
arxiv-2601-05848:
Nate Gillman and 8 co-authors introduce Goal Force in 2026, a way to tell video generation models what to accomplish using physical forces instead of words or target images. Text goals are often too abstract for physical nuance, and goal images may be impossible to specify for dynamic tasks. Humans, by contrast, think in pushes, hits, and falls.

Users define goals through explicit force vectors and intermediate dynamics. The video model trains on synthetic causal primitives such as elastic collisions and falling dominoes, learning to propagate forces through time and space. Despite that simple training, it reportedly generalized zero-shot to complex real scenarios, including tool use and multi-object causal chains. The authors release data, code, weights, and demos.
arxiv-2601-06248:
Hadron decays can hunt for exotic neutrino behavior, show Carlos Henrique de Lima and 3 co-authors in a 2026 paper. They study light particles that love neutrinos and could strengthen neutrino self-interactions beyond the standard model. If such a scalar particle exists, neutrinos can emit it during decays.

Emission turns two-body decays into three-body ones and distorts the measured energy spectra in characteristic ways. The authors compute these effects for charged pion decay and nuclear electron capture, including loop corrections needed to cancel divergences. They then project the sensitivity of the planned PIONEER experiment and assess the current and future reach of BeEST. The spectral tails at low energy give upcoming experiments a powerful probe of these light mediators.
arxiv-2601-06348:
Training models across hospitals without moving patient data is the promise of federated learning. Siqi Zhu and 1 co-author stress-test a leading method under class imbalance in a 2026 paper. Real deployments face label noise and data that differ sharply between sites, which can quietly wreck performance.

Their work reproduces RHFL+, a method designed for clients with different model architectures, alongside all its benchmark rivals under one evaluation framework. They extend it to real medical imaging datasets covering breast imaging and histopathology. A new implementation uses NVIDIA's production federated framework, making the codebase modular and deployment-ready. Ablation studies, noise comparisons, and scaling tests with growing client counts check whether the method's robustness holds up in practice.
arxiv-2601-06548:
Quadrics are the shapes cut out by a square-form rule in space. Mohamad Maassarani fills a gap in their lore in a 2026 math paper. The smooth, full-rank case was worked out long ago by two men of note. The worn case, where the form drops rank, was left open.

Maassarani counts the holes of these worn shapes in two coin types: with whole counts split as parts, and with counts in a two-part coin. Hole counts are the algebra way to log how a shape links and loops at each tier. The two counts, put side by side, fix the full count in whole terms. That ends the tale the old work began. It gives a full map of these shapes for use in shape lore and past it.
arxiv-2601-06948:
Zhuoran Tan and colleagues wrote a 2026 arXiv preprint. The work covers operational runtime behavior mining for Open-Source supply chain security. ArXiv posted the preprint in 2026 under its PAPERS collection. Open-source software (OSS) is a critical component of modern software systems.

Yet supply chain security remains challenging in practice due to unavailable or obfuscated source code. Consequently, security teams often rely on runtime observations collected from sandboxed executions to investigate suspicious third-party components. The work gives specialists a compact account of the problem and one proposed way to handle it.
arxiv-2601-07048:
Hunter McCoy and co-authors published a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint covers GPU-Accelerated ANNS. It appeared in the arXiv PAPERS collection for 2026. Approximate nearest neighbor search (ANNS) is a core problem in machine learning and information retrieval. GPUs offer a promising path to high-performance ANNS through massive parallelism and co-location with downstream applications.

But current GPU indices face three limitations: inability to update without full rebuilds. Lack of efficient quantization for high-dimensional vectors, and poor latency hiding due to data-dependent memory accesses. The preprint gives researchers a focused account of the problem and the approach the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07148:
Zhengxiang Wang and Zeyu Dong wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on how well AI models think about time. They set out a test called Time Puzzles. Each puzzle asks for a date. To find the date, a model must work step by step from clues. The test checks reasoning that loops back on facts more than once.

Each puzzle mixes two kinds of clues. Some clues pin a fact to a set point in time. The rest link dates by the rules of calendars from more than one culture. A puzzle can have one valid date or more than one. A program builds the puzzles, so the test can stay fresh and hard to game. New sets can be made on demand for checks that go on over time. The test gives teams a clean way to grade time-based thought in a model.
arxiv-2601-07848:
A large Project 8 team studies cyclotron signals inside resonant cavities. Many tests in physics need a grasp of signals from single particles in complex field setups. That grasp is key for cyclotron radiation emission spectroscopy, called CRES. In CRES, charged particles give off such signals, and the tone of the signal tells their energy. Project 8 aims to measure the neutrino mass with this technique. Their 2026 preprint studies the signals in cavities.

A resonant cavity shapes the signal in ways free space does not. A wrong read of those shapes would skew the energy result. Neutrino mass is tiny, so the experiment needs extreme precision. To map the signals with care is core work, not a side detail. The paper serves those who build CRES detectors. It supports a measurement that could settle a basic open question about neutrinos. The full chain must be exact.
arxiv-2601-07948:
Yannick Molinghen and colleagues teach local search to choose its own neighborhoods with reinforcement learning. Reinforcement learning has recently been used to improve combinatorial optimization. Its value inside local search metaheuristics is comparatively underexamined. Local search improves solutions by exploring nearby variants, called neighborhoods. Which neighborhood to use, and when, strongly affects results. Their 2026 preprint studies learning methods for that choice.

A learned policy could adapt neighborhood choice to the problem's current state. That beats fixed schedules and hand-tuned rules. The authors come from Belgian universities and a research center focused on applied optimization. Better local search helps routing, scheduling, and planning problems everywhere. The paper serves optimization scholars. It tests reinforcement learning in a workhorse method rather than a showcase problem.
arxiv-2601-08048: Laurin Gray, Katherine Rhode, and Luisa Rebull measure how fast very young stars spin. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses sharp optical spectra from the Hydra tool on the WIYN telescope. The targets are T Tauri stars, which are sun-like stars in their first few million years. The team reports projected spin speeds for 54 stars in IC 5070 and 99 stars in IC 348. Those speeds, plus size estimates, show how young stars shed or keep angular momentum as they form.
arxiv-2601-08148: Seokho Ahn, Sungbok Shin, and Young-Duk Seo enrich user profiles for recommender systems with language models. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that rich profiles of user preferences are key to better recommendations. Yet there is no consensus on how best to build or use such profiles. The authors revisit recent profiling approaches along four dimensions: knowledge base, preference indicator, impact range, and subject. They then fold semantic profiles into a knowledge graph. The aim is recommendations grounded in structured preference knowledge, not just click history.
arxiv-2601-08348: RotCurves is a Python package for fitting galactic rotation curves at high redshift. The package paper is authored by A. Nestor Shachar, A. Sternberg, S. H. Price, and many collaborators. Rotation curves trace how fast stars and gas orbit at each radius in a galaxy. At high redshift those curves test how early galaxies and their dark matter halos formed. Efficient modelling matters because distant galaxy samples are growing fast. A shared open package lets teams fit curves with the same tools and compare results across surveys.
arxiv-2601-08448:
Kexin Bao and four co-authors split few-shot class-incremental learning into static and dynamic stages. Their 2026 arXiv paper targets systems that must recognize new classes from few examples over time. The core tension is the stability-plasticity dilemma: keep old knowledge while gaining new knowledge.

Their framework, Static-Dynamic Collaboration, assigns the two stages distinct roles to balance that trade-off. Freezing what should stay stable and adapting what should move can cut forgetting. Systems that learn in the field, from scanners to wildlife cameras, face exactly this dilemma. The stage split offers a clean pattern for continual learners with scarce new data.
arxiv-2601-08848:
Zihe Zhang and four co-authors build a chat model to help care for kids in their first three years. Most care bots give the same tips to all. But young kids vary in mood type. One child is shy and slow to warm. The next is bold and quick to fuss. Good care advice should fit the child in front of you.

Their model is called PediaMind-R1. It uses a classic mood frame from child study, tied to a graph of facts on mood types. It then tunes its tips to the mood of the child. A reader in child health tech gets a care bot plan with a clear base. It ties each tip to a known view of how young kids differ.
arxiv-2601-09448:
Ioannis Stylianou and four co-authors let a language model turn words into sound settings. Their 2026 arXiv paper maps natural language prompts to equalizer settings for audio playback. Sound control becomes a conversation: a listener can ask for warmer or brighter sound in plain words.

Standard equalization is static and manual, and it adapts poorly when mood, place, or company changes. The authors tune their system to population-level taste rather than one listener. That choice aims at settings that please most users out of the box. The work points toward audio gear that takes requests the way a good DJ does.
arxiv-2601-09548:
Lucas Michel, Pierre Mathonet, and Naïm Zénaïdi refine a basic tool for carving up real space. Their 2026 arXiv paper, bound for the Journal of Symbolic Computation, studies cylindrical algebraic decompositions. Such a decomposition splits space into cells on which a given semi-algebraic set is a clean union.

A decomposition adapted to a set may use far more cells than needed. The authors pursue minimal and minimum versions, asking for the leanest decompositions possible. Fewer cells mean faster algorithms in robotics, verification, and computer algebra. The paper pushes further on when the smallest decomposition can be found and described.
arxiv-2601-09648:
An unnamed team describes PyMUSAS, a framework for tagging the meanings of words across languages. The 2026 arXiv paper mixes rule-based and neural methods, trained on silver standard data. Its target framework is USAS, the UCREL Semantic Analysis System, which sorts words into semantic fields.

Word sense disambiguation has been tested heavily with WordNet, BabelNet, and the Oxford Dictionary of English. For USAS, no broad open evaluation existed beyond lexical coverage or a single language. PyMUSAS aims to close that gap with a hybrid tagger. Reliable semantic tags support corpus studies of how language is used across cultures.
arxiv-2601-09748:
José Ulloa Araya documents, in Spanish, how to run a full Bitcoin node on Linux. His 2026 arXiv paper covers installation, configuration, and day-to-day use. The work starts from compiling the source code by hand and ends with full synchronization with the network.

The paper walks through the technical phases and the main files Bitcoin Core creates. It also tests, empirically, what key settings do: txindex, prune, dbcache, maxmempool, and maxconnections. A full node verifies the chain without trusting anyone else. A clear Spanish guide widens who can take part in that verification.
arxiv-2601-10248:
Laura Grigori, Daniel Kressner, Nian Shao, and Igor Simunec fix a flaw in fast Krylov tools. Krylov tools build a base for a large space step by step. A random form builds that base fast and with a sound shape. But it warps a key link.

The matrix it yields should match the one from the plain path. In the random path, it oft does not. That gap can slow or spike the solve. The team give a fix that brings the link back. They show it on eigenvalue tasks and on functions of a matrix. The fix keeps the speed and the shape.
arxiv-2601-10448:
Naeem Ramzan and Muhammad Tufail Khan grade the look of ultra HD video sent in layers. New codecs pack video into a base layer and a boost layer. Here the base is VVC, a new top codec. The boost is LCEVC, a light add on layer. A third form uses AI in the codec.

Grades from math scores miss how a clip looks to a viewer. The team use human grades. Viewers rate each form on the same clips. That gives a true rank of the layered forms. The work helps broadcasters pick a form that looks best per bit.
arxiv-2601-10548:
Xizhi Liu, Jie Ma, and Tianming Zhu study a core question in extremal graph theory. Given a small graph F, they ask how many copies of F a large graph can hold as induced subgraphs. The inducibility of F is the best share such copies can reach as the host graph grows. Turán graphs, built from balanced complete parts, are the test case here.

The paper works out the inducibility for this family of graphs. The result adds exact values to a problem where few are known. Such values show which host shapes pack the most copies of a pattern. The work will interest readers in combinatorics who study how local patterns fill large networks.
arxiv-2601-10648:
Joseph Rowan, Buu Phan, and Ashish Khisti study a one-shot coding problem for broadcast messages. One source is encoded a single time and sent to many decoders. Each decoder hears the message through its own noisy channel. The send counts as a success if at least one decoder recovers the source well enough.

The setup uses codebook diversity, meaning the decoders do not all rely on the same codebook. A distortion limit sets how close a recovery must be to count. The problem fits alerts and beacons that must reach someone, anyone, on the first try. The analysis helps engineers judge when one broadcast is enough.
arxiv-2601-10748:
