In open nets, joint air move joins liquid entry, giving a seeming speedup. These results show lack of frame move does not promise a tube account. Their results show an edge link between flow and frame, and stress the need to rethink flow in soft packed nets, including froth, gels, and living flesh.
arxiv-2602-15448:
Pinto and Avelino tackle the cosmic smoothing puzzle: linking change of a lumpy cosmos to a smooth spread. They work with links. They study f(R,T) models with f(R,T) = R + F(T), where R is the Ricci scalar and T the trace of the energy-momentum tensor.

This provides a simple, theoretically consistent realization of nonminimal matter-gravity couplings, recast as General Relativity minimally coupled to a modified matter Lagrangian. With K-poles as a toy model, they probe the ratio of the mean of F to F at the mean of T. When F is a curved map of T, this ratio stray from unity, hinging on speck counts. They show that the guess that this ratio matches unity mostly gives an off account. Dust in these theories shows a non-vanishing proper pressure. Their findings stress the weight of counting for smoothing in cosmic models.
arxiv-2602-15648:
Kreber and colleagues tackle inverse design, where many parameter choices can yield the same output and the forward step itself needs a numerical simulation. Discrete parameters and extra constraints block direct gradient methods, so the team turns to diffusion models. Their approach relaxes the design space into a continuous grid form, where gradients flow through the forward simulation by implicit differentiation.

A diffusion model trained on that relaxed space serves as a prior for plausible designs. Sampling by guided diffusion uses gradients from an objective set at inference time. Samples are then backprojected into the original parameter space. The team applies the method to composite material design with a linear finite element forward model. It proposes diverse designs within one percent relative error of target bulk modulus in two and three dimensions. It can also minimise material density at the same time through a multi-objective loss.
arxiv-2602-15948:
Klein and colleagues improve superconducting nanowire single photon detectors by adding a thin silicon cap. Niobium titanium nitride detectors already perform well from X rays to the mid infrared. Surface oxidation and uneven sub five nanometre films have held back quality.

A silicon capping layer blocks oxidation and raises the superconducting transition temperature. With the cap, films as thin as three nanometres still superconduct at three kelvin. Patterned wires then carry higher critical current, and the saturation plateau stretches from visible light out to the near infrared. Timing jitter stays below fifty picoseconds even for wide wires and large areas, so wider wires can ease fabrication and widen the useful temperature range.
arxiv-2602-16248:
Jan Hendrik Bruinier and coauthors study intersections of special cycles on Shimura curves and their link to Siegel Maass forms. They show that the generating series counting pairs of geodesics on a compact Shimura curve gives coefficients of a non-holomorphic Siegel modular form. That form is a theta lift of the constant function. That result retrieves and generalizes counting results of Rickards via the Siegel-Weil formula.

More generally, they study the genus-two theta lift of Maass forms on this Shimura curve. They prove a Fourier-Taylor expansion in terms of generalized Whittaker functions. They also provide a geometric interpretation of all Fourier coefficients of these theta lifts. It uses averages of geodesic Taylor coefficients over special cycles. The paper thus connects counting of geodesic intersections to modular forms and theta lifts.
arxiv-2602-16348:
Arshyn Altybay and Michael Ruzhansky study a heat equation driven by a mixed local-nonlocal diffusion operator whose coefficients vary in space. They begin with the Cauchy problem for bounded measurable coefficients with uniform positivity, with initial data in a first-order Sobolev space. There they prove weak solutions exist and are unique in the natural energy space, and derive an a priori energy estimate.

The work then extends to strictly positive distributional coefficients and compactly supported distributional initial data, handled through Friedrichs-type smoothing. Under suitable moderateness assumptions on the regularising nets, the authors prove very weak solutions exist and are unique up to negligible perturbations of admissible regularised forms. Finally, under convergence assumptions on the regularised terms and initial data, with preserved uniform positivity, they prove the very weak solution agrees with the weak one.
arxiv-2602-16448:
The Euclid Collaboration assesses how galaxy intrinsic alignment choices affect the cosmos. The Euclid galaxy survey will tightly constrain cosmology, but unbiased results demand characterisation and mitigation of systematic effects. Galaxy alignments are among the dominant contaminants of weak lensing probes.

Tests cover models for Euclid's first data release three-by-two-point work using mock data vectors. It compares the two most used models, non-linear alignment and tidal alignment tidal torquing, with several variations. Three perspectives are combined: constraining power on cosmological parameters, and bias when the analysis model differs from the model that generated the synthetic data. The third is degeneracies between alignments and photometric redshift nuisance parameters. Among the models, the redshift-dependent tidal alignment tidal torquing model gives the most flexible description with power similar to simpler models, suitable for the first data release.
arxiv-2602-16648:
Uddalok Nag and co-authors propose a route to much stronger superconducting diode efficiency near a shift between two superconducting states. The trick is to pick settings where, before the system turns normal under rising supercurrent, it flips into a varied superconducting order for one current direction but not the other. That works because critical current hinges keenly on superconducting order.

Detailed sums for a bilayer superconductor in an in-plane magnetic field show the effect plainly. That system hosts both standard BCS order and orbital FFLO order as field strength varies. A sharp peak in diode efficiency appears in the FFLO state near the shift, from interplay of the two orders. Diode efficiency measures thus offer a fresh probe of the BCS-FFLO shift under field and current.
arxiv-2602-16848:
Roshan Kaundinya and co-authors derive step-by-step expansions for generalized steady states in nonlinear mechanical systems. The forcing is moderate and does not repeat in time. Such states were only recently shown to exist. The paper builds a numerical code yielding explicit approximations that can be refined without limit. No early convergence period is needed. That contrasts with direct numerical integration. Its convergence is hard to gauge or even undefined for short, transient forcing.

When at least the linear part of the motion laws is known, the new code beats available data-driven neural-net techniques. Those techniques predict forced response in structural dynamics. In a fully equation-driven setting, computations prove faster than direct integration of forced nonlinear finite-element models. Beams and shells are the test cases. Structural dynamicists get a faster, more assessable route to forced response under realistic, non-repeating loads.
arxiv-2602-16948:
Matthias Christandl, Omar Fawzi, and Ashutosh Goswami show fault-tolerant quantum state preparation with constant space cost for quantum low-density parity-check codes. Preparing a quantum state on a noisy computer necessarily disturbs a share of qubits proportional to gate noise, no matter the protocol. Prior constructions required polylogarithmic cost. The new work improves that to constant overhead.

The advance adds to the toolbox of fault-tolerant schemes for circuits with quantum input and output. The authors build safe interfaces that lower the level of protection for quantum LDPC codes. When info is encoded in multiple code blocks, the interfaces hold constant space cost. In the decoder construction, gradual lowering of encoding level alongside growth in simultaneously decoded blocks circumvents bottlenecks to error pileup and cost.
arxiv-2602-17148:
Aoi Araoka led a two-author paper building cellular automata from Yang-Baxter maps over finite fields. The authors define R-matrices through a map on the field and work out the exact tests for that map to meet the Yang-Baxter equation. In characteristic two, those tests simplify in a striking way, the paper shows.

A full search for one-to-one solutions in small fields turned up counts that explode as the field order grows. Running the resulting automata under helical edge rules revealed a steady match between time period and field order. The authors guess that this period rule holds in general, with full proofs for the two smallest cases, and they argue that one-to-one maps are essential to the pattern.
arxiv-2602-17348:
Charles-Edouard Bréhier led a four-author team studying an explicit exponential integrator for heat-type stochastic partial differential systems driven by Riesz noise. The noise is Gaussian, white in time, with spatial linkage given by a Riesz kernel. Given the equation's coefficients behave, the authors prove strong error bounds and show how the convergence rate depends on the exponent in the Riesz kernel.

Number tests in one and two spatial axes confirm the error results. The paper thus gives workers a studied, direct method for Riesz-noise random equations, with error rates tied plainly to the noise kernel's power rather than left as lab lore.
arxiv-2602-17548:
Henri Truong led a five-author team behind a 2026 arXiv paper on steering tiny man-made swimmers with light. Controlled motion in fluids is hard at that scale, since heat motion scrambles paths fast. Micro-scale particles have made progress, but giving nano-scale particles enough push to beat Brownian motion has stayed a major issue for tiny-scale science and medicine.

The team shows fuel-free motion that can be switched on and off and tuned, in gold-silica Janus nanoparticles driven by light. Single particle tracking gives direct proof of self-thermophoresis, clearly setting active motion apart from thermal noise. The particles form a minimal yet robust photothermal system for studying active matter and steering it at the nanoscale. The work offers a light-driven route to controlled transport with no fuel at all.
arxiv-2602-17948:
Yu Bai and team probe the trade-off between clean scores and adversarial toughness in deep learning, whose geometric origin stays elusive. They use Symmetry-Breaking Dimensional Expansion as a controlled probe: expanding input images by inserting constant-valued pixels, which breaks shift symmetry and lifts clean scores by cutting parameter overlap.

That accuracy gain costs toughness against iterative white-box attacks. A test-time mask projection resetting the inserted pixels to their training values shows the weakness stems almost entirely from the inserted dimensions. That reset neutralizes the attacks and restores toughness, revealing that the model gains scores by creating sharp boundaries, steep loss gradients, along the added axes. The findings give a concrete geometric account of the accuracy-toughness paradox. Tuning deepens the basin pull to lift scores but erects steep walls along added degrees of freedom. That creates fragile sensitivity to off-manifold nudges.
arxiv-2602-18048:
N Naveen Mukesh and Debraj Chakraborty introduce a geometric method for online transfer identification of a deterministic linear time-invariant system. At the start, abundant data exist from a system that is similar but not identical to the true system. Early data from the true system are too thin to pin it down precisely, so several candidate models stay consistent with what has been observed.

Their method picks, at each instant, the model closest to the similar system among those consistent with current data. As more data arrive, the chosen model drifts away from the initial similar system and eventually converges to the true system once the data grow informative. Numerical examples show the incremental transfer identification paradigm working, with models identified from minimal data solving the pole placement problem.
arxiv-2602-18148:
Yannik Mahlau and four co-authors built BONNI, a design tool for tiny light devices that mixes wide search with sharp local tuning. Their 2026 paper tackles a classic bind: wide searches crawl, while local searches get stuck in merely good shapes. BONNI pairs Bayesian search over neural-network stand-ins with gradient-aware steps that pick the next shape to try.

On a ten-layer mirror stack, BONNI reached a mean color error near four and a half percent, beating an older sixteen-layer design at near eight percent. It also handled a wide-band taper and a crystal waveguide junction. The paper shows the mix dodges local traps while keeping the speed of gradient methods. For nanophotonics designers, that means better shapes with fewer costly simulations.
arxiv-2602-18248:
Pietro Sittoni and four co-authors built Neural-HSS, a lean neural solver for partial differential equations. Their 2026 paper starts from a practical bind: learned solvers run fast once trained, but making large, high-quality training sets and training the models costs heavily. The design borrows the structure of Green's functions for elliptic equations.

Built on hierarchical semi-separable matrix structure, the architecture uses few parameters and is proven data-efficient across a broad class of equations, exact even when data are scarce. It links naturally to Fourier neural operator layers and convolutions. On a three-dimensional Poisson problem over two million grid points, it beat baselines in the low-data regime, and it also learned equations from electromagnetism, fluids, and biology. The work points to cheaper, wider use of learned PDE solvers.
arxiv-2602-18348:
Matheus Camilo da Silva and three co-authors open up the black box of AutoClustering. Their 2026 paper notes these systems automate algorithm choice, hyperparameter tuning, and pipeline building through meta-learning over dataset meta-features, yet their recommendations are hard to justify. The hidden influence of meta-features limits trust, bias checks, and smarter feature design.

The team first reviews twenty-two existing methods and sorts their meta-features into a structured taxonomy. They then apply Decision Predicate Graphs to gauge feature importance inside meta-models from selected frameworks, and SHAP tools to explain single clustering decisions locally. Findings show steady patterns in which meta-features matter, expose structural weaknesses that can skew recommendations, and offer concrete guidance for more interpretable AutoML design.
arxiv-2602-18448:
Shubham Kulkarni and three co-authors build a benchmark for auditing insurance calls. Their 2026 paper notes administrative phone work drains roughly one trillion dollars annually from United States healthcare, with over five hundred million benefit verification calls handled by hand in 2024. No public benchmark existed for this phase-aware call auditing.

The team introduces INSURE-Dial: fifty de-identified AI-initiated calls with live representatives, averaging seventy-one turns. One thousand synthetic calls mirror that workflow. Calls carry a phase-structured schema: patient identification, IVR navigation, coverage status, medication checks, and agent identification. Each phase gets labels for information and procedural compliance. Two tasks are defined: phase boundary detection and compliance verification. Per-phase scores are strong for small baselines, but end-to-end reliability is limited by span-boundary errors. Full-call exact segmentation on real calls stays low, exposing a gap between fluency and audit-grade evidence.
arxiv-2602-19048:
Comparing immersive videos is harder than comparing flat ones. Xizi Wang, with three co-authors, studies that problem in 2026. A 360-degree scene spreads information in every direction. Comparison then demands heavy interaction. Good techniques exist for flat media, but immersive comparison remains underexplored.

Borrowing the sliding idea from flat media, the authors build five techniques. They span virtual reality and flat screens, using slide, toggle, and side-by-side views. A study with twenty users probes perceptions, strategies, and workflows. Users must switch approaches across scenarios. No single technique fits all cases. Slide views in both virtual reality and flat screens rate as the most flexible and most liked. The findings guide future immersive comparison design.
arxiv-2602-19448:
Sangchul Oh derives bit-string chance patterns for parts of random pure states and of depolarized random states via the Dirichlet distribution. The exact Beta distribution emerges as the universal statistical law for random quantum states, giving one finite-size account of full-system, subsystem, and conditional statistics. Under depolarizing noise, these patterns scale and shift with noise strength, opening a gap in their support caused by noise.

Notably, random states show exact conditional self-similarity: subsystem bit-string chances conditioned on outcomes of the complementary subsystem match the full-system distribution. This hidden scale invariance lets the full-system statistics be rebuilt from the marginalized Beta distribution by post-selection, and it survives depolarizing noise. The results expose a basic symmetry of Hilbert space and aid validation of random circuit sampling.
arxiv-2602-19648:
Directional data show up wherever observations sit as unit vectors or points on a hypersphere surface. Giuseppe Gismondi and two co-authors propose a local version of statistical depth, a center-outward ranking of data, for classifying such data. They apply the local depth inside the DD-plot, a Depth-versus-Depth plot, as the sorting tool.

An extensive simulation study plus two real-data examples test how well the local-depth classifier performs. The examples move the method from simulated settings to real observations. Readers get a compact method note on using local depth for depth-based sorting of directional data.
arxiv-2602-19948:
Language models are increasingly used for mental health support, yet standard safety tests often miss risks that build up over a therapeutic conversation. A 2026 arXiv paper by Ian Steenstra and four co-authors builds a framework for automated clinical red teaming of such systems.

The framework pairs AI therapists with simulated patients driven by dynamic cognitive-affective models, then scores the simulated sessions against a quality-of-care and risk ontology. Applied to alcohol use disorder, with several AI agents and a clinically validated set of patient personas, large-scale simulation reveals serious safety gaps. These include endorsing patient delusions and failing to de-escalate suicide risk. A dashboard validated with engineers, clinicians, and policy experts lets stakeholders audit the otherwise opaque behaviour of AI therapy.
arxiv-2602-20048:
Coding agents work in contexts far larger than any human can search by hand, yet they often miss architecturally critical files. A 2026 arXiv paper by Tarakanath Paipuru, working alone, names that failure the Navigation Paradox and tests a graph-based remedy, CodeCompass.

Agents fail not because context is too small, the author argues, but because navigation and retrieval are fundamentally different problems. Across hundreds of automated trials on dozens of benchmark tasks in a production FastAPI repository, graph-based structural navigation through CodeCompass reaches near-perfect completion on hidden-dependency tasks. CodeCompass is a protocol server exposing dependency graphs. That result sits well ahead of vanilla agents and lexical retrieval. Yet an adoption gap appears: many trials with graph access make zero tool calls, and agents need explicit prompting to use the tool consistently. The bottleneck, the paper argues, is behavioural alignment, not tool availability.
arxiv-2602-20148:
Two-dimensional superconductors are a fine platform for studying vortex matter. Their stiffness is low. They screen applied fields weakly. A 2026 arXiv paper by Jordan T. McCourt and seven co-authors explores vortices in a thin superconductor on the complex oxide KTaO3.

Several regimes of vortex-mediated transport appear and are studied. Switching patterns in the data are traced to birth of single vortices. Study of that regime shows quantum tunneling of vortices. At higher temperatures, quantum tunneling gives way to heat-triggered motion. Magnetic field dependence reveals rich charts of switching currents, traced to different layouts of pinned vortices. The paper thus maps vortex motion from quantum tunneling through heat-triggered motion in a single oxide platform.
arxiv-2602-20348:
Feeling unheard often comes not from lacking a voice but from gaps between expression and listening, including across language and culture gaps. Earlier empathy VR work often told a story, leaving users as watchers. Yibo Meng and four co-authors present 52-Hz Whale Song, an embodied virtual-reality experience that uses metaphor and role shifts to place users inside the gap.

Built on the real 52-Hz whale, whose calls go unanswered, the experience follows a three-act arc from failed talk through agency to mediation. It stands for no specific social group, using the whale as a lens on failed talk. A small mixed-methods study with thirty people suggests people took other views more and felt less social distance in immigrant-related situations. The work offers design lessons for empathy VR systems built on embodied metaphor and role shifts.
arxiv-2602-20548:
Spiking neural nets promise low-power brain-like computing, but they stay weak against hostile attacks. Shuai Wang and nine co-authors show that neurons sitting near their firing edge are the key weak point in directly trained spiking nets. Such neurons set the ceiling on how strong an attack can be, and they flip state under tiny nudges. The paper proposes Threshold Guarding Optimization to fix this flaw.

The method adds loss terms that push membrane voltages away from firing edges, which thins gradients and lowers the ceiling on attack strength. It also adds noisy spiking neurons, shifting firing from fixed to chance-based and cutting flip odds under tiny nudges. Broad tests in standard hostile settings show the method greatly lifts the toughness of directly trained spiking nets, pointing toward safer brain-like computing in real use.
arxiv-2602-20648:
How clients perceive the therapy alliance shapes counseling outcomes, yet capturing them is hard. Anqi Li and five co-authors note that post-session questionnaires burden clients and arrive late, while computational methods give coarse scores without readable reasons and miss full context. Their system, CARE, predicts multi-part alliance scores and generates readable reasons from therapy transcripts.

CARE builds on the CounselingWAI data set, enriched with over nine thousand five hundred expert reasons, and fine-tunes with reason-boosted training on a LLaMA instruct backbone. Tests show CARE beats leading language models and narrows the gap between counselor and client alliance ratings, reaching over seventy percent higher correlation with client ratings. That training further lifts accuracy, and CARE's reasons pass both automatic and human checks. Applied to Chinese online therapy sessions, CARE surfaces alliance challenges and offers useful insights for mental health care.
arxiv-2602-20948:
Finding a few outer eigenpairs of a huge symmetric matrix is a core numerical task, and restarted Lanczos is the standard tool. Angelo Casulli, Daniel Kressner, and Nian Shao propose a new restart strategy in this 2026 arXiv paper: Lanczos with compression. Instead of polynomial filtering, the method compresses the Krylov subspace with rational approximation, giving up the Krylov decomposition structure in exchange.

Compression stays compatible with later Lanczos steps, and the whole algorithm still uses only matrix-vector products. Theory shows the compression error is small against unrestarted Lanczos, so convergence barely suffers, a guarantee that standard implicit restarting, including Krylov-Schur, lacks. Numerical tests show compression can beat Krylov-Schur in matrix-vector product count.
arxiv-2602-21048:
Hermitian forms have a classical spectral theory, and tensor analogues demand one too. Isaac Dobes introduces higher-degree t-Hermitian forms in this 2026 arXiv paper, a tubal analogue of ordinary Hermitian forms of arbitrary degree. Multilinear matrix multiplication plus the t-product on third-order tensors shows these forms correspond exactly to odd-order tubal tensors with a symmetry called t-conjugate partial symmetry.

Fourier transforming along the tubal mode splits each form into classical Hermitian forms, which characterizes positivity through the spectra of Fourier slices. That yields a tubal spectral theorem for higher-degree forms. The paper then studies contractions along the tubal mode, characterizing when they preserve positivity and bounding the positivity margin of the resulting classical forms.
arxiv-2602-21248:
Streaming graph splitters scale well but suffer when stream order is hostile, cutting many more edges than in-memory methods. Linus Baumgartner, Adil Chhabra, Marcelo Fonseca Faraj, and Christian Schulz narrow that gap in this 2026 arXiv paper with BuffCut, a held streaming splitter joining ranked holding with batch-wise multi-step placing. A bounded rank hold delays poorly based calls and steers node review order.

High-nearness batches are built by slotting the top-ranked held nodes, in effect winning back nearness from the stream, then placed by multi-step splitting. Against the strongest ranked-holding base case, BuffCut cuts about twenty-one percent fewer edges while running nearly three times faster on over eleven times less memory. Against the next-best held method, it cuts about sixteen percent fewer edges at modest extra cost.
arxiv-2602-21748:
Matthew Frosst and two co-authors study stellar bar formation with 145 simulations of disc galaxies in live and static dark matter haloes. They use the bar growth timescale to gauge how disc structure and motion regulate the onset and rate of secular bar formation. The work extends prior work to thicker, more turbulent discs like those seen at high redshift. Revisiting stability criteria, they find the growth timescale, expressed in orbital periods, follows a power law with each criterion.

In Milky Way-like discs in live haloes, bars form within a Hubble time when the disc mass fraction, Ostriker-Peebles ratio, and Efstathiou-Lake-Negroponte parameter meet thresholds. Discs with higher velocity dispersion grow bars later, and a new empirical relation describes all live-halo models. Bars in static haloes grow about half as fast as in live haloes and need far greater disc instability to form at all.
arxiv-2602-21948:
Bahrul Ilmi Nasution, Mark Elliot, and Richard Allmendinger tackle synthetic tabular data, the mixed number-and-category tables used across research and industry. The leading generator of this kind struggles to balance realism against privacy risk. Bayesian versions exist but usually rely on costly sampling methods that store large numbers of weights.

Their method, GACTGAN, instead fits a Gaussian approximation to the weights of the standard conditional tabular generator, cutting costs after training. In their tests it preserves table structure and statistical patterns better than the baseline while leaking less private information. The paper offers it as a simpler, workable route to Bayesian synthesis for tabular data.
arxiv-2602-22448:
Mess usually harms superconductivity, but under the right conditions it can help. Andrzej Ślebarski and Maciej Maśka study swapped-atom mess in Remeika-type quasiskutterudites, joining susceptibility, resistivity, and heat-capacity tests with small-scale modeling. They show rising mess creates local superconducting pockets with a transition point above the bulk transition.

Both the local and bulk transition points vary unevenly with dopant amount and track closely with entropy curves measured against mess. The largest entropy peaks line up with the widest gap between local and bulk transitions, proving mess a thermodynamically set knob. The work reframes mess from flaw to tuning knob.
arxiv-2602-22748:
Matti Lyko studies boundary rules for elliptic operators on non-compact edged shapes through uniform K-homology, a variant tuned to large-scale shape. The work builds relative uniform K-homology and shows boundary rules define classes in relative and plain versions, based on how regular the boundary rule is assumed to be.

An index map is then defined and studied, blending coarse inside data with second-layer edge data. As a test, take a spin shape with product structure and steady positive scalar curvature at the edge. There, the Dirac class maps close to a uniform version of the higher rho-invariant at the edge. A spread-out APS-index theorem of Piazza and Schick follows in this uniform setting.
arxiv-2602-23048:
Abhishek Sadhu and one co-author expose a code-based weakness in standard quantum relay rules. Quantum net security rests on relay rules built for random, known noise, but the authors show that in hostile settings this premise creates weaknesses for compute-limited relay nodes.

The standard BBPSSW distillation rule repeatedly cleans error flags rather than linkage, leaving a low-truth state while checkup metrics show perfect settling. The checker cannot detect the hostile influence through best-guess fit methods, which are blind to compute-limited watchers. To fix these weaknesses, a proposed Code-based Net Stack, built around a trapdoor verification rule, uses secret coin flips to restore working steadiness without needing channel mapping.
arxiv-2602-23148:
Nitin Gupta and three co-authors ask how one plan can serve a whole family of related tasks. Older methods do this with hand-built rules and a clear model of how each action changes the world. Newer transformer planners such as PlanGPT and Plansformer skip that model and predict lists of actions straight from data, which takes large data sets and can drift off course over long plans.

The authors instead train a model to learn the rules of change itself, predicting each next world state in turn and rolling those states forward into a plan. Tests across several problem areas and state encodings, including graph-style encodings of relations, show this route beats direct action prediction on new, unseen cases. It does so with far fewer training cases and smaller models, and the paper is an extended version of a short paper accepted at ICAPS 2026.
arxiv-2602-23248:
The legibility tax is the target of Yegon Kim and one co-author. As language models grow more capable, it matters that weaker systems can check their outputs. Prover-verifier games improve checkability, but they lose accuracy against a baseline trained only for correctness. That gap is the legibility tax.

The fix decouples correctness from checkability. A solver model is first trained purely to maximize correctness. Then a separate translator model learns to turn the solver's solutions into checkable form while keeping the solver's answers. To support this split goal, the authors formulate a decoupled prover-verifier game whose equilibria correspond to faithful, checkable translators, offering checkability without paying the accuracy price.
arxiv-2602-23448:
Sayan Bhattacharya and two co-authors improve the classic minimum-degree spanning tree problem: given a connected graph, find a spanning tree whose largest node degree is as small as possible. The problem is NP-hard. Since the early 1990s, the best method added at most one to the optimal degree but ran in roughly O(mn) time.

The authors break that three-decade runtime barrier. Their deterministic algorithm still adds at most one to the optimal degree but runs in roughly O(mn to the three-quarters) time. Their method rests on a novel use of the blocking flow paradigm. The result is substantive progress toward a long-standing open question, posed repeatedly in the literature, on whether the old runtime bound could be beaten.
arxiv-2602-23548:
Sanjay Manoj and one co-author tackle the continuous p-dispersion problem in three dimensions. The task: place a fixed number of points in a compact set so the smallest distance is as large as possible. That distance counts both point-to-point gaps and point-to-boundary gaps. The problem serves facility placement, network design, sampling, and particle simulation.

Optimal solutions are NP-hard, and prior algorithms focused on two dimensions. The authors introduce an almost-everywhere differentiable optimization model and a global optimization algorithm. It handles convex and non-convex polyhedra under any metric in three-dimensional Euclidean space. Generalizing two-dimensional techniques, the method uses orientation, linear-algebraic projections for point-to-face distances, and ray casting for point-in-polyhedron tests. Validation against analytical optima and empirical benchmarks shows close agreement with optima and gains over benchmarks.
arxiv-2602-23648:
Yao Li and nine co-authors present FAVLA, a force-adaptive fast-slow vision-language-action model for contact-rich robotic work. Force and torque feedback can greatly improve such models. But most methods fuse all modalities at one frequency, ignoring mismatched sensor rates.

Vision-language-action pipelines also run action chunks open loop between costly updates. Unified-frequency fusion then responds late to impacts, stick-slip, and force spikes. FAVLA splits slow perception planning from fast contact-aware control. A slow vision-language model runs at fixed low frequency, encoding modalities and predicting force variation. A fast action expert then runs at variable high frequency on latest force data. A force adapter injects high-frequency force features into expert layers, with execution adapting to predicted force variation. Tests on contact-rich tasks show FAVLA beats baselines on reactivity and success, especially with smaller contact force.
arxiv-2602-23748:
Takumi Hidaka and two co-authors study how electrons move between molecules trapped with light inside a small optical cavity. The 2026 paper uses an exact numerical method that tracks memory effects in the system, rather than simpler methods that treat those effects as small.

The authors find that forming polaritons, mixed states of light and matter, changes the transfer rate in clear ways. In strong coupling the rate levels off, a pattern missed by simpler methods. Adding how molecular charge shifts with nuclear motion creates a three-way link between electrons, vibrations, and light. That link makes the rate rise and fall unevenly as coupling and cavity tone change, through interference between several transfer paths.
arxiv-2602-23948:
Marco D'Elia and two co-authors tackle high-modularity graph partitioning with tools borrowed from natural language processing. The 2026 paper presents Clique-TF-IDF, a framework that represents each vertex by the maximal cliques it belongs to, in the manner of a term-document matrix. It then applies term-frequency weighting and machine learning clustering.

Dense clique structure thus becomes the signal that guides partition choice, rather than edge counts alone. Tests show results comparable to or better than leading partitioning algorithms, whether or not the number of partitions is fixed in advance. The authors note that the same idea extends beyond partitioning. Other hard combinatorial problems with efficiently enumerable substructures could gain AI-driven solutions by the same route. That route turns dense local patterns into features for global optimization.
arxiv-2602-24148:
Keito Suzuki and seven co-authors present HumanOrbit, a method that generates a full orbit video around a person from a single input image. The 2026 paper notes that adapting image diffusion models to multi-view synthesis often yields views that disagree with each other and with the person's identity. Recent video diffusion models produce photorealistic, prompt-consistent results.

HumanOrbit treats multi-view generation as video generation, synthesizing continuous camera rotations around the subject with geometrically consistent novel views that preserve appearance and identity. A reconstruction pipeline then turns the generated multi-view frames into a textured mesh of the person. Tests validate the approach for multi-view generation, and reconstructed models show superior completeness and fidelity over leading baselines. They offer a route from one photo to a usable three-dimensional human model. In short, one photo now gives a full turn. The turn is smooth. The win is clear.
arxiv-2603-01748:
Davide Bizzaro and Luciano Serafini learn world models whose hidden states are simple true-or-false bits. Their 2026 work targets planning and symbolic reasoning, where Boolean states plug in cleanly. A world model predicts how a scene evolves, and past designs kept bits informative by rebuilding inputs or by contrast tricks.

Their method, DWMR, drops both crutches and learns from a prediction loss plus crafted penalties. Penalties push the bits toward high entropy and mutual independence, so each bit carries fresh signal. A locality rule favors sparse changes when an action occurs, which matches how real states shift. A new training scheme also steadies learning through discrete roll-outs. On two structured benchmarks, the models learn sharper states and transitions than rebuild-based rivals.
arxiv-2603-01948:
Yan Wang, Chen Zhang, Lanyun Zhu, and colleagues predict before surgery which Parkinson patients will gain from brain stimulation. Their 2026 model, PreSight, uses only data available before the operation takes place. Imaging signals are subtle and patients vary a lot, which makes per-patient forecasts hard.

PreSight fuses clinical priors with MRI scans and deformation-based morphometry, which maps local brain shape change. A patient-specific weighting module adjusts how much each brain region counts for that person. The model outputs calibrated, decision-ready predictions with explanations at the patient level. On a two-center cohort of hundreds of subjects, it beats clinical, imaging-only, and combined baselines. Accuracy stays high on both internal checks and an external center test, with ablations crediting each main part.
arxiv-2603-02148:
David Woodruff and Samson Zhou define a new streaming problem in this 2026 paper. A large table of numbers arrives one row at a time. At each step, a method must give a compact summary that fits the rows seen so far. The summary should stay close to the best low-rank fit. It should also change little from step to step, a cost called recourse.

The authors bound how much change is needed for two levels of accuracy. A loose target needs only modest change over time. A tight target needs more, and they improve the bound for whole-number data. They also prove a floor: some change is unavoidable for any method. Tests back up the theory with real performance checks.
arxiv-2603-02248:
Sungho Park, Joohyung Yun, Jongwuk Lee, and Wook-Shin Han improve table and text search in this 2026 paper. Questions often need facts split across a table and nearby passages. Early fusion glues each table row to its passages ahead of time, adding clutter. Late fusion fetches pieces alone and can miss key context.

Their system, HELIOS, blends both styles in three steps. First it links fine pieces of tables to passages as edges. Next it grows that link web around the pieces a query needs most. Last, a language model reasons over the grouped stars to handle sums and multi-step questions. On a standard benchmark, recall and ranking quality rose sharply over prior best models.
arxiv-2603-02548:
Sheng Ye, Zhen-Hui Dong, Ruoyu Fan, and colleagues rebuild 3D scenes with meaning from few photos in this 2026 paper. Robots need semantic maps, knowing what objects are, not just their shapes. Older methods demand dense photo sets and per-scene tuning, which limits real use. Their framework, SemGS, works feed-forward from sparse views.

Two branches extract color and semantic features, sharing early layers. Shared layers let meaning borrow texture and structure cues from appearance. A camera-aware attention step models how viewpoints relate geometrically. Features decode into paired Gaussian blobs that share geometry but keep separate attributes. Rendering those blobs yields semantic maps from brand-new viewpoints. A smoothness loss keeps regional labels coherent. Benchmarks show top performance with fast inference and broad generalization.
arxiv-2603-02748:
Hanpeng Liu, Yaqian Li, Zidan Wang, and colleagues give vision-language models eyes that adjust to the question asked. Their 2026 framework, iGVLM, attacks a bottleneck in current systems: fixed vision encoders that describe an image the same way for every task. Fine-grained questions often need specific visual cues that a static summary misses.

The design keeps a frozen branch that preserves the encoder's general visual skill. A second, dynamic branch reshapes features under the instruction using adaptive normalization, shifting focus without breaking prior knowledge. The authors also built MM4, a controlled probe of consistency across many queries and instructions. Across language backbones, the add-on steadily improved instruction sensitivity, suggesting a plug-in path from passive seeing to active reasoning.
arxiv-2603-03448:
An instrument science report from the team behind Hubble's Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph updates how sensitive its echelle modes are. Those gratings spread starlight finely across ultraviolet wavelengths, and turning raw counts into true fluxes depends on sensitivity curves measured in orbit. The 2024 report re-derives the curves for observations taken after the instrument's 2009 servicing mission repair.

The standard candle is a well-studied white dwarf star, G 191-B2B, whose expected brightness comes from the newest CALSPEC models. Those models shifted standard star fluxes by a few percent depending on wavelength, enough to matter for precision work. Alongside the new throughput curves, the team released updated blaze shift coefficients and echelle ripple tables. The report documents each procedure in detail so observers can trust and reproduce the calibration.
arxiv-2604-00248: Taechoyotin and Acuna introduce REM-CTX, a reinforcement-learning review system that adds auxiliary context, such as figures and outside research signals, to manuscript text. It trains an 8-billion-parameter model with group relative policy optimization, pairing a quality reward spanning several aspects with two correspondence rewards that tie reviews to that context. Across computing, life, and physical science papers, it posts the highest quality among six baselines, beating larger commercial systems. Ablation tests show the two rewards complement each other, while criticism scores move against other metrics during training.
arxiv-2604-00348: Hakim and Agrawal propose making gray swans, plausible unobserved extremes, from the observational record, via gradient descent with a differentiable model. Minimizing the loss yields perturbed initial conditions giving a measurable outcome under size constraints. They turn Hurricane Fiona (2022) into a Sandy outcome: a Sandy track, warm core, and minimum pressure over 20 hPa lower than Sandy's. Extratropical perturbations matter more than hurricane ones, driving merger of a trough and the hurricane. Four Atlantic hurricanes yield swans, though the core goes unresolved and probability stays unknown.
arxiv-2604-00448: Brand, Gay, and Licata examine Morse diagrams under the connect sum of open books. A diagram of this kind codes a mapping class on a surface with boundary. It also fixes an open book decomposition of a three-dimensional manifold, and with it a contact structure. The paper looks closely at negative stabilisation and extracts a diagram test for overtwisted contact structures. When the open book pages are one-holed tori, the authors sort all diagrams that belong to one fixed decomposition.
arxiv-2604-00848: Benjamin Smith reviews and replicates a debiased estimator for many-variable regression by Javanmard and Montanari, where penalized fits like the LASSO add bias. The debiased fit restores a normal limit shape, so tests and intervals built from it are valid. He reruns part of the original simulations and real-data work, adding the desparsified LASSO, and finds good coverage and Type I error control. The projection fit wins power when signals are weak, while the original method holds up better when variables correlate in complex ways.
arxiv-2604-00948: Zhai and team develop a meshfree physics-guided neural network method for two-phase flow with moving edges, where two non-mixing fluids with different traits meet at a shifting edge. They address set edge motion, with speed plainly given, and flow-driven motion, set by the flow's speed field. Patched deep networks and space-time sampling in each zone power the method. The framework recasts the problem as a least-squares fit over rule, edge, and initial gaps, with strict estimate analysis via the Reynolds transport theorem.
arxiv-2604-01148: Saha and colleagues present BugScribe, a language-model approach linking user bug reports with app execution data to infer accurate observed behavior, expected behavior and steps to reproduce. A component-specific grounding strategy gives the model the context per report part, guided by a quality model. Tested on 48 bug reports from 26 Android apps with built ground truth, BugScribe beats the original reports and three language-model baselines. It improves steps-to-reproduce quality by 44 to 82 percent and observed/expected behavior quality by 4 to 35 percent.
arxiv-2604-01248: Ji and Piasecki trace the origin of the covariant Wigner operator as a quantum amplitude in QCD. The Wigner function encodes links among quarks, antiquarks, and gluons, yet its meaning stays subtle because of its quasiprobabilistic nature and negativity. Building on a Koopman-von Neumann-Sudarshan Hilbert space view of classical mechanics, they build a Koopman account of the quark Wigner operator. The operator proves isomorphic to a phase space spinor, so the Wigner function keeps its amplitude reading even relativistically and clarifies negativity and parton functions.
arxiv-2604-01348: Wu and colleagues argue that reasoning models waste know-how buried in past solution traces, which record how to reframe a problem, pick an approach and check or backtrack. Their Reasoning Memory system chops trajectories into subquestion-and-subroutine pairs, building a store of 32 million procedural entries. At test time the model states its subquestion and pulls matching subroutines inside its reasoning trace, reasoning under those priors. Across six math, science and coding benchmarks it beats document, trajectory and template retrieval, improving over no retrieval by 19.5 percent.
arxiv-2604-01948: Tagani, Fakhredine and Autieri chart how a field switches on quantum anomalous Hall conduction in a d-wave altermagnet on a Lieb lattice. Altermagnetic order splits spins by momentum without net magnetization, giving spin bands at X and Y valleys. The field breaks valley symmetry at zero total magnetization, so each valley shapes topology, with Chern numbers set by field and bandwidth. Berry curvature analysis finds gapped phases with total Chern numbers plus or minus 1, split by gap closings in valleys, offering fast magnetic control near the semimetal phase.
arxiv-2604-02048: Sugiura and colleagues build Jagle, the largest Japanese multimodal post training set, with about 9.2 million instances. English sets aggregate pools, but that path fails there, where sets are limited in scale and coverage. Instead the team gathers data and generates pairs through generation, translation and rendering. A model at 2.2B scale trained with Jagle beats InternVL3.5-2B on ten Japanese tasks, no more than five points from Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct. Combining Jagle with FineVision lifts English scores over FineVision.
arxiv-2604-02248: Kar and colleagues predict survival risk from data held by separate parties without pooling it. Their Bayesian vertical federated frame lets each client model one data type with a Bayesian neural net while a server merges mid level features. Privacy noise on client features guards against leaks during training. Against single type and pooled baselines it lifts ranking by up to 0.02 in C-index, staying robust under strict privacy budgets while reporting uncertainty.
arxiv-2604-02448: Dey and team review fundus image sets for diabetes eye care with a data centric lens. Auto finding and grading with deep learning can ease doctor burden but suffers scarce, narrow, uneven labeled sets. The review tests sets across binary sorting, stage grading, lesion finding and multi disease screening, and sorts them by size, access and label type. A recent dataset case study shows broader building issues, and the review flags missing standard lesion labels and over time data, with advice for future sets.
arxiv-2604-02548: Shahzad and four colleagues build a dataset of vulnerable code examples tied to CAPEC attack patterns and CWE weakness descriptions, a resource current datasets lack. They generate the snippets with GPT-4o, Llama and Claude models, and the three models agree closely, with codes at 0.98 cosine similarity. The final set holds 615 CAPEC snippets in Java, Python and JavaScript for training vulnerability detectors.
arxiv-2604-02848: Hasegawa, Kanai and Oki study when multinorm one tori, geometric objects tied to finite étale algebras, count as rational. Results hinge on d, the greatest common divisor of the degrees of the factors. The tori are stably rational for d equal to 1, and the team gives a criterion for retract rationality drawn from earlier work. For d above 1, they give conditions under which retract rationality fails. They also extend Endo-Miyata and Endo results to tori splitting over Galois extensions whose Sylow subgroups are cyclic, and over dihedral extensions.
arxiv-2604-03048: Neumüller and three colleagues test whether mixing language models with static code analysis improves automated algorithm spotting in source code. The team compares combined and standalone methods across prompting strategies, filter patterns, and systematic name obfuscation. Mixing models with lightweight static analysis cuts required model calls by 72 to 98 percent, while lifting F1-scores by up to 12 percentage points. In-context learning with two examples balances results and runtime at F1-scores of 75 to 77 percent. Models still identify most programs when names are obfuscated.
arxiv-2604-03448: Tang and colleagues offer ExpressEdit, a free Photoshop plugin that edits stylized face expressions without the global noise and pixel drift of other AI tools. It changes one within 3 seconds on one home graphics card and works with native tools like Liquify. A set of 135 tags with stories and images supports retrieval-based story work.
arxiv-2604-03848: Ahmed Bchatnia and team studied blow-up for a 1D damped nonlinear wave equation with derivative nonlinearity and scale-invariant damping. For large smooth starting data, they proved the blow-up curve has a well-defined slope everywhere. A key step mapped the blow-up shape. The proof turns the wave into a first-order system, using the Sasaki take on the Caffarelli-Friedman method for cases with time-derivative terms.
arxiv-2604-04248: Floricel, Plosker and Sadikov build distance rules for completely bounded maps between operator algebras. Their Bures-Kuratowski metrics stretch the Bures metric from completely positive maps to the wider class, using a Kuratowski embedding based at one map plus a coordinate from regular models. Each metric splits the space into the Bures cone and an outside part, joined at the anchor. The authors then study Vietoris-Rips and Čech complexes of these spaces. They give tests for mixed simplices; the mixed shape follows from the two part metrics.
arxiv-2604-04648: Yu, Wu and Block tackle reward hacking in best-of-N sampling, where N responses are scored and the best is picked. Performance can fall as N grows, because selection favors responses exploiting reward flaws. Their approach, called caution, reverses curiosity: curiosity rewards prediction error as novelty, while caution penalizes it. The authors explore pessimism, using lower confidence bounds to avoid uncertain out-of-distribution actions. Caution trains an error model on typical responses and lowers atypical estimates. Tests show caution mitigates reward hacking in best-of-N sampling.
arxiv-2604-04748: Shang, Yu and Chen present RegGuard, a framework that adds rule-based legitimacy checks to optimistic rollups for regulated finance. It pairs a rule language, RegSpec, that codes regulatory limits in a form a machine can decide, with a check that spots mismatched state between layers one and two. A third part orders trades in a checkable crypto way, with a tiny breach chance. A 15,000-line prototype built on Optimism cuts failed settlements by over 90 percent, blocks spotted order rigging, and keeps 85 percent of base speed.
arxiv-2604-04848: Bürger extends an earlier result on survival chances in supercritical Galton-Watson processes, branching models used in population genetics. The addendum proves that a fractional linear lower bound for the negative binomial generating function, proved earlier only up to the extinction probability, holds for every value between zero and one. That wider range closes a gap in Theorem 4.6 of the 2026 Journal of Mathematical Biology paper, making the bound usable across the full interval.
arxiv-2604-05248: Goyal and three colleagues present a line to refit models with memory modules, giving learning on hardware. Standard methods like full tuning face fatal loss, as changing dense codes causes clash across tasks. Sparse Memory Tuning pins updates to a subset of knobs in open memory layers. They extend with slot choice based on Kullback-Leibler gap, picking odd-token updates against a background spread. Refit models acquire new knowledge with loss of held-out skills, proving sparse updates in practice.
arxiv-2604-05448: Teng and Choo study how foreign domestic workers in Singapore use a language-model chatbot for daily, non-clinical emotional support. Caregiving strain, language gaps, and isolation weigh on these workers. Interviews and guided chats point to three themes. The bot felt safe and validating, it coped with broken language, and workers reused it for reassurance, guidance, and company. The authors draw design lessons around safety, access, and flexible use.
arxiv-2604-05848: Park and four colleagues judge learner profiles for tutoring AI without waiting for lesson results. Their distinctiveness score rates how each learner stands apart from cohort peers by pairwise distance, needing no clusters, labels, or task tests. Learner-level profiles split students better than interaction-level ones, giving a handy pre-deployment check.
arxiv-2604-06448: Madabhushi and five colleagues build a graph-based anomaly detector for Prime Video microservices, linked services behind video streams. Load tests mimic spikes from Thursday Night Football and Rings of Power, yet miss quirks seen only in real traffic. Their system learns node-level graph embeddings from directed service graphs with a GCN-GAE model, flagging gaps between load-test and event embeddings. It spots incident services, and a synthetic injection test reports 96 percent precision, false positives under a tenth of a percent, and recall of 58 percent.
arxiv-2604-06648: The Euclid Collaboration presents an end-to-end pipeline for finding strong galaxy-galaxy lensing systems in Euclid's first quick data release. Starting from VIS catalogs, the pipeline drops point sources, cuts deflectors by magnitude, and filters artifacts into small image cutouts. A seed classifier plus morphology-balanced negatives trains a modified VGG16 model, refined over three rounds. Human grading of the top 4,000 candidates yields 441 Grade A or B systems, including 130 new ones, while the model recovers 740 of 905 known candidates in its top 20,000 predictions.
arxiv-2604-06848: Klurman and Mangerel prove a sharp mean value formula for bounded multiplicative functions and draw out several long sought gains. Their formula sharpens a twenty year old bound of Granville and Soundararajan for fully multiplicative signs, giving a firm floor for a weighted sum that falls slowly with size. When the function does not mimic the Liouville sign pattern, the fall rate can be pushed near the best possible pace. For a random sign function, they show the chance the sum dips below zero shrinks fast.
arxiv-2604-06948: Gholami tackles nonstationary wavelet phase gauging with tuned fitting. Seismic wavelet phase drifts in space and time from fading, spread, and tuning. Raising kurtosis and skewness pushes signals toward non-Gaussian or uneven zero-phase states, but window methods prove unstable. Gholami casts the task as tuned fitting solved by ADMM. He derives the first closed-form nearness tools for inverse kurtosis and skewness. Signed swaps reduce tasks to 1D root-finding, and tests on fake and real data show linear cost and calm.
arxiv-2604-07448: Paganelli and four colleagues ask when randomization helps Hamiltonian simulation. Their sparse-QSVT method treats large terms exactly and samples small terms at random, tracking error growth through block-encoding and QSVT steps. On random Hamiltonians built to favor randomization, gate counts fall up to tenfold for many-term, uneven cases. The edge holds only at moderate precision: near an error of ten to the minus three, deterministic methods win, and real chemistry structure likely favors them more.
arxiv-2604-07548: Munira and Manikonda analyze 210840 Google Play reviews of Character AI, tying each review to the app version live at posting. Ratings fluctuate across versions, with certain versions drawing stronger bad ratings. Theme analysis finds complaints cluster on tech glitches and errors, while a subset of reviews frames concerns in mental-health or habit-related terms. The findings show how overall ratings and voiced concerns vary across software rounds, showing the value of steady behavior and clear talk in changing AI apps.
arxiv-2604-07648: Mota investigates vacuum current density for a scalar field in dispiration spacetime threaded by flux. The background joins a cosmic string and a screw dislocation, giving a twisted geometry. From Klein-Gordon mode functions, the author evaluates the Wightman function for the current density. Beyond the azimuthal component of current around the defect, a nonzero axial component is induced by the structure. Both components are periodic in flux, depending only on its fraction. The screw dislocation regularizes the axial component at the origin and sets its size.
arxiv-2604-07848: Zhang and Cheng uncover a hidden assumption behind gradient-based task analysis in multi-task learning. Joint training sometimes helps a lot and sometimes actively harms, with no principled way to predict which. They show gradient conflicts reveal genuine task relationships only when tasks share training instances. Measured on disjoint inputs, apparent signals mix task relationships with distributional shift. The sample-overlap requirement turns sharply: below 30 percent overlap, gradient-task correlations look like noise, while above 40 percent they reliably recover known structure.
arxiv-2604-07948: Sipacheva proves that every countable-dimensional topological vector space over a suitable field has a closed discrete basis. The field may be a complete nondiscrete second-countable valued field, such as the real or complex numbers, or a finite field. The result gives a clean structural guarantee: however large the countable dimension, a basis can be chosen that is both closed and discrete. That combination matters because closed discrete sets behave well under topological operations. The short proof settles the existence question for this whole class of spaces.
arxiv-2604-08148: Kuntur and four colleagues offer a lightweight hybrid approach to clickbait detection using OpenAI semantic embeddings with six compact heuristic cues for style and information. To improve speed, vectors are reduced using PCA and tested with XGBoost, GraphSAGE, and GCN models. While simple feature design yields slightly lower F1-scores, graph models achieve competitive performance with much reduced run time. High ROC-AUC values further indicate strong discrimination power, supporting reliable spotting of clickbait headlines under varying decision thresholds.
arxiv-2604-08248: Ziampras, Qiao, and Haworth study parts in outside-lit protoplanetary disks: spirals and rings in 2D flows. Light from nearby massive stars can strip mass from such disks and shape their growth, but its motion impact on the disks is new in detail. They aim to study how uneven outside irradiation shapes the structure of such disks. They run 2D multi-fluid light hydrodynamics models of such disks under external irradiation with the PLUTO code, treating it as a flat flux with a simple heating rate.
arxiv-2604-08348: Illesca and three colleagues study SMC star cluster kinematics, using residual motions to disentangle perturbations. The SMC's motion behaviour remains challenging, tackled diversely by many authors. Observational evidence has grown for tidal perturbations from the Large Magellanic Cloud on the SMC, especially outward. Star clusters serve as kinematic tracers of the SMC. They analyse 36 clusters across regions: Northern Bridge, Southern Bridge, Wing/Bridge, West Halo, Main Body, and Counter-Bridge. From proper motions, radial velocity, and distance per cluster, they estimate Cartesian velocities in the SMC frame.
arxiv-2604-08448: Wanzare and sixteen colleagues release AfriVoices-KE, a speech dataset of about 3,000 hours across five Kenyan languages: Dholuo, Kikuyu, Kalenjin, Maasai, and Somali. Recordings from 4,777 native speakers mix 750 scripted hours with 2,250 hours of spontaneous speech, gathered by phone app across varied regions. Layered checks on sound quality and content accuracy support speech recognition and synthesis work for languages long left out of speech technology.
arxiv-2604-08648: Mishra-Sharma and three colleagues bring differentiable probabilistic programming to the gamma ray sky, targeting the long standing Galactic Center excess puzzle. Their differentiable forward model and likelihood use GPU acceleration to weigh a continuum of spatial shapes for the excess in one probabilistic fit, with variational inference over the large model space. Beyond gamma rays, the work showcases the method as a flexible tool for astrophysical data analysis.
arxiv-2604-08748: Abe and colleagues test Cherenkov Telescope Array Observatory plans for chasing GeV to TeV signals. Their target is binary neutron star mergers in observing run O5. Using mock merger samples with gravity wave finds and model based short gamma ray burst output, including off axis jets, they model observations with device response, sky tiling, and varying skies. A tuned plan makes about 5 percent of mock gravity wave linked short bursts seen, with jet and viewing angles driving whether they are seen.
arxiv-2604-08948: Hu and seven colleagues introduce TaxPraBen, the first benchmark built for language models doing realistic Chinese tax work rather than isolated language tasks. It combines ten standard application tasks with practical exercises graded against Bloom's taxonomy of learning levels. The field is knowledge-heavy and rule-bound, and general models show clear gaps there. Tests of 19 models find large gaps in scores: big closed-source models lead, Chinese models such as Qwen2.5 generally beat rivals in other languages, and a tax-tuned model improves only modestly.
arxiv-2604-09248: Sambale, Schulte, and Thaele study limit laws for the longest edges in empty region graphs. In such graphs, vertices are points, and an edge joins a pair when an associated region holds no other vertices. For graphs from a stationary Poisson process, they let intensity tend to infinity and track edge midpoints, transformed lengths, and directions. They prove the transformed process converges to a Poisson process, and the longest edge length in a window converges to a Gumbel variable, with explicit error bounds.
arxiv-2604-09648: Islam and five colleagues present TRACE, the first framework measuring exhaled carbon dioxide from free-roaming cattle by thermal video. No current system gives continuous, spatially resolved readings without touching the animals. TRACE segments carbon-dioxide plumes per frame and classifies emission flux per clip from mid-wave infrared footage. Gas-aware attention and temporal fusion capture breath-cycle dynamics. Against fifteen leading models on a farm thermal-gas dataset, it scores 0.998 mean intersection over union and tops every metric at once.
arxiv-2604-09848: Rosa da Silva and Rossi study two local-nonlocal systems on a domain split A and B. First, a local parabolic equation in A pairs with a nonlocal elliptic balance in B; then roles reverse. A nonlocal kernel moves mass across the interface, with Neumann boundary conditions in both. The authors prove solutions exist and are unique, show total mass is preserved and the parabolic part decays toward a constant elliptic solution. The coupled problem is also the limit of a purely parabolic problem as one component slows to zero.
arxiv-2604-09948: Zhu and Xu present a split-guided spatial-spectral Mamba for many-band image sorting, tackling mixed spectra and fragile edges. A spectral split network learns pure pixels and spread maps, handling pure-pixel shifts and splitting mixed pixels. Spread clusters drive tuned Top-K token picks for Mamba chains, and a split-guided Mamba module lifts token learning and order. A multi-task scheme learns pure-pixel-spread patterns and labels, giving sorting maps plus a spectral library. Tests on four sets show large gains over rivals.
arxiv-2604-10048: Raj, Jha, Anand, and Saha reframe conversational recommendation as structured decision-making. Most systems chase search scores or fluent replies instead of good recommendations. Their HARPO framework splits quality into relevance, diversity, satisfaction, and engagement, weighted by context. Tree-search reasoning guided by a learned value network then picks the best paths. Tests on ReDial, INSPIRED, and MUSE show steady gains in recommendation quality with strong reply quality.
arxiv-2604-10148: Randeep and Saha build a closed-form account of inflation with a derivative-coupled scalar field. In their model, gravity and the scalar field interact through the Ricci tensor times field derivatives. They estimate the scalar spectral index and tensor-to-scalar ratio for power-law, exponential alpha-attractor, Arctan, Hilltop, and polynomial potentials. Higher derivative terms from the coupling cause no singularity in slow-roll. For each potential set, the index and ratio values match ACT and Planck observations.
arxiv-2604-10248: Su and Fang model factory forecasts under shifting work conditions with a multi-head attention fusion network. Engines, turbines, and machines wear in their own ways as work shifts, making forecasts hard. Their method fuses three signal parts: a wear trend, discrete work states from grouping encoded as vectors, and leftover noise. BiLSTM networks capture time links, weighting time steps and sensor signals as needed. A fusion module joins the trend branch with state vectors to capture their links. Tests on a NASA data set confirm the method works.
arxiv-2604-10348: Gabarrete, Montoya, and Raudales derive the entropy vector field for a relativistic kinetic gas of free, spinless, massive, neutral bits on bound orbits in space-time. With dependence on orbit tilt, they model spinning and still gases around a Schwarzschild black hole. They analyze readings built from bit density, energy density, and main pushes, like the skew index and kinetic heat. Spinning and still cases differ sharply, most in far-out shape of skew, heat, and average pressure, showing angular spin in shaping free gases under strong gravity.
arxiv-2604-11148: Aksoy and two colleagues propose a compound integrated circuit protection system with light cryptography. Many methods protect integrated circuits from threats in the supply chain, such as excess and theft. Most prior methods are weak because they do not rely on proven secure rules. Earlier methods increase hardware cost and are open to removal and power attacks. The system uses a light cryptography method with logic locking and hardware obfuscation. Tests show secure designs from the tool have less hardware cost than earlier designs and resist existing attacks.
arxiv-2604-11248: Berdica and three colleagues evolve populations of Petri Dish neural cellular automata toward open-ended complexity. Standard systems collapse into frozen patterns or noise and depend heavily on settings, so their PBT-NCA algorithm rewards both past behavioral novelty and present visual diversity. The evolving substrate produces coordinated waves, spore-like clusters that colonize new ground, and shape-shifting structures with active interiors. This sustains complexity at the edge of chaos.
arxiv-2604-11448: Vergara studies p-variational capacity of condensers, where both plates come from one phase function via level sets. Restricting potentials to phase forms and applying the coarea formula reduces the problem to a level function. An energy weight governs it, combining phase gradient and level-set shape. He derives a formula for the reduced problem, builds an optimal profile, and bounds the capacity by fibered restriction. He bounds the energy weight, studies critical levels, and gives exact-reduction models, plus a tangential obstruction in the linear case.
arxiv-2604-11648: Coccaro, Schiavi, and Zaio present a hit filter to speed online track reconstruction at hadron colliders. Trigger systems must judge collision products fast, and rebuilding charged-particle paths in inner detectors is combinatorial, with run time growing with pile-up. The High-Luminosity LHC upgrade will raise hit counts and swell costs. Their convolutional-neural-network filter drops unneeded detector data and runs easily on accelerator cards. The paper covers the filter, weighs its impact, and discusses next steps.
arxiv-2604-11748: Chen and six colleagues present LangFlow, the continuous diffusion model matching discrete diffusion. Continuous diffusion excels at fast images, but prior language models lagged discrete rivals given sparse data. LangFlow links embedding diffusion models to Flow Matching via Bregman divergence. Its innovations are an ODE-based NLL bound, an information-uniform noise schedule motivating a tuned Gumbel scheduler, and revised training with self-conditioning. LangFlow rivals discrete models on perplexity measures, reaching 30.0 on LM1B and 24.6 on OpenWebText, and beats autoregressive baselines on 4 of 7 zero-shot benchmarks.
arxiv-2604-11948: Shen and five colleagues propose AILFM, an active imitation learning scheduler for large foundation model inference on 3D-stacked static non-uniform cache many-cores. Such systems offer bandwidth and locality but suffer severe thermal problems and uneven cache latencies from 3D networks-on-chip. Thread migration and voltage-frequency scaling face kernel diversity and system heterogeneity. AILFM learns near-optimal thermal-aware policies from Oracle demonstrations with minimal run-time overhead, accounting for core and kernel differences, and beating state-of-the-art baselines across diverse workloads.
arxiv-2604-12348: Goswami and two colleagues present PrivEraserVerify, one system for federated unlearning that joins speed, privacy, and a way to prove removal. Adaptive checkpointing keeps key past updates for fast rebuilding, layer-wise differentially private calibration removes a departing client's influence with little accuracy loss, and fingerprint checks let participants confirm removal without central control. Tests on image, handwriting, and medical data show removal two to three times faster than retraining.
arxiv-2604-12848: Yannis Voet and three colleagues fix bad systems in immersed finite element methods. Trimming in design tools merges or drops shape parts, creating tiny cut pieces. Tiny cut pieces wreck matrix health, needing fixes. The paper first sizes up the scaled matrix and shows where standard fixes fail. A robust deflation fix tailored to immersed methods is then put forth.
arxiv-2604-13348: Srivastava and three colleagues present CONCORD, a setup in which assistants that listen all the time work together without sharing raw speech. Only the owner's voice is kept, checked by speaker verification, leaving a one-sided transcript that guards privacy but leaves gaps. CONCORD fills needed gaps with place-and-time clues, gap detection, and short queries between assistants, limited by how the speakers relate. On a dialogue dataset across many domains it reaches about 91 percent recall in gap detection, 96 percent relationship accuracy, and 97 percent true negatives on sensitive disclosures.
arxiv-2604-13748: Ma and three colleagues forecast many series over time, where each series behaves differently. One model for all can miss the differences. A model per series can go wrong. Their framework groups series by out-of-sample predictive performance, not by similar representations. Assignments update from validation losses for point and probabilistic forecasts. A fallback returns to the global model when specialization fails to help. Traffic tests show gains without degradation when differences are weak.
arxiv-2604-13948: Xiao-Jing Gao, Yanfeng Ge, and Yan Gao propose a boron crystal, P63-B30, where a two-dimensional nodal surface coexists with several kinds of Weyl fermions. Time-reversal plus screw symmetry pins the nodal surface to one plane, while rotational symmetries protect double, type-I, and type-II Weyl points. Wide separation between surface and points lets each be resolved on its own, and surface states show Fermi arcs linking nodes of opposite chirality.
arxiv-2604-14048: Dai and Yang let feed-forward 3D reconstruction models improve themselves at test time without ground truth. Free Geometry masks some frames to build a self-supervised task, enforcing cross-view feature consistency between full and partial observations while preserving relations implied by held-out frames. Lightweight LoRA updates recalibrate a model in under 2 minutes per dataset, lifting camera pose accuracy by 3.73 percent and point-map prediction by nearly 3 percent.
arxiv-2604-14348: Liao studies how transit access shapes who shares city venues, using phone location data from nine Swedish cities and three American ones. Places draw a mix of visitors, measured by the birth backgrounds of their home areas, and transit catchment mix predicts visitor mix. The link holds only in the biggest metro areas; in smaller Swedish cities it fades once centrality, venue density, and catchment makeup are held fixed. Transit-diversity hotspots sit not in mixed venues but in quieter, less commercial spots with few other paths to mix.
arxiv-2604-14448: Almeida and eight colleagues present MARCA, a bilingual English-Portuguese benchmark for testing language models on web-based information seeking. Fifty-two hand-written multi-entity questions pair with hand-checked checklist rubrics that score answer completeness and correctness. Fourteen models run under two setups: a basic path with direct search and scraping, and an orchestrator path that splits tasks across delegated subagents. Orchestration often improves coverage, scores vary widely across models, and transfer between English and Portuguese proves uneven.
arxiv-2604-14848: Remlein, Esposito, and Avanzini ask when open reaction network behavior emerges from closed ones. Open networks model out-of-equilibrium chemistry via chemostats exchanging species, yet finite systems relax to equilibrium. Open-network behavior arises from closed networks under two conditions: fast reactions as exchanges, and abundant species acting as chemostats. Here, stochastic dynamics and thermodynamic structure, including entropy production and free-energy balance, emerge to leading order. The regime lasts up to a time proportional to the abundance scale, giving a test of how long closed systems act open.
arxiv-2604-14948: Berti, Polimeni, and Terracini study outward N-body paths driven by homogeneous Newton fields. Half-entire outward motions exist with given setup and course for many powers. Their approach minimizes a tuned action, treating hyperbolic, parabolic, and hyperbolic-parabolic regimes jointly. They derive refined series with higher fixes, lifting growth bounds. For hyperbolic-parabolic paths, linear cluster-center escape meets internal parabolic motion, stretching cluster spreading to general fields.
arxiv-2604-15048: Ahmed and four others propose GAT-QNN, a genetic framework for hybrid quantum neural networks. Hybrid networks combine classical learning with quantum circuits, but NISQ noise and large design spaces limit performance. GAT-QNN trains a macroCircuit by sampling microCircuits, reintegrating their parameters. After training, a genetic inference stage evaluates microCircuits with macroCircuit weights and selects top architectures. Backend-aware selection needs no retraining and can cut gates. On four-class MNIST, genetic inference gains 22 to 23 percent accuracy across backends.
arxiv-2604-15148: Liang and colleagues sharpen search-augmented reasoning with IG-Search, a framework that rewards each search step by information gain. For every step, the gain measures how much retrieved pages raise confidence in the gold answer versus random pages, judging the query itself. That signal flows back to query tokens through per-token advantage modulation in GRPO. Across seven question-answering benchmarks the method beats the strongest trajectory-level baseline by 1.6 points, and it still learns when every sampled trajectory fails.
arxiv-2604-15448: Pal and Kadioglu ask whether pre-trained embeddings built for mixed-integer programming can transfer to Boolean satisfiability. Mapping CNF formulas onto the same bipartite constraint-variable graphs lets them reuse the model with no design change or labeled fine-tuning. The vectors capture SAT structure well enough for unsupervised grouping and distribution spotting, a first step toward one shared code for optimization and decision problems.
arxiv-2604-15848: Mikkelsen and three colleagues present a phase-only time-reversal method for steering photonic nanojets, tight beams of light, without moving parts or amplitude control. A source placed at the target spot defines a phase pattern for a control line, fit for a spatial light modulator, that shapes the desired jet.
