Full-wave simulations show robust lateral and axial steering with tight subwavelength focus and low sidelobes. The design also survives moderate shape, making, and alignment errors.
arxiv-2604-16348: Hausladen and five co-authors study spatial anchoring and LLM agents for public planning, in an experiment with 200 participants. People learned about a green project from a street redesign, through text and images, or through narrated 360-degree video with spatial audio. They then engaged with LLM personas. The video condition improved recall and changed replies. They named winners more often, asked more project questions, and gave more positive feedback. The authors offer a framing of LLMs as dialogue partners, causal evidence, and a test method for cities.
arxiv-2604-16748: Ao proposes TriTS, a cross-modal framework projecting time series into time, frequency and two-dimensional vision spaces. Long-term forecasting struggles because real signals carry entangled dynamics that a purely one-dimensional view misses. Period-Aware Reshaping plus Visual Mamba bridges the gap at linear cost, modelling cross-period links as textures. A Multi-Resolution Wavelet Mixing module splits non-stationary signals into trend and noise for time-frequency localization. A streaming linear branch anchors stability, and fusion lets TriTS adapt across contexts with state-of-the-art results.
arxiv-2604-16848: Cui and colleagues open Tower, a benchmark for transmission-corridor point cloud cutting. Fine-grained cutting of corridor point clouds backs power-line checks, but data lack and long scenes limit progress. The dataset holds 661 scenes and two point four six six billion points, with a 22-class list and set splits. A global-local fusion framework joins a whole-scene branch capturing long-range topology with a local branch retaining fine geometry. Fused predictions pass geometric validation, and experiments show the benchmark's challenge and the framework's robustness.
arxiv-2604-17248: Lin and three colleagues propose VIBE, a framework for evaluating generative bias in large audio models through open tasks with human speech. Existing speech fairness benchmarks rely on synthetic speech and choice questions, giving only a fragmented view of fairness. Open tasks such as personalized recommendations let stereotypical associations surface without preset options and extend easily to new tasks. Testing 12 top models reveals systematic biases in realistic scenarios: both gender and accent cues trigger statistically significant distributional shifts, and bias magnitude depends strongly on the task.
arxiv-2604-17348: Yuliia Samoilenko and Valerii Samoilenko build soliton-like and peakon-like solutions of the Camassa-Holm equation with varying coefficients and small dispersion. Each solution pairs a shared regular background with a singular part carrying their own features, with the main singular term defined. In the one-phase case that term is pinned down and higher corrections are shown solvable, giving solutions as close as desired in the small parameter. Two-phase solutions are also built, with accuracy theorems and examples shown as graphs.
arxiv-2604-17448: Kumar and four colleagues introduce AVICA, a fully automated pipeline for calibrating big VLBI radio-telescope data sets in CASA. Data from the Very Long Baseline Array span three decades of formats, and the SMILE project alone needs some 5,000 sources done. AVICA automates prep work, choice of calibrator and antenna by fringe detection, and the full workflow, tracked live by its ALFRD system. Tested on 1,000 archival sources, it finished 978 of them in about 30 minutes each, proving blind calibration at scale.
arxiv-2604-17648: Olabisi, Mitra, and Agrawal introduce ThreadSumm, a multi-stage framework for summing up deeply nested threads, where tangled replies, quotes, and mixed topics defeat standard tools. The method first plans content by pulling discourse aspects and Atomic Content Units, then orders lines into thread-aware chains showing multiple views rather than one linear strand. A Tree of Thoughts search then drafts and scores multiple passage options, jointly tuning flow and breadth. The design yields summaries with clear logic beating current rivals.
arxiv-2604-17848: Hamada and Misumi test whether the confined phase of a large-N gauge theory with one adjoint Dirac fermion survives shrinking one spatial direction. They use a partially reduced twisted Eguchi-Kawai model on a small lattice, tracking the Polyakov loop and order parameters for volume independence. At N equal to 36 with periodic boundaries, the loop stays near zero for light fermions as the circle shrinks, supporting adiabatic continuity between large and small circles. With antiperiodic boundaries, by contrast, the loop shows a clear deconfinement transition.
arxiv-2604-18048: Díaz and nineteen colleagues present the first X-ray polarization results for the atoll source 4U 1735-44 from joint IXPE, NICER, and NuSTAR observations. Over 2 to 8 kilo-electronvolts they find a weak polarization signal of 1.4 percent at an angle of minus 29 degrees, with an upper limit at three sigma of 3.5 percent. The best-fit spectrum mixes disk heat, a Comptonized blackbody, and reflection. From reflection they infer a disk inclination near 40 degrees, like other atoll sources, where low tilt likely explains the weak signal.
arxiv-2605-00048:
Dechao Li and Yuhui Zhu build a hierarchical reasoning system for fuzzy inference. Restricted equivalence functions can measure how similar two fuzzy sets are. That makes them natural fuel for similarity-based approximate reasoning, a scheme that draws conclusions by comparing a new case with known ones. The authors set out to integrate the two and strengthen the inference that results.

They first characterize restricted equivalence functions built from a given aggregation function. They then examine the approximation quality of an existing reasoning method when equivalence functions are used. Finally they propose two hierarchical versions of that method, layered so that the explosion of fuzzy rules that plagues flat systems is efficiently restrained. The hierarchy keeps the reasoning tractable as rule bases grow.
arxiv-2605-00148:
Sergey Pirogov and Elena Zhizhina ask a stark question in mathematical population theory: can a local disaster wipe out a whole population? Their model is a contact process spread over a continuous space, where birth and death rates vary from place to place. Earlier work needed a balance between birth and death on average.

Here the authors drop that balance condition and study what follows. The change turns the model's core operator into one with a negative potential term. Even so, they prove that a family of stable long-run distributions still exists, and they describe those distributions with a Feynman-Kac formula. In plain terms, sharp local peaks in mortality do not, in general, force extinction.
arxiv-2605-00548:
Nadav Z. Cohen, Ofir Abramovich, and Ariel Shamir find a simple lever for controlling the broad look of images made by text-to-image diffusion models. These models turn white noise into a picture step by step. White noise has no structure, which gives variety but leaves global attributes like layout and color palette hard to steer or predict. The authors investigate which parts of the noise actually decide what.

Although all frequencies in the noise carry similar energy, the low-frequency parts mainly fix the image's global structure and color composition, while high frequencies fill in fine detail. So they manipulate only the low-frequency noise, using low-frequency cues taken from a guide image. The training-free method reconstructs those broad cues in the output while letting details emerge freely, preserving variety between samples. It adds minimal overhead, offering direct control over an image's structure and coloring.
arxiv-2605-00748:
Z. Rajabi Najjar, M. Ahmadi, and K. Azizi calculate the masses of particles that would contain a single top quark, a type not yet seen in nature. Their study covers several baryon forms, which combine three quarks, and meson forms, which combine a quark with an antiquark. Interest was partly sparked by hints near the top-antitop threshold reported by the CMS and ATLAS experiments.

Using two-point QCD sum rules, a method that links quark behavior to particle properties, the authors include effects up to a high level of detail. Several predicted masses sit slightly below the sum of their parts, which may point to weak binding. The results give search teams at the LHC and future colliders clear targets to test.
arxiv-2605-01048:
Zihao Yang and three co-authors argue that counterfactual prompting studies need meaning-preserving baselines before attributing effects to a chosen factor. Changing one factor, such as patient gender, also changes surface form, so the edit bundles two treatments. On a medical question dataset, changing gender flipped predictions at a rate statistically indistinguishable from simply rewording the input.

Their method compares target interventions against paraphrase effects with statistical testing. Revisiting a published perturbation analysis, most reported demographic and style effects dissipate. Only a small fraction of tests stay significant. On biography classification, the same method detects clearly marked gender bias in one direction. Per-sample metrics prove far more powerful than aggregate ones. Regression best shows which way the bias runs and how large it is.
arxiv-2605-01148:
Sheridan Feucht and eleven co-authors study how a Llama model reasons about cyclic concepts such as months, asking whether representational structure implies computational structure. The model's representations for cyclic concepts are circularly structured, yet the authors find it does not compute modular addition in the concept's own period. Instead it reuses a generic addition mechanism that operates independently of concept-specific geometry.

First the model adds the two inputs in base ten, then maps the sum back into cyclic space. Fourier features used for the sums have periods matching base-ten addition, not the cyclic period. A sparse set of neurons at one layer is reused across tasks, partitioned into clusters each computing a sum for a different Fourier period.
arxiv-2605-01248:
Goel and four colleagues train language models to search the web step by step before answering. Models that answer from memory alone struggle with hard, multi-hop questions, where the answer needs several rounds of evidence. Sparse rewards make this worse: a model only learns whether its final answer was right. Their framework, S3-R1, pairs synthetic training questions of middling difficulty with rewards for good intermediate searches as well as correct final answers.

A pipeline builds the training questions from existing documents and checks them by retrieval, keeping only questions that demand real digging. Rewarding the search path itself helps the model learn deeper, more careful strategies. In tests, S3-R1 beat earlier baselines and improved generalization on out-of-domain question sets by up to ten percent. The work shows that denser feedback can turn a shallow searcher into a steadier researcher.
arxiv-2605-01748:
Rahul Bothra and six co-authors run traffic engineering, the art of routing flows across a wide-area network, on a graphics processor. Operators must balance placing traffic well against reacting fast when demand shifts or links fail, and as networks grow the exact solvers slow past usefulness while fast approximations waste capacity.

GATE decomposes the optimization into pieces a GPU can grind in parallel, then iterates toward the provably best routing rather than settling for a near miss. The design grows more parallel as the network grows, accepts a wide range of fairness goals, and carries convergence guarantees, with near-best answers inside a bounded time. On production traces from two large cloud backbones it reaches near-optimal routings four to ten times faster than the state of the art. The result targets the control rooms of hyperscale networks, where minutes of routing delay cost real money.
arxiv-2605-01848:
Umut Dundar and Alptekin Temizel synthesize colonoscopy images at chosen stages of ulcerative colitis while keeping the patient's anatomy fixed. Making such staged images is blocked by entanglement: in real frames, disease texture and anatomy are woven together, so a generator told to worsen the disease tends to redraw the patient.

Their diffusion framework conditions on two separate codes, one for anatomy from an image encoder and one for severity from an embedder trained on the Mayo score's ladder. A purifier scrubs disease-correlated channels out of the anatomy code by cross-attention erasure. Both codes enter through a three-path attention scheme whose gates shift with resolution, matching the split between global shape and fine texture. A training-free steering signal from the ordinal codes walks severity up or down in one pass. On the LIMUC set, images hold up across stages and rebalance class counts for classifiers.
arxiv-2605-02048:
S Carmona-López and colleagues explore using superfluid atom currents in a shaken ring lattice to measure angular acceleration. The device is an atomtronic accelerometer, where ultracold atoms circle a ring that is shaken and also rotated from outside. Within the Bose-Hubbard model, the authors combine analytic and numerical work on when a net current appears.

A strong current arises when the shaking frequency hits an integer fraction of the Bloch frequency, and it nearly vanishes elsewhere. For single particles, resonance width shrinks with averaging time, setting a Fourier limit on sensitivity. Adding weak interactions between atoms lets simulations pass that limit. The result suggests interactions can improve inertial sensing, not just complicate it.
arxiv-2605-02148:
Amir Shee and P S Pal solve exact moments for a self-propelled particle held in a harmonic trap, where ease of motion differs by direction. Such a setup fits wheeled or gliding particles better than rods in a fluid. The authors work in two dimensions. They give closed forms for mean position and for mean squared displacement.

At high persistence, both measures reach a near-steady plateau with small fluctuations, then relax in a second step. The steady excess kurtosis is negative. It varies in a non-monotonic way with the ratio of two time scales. The particle is also pushed beyond the usual ring set by activity and confinement. The two-step pattern appears when sideways relaxation is slow.
arxiv-2605-02248:
Matthew Herman and Stephen Doro derive the population statistics of a multi-factor function from its Fourier transform alone. The function depends on many factors and is defined on a finite abelian group. Their main result, an annihilation theorem for coefficients and indices, states that each moment becomes a series whose terms each hold a fixed number of Fourier coefficients.

Surprisingly, the coefficient indices in each term sum to zero under group addition. That condition filters which terms can appear and can reveal deeper links among the variables that drive the function. The tools can serve analysis and design, or act as feasibility checks in search. For binary groups, the authors derive skew and kurtosis of a binomial distribution from the Fourier side, among other examples.
arxiv-2605-02348:
Muneeb Ur Raheem Khan debiases language model output at decoding time, without retraining or touching model weights. Models pick up social biases from training data and can reinforce stereotypes around gender, race, religion, disability, age, and social status. Standard fixes are costly, need weight access, and can harm other tasks.

Khan treats debiasing as a search over candidate tokens, judged by a separate process reward model that scores fairness and fluency together. Three schemes grow in sophistication: best-of-N selection, sequential critique and revise, and constitutional self-audit. Tests cover four models on a two-hundred-prompt bilingual benchmark in English and Urdu, across the bias categories named in the paper.
arxiv-2605-02548:
Max Rang and Paul J. Kelly calculate how orbital currents behave when injected into transition metals, using first-principles scattering methods. Spin currents in such metals fade over a length scale that is fairly well understood. Orbital currents, tied to the orbital motion of electrons, have been read in experiments as fading in a similar slow way.

The calculations tell a different story. Orbital currents decay within a few atomic layers of entering the metal, far faster than the experimental reading suggests. When spin-orbit coupling is included, part of the orbital current converts into a spin current within those same few layers. That conversion, the authors argue, reframes the physics behind the orbital Hall effect and how its signals should be interpreted.
arxiv-2605-02848:
Members of the CMS Collaboration search proton collision data for a new heavy particle that decays into a Higgs boson plus another new scalar. Each of those two then decays into a bottom quark pair, so the final state holds four bottom jets. Such patterns are a clean probe of physics beyond the standard model.

The data come from the Large Hadron Collider's second run, at a set collision energy, gathered by the CMS detector. Hypothetical masses span a wide grid for both new particles. Observations agree with the background-only picture. The largest excess sits at one mass pairing, with modest local significance that shrinks once the full search range is counted. Upper limits on the production rate are set, and results are read within a supersymmetric model variant.
arxiv-2605-02948:
Yuxin Lu and three co-authors present AsymTalker, a diffusion method for generating long talking-head videos that keep one identity steady. Quality in this task is now high for short clips, but the standard chunk-by-chunk approach breaks over time. A still identity photo misaligns with a moving audio stream, and each chunk's self-made bridge to the next carries identity drift forward, compounding the error.

One component turns the still photo into a time-coherent latent form by encoding a repeated pseudo-video, adding no new parameters. The second breaks a training dilemma with an asymmetric design: a teacher anchored on true bridge frames gives clean, drift-free guidance per chunk, while the student learns under realistic conditions. Drift and misalignment are attacked at their shared root.
arxiv-2605-03048:
Members of the MicroBooNE Collaboration report a better way to estimate muon energy inside their liquid argon detector at Fermilab. Muons bend slightly as they scatter off nuclei along their path, and the size of those bends reveals their energy, if detector flaws are handled well.

The new estimator models those non-ideal effects in detail. In simulation it keeps bias within about one percent for contained events, with far better resolution and smaller bias than the earlier MicroBooNE method. Checks on real data agree well with the model within its stated uncertainties, for contained and exiting tracks alike.
arxiv-2605-03348:
Hahyeon Choi and Nojun Kwak propose S3, a mixture-of-experts framework for multimodal learning. It builds representations from selectable semantic parts, instead of one fixed embedding. Forcing all signals into a single vector can waste capacity. It can also blur structure that a task needs.

Three steps define the method. Specialization forms concept-level experts in a shared space. Selection routes them per task. Sparsification prunes low-value paths for compact results. Across four MultiBench benchmarks, accuracy improved. Performance followed a reverse U shape in sparsity, peaking in the middle. The authors present selectable parts as a principled option for multimodal models.
arxiv-2605-03648:
Surya Jayakumar and four co-authors model how Irish dairy farms might adopt low-emission fertilizers over fifteen years. Their agent-based model covers 295 farms and treats decarbonization as a social process, not just a cost calculation. Farms influence each other through a communication network, while farm size, subsidies, and carbon taxes also shape adoption chances.

The framework tracks sector greenhouse gas emissions, cumulative abatement, and private and social costs, with Monte Carlo and sensitivity analyses for uncertainty. It matched observed adoption data closely and reproduced a realistic saturation plateau of about ninety-one percent, with a stubborn laggard group remaining. The authors offer it as an exploratory tool for testing climate policies before rollout.
arxiv-2605-03848:
Edoardo Bianchi and Antonio Liotta survey three recent contributions to multi-view proficiency estimation, the task of judging how well a person performs an action rather than which action it is. Proficiency hides in subtle timing, balance, and body mechanics, spread across camera views and brief events, which makes it central to coaching, rehabilitation, and talent identification. All three methods are evaluated on the Ego-Exo4D dataset.

SkillFormer fuses multiple views selectively with a parameter-efficient design. PATS improves temporal sampling by keeping dense excerpts of fundamental movements. ProfVLM turns estimation into language generation, emitting both a proficiency label and expert-style feedback. Together they reach state-of-the-art accuracy with far fewer trainable parameters and training epochs than video-transformer baselines.
arxiv-2605-04548:
Ivica Dimitrovski and four co-authors build an early warning approach for disease risk in vineyards, using weather and environmental time series from a multi-year case study. Warning growers days ahead supports timely, more sustainable crop protection, but many studies only predict each day's disease status, which rewards models that simply repeat yesterday.

Their reformulation asks models to predict the start of a risk period within the next three to seven days, with new events counted only after a minimum disease-free gap. Input features capture humidity and related precursors of upcoming risk. The event-based framing pushes models to learn genuine warning signs rather than persistence.
arxiv-2605-04648:
Sergi Vidal, Alba Mayor-Fernandez, and Rosa Lopez examine how quantum coherence affects the fundamental precision limits of thermal machines. Thermodynamic uncertainty relations bound how steady a device current can be for a given amount of entropy production, and a matrix version links several currents at once.

Their test device is a two-terminal conductor. It can run as a heat engine, a refrigerator, or a heat pump. They show classical limits on efficiency and performance still hold under these bounds. That is true whenever useful power or uphill heat flow is maintained. It holds even where coherent transport dominates. They also find conditions that maximise violations of the bounds, showing cross-correlations between charge and heat currents can sharpen joint precision near equilibrium.
arxiv-2605-05248:
Alan McCann argues that when AI systems create runnable code at runtime, the step from form to running should be governed like any other powerful effect. In classical languages, running a program form is a free, basic act. McCann calls that step an authority boost, since it converts written structure into the power to act, and proposes guarded materialisation instead.

His governed metaprogramming design keeps program forms as plain values that can be handled purely. Before execution, a control layer inspects what the program needs, policy fit, and resource costs, issuing exactly one governed directive. He formalises the rules, proves key traits including a no-bypass theorem, and builds the design in a workflow language for AI systems.
arxiv-2605-05448:
Bird-like flocks with a twist can settle into rotating, chiral patterns. Charlotte Myin, Suropriya Saha, and Benoît Mahault show that such order is fragile in two-dimensional mixtures where interactions are nonreciprocal. Their evidence combines large agent-based simulations with a continuum model of the same system.

As topological defects multiply, the rotating states fall apart into chaotic motion. Below a certain length scale, fluctuations still look scale-free, but with exponents that refuse to stay universal. The coupling between density and orientation makes defects keep stirring the system, which explains the odd scaling the team observed.
arxiv-2605-05548:
Some dwarf galaxies glow with helium emission that demands very hard ultraviolet light. Ivan Altunin and eleven co-authors test one suspect: accreting X-ray binaries inside those galaxies. Ordinary star populations cannot supply the needed radiation, and the answer bears on how the earliest galaxies formed.

The team studied twenty-one nearby star-forming galaxies with the Chandra X-ray observatory, adding new and archived observations. They compared the ultraviolet output the helium line requires with what the X-ray sources can actually provide. The X-ray output fell systematically short, so accreting binaries alone cannot explain the emission, and other sources must contribute.
arxiv-2605-05948:
Rehana Yasmin and two co-authors propose moving public key trust services for satellites into orbit. More independent operators now fly spacecraft, and secure, fast coordination between them needs reliable authentication. Ground based public key systems face delays and bottlenecks that limit growth in busy space settings.

The authors sketch two designs. One joins space and ground, with validation authorities in orbit, and the other issues and checks certificates fully in space. They weigh both designs on scale, availability, security, cost, and daily complexity for multi operator use. A baseline study of delay shows what in orbit trust handling could save. The goal is smoother joint work between separate space entities.
arxiv-2605-06048:
Marco Pasquale and three co-authors apply quantum optimization to reconfigurable intelligent surfaces, panels that steer radio signals. Setting such a surface is a high dimensional combinatorial task. Many quantum studies simplify it by ignoring mutual coupling between elements, which badly hurts real world performance.

The team embed progressively richer coupling models into optimization problems for the quantum approximate optimization algorithm. Four interaction models range from idealized phase only forms to fully dense physical ones, tested on a five by five grid. Full coupling gave the most precise beam pointing, but dense models burden near term quantum hardware with routing overhead. Sparse, distance penalized models remain the workable compromise for today's noisy devices, the authors conclude.
arxiv-2605-06148:
Bowen Zheng, Yihong Luo, and Tianyang Hu fix a mismatch in how discrete image tokenizers are trained. Tokenizers usually learn reconstruction first, with a prior model fitted afterward to the frozen token sequences. That split leaves the tokenizer blind to the model that must later predict its tokens, so tokens can store images well yet be hard to generate in order.

The authors analyze the split through a three part consistency lens, showing the prior side never enters tokenizer training. They add a distribution level prior matching signal during training, optimized with a Wasserstein gradient flow update. The update compares two autoregressive models by forward passes only. The resulting tokenizer lowered generation loss and improved image quality scores at similar reconstruction quality.
arxiv-2605-06648:
Jonah T. Hansen and nine co-authors explore how long the baselines of the planned LIFE space mission need to be. LIFE aims to find and characterize dozens of habitable exoplanets using nulling interferometry, where telescope light is combined to cancel a star's glare. Earlier studies assumed baselines between ten and one hundred meters, a costly range to build for.

Using the LIFEsim simulator with updated planet statistics, they test whether a narrower range, such as twenty-five to eighty meters or even discrete settings, keeps planet yield and fringe tracking nearly intact. Losses stay under ten percent, though target-specific tuning and spectral weighting still need care in the trade-off.
arxiv-2605-06748:
Mohamed-Yacine Hachani and five co-authors report a memory effect in cold sapphire resonators, the heart of ultra-stable oscillators used for exact timing. Chromium impurities in the lab-grown sapphire create a temperature turning point needed for best frequency stability. The team finds the impurities relax slowly, so frequency depends not just on temperature but on how fast temperature is changing.

This dynamic thermal response produces hysteresis and a wide bump in noise near ten-second averaging times, hurting performance. The size of the harm depends on which paramagnetic impurity is chief and how much of it is present. The finding matters for running the world's most stable microwave sources.
arxiv-2605-07048:
Xujun Che, Xiuxia Du, and Depeng Xu generate molecular structures directly from mass spectra, a hard reverse problem. Deciding atom types and bond types depends on each other in a circle, since an atom's setting is defined by its bonds. Earlier diffusion methods handled atoms and bonds in one stream, letting them sync only indirectly.

Their DualLGD model separates atom-level and bond-level reasoning into two streams, linked by attention that respects real chemical connections. On two benchmarks, it reaches top accuracy roughly three times higher than the previous best. Tests removing parts of the design confirm the two-stream architecture, not pretraining, drives most of the improvement.
arxiv-2605-07148:
Haoming Wang and Wei Gao ask whether vision-language models build an inner map of three-dimensional scenes. People navigate using cognitive maps that preserve the layout of space. Models show spatial skill from flat images, but whether they form a similar map was unclear.

The pair isolate a clean spatial subspace inside the model, hidden under stronger color and shape signals, and show it controls spatial outputs. They prove the subspace matches a mathematical map of the scene's geometry. A regularizer based on that insight, applied in brief fine-tuning, improved real-world spatial benchmark scores by up to about twelve percent.
arxiv-2605-07248:
Youngsik Yoon and five co-authors save computing cost in code generation by planning only after a first try fails. Most test-time methods plan before attempting anything, paying planning overhead even on problems a model solves directly. Their Planning-after-Trial policy instead invokes a planner only when verification of an attempt fails.

That timing naturally supports a mixed setup: a cheap model makes attempts, and a strong model plans only when needed. Across benchmarks and model families, the approach pushed the cost-performance frontier outward. One mixed configuration matched a large uniform model's performance while cutting inference cost by roughly two thirds, a substantial saving for code assistants.
arxiv-2605-07348:
Fukutaro Miya and Ryosuke Sato generalize the Cho-Maison monopole, a magnetic monopole configuration inside electroweak theory that behaves singularly at its center. Because its structure rests on electroweak-style symmetry breaking, similar monopoles should appear in any gauge theory with that structure. The authors construct such configurations explicitly across a broad class of models.

They also embed the Cho-Maison monopole inside the classic 't Hooft-Polyakov monopole as a low-energy effective description. A monopole in the Pati-Salam model, for instance, behaves exactly like the electroweak one once heavier degrees of freedom are integrated out. The work widens where such monopoles can be expected.
arxiv-2605-07448:
Zihao Song and three co-authors make tensor regression robust to outliers and heavy-tailed noise. Tensor data, arrays with several axes, arise across science, but existing regression methods ignored outlier sensitivity. Their method uses a low-rank structure relaxed in a nonconvex way, inside a framework allowing nonconvex losses and penalties alike.

An implementable algorithm is shown to converge globally under mild assumptions. Statistical theory covers convergence rates and prediction error bounds for stationary points across many model types, from linear and generalized linear models to robust Huber regression. Simulations and application studies back the theory with numerical evidence.
arxiv-2605-07548:
Matti Schulze and two co-authors address a portability problem in confidential computing, where sensitive programs run inside protected enclaves. Intel SGX is widely used for such work, but its programs are tied to Intel-specific interfaces. As Arm processors spread through cloud data centers, those programs cannot simply move over.

Their system, CCX, rebuilds SGX functions inside Arm CCA firmware so existing enclave programs run with no source changes at all. They prototyped it on an emulator and on a Nitrogen8M development board. Tests showed unmodified SGX programs running with security comparable to SGX itself, and with better performance in the settings they measured.
arxiv-2605-07748:
Jiaxiu Jiang and twelve co-authors bring the visual diffusion recipe to language modeling. Diffusion transformers trained with flow matching in a learned latent space have unified image and video generation, but text is discrete, so the transfer is not obvious. Their system, TextLDM, first maps tokens into continuous latents with a transformer autoencoder.

The key finding is that reconstruction fidelity alone does not make latents good for generation; aligning them with a frozen pretrained language model's representations proved critical. A standard diffusion transformer then performs flow matching in that latent space, architecturally identical to its visual counterpart. Trained from scratch on OpenWebText2, TextLDM substantially beat earlier diffusion language models and matched GPT-2 under the same settings.
arxiv-2605-07948:
Anaïs Defossez and three co-authors turn a classic condensed matter formula into a microscope for quantum geometry. The Středa formula links an insulator's Hall conductivity to how its particle density responds to a magnetic field, giving a local probe of the topological Chern number. An energy-resolved version of the marker can reveal the fine shape of energy bands.

They show that driven-dissipative bosonic lattices, pumped uniformly with random phases and losing particles evenly, give direct access to both the integrated and energy-by-energy responses. From them the team builds a coarse-grained energy-resolved marker for plain dispersive bands. As a striking use, the marker tracks what happens to topological bands under strong disorder, catching the quantum geometry behind topological Anderson insulators.
arxiv-2605-08048:
Yo Ehara measures how broadly a word is used across contexts, a quantity that helps lexicographers decide when senses should be split in thesauri and dictionaries. Modern embeddings place each use of a word as a point in space, and the spread of those points acts as a proxy for breadth.

Ehara shows that naive tests can confuse a change in average direction with a change in spread, creating false significant results. The proposed fix is a permutation test aligned by a Householder reflection, which separates direction from dispersion. The method gives more accurate and efficient tests for comparing the semantic breadth of two words.
arxiv-2605-08148:
Renato Vieira dos Santos proposes an experiment on a foundational assumption of electromagnetism. The electric Aharonov-Bohm effect, where a time-dependent potential shifts an electron's phase in a field-free region, has never been tested in its original shielded form. Textbook theory also imposes the Lorenz condition, which removes a scalar degree of freedom by fiat.

Santos asks what happens if that scalar field is physical and couples to matter. It would add a phase shift with a one-minus-cosine signature, distinct from the standard sine pattern and separable by sweeping the frequency. Single-electron interferometry with picosecond timing, already within reach, could run the test.
arxiv-2605-08248:
Abdelmalek Bouzenada and Rami Ahmad El-Nabulsi build one algebraic frame for cat-like quantum states. Catability is a score for how clean a mixed state is. The pair extend that score to fast-moving systems of any spin. They do the work with Lie algebra tools, step by step.

Inside the frame, they set up a broad Foldy-Wouthuysen swap. That swap is the standard way to split a Hamiltonian into its plus and minus energy parts. They also add an operator that is keen to phase, so it can track how parts of the state line up. At the end, they work the whole scheme out for Dirac spin one-half particles in full detail.
arxiv-2605-08348:
Michael Li and Nishant Subramani measure two virtues of interpretability circuits. Circuit analysis hunts the sparse set of model parts behind a behavior. It usually checks necessity and sufficiency. Those checks say little about consistency. They also say little about whether a circuit belongs to one task alone.

The team studied six tasks and five models. Component-level circuits proved highly consistent and causally strong. But they were not specific. Cutting one task's circuit hurt about as much as cutting another's. Neuron-level circuits flipped the pattern. They were specific but inconsistent. The authors trace the tension to how components are shared. It is a caution for anyone reading circuits as task explanations.
arxiv-2605-08648:
Josue Ortega Caro and five coauthors model how cell and brain populations change over time when only unpaired snapshots exist. The same cells or animals are rarely tracked, yet states are sampled stage by stage, and hidden regimes like learning or growth phases switch the rules midstream. Their FLUX framework learns a curved geometry from the data and routes motion through sparse expert fields.

Tests span controlled manifolds, a switching chaotic system, brain imaging during learning, and cell differentiation data. Geometry proves essential: without it, local motion fits but regime discovery fails. Biology gains a way to recover both transport paths and hidden state changes from snapshot data alone.
arxiv-2605-08748: Sujoy Majumder, Debabrata Pramanik, and Shantanu Panja prove sole form claims for whole functions of more than one input. The functions share two values with their own part slope maps. With tools from normal family theory, they show such tight sharing locks the function down. The work takes past one input results into the many input case. Sharp cases show the terms can not be loosened.
arxiv-2605-08848:
Tung Nguyen and Sang-il Oum bound the hues a graph needs when it bars set patterns. A graph class is chi bounded when its hue count is tied to its top clique size. They prove one clean case first. Graphs that bar any fixed path and the four loop need just a line rate of hues. Then they ask the broad form. The pair is a forest and a full multi part graph.

Two broad cases say yes. One pairs broom shaped forests with any full multi part graph. One pairs any forest with a full two part graph. The proofs join many past line and square rate results. A new, sharp proof of a fresh tree find claim is in the work too.
arxiv-2605-08948:
Mateusz Mojsak, Elfi Kraka, and Adam Michalchuk measure bond strength inside crystals with localized vibrational modes built like Wannier functions. Molecular chemistry has local mode theory for interpretable bond strengths, but periodic solids lacked a direct analog. Their construction superposes wave resolved local modes into smooth, real space modes tied to individual internal coordinates, with no extra phase fixing needed, yielding well defined force constants and frequencies per bond.

Phonon dispersion turns out to matter for the computed strengths. Tests span ionic and covalent representatives, including magnesium oxide, carbon, silicon, silicon carbide, and two forms of calcium carbonate. Solid state chemistry gains quantitative, chemically readable bonding analysis for fully periodic materials.
arxiv-2605-09248:
Wang and three colleagues fix a bias in galaxy counts from confusion limited submillimetre surveys, where faint galaxies blend into background fluctuations. Standard P(D) analysis assumes galaxies are Poisson distributed, but real galaxies are clustered, which systematically biases the counts it recovers. The team presents an empirical method that measures and corrects this bias together, using both the 1 and 2 point statistics from the map.

Applied to deep Herschel SPIRE data from the GOODS-N field, it gives revised counts at 250, 350 and 500 micrometres. At 500 micrometres, clustering inflates counts 1 point 6 fold near 10 mJy and slightly cuts the faintest sub mJy counts, with gentler effects at 350 and 250 micrometres from smaller beams. The method applies broadly to other confusion limited surveys with known beam and noise traits, including SCUBA-2 and CCAT. It enables unbiased use of the full statistical information in far infrared and submillimetre surveys.
arxiv-2605-09348:
Egami and seven colleagues present HOME-KGQA, a benchmark for multimodal knowledge graph question answering over household daily activities. Large language models bring easy language handling and knowledge graphs bring explicit structured knowledge. Joined, they promise more reliable and verifiable AI, and question answering over graphs can cut hallucinations and reach beyond training data.

Current benchmarks lean encyclopedic, cover one modality only, and lack fine-grained spatiotemporal data, limiting their use for Embodied AI tasks. HOME-KGQA instead pairs complex, multi-hop natural language questions with graph query languages, adding harder questions with multi-level spatiotemporal reasoning, multimodal grounding, and aggregation. In tests, LLM-based question answering methods fall short of their performance on existing datasets, showing the benchmark poses real challenges for using such systems, and the dataset is public.
arxiv-2605-10048:
Zhang, Li and Yan investigate the link between the generalised i-boson model and boxed BUC plane partitions, two objects from quantum integrable models. First comes a representation of the generalised i-boson algebra, plus how monodromy matrix operators act on basis vectors. Neutral fermion vertex operators acting on state vectors are then treated through the neutral fermionic Fock space.

Using the scalar product of the generalised i-boson model, the authors derive boxed BUC plane partitions' generating function, showing it matches products of Schur Q-functions. A generating function for BUC plane partitions under the double scaling limit is also presented. The work sits inside the Quantum Inverse Scattering Method tradition. There the i-boson model turns out to be one special case of the q-boson model, when q approaches the imaginary unit.
arxiv-2605-10148:
Setyawan and co-authors present MicroViTv2, a lightweight vision transformer tuned for real-device efficiency at the edge. The first vision model is accurate but too costly for phones and edge hardware. Built on MicroViT, the new model uses reworked design for faster inference. It includes reworked patch coding and a reworked depth-wise mixing unit, plus Single Depth-Wise Transposed Attention to capture long-range links with little redundancy.

Despite slightly higher FLOPs, MicroViTv2 improves scores by up to half a percent over its forerunner. It beats MobileViTv2, EdgeNeXt and EfficientViT while keeping run time fast and energy use low on Jetson AGX Orin. Tests on ImageNet-1K and COCO support the paper's thesis. Hardware-aware design and built-in reworking matter more than raw FLOPs when judging efficiency, and efficiency must be measured beyond flop counts.
arxiv-2605-10348:
Wan Nie and four colleagues speed up a core task in computational chemistry: describing electron correlation well. Selected configuration interaction nears the exact full limit by picking key determinants, but recent machine-learning versions suffer a goal mismatch, judging determinants alone rather than by relative rank. Their 2026 paper introduces ranking configuration interaction, or RCI, which reframes selection as pairwise ranking.

Built on a Transformer that captures non-local orbital links, RCI tunes the partial order of determinants step by step. That aligns training with the ranking nature of the task. Across plane-wave and Gaussian basis sets, it cut total computing time by 23 percent to over 50 percent against sorting baselines. It needed only 55 percent of the determinant count for N2 and CO. On a hard iron-sulfur cluster it hit chemical accuracy using just 12 percent of the full space.
arxiv-2605-10748:
Li Shen and co-authors propose FedMITR, a shared model flip and token relabel framework for one-shot shared learning with vision models. In one-shot shared learning a central server learns a global model in a single contact round, but under highly non-IID settings current data-free methods make low-quality data badly misaligned with ground-truth labels. FedMITR trains the global model by fully using all patches of made-up images. It uses sparse model flips during data generation to selectively invert key foregrounds while halting flips of blank backgrounds.

To address meaning-free tokens hindering vision model predictions, patches with high information density use pseudo-labels. Low-density patches are relabelled via group models for robust teaching. Stability analysis shows sparse flips eliminate gradient wobble from background noise, while token relabel reduces gradient spread, together giving a tighter general bound.
arxiv-2605-10948:
Lilly Horvath-Makkos and Fayyaz Minhas model how vegetation loss reorganizes Amazon rainfall, hour by hour. Deforestation shifts rain through tangled, seasonal, nonlinear land-atmosphere feedbacks, yet most models blur convection at coarse scales and resolve correlations rather than causal pathways.

A neural network forecasting hourly rainfall across the Amazon Basin, paired with pathway diagnostics and sensitivity tests, checks whether the model internalizes physically consistent links from canopy to atmosphere to rain. The model predicts occurrence and intensity well, and sustained canopy loss shows threshold-like reorganization in rainfall patterns. Climate and water planners get an interpretable warning system for hydrological disruption.
arxiv-2605-11148:
Miguel Alejandro Mantilla and four colleagues design a testing method for a prototype wristband reading muscle signals and upper-limb movement. Surface electromyography drives myoelectric prosthetic limbs and human-machine interfaces, but store-bought systems cost too much for many school, lab, and factory settings, especially in poorer countries.

Their plan follows global standards IEC 60601 and ANSI/AAMI EC13, running safety tests for power for leakage currents, double insulation, and electrode-circuit links. Use tests compare an eight-electrode wristband sample against the store-bought PortiLab2 reference using Pearson correlation, Bland-Altman analysis, and mean squared error, extended to signal steadiness at rest and during movement. Low-cost prosthetics teams get a standards-based testing route for affordable recording gear.
arxiv-2605-11348: Jeong and five colleagues test whether large language models can pull causal links from disaster posts on social media. Such posts are informal, fragmented and context-bound, and often tell personal stories rather than stating causes. The team builds an expert-grounded framework that compares model-made causal graphs with reference graphs from disaster reports, and checks whether links rest on post-event evidence or on model priors. Their findings show both promise and risk for disaster decision support.
arxiv-2605-11448: Lee and Kondor argue that neural probes should hold steady under representation symmetries, not hinge on one basis. Even when two systems run the same computation, hidden coordinates may differ by reparameterization. They prove that, under standard assumptions, behaviourally equivalent models have hidden representations linked by an invertible affine map. That symmetry principle picks out a unique ladder of shallow coordinate-stable probes, with linear probes first. They also show that a probe-visible quotient, the representation modulo unseen directions, is the basis for cross-model probe transfer.
arxiv-2605-11748: Li and Himstedt present BronchoLumen, YOLO-based architectures for real-time bronchial orifice detection in video bronchoscopy. Navigating branching airways challenges pulmonary clinics and intensive care units, and BronchoLumen assists navigation and diagnosis systems. The study compares YOLOv8 and YOLOv12, the latter adding attention modules, trained and tested solely on public datasets. YOLOv8 reaches mAP at 0 point 5 of 0 point 91 in-domain and 0 point 68 cross-domain; YOLOv12 reaches 0 point 84 and 0 point 68 with better localization. Motion blur and low contrast occasionally cause uncertainty, but the system proves robust overall.
arxiv-2605-11948: M. Niţă studies topological edge states in a 1D chain of hexagonal unit cells. Two hopping strengths that switch back and forth produce a rich spectrum with spread-out and flat bands. Under periodic versus open ends, he finds two insulating phases split by a gap-closing switch set by the hopping ratio. In this phase, below a key ratio, edge states emerge that are sharply pinned at the edges of finite chains.
arxiv-2605-12648: Wang and seven colleagues give risk bounds for clipped DP-SGD with noise in KANs. Time links break centering, projection blocks cuts of linked noise, and clipping breaks gradient shape. They address these issues through shifted moves, a weighted loss, and focus. Their bound shows time links reduce noise terms, clipping enters through a step size, and training admits a width range. Synthetic and MNIST experiments support the seen time-link effect.
arxiv-2605-12748: Do, Sonkar and Sachan test whether language-model student simulators truly hold misconceptions or merely flatter the tutor. Such simulators fluently mimic student replies, making them attractive for training tutors and teachers. Yet they are usually judged by output similarity, not by whether they maintain a coherent wrong-belief state. The team introduces a framework for faithfulness to wrong beliefs, with a contrastive feedback protocol comparing targeted feedback against misaligned and generic controls.
arxiv-2605-13248: Cui and colleagues present CLMT, a compact model that turns one body signal into another across devices. Heart traces and pulse traces differ in form and sampling rate, which blocks shared analysis. A universal tokenizer splits signals into discrete tokens, and a translator maps those tokens across forms and rates. The small model beats much larger baselines, lifting heartbeat detection sharply and rebuilding fast sampled signals with near perfect correlation.
arxiv-2605-13348: Matteo Capucci and four colleagues present a logic for stating safety rules for neural parts built into symbolic software, even safety-critical software. Such rules must suit both a plain true-or-false reading and training, which needs a smooth numeric reading. The authors give a family of calculi, pQLL, keyed by a hardness degree. They prove cut-elimination for these calculi and completeness against enriched residuated soft lattices. At infinite hardness, pQLL reduces to multiplicative additive linear logic, and they prove numeric adequacy of neuro-symbolic loss functions.
arxiv-2605-13548: Daojie Peng and nine colleagues introduce AttenA+, a framework that rectifies action inequality in robotic foundation models. AttenA+ prioritises critical segments through speed-based action focus, reweighting training by the inverse speed field. As a plug-and-play add-on, it integrates into existing backbones without design changes or added parameters. It lifts OpenVLA-OFT to 98.6 percent on Libero and FastWAM to 92.4 percent on RoboTwin 2.0, with real-world validation on a Franka manipulator.
arxiv-2605-13648: Tony Shardlow studies the sticky CIR process, a diffusion on zero-and-above reals with a sticky boundary at the origin. For settings between one and two, where the origin is open but not trapping, he proves soundness and a unique invariant measure. For non-trivial forces, he proves a unique tilted invariant measure via a Girsanov change of measure. He builds two samplers: an exact Metropolis-Hastings fixed sampler and a cheaper biased Langevin method.
arxiv-2605-13748: Ishaan Mahajan and six colleagues introduce TinySDP, the first semidefinite coding solver built for on-chip systems. TinySDP mixes SDP cone casts into a cached-Riccati-based ADMM solver, using compute shape for on-chip ease. An after-the-fact rank-1 proof turns relaxed solutions into plain shape pledges at each timestep. On cul-de-sac and moving blocker dodging tests, TinySDP achieves crash-free driving with paths up to 73 percent shorter than state-of-the-art rivals. A drone test shows SDP limits held at real-time rates.
arxiv-2605-13948: Esposito, Sanchez, Bel and Ruiz give new fit formulas for velocity-divergence auto- and cross-spectra, tuned on gravity-only N-body runs. With the Evolution Mapping frame, they tie the fits to the clump strength smoothed at twelve megaparsecs. Strict convergence checks and a safe patch plan yield firm measures up to a wave number near 0.56 per megaparsec, with errors within a few percent for both spectra.
arxiv-2605-14148: Almeida studies how operator ordering shapes spectra in Dirac systems with spatially varying mass. Unlike the nonrelativistic case, where many orderings pass muster, the relativistic Dirac operator admits just one ordering that fits probability-current conservation. That requirement adds a logarithmic-gradient term tied to how the mass profile varies in space. The term alters the effective kinetic operator and warps the spectral quantization rule, with a mode-wise second-order shift that grows sharply near the mass-inversion threshold.
arxiv-2605-14248: Kang and seven co-authors dissect the origins of altermagnetism in three cases, MnF2, MnTe and RuO2, using DFT+DMFT. In MnF2, strong local correlations in Mn-3d states open a clear Mott gap, pin the electrons down, narrow the spin bandwidth, and cut spin-band splitting. MnTe proves an ideal platform, with large local moments from strong correlations and wide splitting from Mn-3d-Te-5p orbital mix. RuO2 acts as a Pauli paramagnet with no local moments, yet shows strong splitting, pointing to itinerant behavior.
arxiv-2605-14348: Singhal and four co-authors present a Z1-squared framework for pulsar spin and derivative estimation from photon lists. Peak width alone is not the statistical uncertainty on recovered parameters. Three estimators are compared. For sine signals, the local Z-squared response versus frequency and derivative is derived, and midpoint frequency removes the leading-order covariance between the parameters. This gives simple uncertainty values from fitted peak amplitude and local widths. The framework is applied to Crab, Swift J0243.6+6124, and SAX J1808.4-3658.
arxiv-2605-14448: Think When Needed, from Zhang and colleagues in 2026, is a unified multimodal embedding system with adaptive reasoning. Recent methods add chain-of-thought to embeddings but cost heavily. For simple inputs, plain embeddings already work well. Think When Needed uses dual-LoRA adapters for reasoning and embedding on a shared frozen backbone. An adaptive think switch decides per input whether to use chain-of-thought, skipping needless reasoning. On MMEB-V2, it reaches state-of-the-art embedding quality with only 3 to 5 percent extra weights.
arxiv-2605-15048: M. Orte-García and nine others present an even-handed study of electron temperature links across ionized species in star-forming regions. Drawing on 699 spectra of Galactic and far-off H II regions and star-forming galaxies from the DESIRED-E database, they redo densities and temperatures with updated atomic data. Low-ionization diagnostics show large intrinsic scatter, likely from uneven density and recombination effects. Nitrogen-based diagnostics prove steadier, making them the more reliable temperature tracers.
arxiv-2605-15148: F. Güngör and C. Özemir derive conservation laws for a class of time-dependent damped nonlinear multidimensional wave equations via Noether's theorem. For any nonzero damping and nonlinear interaction, the variational symmetries form a Euclidean algebra of space shifts and turns, yielding linear and angular momentum laws. For special forms of the two terms, the algebra widens into part of the conformal algebra, giving extra, more rich laws.
arxiv-2605-15248: Yifei Ge and nine others probe privacy leaks in code-generating language models through test generation. Code sets may contain personal information that models memorize and repeat, but old detection prompts poorly match real contexts where such data appears. Their setup mocks real privacy-related code cases and uses a test-driven strategy to draw memorized details from made tests, guided by an on-its-own built privacy feature library. Across five models it detects 2.56 times more proven leakage than baselines.
arxiv-2605-15348: Jagannath Das and four colleagues study Clifford-deformed zero-rate quantum low-density parity-check codes under biased noise. Rotating Pauli axes by single-qubit Clifford unitaries tailors a fixed code to anisotropic noise. Biased logical operators may grow slower than distance, or a logical basis may meet certain overlap scalings. In either case the deformed code-capacity threshold under pure dephasing nears 50 percent. This explains known 50-percent examples like XY and XZZX surface codes and color codes, and the authors map a similar phase diagram for tile codes.
arxiv-2605-15448: Changfeng Gui and Amir Moradifam prove symmetry for solutions of the mean field equation on the sphere. They cover a parameter range from one third to one, under a set geometric condition. The proof uses a sphere covering inequality and ideas about shape. The results then give a rigidity fact for the Hawking mass of stable spheres of constant mean curvature. This answers a 2002 question from Robert Bartnik. It also extends past work beyond nearly round cases.
arxiv-2605-15548: Martin Peticco and Pulkit Agrawal present KaRMA, a gauge for fine hand skill in robots. Old gauges track still traits like workspace and grasp hold. KaRMA asks how far a hand can shift and turn a small ball in a two-finger pinch while holding touch. It obeys joint caps, crash bans, rolling touch, and force rules. It then searches reach poses by breadth-first steps. It reports shift cover, turn cover, and grasp touchiness. On sixteen hands it splits ties from still gauges and bares shift-turn trade-offs.
arxiv-2605-16048: Farsang and three colleagues shrink state space models, compact recurrent rivals of large language models on edge devices. Looping a small model through depth recurrence matches a much larger standard model with no performance loss. Presenting inputs at a fixed, consistent time granularity also lifts performance. Both gains held across four architectures: LRU, S5, LinOSS, and LrcSSM.
arxiv-2605-16348: Tan and three others present Flow-Direct, a framework that guides flow models with a persistent guidance field built from all accumulated reward-evaluated samples. Existing training-free guidance wastes feedback, using it only transiently for local gradient approximations or discrete search choices. Flow-Direct derives its field from the log-density ratio between base and reward-weighted target distributions. Every evaluated sample refines the global field, so no reward information is wasted, and the field can be reused for new target samples without further reward evaluations.
arxiv-2605-16848: Jian and colleagues tackle visual planning with vision-language models, where raw visual input exceeds one-step perception. Following image-thinking, they treat planning as building and reflecting a world model from local evidence. A training-free strategy lets models solve tasks beyond initial reach, but many image-thinking steps raise compute cost. Pattern Inference lets models spot patterns in new tasks and infer world-model structure. Pattern Induction discovers and optimizes such patterns as experts. Tests on FrozenLake, Crafter, and CubeBench show balanced accuracy and efficiency.
arxiv-2605-17048: Porto's team shows nonlinear electrodynamics alters photon travel near magnetars, bending light from its standard paths. Missing these fixes biases stellar radius reads by about 10 percent. It also induces a steady minimal travel-time delay near 350 ns, far above the 100-ns resolution of NICER. The findings matter for reading X-ray pulse profiles from observatories such as eXTP, which rely on precise light-bending and timing models for masses and radii. They thus offer a window into dense matter and extreme fields, with glitches and anti-glitches also hit.
arxiv-2605-17148: Rubio-Solis improves manta-ray foraging optimization with Lévy flights and uses it to train extreme learning machines, single-hidden-layer networks whose output weights come from a generalized inverse. The method predicts formation energies for binary crystal compounds, relaxed and unrelaxed, against their pure-component ground states. Tests compare it with other nature-inspired algorithms under matched conditions.
arxiv-2605-17348: Zhang and colleagues introduce AgentRevive, a framework that stops multi-agent systems from permanently discarding agents that could still recover. Instead of hard pruning, agents move among Active, Standby and Terminated states under a risk-aware policy, with standby agents kept for later rounds. Edges follow learned states, so only terminated nodes leave for good. Tests show it beats strong baselines and cuts token use through state-aware scheduling.
arxiv-2605-17448: Son and colleagues recast CAD generation as an industry-native task. Models must produce a fully built multi-part STEP document from a free-form note, then validate it by finite element analysis. First-attempt sweeps find leading agents produce no strict-passing artifact, meeting only about a fifth of typed requirements at best. Two new feedback signals, a text-only blueprint plan and a 21-view image renderer, lift geometric reconstruction markedly on S2O and Fusion360.
arxiv-2605-17648: Zaiyi Zheng and colleagues present Step-Aligned Policy Optimization (SAPO) for reasoning tasks. Recommendation treats next-item picks as semantic identifier generation. In large catalogs, exact-match feedback only says whether the final item is correct, not which token caused it. The credit unit is one step: one thinking block plus one identifier token. SAPO computes a separate advantage per step, applied only to the corresponding thinking block and token. Across three datasets, SAPO stabilizes training and improves over baselines, with the largest gains where feedback is sparse.
arxiv-2605-17748: Yu Li and five colleagues introduce GLIA, an adapter that lets pretrained vision transformers judge image quality without retraining the whole model. A dual-stream design reads both the broad meaning of a scene and fine local detail, then fuses the two views interactively, keeping trainable parameters low. Across several benchmarks for blind quality assessment, where true distortions vary widely and labeled data are scarce, the method beats existing approaches on accuracy and robustness.
arxiv-2605-18048: Jingjing Liu and eight colleagues introduce proactive document-guided action for GUI agents in open-web settings. GUI agents lean on static knowledge from pre-training, limiting long-tailed tasks needing explicit procedural knowledge. The new paradigm lets agents search alone for relevant documentation to resolve long-tailed tasks. The team proposes DocOS, a benchmark requiring agents to browse, locate documentation, and ground instructions into GUI actions. Tests reveal dual bottlenecks: locating relevant information during proactive search, and grounding retrieved instructions into precise actions.
arxiv-2605-18248: Alexander Rabinovich's 2026 paper asks whether MSO encodings over countable chains can be cut to lower dimension. Encodings place one structure inside another by logical rules, with inner elements standing for tuples of host elements. Cutting one down means finding a reparameterization that lowers its dimension. The main result shows it is decidable whether a formula admits a d-dimensional reparameterization over countable labelled linear orders. Any encoding whose domain admits one thus equals a d-dimensional point encoding.
arxiv-2605-18348: Angelos Koutsianas and Nikos Tzanakis study the equation x to the k plus x plus one to the k equals y to the n, for k congruent to 2 modulo 4. They prove the only solutions have x equal to 0 or negative 1, either for k between 6 and 100 or for k with odd prime factors congruent to 3 modulo 4. Their 2026 proof uses linear forms in logarithms, the modular method, and Thue equations.
arxiv-2605-18448: Yuan Liao and three co-authors develop, in a 2026 paper, limit theory for principal component analysis of a high-dimensional factor model. The working size R is fixed and need only meet or beat r, the true factor count. From anisotropic local laws in random matrix theory, extra sample eigenparts past r prove noise-led, unlinked, and nearly orthogonal to factor loadings. Two rotations, wide and narrow maps, both give consistent factor estimates. A factor-boosted test case proves root-T limit normality for every fixed R.
arxiv-2605-18548: Tingfeng Hui and seven co-authors present STT-Arena, a 2026 benchmark of 227 interactive tasks for tool-using models under spatio-temporal dynamics. Injected triggers abruptly invalidate ongoing plans, forcing models to detect state shifts and replan. Even the best proprietary models score under 40 percent overall. Failure analysis finds three recurring error modes, and an iterative trajectory refinement method plus online RL yields STT-Agent-4B, which beats frontier models on the benchmark.
arxiv-2605-18648: Maja Pavlovic, Silviu Paun, and Massimo Poesio audit, in a 2026 report, how human soft labels shape learning and calibration. Past work mixed two effects: the gain from soft labels and the silent fix of mislabeled data. By re-annotating subsets of MNIST and a synthetic variant, they separate the two. Human soft labels give small accuracy gains, but their larger value is regularization: better calibration on hard samples and steadier convergence across runs. Models trained this way mirror human uncertainty, while synthetic-label models fail to align with people.
arxiv-2605-18748: Yongsheng Yu and six colleagues build Aurora, a 2026 system that turns rough video edit requests into finished edits. Current unified editors expect ready-made text, reference pictures, and exact locations for local changes, which users rarely supply. A vision-language agent first turns a raw request into a clear edit plan and picks reference pictures. That plan then guides a video diffusion model through replacement, removal, style change, and insertion.
arxiv-2605-19048: Srinivas Ravishankar and Virginia de Sa ask if motor cortex handwriting rests on shared move bits. Felt handwriting links serve Latin well but need each sign in train, a wall for tongues with thousands of signs. Their frame lines brain fire to felt moves and trains a zero shot decoder. It scores sixty four percent top three hits on unseen letters, backing shared stroke codes and easing open word links with light retune.
arxiv-2605-19248: Sagar Dubey shows entanglement nearly halves bandwidth for oblivious updates in MDS-coded storage. In the oblivious update problem, one symbol changes unknown to helpers and node, and the classical bound is alpha k log base 2 of q bits. With entanglement, bandwidth falls to ceiling of alpha over 2 times k log base 2 of q, a factor approaching 2. For alpha 2, a CSS code reaches bandwidth with one qudit per helper. A converse uses the superdense coding bound, and the result holds for all n and k with large prime q.
arxiv-2605-19948: Damgaard and three co-workers expand the Kerr black hole metric step by step from the Einstein equations. The metric depends on Newton's constant and the spin parameter, so the expansion runs in two parameters at once. In harmonic gauge the recursion solves to any order, yet summing it back into closed form needs extra terms tied to harmonic functions added to the coordinates. The paper also explains how dimensional regularisation handles the Fourier transforms involved.
arxiv-2605-20048: Vincent Alexander Croft replaces per-bin uncertainty factors in Large Hadron Collider template fits with a small set of eigenmodes. HistFactory uncertainty scales with bin count, hurting multi-way fits and templates from limited Monte Carlo samples. His eigenmode decomposition uses smooth functions from log-Gaussian Cox process posteriors on Monte Carlo data, with rank-one updates per shape shift. Keeping only the leading eigenmodes yields a few Gaussian amplitudes, recovers Barlow-Beeston as a limit, and caps posterior variance at the Barlow-Beeston level in each bin.
arxiv-2605-20248: Brown Zaz and four co-workers revisit the objective for node classification in the transductive setting, where the graph is seen but labels cover only some nodes. Transductive models predict nodes, but standard objectives discard unlabeled predictions for lack of ground truth. Splitting cross-entropy into label alignment and entropy terms, they propose prediction confidence as a way to extract signal without labels. Transductive Sharpening: a loss change minimizing prediction entropy on unlabeled nodes while counterbalancing labeled ones. Tests across benchmarks show steady gains with no backbone changes.
arxiv-2605-20348: Koulouris and Campajola ask whether deep reinforcement-learning agents can sustain supra-competitive outcomes when liquidating assets. In a two-agent Almgren-Chriss liquidation game, agents first set full sale plans in advance, then learn with live feedback. Access to recent prices and their own past moves makes above-competitive results far more common and lasting. The driver is memory and state-based feedback along the sale path, not group learning or price watching alone.
arxiv-2605-20548: Yong Jin Chun and Iftekhar Ahmed examine what agents actually tell each other in multi-agent language-model systems. Early errors can spread and spoil later reasoning, yet which shared facts matter most was unclear. Their systematic analysis finds that missing reasoning and verification in messages sharply hurts performance. They then propose a recovery method that restores missing critical facts, recovering up to 86.2 percent of failed cases.
arxiv-2605-20648: Benedict Quartey and five colleagues propose Predicate Action Skills, a way for robots to compose learned skills without retraining. Learning from demonstration often fails on new combos of known skills, since policies model motion alone. Their PACTS policies jointly model action paths and the symbolic results those actions bring about. Generating both together improves motion and result prediction, and planning over the joint model enables zero-shot composition of skills.
arxiv-2605-20848: Arhrib and seven colleagues present VLQBounds, a public Python tool for testing vector-like quark scenarios against collider limits. It uses public ATLAS and CMS results on pair and single production. It supports mass-mixing, mass-coupling, and mass-width parameterizations. For each parameter point, predicted values are compared channel by channel with observed and expected limits, and the most sensitive analysis is auto-identified with a 95 percent confidence verdict.
arxiv-2605-21148: Tanumoy Mandal, Subhadip Mitra, and Rachit Sharma show that photon-initiated production matters for heavy, highly charged colored particles at the LHC. Mixed gluon-photon contributions, scaling with charge squared, raise leptoquark pair rates by up to about a third for a charge-five-thirds state, rivaling next-to-leading-order QCD corrections. Recasting ATLAS muon-jet data, they find these overlooked effects tighten mass exclusion limits.
arxiv-2605-21248: Keren Censor-Hillel, Aditi Dudeja, and George Giakkoupis study stochastic graph optimization in a distributed setting. A random subgraph keeps each edge of a known base graph with a known chance, and the task must be solved despite edge doubt. Here each vertex knows only its own edges and talks only over them, with cost counted in sync rounds. The authors show distributed stochastic methods can beat non-stochastic methods and known lower bounds, with fast approximations for maximum matching and related tasks.
arxiv-2605-21348: Alicja Polanska and co-authors present physics-based acquisition, an active learning method for data-efficient neural operator training. Neural operators cut simulation cost but need large training sets, and active learning selects the most informative samples in turn. Their method uses the partial differential equation residual to guide selection, adding a physics bias so simulation cost goes where the model's physical grasp is weakest. Tests on Burgers and Navier-Stokes equations show it beats random selection and matches the best prior data efficiency.
arxiv-2605-21648: Lucas Fernandez Sarmiento asks whether dropout should stay a static setting or vary over depth. He develops a mean-field account of dropout near the edge of chaos, finding distinct classes for smooth and kinked units with their scaling powers. The resulting propagation theory, bound by maximizing dropout's regularization, points to putting dropout near the input. Tests on vision, speech, and finance time series show gains often in MLPs, with smaller gains in attention models.
arxiv-2605-21948: Xucheng Yu and co-authors present SCI-Defense, a defense for ranking systems based on large language models against Generative Engine Optimization attacks. Attackers inject meaning signals into product descriptions to lift rankings falsely, and current filters miss such tricks. SCI-Defense combines perplexity checks, semantic integrity scoring, and inter-candidate detection. Tests show perplexity-only filters, content classifiers, and paraphrasing score zero recall against such tricks, while new attacks expose it as a structural blind spot.
arxiv-2605-22048: Yong-Xin Gao and Ze-Hua Zhou characterize the spectra of generators of hyperbolic composition and weighted composition semigroups. They give full accounts of the spectrum, the essential spectrum, and the point spectrum of weighted composition C0-semigroups from such semiflows on Bergman spaces. They also give an example showing spectral properties can shift with the semigroup near self-contact points that are non-fixed.
arxiv-2605-22248: Stanley-Clamp and colleagues argue that climate emulation is at heart an out-of-distribution task, since a warming world shifts atmospheric patterns beyond training data. They show seasonal change works as a real-world proxy for those long-term shifts. Current hybrid machine learning emulators degrade sharply under such seasonal tests. The authors point to compositional generalisation, recombining observed parts in new ways, as the principled route forward. Physically motivated decompositions already lift out-of-distribution skill at modest cost.
arxiv-2605-22948: Joksimović recasts pitch-class set theory in graph terms. Each set in Z_n becomes a complete weighted graph, with interval classes as edge weights. The build is invariant under the dihedral group. A cyclic step composition encodes the whole structure, recovered through an additivity rule. The framework ties T/I equivalence to graph isomorphism. It reinterprets Z-relation as non-isomorphic graphs sharing edge-weight multisets. The graph view makes hidden links plain. That gap is the heart of Z-relation.
arxiv-2605-23048: Pradhan and five coauthors offer StanBKT, an open-source Python package for Bayesian Knowledge Tracing in tutoring systems. Most tools use EM and yield only point values. That limits uncertainty estimates and fair comparisons. StanBKT uses Bayesian methods in Stan. It supports Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, variational methods, Pathfinder, and optimization, while keeping the hidden Markov structure. On ASSISTments 2020, its methods match on prediction while differing in speed and posterior fidelity. Posteriors enable fair comparisons of learning, forgetting, guessing, and slipping parameters.
arxiv-2605-23348: Reddy and colleagues route large language model inference to wind-powered sites instead of straining grids, in a plan they call AI green inferencing. Their survey finds over 890 gigawatts of wind capacity within 50 milliseconds of Azure data centers, and right-sized sites can match standard fleet use. Their router, XWind, splits requests using live latency, cache use, and queue depth alone. On a 64-GPU testbed with real Azure traces, it cuts the slowest-request latency by up to 52 percent against the best rival.
arxiv-2605-23448: Zhang examines a lopsided habit in AI security research: attacks on AI systems far outnumber defenses. Surveying related papers, he finds attack-heavy ratios across federated learning, speech recognition, membership inference, and large language models, and other subfields. The skew runs deeper than counts, he argues, because attack papers often enjoy friendly test conditions that inflate threats, while defenses face a stricter bar few can clear. The literature thus overflows with shown flaws and starves for usable, deployed protections, so he urges stronger incentives for defense work.
arxiv-2605-23548: Mukherjee, Pramanik, and Rakshit count Pfaffian orientations on punctured polygonally cellulated surfaces, giving a formula for their number. The notion extends Pfaffian orientations from planar graphs: a planar graph counts as a punctured two-sphere embedded in three-dimensional space. As a direct corollary of their main theorem, they derive the number of Pfaffian orientations on a planar graph.
arxiv-2605-23848: António Antunes and Junchen Rong study the boundary between two critical spin chains, the Ising and tricritical Ising universality classes, as a conformal interface. They emphasize non-invertible symmetries and modular consistency. Using defect couplings and spectra, including mixed boundary cases, they make sharp predictions testable in Rydberg atom arrays. The observables hinge on a newly found pattern: an emergent W3 chiral symmetry at the interface. That structure ties the abstract field theory to a concrete laboratory platform.
arxiv-2605-23948: Brugière and Chapuis offer comokit4py, a Python package that plugs COMOKIT simulations into high-performance computing workflows. COMOKIT models the lives of city residents in Vietnam to test policy moves against COVID-19 spread scenarios, but running its many replications over parameter ranges demands heavy computing. The package lets users generate, explore, and report on any COMOKIT experiment headed for such machines.
