Agent-based models of this kind simulate self-directed programs interacting in a shared virtual world, a tool used for segregation, opinion shifts, and epidemics.
arxiv-2605-24048: Zhang and five co-authors reframe picking bidders for language-model teams as a feature-selection problem, where a model's value lies in backing the others. Current methods stress scores or variety but miss links among bidders and with the editor, and feature-picking rules cost too much time here. The team therefore tests a wide range of feasible greedy-style pickers that judge fit from a small tagged set. Tests confirm fit as a guiding principle and name the methods with the best score-cost trade-offs in practice.
arxiv-2605-24148: Nair and Zhou prove a fresh case of the Harris-Viehmann conjecture, a parabolic induction formula for cohomology groups of non-basic local Shimura data. The conjecture implies supercuspidal representations on a Shimura variety concentrate on the basic locus, tying it to the Langlands program. This proof too assumes Hodge-Newton reducibility. Building on Mantovan's and Hong's cases, the authors extend the proof to unramified non-basic Shimura data of abelian type. They use Shen's Rapoport-Zink spaces of abelian type at hyperspecial level.
arxiv-2605-24548: Yan Leng, Thibaut Mastrolia, and Hao Wang present Deep ZakaiJ, a 2026 latent-state model for jump-diffusion systems. It embeds the Zakai filtering equation for half-seen systems in a neural encoder-decoder design. The encoder updates beliefs about the hidden state by Strang splitting into three steps: prior propagation, diffusion innovation, and jump innovation. The decoder keeps smooth dynamics and sudden shocks apart in a structured jump-diffusion model. On synthetic, financial, and ocean data, the model gave better distributional forecasts while staying competitive on point accuracy.
arxiv-2605-24648: Ildar Khabibullin and others report a massive galaxy cluster hiding behind the plane of our own galaxy. In the Zone of Avoidance, dust and foreground stars can mask even huge systems. The SRG/eROSITA all-sky survey picked out SRGe CL0512.7+3712. Radio, optical, and infrared data show red-sequence galaxies plus a likely brightest member. Follow-up work confirms a very massive cluster at redshift 0.0745. Its place and stretch fit local large-scale structure, and about ten similar clusters may still await discovery.
arxiv-2605-25148: Marco A. A. Paula, Carolina L. Benone, and Luís C. B. Crispino calculate how heavy scalar waves are absorbed and scattered by charged black holes without a central singularity. For the Ayón-Beato-García and Bardeen geometries, a heavier incoming field lowers total absorption at fixed charge. It also widens the interference pattern in scattering above a critical speed. Their numbers match classical and semiclassical estimates where those apply, and sometimes make regular and ordinary black holes look alike.
arxiv-2605-25248: Filipi Silva and colleagues tackle network grouping when every group must fall inside a size range set by the user. Standard tools only steer average group size through a tuning knob, leaving single groups free to balloon or shrink. Their new heuristic optimizes a standard quality score, called modularity, while respecting those size limits directly. An exact integer model serves as a check on synthetic and real networks, and the method ships inside the Python Leiden package.
arxiv-2605-25548: Shubhajit Roy and Anirban Dasgupta fuse space and time inside one graph message pass. Temporal-first and spatial-first networks force the second stage to read a compressed summary from the first, so a neighbor's past path never weights its message. SiST-GNN keeps a history state per node, pairs it with current features across a cross-time edge, and runs convolution on the augmented graph. It leads methods on link prediction and live-update sets, and beats discrete-time baselines on classification tasks.
arxiv-2605-25948: Pan and sixteen colleagues run both kinds of qubit operation through a single flux line. Fluxonium qubits are circuits that hold quantum states for a long time. One shared line, driven by one waveform generator, must pass slow reset signals while blocking noise near the qubit frequency. Cold filtering plus corrected waveforms resolve that tension. Coherence stays above one hundred microseconds, reset fidelity reaches about 98 percent, and twenty-nanosecond gates top 99.99 percent.
arxiv-2605-26248: Ethan Caballero and three colleagues propose a Unified Neural Scaling Law, a single form modeling how deep-network scores vary as parameters, data, training steps, inference steps, compute, and hyperparameters change together. It covers vision, language, math, and reinforcement learning tasks, upstream and downstream. Compared with other scaling formulas, it extrapolates considerably more accurately across architectures and tasks. The law thus offers one form for many scaling dimensions at once.
arxiv-2605-26348: Zhengye Han and Quanyan Zhu study near-miss commitment: a safe-looking robot velocity can trap it in a passage moving obstacles will soon shut. Their Risk-Sensitive Conjectural Scenario Planning layer tests commands against plausible obstacle futures, keeping a light belief over conjectures and penalizing risky tails. In MuJoCo tasks, it reaches the goal collision-free with better safety and path scores than a plain predictor, at extra latency. Added to a Nav2 stack in ROS2 and Gazebo, its safety layer cuts near-miss failures.
arxiv-2605-26448: Ujwal Kumar and seven colleagues run an adversarial arms race between language-model constitutions in public-goods games. Blue cooperators face Red free-riders across 30 generations in a Public Goods Game and a spatial grid world. In the goods game both sides settle near parity, around a score of 0.78, across tested multipliers. Separately scored worlds yield no real adversarial pressure, but a score-advantage fitness target restores it. Under pure-adversary fitness, two evaluation seeds let specialists regress, while five sustain a strong specialist all 30 generations.
arxiv-2605-26548: Hwiwon Lee and six colleagues benchmark long-horizon security work with SEC-bench Pro. Finding a real flaw demands reasoning across a codebase to craft a working proof-of-concept. Each task pairs a bug with trigger instructions, asking frontier models to reproduce proof-of-concept inputs. Rule-based judges grade such proofs poorly, so the team offers a language-model judge instead. Across 344 validated flaws in V8, SpiderMonkey, and the Linux kernel, Codex with GPT-5.5 solves 58 percent overall. Building it surfaced three new flaws, one earning a 20,000 dollar bounty.
arxiv-2605-26748: Skresanov generalizes a 2012 polynomial-time isomorphism test for solvable groups to the wider class of solvable A-groups, groups whose Sylow subgroups are abelian. The group isomorphism problem asks whether two finite groups given by Cayley tables are the same up to relabeling. His algorithm builds on methods of Babai and Qiao plus structural properties of A-groups, extending their result beyond groups with abelian Sylow factors in a normal series.
arxiv-2605-27148: Sharma and co-authors offer a modular frame for combining machine learning defenses that are usually tested alone. Their Landseer system wraps each defense as a plug-in module and runs tests across many measures, alone and in combination. A first survey found 35 current defenses, and after filtering for work that could be rerun, the tests exposed gaps in how well defenses reproduce across families. The authors present the frame as a base for more reliable combined defenses in real deployments.
arxiv-2605-27348: Jihyeon Kim and colleagues detect fake images from gaze: whether the eyes, head, and pupils of people in a scene agree with each other. Their supervision holds a fixed five-block reasoning skeleton across many captions, blocking shortcuts from paired edits. The same training lifts a vision-language detector and a vision-only detector, with real and fake recall rising together.
arxiv-2605-27448: Jongmin Kim and colleagues scramble spin-state ensembles by tuning chaos in a nonlinear spin-1 system. Weak wobble of a linear Zeeman field moves ensembles across energy shells toward a Haar-random spread. Overdriving instead stalls scrambling at set amplitudes, as sticky phase-space zones form when the leading drive harmonic cancels out.
arxiv-2605-27548: Arjyama Bordoloi, Daniel Kaplan, and Sobhit Singh find that letting twisted bilayer BiSb relax creates tunable topological domains. Within a single moire unit cell, nontrivial and trivial regions coexist, and shrinking the twist angle grows a network of topological regions whose boundaries host protected gapless edge states. An out-of-plane electric field reversibly tunes the domain pattern and its edge channels.
arxiv-2605-28148: Aditya Pujara, Xiaogang Zhu, and Hsiang-Ting Chen keep AI tool servers in step with changing enterprise APIs. DeltaMCP regenerates only the tools touched by a new API specification, instead of rebuilding everything from scratch. Tested on Azure specifications, it cut developer overhead while improving upkeep and version consistency across releases, easing life for teams that ship LLM-based systems.
arxiv-2605-28248: Clare Burrage, Angus Macdonald, and Elisa Todarello use a satellite's orbital precession to hunt ultralight dark matter. Quadratically coupled scalars would shift constants and mediate fifth forces, nudging LAGEOS II's pericentre. The measured precession constrains the scalar's mass and couplings, biting hardest at strong couplings where other satellite and tabletop bounds break down.
arxiv-2605-28348: Seutin and colleagues free vision-language segmentation from semantic labels, segmenting from shape, geometry, and texture descriptions alone. Their SANSA paradigm generates meaning-free prompts by dictionary rules or example guidance, then fine-tunes models under meaning-free supervision. It gained up to twenty percent on the new task while holding strong performance on standard semantic prompts.
arxiv-2605-28848: Mohd Ariful Haque and three colleagues present GPF-LiveNews, a streaming testing system for group-based framing in outputs. Live models face a shifting world where versions, search layers, and inputs change over time, and static benchmarks miss how models frame fresh events for prompted crowds. The system expands BBC and Reuters anchors across 42 group labels and seven families, then scores bundles using meaning shifts and sentiment gaps. In a pilot over 12 runs and 23 models, policy and action prompts produce the strongest movement, while feeling spread stays flatter across axes.
arxiv-2605-29048: Lauren Levine and Amir Zeldes introduce LLMBridge, a language-model pipeline for referential bridging resolution in English. The pipeline pairs heuristic pre- and post-processing with language-model inference ability. Tested on ISNotes, BASHI, and GUMBridge, it beats prior best systems on all three datasets. It wins in both the end-to-end setting and the basic setting with gold bridging anaphors given. Error analysis probes which bridging varieties still challenge language-model systems, and the authors release the pipeline code.
arxiv-2605-29448: Jeff A. Bilmes, Gantavya Bhatt, and Arnav M. Das ask how much a dataset is worth, comparing size-based scaling laws with the Vendi Score. Both objectives are submodular, and the Vendi Score is one case of matrix spectral functions. Secular-equation updates avoid eigendecompositions, making Vendi optimization feasible at ImageNet scale. Facility location predicts held-out value best, and the Vendi Score predicts well only over moderate ranges. Random fixed-size subsets prove concentrated in scores and performance, showing size and budget alone do not fix data value.
arxiv-2605-29548: Jing Huang and eight colleagues explain why larger models learn tasks smaller models miss, from data. An argument suggests bigger models capture data parts smaller ones fail on, even with unlimited training. In mixtures, smaller models spend neurons on frequent or simple tasks and fail rare, complex ones, even when a solution exists. Larger models ease this bottleneck because common gradients weaken once covered, leaving rare-task features intact. OLMo pretraining from four million to four billion parameters mirrors this, with only larger models learning infrequent, complex tasks.
arxiv-2605-29748: Marius Potfer and Vianney Perchet refine regret bounds for Lipschitz bandits, where a learner probes a smooth function with noise. Old bounds run worst-case or lean on zooming dimension, which tracks only near-optimal level-set growth, missing finer shape in the function. The team ties regret to integrals of the gap over level sets, so bounds adapt to local growth, not asymptotics alone. When maximizers form a positive-dimension set, their rates beat zooming bounds. The analysis stretches to full-information Lipschitz experts with softened regularity demands.
arxiv-2605-29848: Renan J. S. Isneri traces the origin of the Gibbons conjecture, a name tied to symmetry results for the Allen-Cahn equation. The label circulates widely, yet its birth proves murkier than frequent citation suggests. Revisiting its emergence, the note roots it in a paper by Carbou and in later literature developments. The attribution, Isneri argues, likely grew from informal communication rather than a formally stated conjecture. The short study thus shows how mathematical names can form through transmission and collective use rather than formal declaration.
arxiv-2605-29948: Bohan Li and eight colleagues build HoliTok, a speech tokenizer serving both speech making and understanding in one model. It squeezes high-rate speech into a stream of compact latents, staged to keep signal truth, sense, and ease of learning. One model both speaks and listens from the same latents, with no extra training tricks. Tests show strong rebuild quality, easier learning for controlled synthesis, and the only steady run among rivals in the joint setup. HoliTok offers a shared base for spoken models that must both hear and speak.
arxiv-2605-30048: Nik Weaver reviews linear and matrix extensions of four classic min-max theorems. Hall's marriage theorem and König's theorem on bipartite matchings anchor the survey. Dilworth's theorem on chains and antichains in ordered sets and Menger's theorem on disjoint paths in directed graphs complete the set. The paper relates the linear and matrix versions, showing how matching, ordering and path ideas extend beyond their first settings. It maps generalizations carrying min-max principles into linear algebra and matrix theory.
arxiv-2605-30348: Yaxin Luo and seven co-authors define Data Mixture Surgery: given only text from an LLM, estimate the spread of its training corpus under a scheme. They propose LLMSurgeon, casting Data Mixture Surgery as an inverse problem under label shift. Rather than pooling model outputs, LLMSurgeon finds a soft confusion matrix and solves an inverse problem to correct domain confusion and rebuild the latent mixture prior. To test, they introduce LLMScan, a test suite built from LLMs with open training mixtures. Across LLMScan, LLMSurgeon finds domain mixes well.
arxiv-2605-30448: Munawar Hasan defines bounded behavioral indistinguishability for black-box LLM distillation. He frames the idea with bounds on telling advantage, oracle queries, compute, and adversary class. He tests it on Qwen and Llama teacher-student pairs with a 5,000-prompt probe set. Yet foe tests show leftover behavior gaps: trained tellers keep nonzero edge. With a different-family Llama judge, Qwen tell edge roughly halves after LoRA distillation. Results show fidelity helps but falls short: distillation needs bounded, foe-aware, category-aware evaluation.
arxiv-2605-30648: Vaswani, Sun, and Babanezhad study steepest descent and Adam under uneven smoothness, where curvature tracks the loss value. The class covers logistic regression, softmax policy gradients, and some neural nets. Under this rule plus gradient dominance, they prove convergence rates for steepest descent, RMSProp, and Adam. Sign descent runs linearly and beats plain descent on separable logistic data and softmax gradients. RMSProp and Adam run linearly on a two-layer net class, and a lower bound shows both beat AdaGrad, AMSGrad, plain descent, and heavy-ball momentum.
arxiv-2605-30848: Li and colleagues study text anonymization under a threat. Agentic models with web search can turn weak cues into evidence for re-identification, while details carry downstream analytic value. Existing defenses remove identifiers, perturb text, or test rewrites against non-web models. They introduce AURA, a mask-reconstruct framework decoupling privacy localization from reconstruction. Evaluated on interview transcripts under attacks by web-search agents, adaptive-scope AURA yields the lowest counts under three models. At matched scope, AURA retains more utility than the anonymizer, with over six points higher recovery.
arxiv-2605-31148: Tianhui Liu and colleagues benchmark whether vision-language agents can turn spatial reasoning into action inside 3D scenes. Their SpatialAct suite moves from multi-turn interactive refinement down to single-step error fixing plus five basic spatial skills. Models handle isolated reasoning tasks well, the experiments show, yet falter at holding a coherent picture of the scene across turns, trailing humans badly. The gap, they argue, is tracking spatial state as actions change the world.
arxiv-2605-31248: Mejia and colleagues solve linear partial differential equations with trainable quantum spectral models. Rather than learning solutions in physical space, these models learn the inverse operator in a basis matched to the equation's spectrum. A mixer parameter blends near-diagonal and fully mixing designs, and an intermediate setting near 0.5 gives the best balance of expressiveness and trainability. Models inspired by the HHL algorithm converge fastest, and spectral training beats standard variational circuits on Poisson and Helmholtz tests.
arxiv-2605-31348: Brubeck, Liang and Parker study a Stokes complex from finite elements on an Alfeld split mesh. They show its cohomology matches the continuous Stokes and de Rham versions. They also build small conforming element complexes. Here the H1 space is the lowest-order Guzmán-Neilan space, and the L2 space holds piecewise constants. Those small complexes share the same cohomologies. The team also builds bounded local cochain maps for them. All of this holds on strongly Lipschitz domains with nontrivial topologies and mixed boundary rules.
arxiv-2605-31548: Ferreira and team match the Fundamental Plane of early-type galaxies with the IllustrisTNG100-1 hydrodynamical simulation. Yet models have long missed its seen tilt, a gap often blamed on flawed feedback physics or poor resolution. Using observation-based ways, including Sérsic photometric values and measured velocity dispersions, the team shrinks the gap between the model plane and the seen plane. Adding bottom-heavy, mass-dependent initial mass function variations yields plane coefficients that match observations for direct and orthogonal fits.
arxiv-2606-00048:
Barmettler tests whether the political leanings of language models survive contact with real votes, in this 2026 arXiv paper grounded in Swiss democracy. Earlier studies found instruction-tuned models lean left, but only on abstract questionnaires. Barmettler administered the 75-question Smartvote survey to 66 models and compared them with Swiss national councillors, replicating the leftward pattern. He then confronted 9 flagship models with 48 federal referenda, asked in Switzerland's 4 national languages under 3 information conditions.

The concrete votes told a different story. Model agreement peaked with centrist parties rather than the left, and abstract scores failed to predict referendum behavior. Language itself swayed some models more than content did, with cross-language consistency ranging from about half to nearly full agreement depending on the model. Two models simply voted no on over 80 percent of proposals regardless of ideology. The author concludes models behave less like left partisans and more like cautious, change-averse civil servants.
arxiv-2606-00148:
He and co-authors pinpoint where multimodal models fail at abstract visual puzzles in this 2026 arXiv paper on StemBind. A model may describe an image correctly and name the governing pattern, yet still pick the wrong completion. Existing benchmarks merge perception, rule discovery, and answer selection into one score, hiding which step broke. StemBind instead probes the same visual stem with three aligned questions covering perception, the rule, and the full task, across roughly 2,300 stems.

Testing 24 frontier model configurations produced four findings. Rule accuracy exceeded full-item accuracy on nearly every model, so most failures occur after the rule is known. Even when perception and rule answers were both right, models still answered the full item wrong about half the time. Analysis localized the bottleneck to mapping, the step binding a rule to the correct candidate instance. Neither larger models nor explicit thinking modes reliably closed that binding gap.

arxiv-2606-04048:
Yifeng Liu and Quanquan Gu derive in 2026 scaling rules for Gated Delta Networks, a memory-efficient alternative to the standard Transformer design for language models. Efficient architectures only help if their training settings can be tuned cheaply as models grow.

A method called maximal update parametrization lets engineers transfer good settings from small models to large ones, but it had not been worked out for this gated, recurrent design. By tracking how signal sizes flow through the gates and the memory state, the pair derived rules for this family. Language model training runs confirmed the payoff: the best learning rate carried across widths under two common optimizers, while standard settings failed to transfer, which validates their analysis.
arxiv-2606-04748:
Perradin and colleagues reinterpret the squeezing of silica glass as a percolation transition, in a 2026 arXiv physics paper. When silica glass is compressed, it jumps from a low-density to a high-density amorphous form. The authors run large-scale molecular dynamics simulations of up to a million atoms at pressures from zero to 35 gigapascals, tracking how structural motifs emerge and grow to system-spanning scales under compression.

The results reveal critical percolation transitions of silicon-oxygen clusters as their coordination number rises with pressure. Analyzing silicon-silicon clusters with a non-bonded approach complements the bonded picture. Together, the authors argue, the two views illuminate pressure-induced structural transformations and mechanisms shared by bonded glasses like silica and non-bonded ones like amorphous ice, two families usually studied separately.
arxiv-2606-04948:
Kaur and Ashokan watch a chain of interacting fermions refuse to thermalize when disorder gets strong enough, in a 2026 arXiv condensed matter paper. Many-body localization is the failure of an isolated quantum system to act as its own heat bath. The authors study the disordered one-dimensional Fermi-Hubbard model, initialized in a charge-density-wave state.

A clear crossover from ergodic to non-ergodic behavior appears. Under weak disorder, imbalance decays rapidly and entanglement grows fast. Under strong disorder, imbalance persists and dynamics slow, the breakdown of ergodicity. Charge and spin sectors relax distinctly. In the interacting regime, entanglement entropy grows slowly and logarithmically, the dephasing-driven signature of the many-body localized phase.
arxiv-2606-05248:
Yigit Yildirim, Giuseppe Rauso, Riccardo Caccavale, and Alberto Finzi build a framework for inverse manipulation in this 2026 arXiv paper: teaching a robot to undo a task it has performed. Undoing is more than reversing symbolic state changes or rewinding joint trajectories. Such an inverse plan often fails to restore the world exactly under real contact dynamics, as when a pushed object cannot simply be pulled back.

Their framework extracts STRIPS-like operators from demos using soft geometric predicates. For each operator it builds an inverse objective that preserves preconditions, restores delete effects, and negates add effects. A task planner tries to satisfy that goal with action primitives at hand. Whatever remains unresolved defines a residual learning problem, solved with reinforcement learning. On the ManiSkill3 PushCube task, the symbolic inverse performed a restoration while a residual Soft Actor-Critic policy refined the cube's pose until the predicates held.
arxiv-2606-05348:
Fabian Zaiser and colleagues bring incremental computation to inference in probabilistic programs in this 2026 arXiv paper. Scoring many possible program runs to find the high-density ones means the same results get recomputed from scratch. Incremental computation, which updates a deterministic program's output when its inputs change slightly, is the remedy, but wiring it into probabilistic inference has been ad hoc and bug-prone.

First, expressive programs are compiled into deterministic programs that compute their density functions. Then, building on the incremental lambda calculus, a technique incrementalizes those programs step by step. The resulting densities speed up a range of Monte Carlo inference algorithms, including nonparametric models that systems support poorly. Because the steps are separate, logical-relations proofs cover each one, fixing the soundness bugs that plague ad-hoc versions. A Julia prototype shows runtime gains that grow with dataset size across models.
arxiv-2606-05448:
Hannah Lu and colleagues couple machine learning stand-ins with Bayesian inference for carbon dioxide flowing underground, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Predicting the parameters of multiphase flow in porous rock is central to carbon storage, but the physics is nonlinear, the parameter space is huge, and observations are limited.

A convolutional neural network stand-in is trained on high-fidelity simulations to predict how the carbon dioxide saturation fields evolve across a range of rock-layer properties. Embedding that surrogate inside a Markov chain Monte Carlo sampler then makes Bayesian inference from the experimental photographs feasible, running about a million times faster than the original simulator. Using the full time-resolved images, the framework matched experiments better than manual calibrations. Data became much more informative once the plume reached major features such as faults and sealing layers.
arxiv-2606-05648:
Zhiyu Sun and colleagues expose a location leak in nearest-neighbor queries in a 2026 arXiv paper. People-nearby features answer which users sit closest to a point. The team shows those answers can betray the very locations they should hide. They craft two inference attacks, one geometric and one based on black-box optimization. Both reconstruct a target's position from query results alone.

The defense, DPRS, adds differential privacy with a twist. Noise is drawn inside a bounded interval, and draws that fall outside are rejected and resampled. A private method builds that interval so noise stays useful rather than wild. On real spatial data sets DPRS beat earlier defenses on both privacy and query utility. The trade-off between the two, long treated as steep, proved gentler here. The paper is a warning that handy location features need privacy engineering from the start.
arxiv-2606-05848:
Adrian Piedra, Jeffrey, and Khatib build a robot that performs abdominal ultrasound scans on its own in a 2026 arXiv paper. Good scans depend on an expert's hand: path, pressure, and angle all matter. The team first records radiologists scanning freely, capturing probe motion and force. Stereo cameras map the patient's belly in three dimensions. Stiffness probes at key points outline the rib cage boundary.

The replayed expertise drives a seven-joint arm with closed-loop force control. Two scan paths cover the anatomy: an angled sweep tucked under the ribs, and a straight sweep across soft tissue. Contact pressure stays steady as the surface curves change. Bench experiments produced images matching expert scan quality. The robot then goes past the experts: it assembles full three-dimensional volumes from its sweeps. Those volumes open the door to richer diagnosis and later analysis. Perception and touch, combined, carry the skill transfer.
arxiv-2606-06248:
Hanna Parul and colleagues study how the Milky Way's central bar bends the tails of star clusters in this 2026 arXiv paper. Open clusters slowly shed stars, forming tidal tails that stream along their orbits. Our galaxy's bar, a rotating bar shaped mass of stars, should tug those tails off their expected paths. If the effect is measurable, tail shapes could reveal how fast the bar rotates, its pattern speed.

The team simulated about one thousand four hundred fifty real clusters from a recent catalogue. They used a smooth reference galaxy and eight barred versions. Pattern speeds ran from twenty to fifty five kilometers per second per kiloparsec. Each tail's deflection angle was measured against the unbarred case. Deflections grew largest near the outer Lindblad resonance and flipped sign with orbit orientation. The observed long tails of NGC 2632 and the Hyades already rule out some moderate pattern speeds.
arxiv-2606-06348:
Wolfgang Rowell Jr and Lucas Kupssinskü benchmark an AI weather model over Brazil in this 2026 arXiv paper. GraphCast, a machine learning forecaster, now rivals the physics based systems that have run global prediction for decades. Most validation, though, comes from temperate regions, leaving its skill in Brazil's convective tropics largely untested. The authors compare operational GraphCast with the ECMWF IFS HRES model across four Brazilian climate sub regions and four seasonal windows.

Skill depended on the regime. In the austral winter, GraphCast lagged on days two to seven for upper air heights over fast southern systems. It then regained the lead at longer ranges, where its smoothing of chaotic detail helps. In the wet summer, it captured large scale moisture transport accurately and damped the rapid convective swings that degrade the physics model's temperature forecasts. The study sets a baseline for Brazil.
arxiv-2606-06448:
Yasmine Omri and co-authors profile the memory systems that give AI agents a past in this 2026 arXiv paper on computer systems. Long horizon agents must store, retrieve, and update their own memory across sessions, and a crowded ecosystem of designs has sprung up, from flat retrieval to consolidating fact stores. Nobody had measured what these systems cost a serving stack, or where the time actually goes. This paper is the first such characterization.

The team built a taxonomy along four axes and a harness that splits cost into construction, retrieval, and generation. They measured ten representative systems on two benchmark suites. The headline finding: building memory dominates the bill, not answering queries, and construction is heavy on embedding work that clashes with live question traffic. The paper distills ten recommendations for deploying memory at fleet scale.
arxiv-2606-06948:
Swapping the spins of two electrons is a basic operation for quantum computing. Sierant, Czarnecki, Szafran, and Wojcik simulate that SWAP in an oxide platform in this 2026 arXiv paper. The stage is a double quantum dot at an interface between two oxides, lanthanum aluminate and strontium titanate. Such oxides promise weaker hyperfine noise for spin qubits.

The study starts with one electron's spin dance. Spin orbit and interorbital couplings shape that dance. Simple semiclassical equations matched the full quantum simulations well. Then the team crosses between two dot regimes. Large dots live in one orbital family, with Rashba type coupling in charge. There the SWAP stays anisotropic but faithful. Small dots recruit higher orbitals into play. Fidelity drops significantly in that regime. The message for device design is concrete: keep the dots large, in orbital terms.
arxiv-2606-07048:
Grid operators often need a stand in circuit for a load they can only measure at its terminals. Montoya, de Leon, Arrabal-Campos, and Alcayde recover that stand in geometrically in this 2026 arXiv paper. Voltage and current waveforms become paths traced through a signal space. The shape of those paths encodes the hidden circuit's parameters.

The method extends an earlier single phase version to three phase systems. Three wire setups get special care, since no neutral voltage exists there. Terminal data must obey coupled Kirchhoff constraints on its own. A sampled data version works in short local windows. It adds normalization, harmonic based coordinates, and explicit identifiability tests. When a window carries too little information, the method says so. It reports low confidence instead of forcing a fit. Noise and sensor delay tests confirmed accurate recovery on informative stretches.
arxiv-2606-07248:
Sundaresan tackles a queueing annoyance for people running language models on modest hardware in this 2026 arXiv paper. Local backends such as Ollama answer requests one at a time in arrival order. That creates head-of-line blocking, where a two-second question waits minutes behind a long essay generation. Cloud systems avoid this with batching, but batching needs far more graphics memory than edge machines have.

His system, Clairvoyant, sits in front of the backend as a proxy and predicts each request's answer length before dispatch. The predictor uses nineteen simple word features and runs in a small fraction of a millisecond per request. Requests are then served shortest first, with a timeout guarding against starvation of long jobs. On a high-end consumer graphics card, median latency for short requests fell by roughly seventy percent under heavy queue pressure in his benchmarks.
arxiv-2606-07348:
Balbiani and Gencer develop the logic of four modal connectives within intuitionistic logic in this 2026 arXiv paper. Modal logic reasons about necessity and possibility, while intuitionistic logic rejects the principle that every statement is either true or provably false, demanding constructive evidence. Combining them requires care, because possibility and necessity each split into versions proposed by writers. The authors build a system with a possibility connective and its necessity connective, plus a pair from a different tradition.

With syntax and semantics defined over relational frames, they analyze which classes of frames each connective can define. They then study whether the valid formulas for those classes admit axiom systems, meaning every truth can be derived from listed rules. The minimal logic over all frames turns out to be decidable, so an algorithm can settle whether a formula holds. The results clarify how the connectives interact and where tradition's choices lead.
arxiv-2606-07548:
Bajaber and Alliheedi show that prompt design matters as much as model generation for biomedical question answering, in this 2026 arXiv challenge paper. The MedHopQA task requires multi-hop reasoning, chaining several facts to answer clinical questions, a high-stakes setting for accuracy. Working through the public API, they built a prompt for Gemini 2.0 Flash combining role-playing instructions, chain-of-thought examples showing multi-step reasoning, and formatting rules. The model itself stayed unchanged between runs.

Their best run with the complex prompt scored about 0.72 on the challenge's concept-level metric. The baseline prompt scored about 0.57, so prompt engineering alone produced most of the system's quality. The tuned older model performed almost identically to the newer Gemini 2.5 Flash under the same treatment in their comparison. The authors conclude that for production models, unlocking reasoning through prompt architecture is a critical and underpriced lever, especially in specialized domains.
arxiv-2606-07748:
Aboulker and many co-authors introduce a new way to measure how close a directed graph is to being orderly, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A digraph assigns a direction to every connection. The new parameter, the partial order decomposition number, counts how few partial orders are needed to cover all its arrows. A partial order is a ranking in which some pairs stay incomparable.

The team proves this number controls the dichromatic number, the directed analogue of graph colouring, through an exponential bound involving the largest directed clique. One consequence is that any family of digraphs with bounded decomposition number is well behaved for colouring. Applied to tournaments, where every pair of vertices meets exactly once, closing a well-behaved family under substitution keeps it well behaved. That advances an open question in the area, and the same tool answers a conjecture about explicit tournaments and bounds their domination number.
arxiv-2606-07848:
Nanayakkara and co-authors map how platinum silicide films form on silicon, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Platinum silicide, PtSi, suits silicon-based quantum devices because it fits standard CMOS fabrication, survives air exposure, and turns superconducting near one kelvin. Device makers need a reliable recipe for phase-pure films.

Using X-ray diffraction, X-ray reflectivity, and transport tests, the team tracked phase formation, structure, and interface quality across annealing conditions. Phase-pure PtSi formed within minutes under thermal processing at six hundred degrees, and stayed stable under extended annealing. Even thirty-second anneals from three hundred to six hundred degrees gave equal film quality, with the same structure and superconducting properties. One finding: roughening at the interface is built into the chemical conversion from Pt2Si to PtSi, not a side effect of heat or long annealing. The results define a forgiving processing window.
arxiv-2606-08048:
Juntong Shi and co-authors close most of the gap between fast diffusion language models and slower autoregressive ones, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Diffusion models generate many tokens in parallel, but ignoring dependencies costs quality. Earlier bridges used importance sampling with the diffusion model proposing and the autoregressive model as target. The two distributions sit so far apart that sampling needs huge particle counts.

Their PoE-Bridge inserts a halfway distribution: a product of experts combining the diffusion proposal and the target. The diffusion model drafts continuations in parallel. Rejection sampling moves candidates toward the halfway point, and importance sampling corrects them the rest of the way. The result is about five times faster than standard diffusion decoding, with accuracy back to at least ninety-five percent of the target model's. The idea is general: when two distributions are too far apart to sample between, build a stepping stone.
arxiv-2606-08148:
Yonatan Kurniawan and co-authors design atomistic simulation models backwards, starting from the property they must predict, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Interatomic potentials let computers simulate materials at scales basic methods cannot reach, but their reliability hinges on training data, uncertainty control, and model range. Active learning usually shrinks parameter uncertainty in general, ignoring which property the potential will be used for.

Information-matching instead demands that chosen training data carry as much information about the parameters as set error targets for specific quantities of interest require. The team applies it to plastic strength in metals, an expensive property to simulate, via an indirect strategy targeting cheap intermediate values tied to strength. The method gave precise parameter limits from minimal data, and precise predictions for both the intermediate values and strength itself. Model error, not data, remains the key limit, partly eased by a post hoc uncertainty correction.
arxiv-2606-08248:
Hsiao, Kai-Lei Wang, and Juan Wang analyze a rare decay of a heavy baryon in this 2026 arXiv paper. The particle is the Lambda-b baryon, which can decay into a proton plus three lighter particles. That decay produced the first observation of CP violation in baryons, meaning matter and antimatter versions proceed at different rates. Unexplored was the role of intermediate resonances, short-lived excited states through which the decay can pass.

Working within the constituent quark model, which treats baryons as bound states of massive quarks, the authors identify the relevant excited states feeding the two-body subprocesses. They compute the branching fraction, the share of decays following this path, finding close to thirty parts per million in their calculation reported here. The work clarifies which resonances drive the matter-antimatter asymmetry.
arxiv-2606-08348:
Xiaojun Wu and co-authors propose a principled way to improve the reusable skills of language model agents, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Agents depend on assets outside the model itself: prompts, tools, memory, standard operating procedures, and skills bundled in a harness. These assets are usually revised by rough reflection, or judged by raw success counts. The authors treat each skill instead as a hypothesis about whether a frozen model will succeed under a given setup.

Their framework, Bayesian-Agent, records verified evidence from agent runs. It keeps a probability distribution over each skill's outcomes, updated as evidence arrives. That posterior maps into inspectable actions: patch a skill, split it, compress it, retire it, or explore alternatives. Model-facing prompts get guardrails and failure-mode patches, while summaries stay open for human audit.
arxiv-2606-08448:
Zilin You, Xu, and Cai teach a neural network to image the inside of materials from scattered waves, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Inverse medium problems, reconstructing unknown material properties from wave measurements, arise in radar imaging and medical diagnostics. The governing Helmholtz equation describes wave propagation, and highly oscillatory media are especially hard. The authors propose an operator learning method based on a multiscale Fourier neural operator. It maps oscillatory medium profiles to the scattered wavefields they produce.

The multiscale design reduces spectral bias, the tendency of neural networks to ignore fine, high-frequency structure. For the recovery itself, a plug-and-play scheme uses a diffusion model to steady the least-squares fit to measured data. Numerical results on partial-aperture inversion of wavy media show accurate reconstruction. The method suits problems that defeat old solvers in daily use at scale in the field and the lab.
arxiv-2606-08648:
Qi Guo and colleagues resolve a question about sphere-valued harmonic maps left open since the nineteen eighties, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Harmonic maps are the critical points of an energy functional, the smoothest maps between geometric spaces in a variational sense. The problem concerns maps from the unit disk to the two-sphere satisfying a specific nonlinear equation, with boundary data tracing a circle of latitude. In nineteen eighty-three, Brézis and Coron proved the existence of two explicit solutions and showed each is the unique minimizer in its relative homotopy class.

The open problem, posed in that work and later listed by Brézis, asked what other solutions exist beyond the two minimizers. The authors resolve the question for this boundary-value problem, a result that has stood for roughly four decades. Harmonic maps into spheres also model liquid crystals and ferromagnetic materials.
arxiv-2606-08848:
Pellarin reviews two rival ways of building zeta functions in positive characteristic, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Zeta functions package arithmetic information. David Goss built analogues for function fields, where values are formal series, not complex numbers. His theory, begun in 1979, grows from Carlitz zeta values and leans on analogies with classical theory. A newer approach defines zeta and L-functions over curves, with values in complete algebraically closed fields of matching characteristic.

The two families interact but remain fundamentally different, and Goss's functions lack a known functional equation. Pellarin explains a rationality theorem of Ferraro that yields an analogue of Riemann's zeta function, presenting tools such as shtuka divisors, Anderson motives, and Drinfeld modules. He treats relative zeta functions, counterparts of Dedekind's, and shows they extend to entire functions. An appendix by Ferraro adds a conjecture, with evidence, on how deeply the function vanishes at its canonical point.
arxiv-2606-09248:
Zheng and colleagues teach video AI to reason about time when finding the moment a query describes, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Video temporal grounding locates the segment of an untrimmed video matching a query. Multimodal models trained with reinforcement learning generate reasoning paths that are often superficial narration, barely helping precision. The authors blame inefficient exploration and rewards grading only the final answer.

Their framework, TaRO, attacks both causes. Constructive Reasoning Exploration builds paths from dense captions, grounded in visual cues and timestamps. A Temporal-Sensitivity Reward grades reasoning quality directly. Good thinking anchors to events and timestamps; disrupt its boundary, and the path's probability drops, the critique signal. Training is a progressive curriculum: select better constructed paths with this reward, then free the model to explore. TaRO reached state-of-the-art results on grounding benchmarks: grading the thinking, not just the answer, sharpens temporal precision.
arxiv-2606-09648:
Luciano Duarte, Olga Ovcharenko, and Sebastian Schelter release a large mixed museum dataset in this 2026 arXiv paper. Database research lacks big real sets that join tables, text, and images in one place. ArtiFact fills that gap with six hundred fifty-one thousand records from three famed museums: the Met, the Art Institute of Chicago, and the Rijksmuseum.

Each record mixes fields, prose, and art images. To test data quality tools, the team planted seven kinds of error into about one hundred thirty thousand records. The planted flaws span wrong dates and materials that clash with a work's era. Today's systems still miss many of these fine, field-aware errors. A second test covers search with hard queries, like objects tied by culture or terms whose sense shifts with era. Systems stumbled there too. ArtiFact thus sets a stiff bar for mixed-data tools.
arxiv-2606-09748:
Rishabh Sabharwal and his co-authors test whether deep research agents get better when given notes on their drafts in this 2026 arXiv paper. These agents plan, search the web, and write cited reports. Most tests grade one shot only. Real users, though, send drafts back with comments. The team ran multi-turn trials under two kinds of feedback.

One kind was self-reflection, with no outside signal. Agents there added and lost rubric points at near equal rates, for no net gain. The second kind was process-level feedback, aimed at gaps in the research plan itself. A new method reads the pattern of met and missed rubric items to infer those gaps. One round of it raised scores by about eight to fifteen points. Later rounds stalled: full rewrites dropped up to a quarter of the points won before.
arxiv-2606-10048:
Yin and colleagues test whether indoor wireless signals can recover a walking person's pose, in a 2026 arXiv paper on wireless sensing. Their network operates in the six gigahertz band and records channel state information, measurements of how radio signals change as they cross a room, from multiple links. Four existing deep learning architectures for pose estimation are adapted to this signal structure.

The models estimate the pose of a person walking inside the network's coverage area, judged by standard error metrics on joint positions. Reliable pose reconstruction proved possible from these radio measurements, with the DT-Pose model giving the best overall accuracy. On average, amplitude alone performed comparably to using amplitude and phase together. Phase information helped more as a complementary feature than as a standalone input, a practical guide for designing sensing systems that reuse communication hardware instead of cameras.
arxiv-2606-10448:
Liu and co-authors try to steady automated trading in this 2026 arXiv paper, where financial data has a low signal-to-noise ratio, meaning real patterns are weak beside random market jitter. They study Soft Actor-Critic, a reinforcement learning method that learns a trading policy while favouring varied actions. In noisy markets its value estimates turn unreliable, and reusing them compounds the error, a failure named the Financial Entropy Trap. Their variant passes market data first through a small parameterised quantum circuit.

On real portfolio tasks, FPQC-SAC earns a 66.89 percent relative gain in cumulative return over the standard method in out-of-sample tests. It beats the best competing continuous-control baseline by roughly twenty-seven percent and shows the lowest variance in its value targets. The claim is that a quantum circuit can serve as a geometric restraint that keeps noise from swamping weak trading signals.
arxiv-2606-10948:
Mahmoodi and colleagues propose a diagnostic for adaptive systems in this 2026 arXiv paper. Average performance says whether a system works, not how its parts mesh or where to step in when it fails. Their measure, complexity synchronization, tracks whether the changing complexity of coupled parts rises and falls together, using entropy and fluctuation scaling exponents.

In a multi-agent predator-prey testbed, entropy-based sync grows alongside cooperative success, while the DFA version marks a separate persistence mode. When learning in one subsystem was deliberately weakened, a CS-guided repair restored cooperation to near baseline. It also shrank the search from 15 candidate threshold pairs to the single right one.
arxiv-2606-11648:
Kazuki Iwahana and five colleagues propose an unusual defence for language models in this 2026 arXiv paper. A backdoor attack poisons training so a model behaves normally until a hidden trigger phrase appears, then produces the attacker's chosen response. Removing an unknown backdoor is hard because the defender knows neither the trigger nor the attack type.

The key finding is that different backdoors built for the same task create similar trigger-driven changes inside the model. So the defenders deliberately plant their own dummy backdoor with a known trigger, then fine-tune it away by pairing dummy-triggered inputs with clean responses. Because the dummy and the real backdoor share internal machinery, erasing one weakens the other. Tests span three attack types and several model families. The method cuts the unknown backdoor's attack success rate substantially while preserving normal usefulness, beating representative existing defences on both removal and utility.
arxiv-2606-11748:
Niamh Ferguson and four colleagues compute atomic data for interpreting kilonova light in this 2026 arXiv paper on astrophysics. A kilonova is the glow from merging neutron stars, where the heaviest elements are forged. As the debris expands, electrons recombine with ions, and dielectronic recombination, capture helped by exciting an inner electron, is expected to dominate. Reliable rates for heavy ions are largely missing, forcing spectral models to guess.

The team develops an optimisation strategy for ions with open f-shells, a complex electron layout, using the AUTOSTRUCTURE code. They target uranium ions at three charge states found in kilonova debris. Neodymium is the benchmark case validating the treatment. The computed rates land in the expected range across kilonova temperatures, and the benchmark shows refining the atomic structure changes spectral features measurably. The rates are intended for the SUMO transfer code, to test how better physics changes predicted spectra.
arxiv-2606-11948:
Victor Daniel Reyes Dreke and Rahul Rane auto-tune controllers for high-voltage power links in this 2026 arXiv paper. Modular multilevel converters drive modern high-voltage direct current links, prized for integrating renewable energy. Their dynamics are strongly coupled and uncertain, which suits model predictive control, but tuning it by hand guarantees neither stability nor robustness.

The method computes the weighting matrices by solving one convex fitting problem with matrix inequality constraints. The result can be reproduced exactly, and the online computation burden does not grow. Tests used a real-time digital simulator model of a point-to-point high-voltage link. Against the standard tuning, the robust version guarantees closed-loop stability and enforces the phase and gain margins grid operators specify. Across scenarios it damped oscillations faster, reduced high-frequency ringing and kept overcurrents lower, even under parameter uncertainty and nonlinear conditions.
arxiv-2606-12048:
Balázs Gyenes leads an eight-author team putting surgical clips in place autonomously in this 2026 arXiv paper. Laparoscopic gallbladder surgery involves clipping vessels precisely, allowing almost no error. The team presents the first robotic system to position clips on its own on a physical phantom, a tissue model, for this operation. The robot works from a colourless three-dimensional point cloud from one camera.

A segmentation model, trained on only sixty hand-labelled real point clouds, finds the target structures. Scarcity of surgical data is offset by pretraining on one hundred twenty-eight thousand synthetic clouds. Spline fitting extracts clip target positions, which the human operator can adjust. In real robot experiments the system localised targets within the required precision at a ninety-five percent success rate. Clip positioning itself succeeded in every trial, while respecting the motion constraints of minimally invasive surgery.
arxiv-2606-12148:
Dürfeldt-Pedros and co-authors cap the hidden magnetic fields inside pulsating stars, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their tool is asteroseismology, reading a star's vibrations to probe its interior. They use gravity modes, slow buoyancy waves that reach deep near the core. A strong near-core field would wipe these modes out, so seeing them sets a ceiling on the field. The team models three stars with vibration patterns already identified from space data.

For two gamma Doradus stars, the radial field near the core must stay below about 130 kilogauss in one and about 13 kilogauss in the other, assuming a dipole shape. The evolved star 44 Tau allows a far higher ceiling near 1,771 kilogauss from its mixed modes. Ring-shaped parts barely matter: they must exceed the radial part two hundredfold to suppress the modes. The limits fit field estimates for red giant descendants.
arxiv-2606-12248:
Xiao and co-authors type disaster damage building by building from a single post-event photo, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Most automated tools grade harm on one severity ladder, or need before-and-after image pairs that emerging hazards rarely allow. Their model assigns a damage typology: five classes separating roof from structural damage, each split by extent. The system works from one aerial image plus the building's footprint outline.

A new benchmark draws on disaster imagery from Hurricane Michael, Hurricane Helene, and the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires. It extends a DINOv3 vision backbone with finer pooling, a two-stage gated head, and a side severity task. It reaches macro F1 scores of 0.624 in validation and 0.619 on held-out tests. It is strongest where triage needs it most: F1 of 0.91 for undamaged buildings and 0.84 for total structural collapse. Only the rare total roof class stays hard, with few examples.
arxiv-2606-12348:
Bhatt and co-authors teach a physics-informed neural network to grade its own homework, layer by layer, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The coupled Burgers' equations model interacting flows that develop sharp shock fronts as time passes. At high Reynolds numbers, low viscosity, those fronts break mesh-based solvers through instability and grid dependence. Physics-informed networks bake the equations into training, but balancing the physics residual against starting and boundary conditions is delicate. One fixed weighting rarely serves all layers equally.

Their layerwise self-adaptive framework adjusts penalty weights dynamically during training, separately for each layer's terms. A dual-phase optimization strategy steadies convergence further. Tests across one, two, and three dimensions compare it with standard physics-informed networks, with and without a popular second optimizer. The adaptive version wins on relative error throughout. It also captures the birth and growth of sharp shock fronts that defeat conventional training.
arxiv-2606-12548:
Sylos Labini and Capuzzo-Dolcetta argue that the Milky Way's dark matter may be flattened into a disk, not balled into a sphere, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Using Gaia satellite data, they derive how stars orbit at heights up to two kiloparsecs above the galactic plane, across the disk. Rotation speeds there are measured to better than five percent. Vertical accelerations, the pull back toward the plane, carry larger model uncertainties.

Models pairing the stars with a spherical dark halo fail. They cannot reproduce how rotation speed changes with height, nor the vertical pull's pattern. A halo sphere fifteen kiloparsecs in scale barely contributes off-plane in the inner disk, leaving those features to the stars alone. Flattened, disk-like dark matter contributes to both signals and matches the data better. The authors conclude disk-like distributions are favored. Future Gaia releases should sharpen the test of dark matter's shape.
arxiv-2606-12848:
Zhu and colleagues argue that reliable AI-assisted social science comes from decision architecture rather than model capability alone, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Language models are delegated research tasks more and more, such as writing hypotheses, choosing specs, and drafting reports. The authors build their workflow around behavioural-science principles: pre-commitment, decision sequencing, accountability, and attention allocation.

In a set 2 by 4 factorial experiment with 280 research runs across 4 data sets, a free multi-agent baseline caused critical failures in 72 percent of runs. The same model, agent split, and prompts, rebuilt under 3 architectural pledges, failed in only 16 percent of runs. Those pledges restrict language models to reasoning, and run data handling and estimation by fixed rules, and insert 3 human gates. Gains were largest on the least covered data set, a Qing-dynasty population register. The authors frame their harness, HLER, as decision infrastructure, not an autonomous scientist.
arxiv-2606-13048:
Abyzov and colleagues investigate 3 clean-like properties of rings, in this 2026 arXiv paper. They ask when rings, matrix rings, and endomorphism rings admit decompositions of their elements into units combined with idempotent or nilpotent parts. Clean-type properties generalise the classical notion that every element of a ring is a sum of a unit, an invertible element, and an idempotent, an element equal to its own square. They connect a ring to the abelian groups whose endomorphisms form it.

The authors establish when a ring is weakly strongly k-nil-clean for a fixed natural number k at least 2. They also settle when the matrix ring over a finite field is quasi 2-nil-clean or quasi 3-nil-clean. And they settle when the endomorphism ring of an abelian group is weakly clean. Their theorems improve earlier results by Goldsmith and Vamos, Breaz, Kosan and Zhou, Su, and others.
arxiv-2606-13148:
Nguyen and colleagues present TerraBench, a benchmark testing whether language-model agents can reason over heterogeneous Earth-system data, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Climate and environmental decisions require reasoning across gridded data, satellite imagery, geospatial context, and simulator outputs.

TerraBench is built on TerraAgent, a ReAct-style framework coupling language-model planning with scientific tools for environmental retrieval, geospatial processing, simulation, and computation. The benchmark has 403 agentic tasks across 3 tracks, fundamentals, simulator-grounded, and document-grounded verification, spanning 8 application domains with 24,500 execution steps; only about 51 percent of samples survived review. The strongest frontier model, Claude Sonnet 4.6, reaches only a tool-use score of about 59 and a tolerance-aware hit rate of about 23, while the strongest open-weight model trails at 40 and about 6. The gap is driven mainly by argument and numeric grounding failures, not tool selection: over 84 percent of numerical answers fall outside acceptable error margins across all models.
arxiv-2606-13248:
Chehimi and colleagues outline Q-Backbone in this 2026 arXiv paper, a design for adding quantum computers to future network control systems. Modern networks must constantly route traffic, divide capacity, and tune wireless links under tight limits on delay, energy, and reliability, and the maths grows hard for ordinary computers. Q-Backbone places quantum processing units, machines that compute with quantum states, beside classical servers as accelerators for the hardest tasks. A policy layer decides case by case which machine should handle each job.

The design has four layers, covering hardware, shared runtime services, task scheduling, and network applications. A case study on scheduling quantum jobs across different machines under deadlines shows more work finishing on time. The authors stress that hardware access alone is not enough for real networks. They close with a roadmap of design problems to solve before such control planes can run.
arxiv-2606-13948:
Bovill, Jurik, and Malde redraw the map used to measure a key angle of particle physics. The angle gamma tests the Standard Model's account of matter-antimatter asymmetry. It is extracted from Dalitz plots, maps of D meson decays. Analysts divide the map into bins, and bin shapes affect precision. Their 2026 arXiv paper optimizes the binning with a new figure of merit tracking sensitivity to gamma.

The new scheme uses ten bins, with fuller treatment of backgrounds and of entanglement with other fitted parameters. Expected precision on gamma improves by about five percent over the CLEO_OPTIMAL scheme now in use. Strong-phase inputs should also cut their propagated uncertainty on gamma by ten percent. Separately, the first dedicated binning for charm mixing observables gains about twenty percent in statistical sensitivity. Event migration between bins, from detector blur, stays comparable to today.
arxiv-2606-14048:
Li and colleagues teach a robot world model real three-dimensional structure without paying for it at run time. World action models predict future observations and robot actions, but most work in flat video space, missing the spatial constraints and contact geometry precise manipulation needs. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents WAM4D. In training, lightweight spatial register tokens act as future-depth readouts, transferring priors from geometric foundation models into a causal video-action transformer. The branch is then removed for fast inference.

A causal mixture attention design stops video, action, and geometry tokens from leaking future information into the past. Experiments span the RoboTwin 2.0 simulator and real-world manipulation tasks. WAM4D improved spatial consistency and reached competitive action prediction with efficient inference. Two limits are noted: no explicit long-term object memory, so severe occlusion can produce identity-inconsistent completions, and speed still below direct vision-language-action policies.
arxiv-2606-14348:
Zarcone, Micciche, and Sanchez read sixteen years of a newspaper as a physical system, letting turning points emerge from data, not labels. Pre-digital diachronic corpora are scarce, so they rebuilt one: 600,000 La Repubblica articles from 1985 to 2000, spanning the First Republic's fall and two wars. Their 2026 arXiv paper analyzes it at lexical and semantic levels with complex-systems tools.

At the word level, salience varies: some terms drift slowly while others burst, spiking and decaying fast. The heavy-tailed spread of Fano factors shows this intermittency is systematic in the vocabulary that carries content. At the semantic level, a semantic trajectory and cosine similarity matrix show bursts aligning into mesoscopic regimes, quasi-stable phases visible as block structure. The mid-1990s emerged as the biggest change, matching the First-to-Second Republic transition, detected with no prior labeling. Word bursts, they conclude, are how events reorganize public discourse.
arxiv-2606-14548:
Talebi, Ekh, and Meyer speed up plasticity simulations with neural networks in a 2026 arXiv paper. Finite element simulations predict how structures deform. But advanced material models solve coupled equations at every point, step, and iteration. That makes them costly. Plasticity means permanent deformation that stays after loading.

Their framework lets neural networks compute the state updates directly. This allows large time steps at low cost. The networks act on invariants, values unchanged by rotation. The needed evolution directions are fixed from the training data by analysis. One key rule is enforced exactly. It is the plastic consistency condition, which keeps stress on the yield surface during flow. Training used just ten cycles of multiaxial loading. The integrator stayed accurate and stable in point tests. It also held up in full finite element tests, with a clear gain in computing time.
arxiv-2606-14648:
Chumpitaz-Flores and co-authors ask which uncertainty directions a robust model must cover in a 2026 arXiv paper. Robust optimization plans against a set of possible disturbances, but covering every direction is intractable, so the set is built from a finite dictionary under a budget. Choosing a subset gives an atomic uncertainty set with a closed-form support function, keeping robust programs with affine objectives tractable.

The authors propose a data-driven selection rule based on a coverage objective over evaluation directions such as gradients, adversarial perturbations, or shifts seen in held-out data. They prove the objective is monotone and submodular, so a greedy method achieves a constant-factor approximation guarantee with a matching hardness barrier. They add a certificate bounding the loss from the chosen subset and a radius calibration rule with out-of-sample control.
arxiv-2606-15148:
Yang and coauthors learn inverse kinematics from human teleoperation data for smooth real-time robot control in a 2026 study. Inverse kinematics converts a target hand pose into joint angles, and classical solvers jump between branches near singularities. Learned solvers often trade accuracy, smoothness, and speed against each other. Training data from human operators adds noise on top.

Their system, MimicIK, uses conditional flow matching to predict small joint updates from the current pose and target. A two-step iterative policy keeps inference fast enough for live control. A forward-kinematics consistency loss penalizes pose error during training, anchoring predictions physically. Training uses nearly nine thousand real demonstrations on a six-axis robot. Mean position error lands under five millimeters, with most trials inside a ten-millimeter success band. Latency drops to about a third of a diffusion baseline's, and the system stays stable where plain network baselines diverge near singularities.
arxiv-2606-15348:
Kanai and Ma ask when a simulated brain could be conscious in a 2026 philosophy of mind paper. The objection says simulated water is not wet, so a simulated brain is not conscious. Their framework, Intrinsic Computational Functionalism, replies that constitution matters, not labels. What counts is the structure a system realizes through its causal setup. An earlier version, Canonical Functionalism, picked out states by future input-output behavior. The authors argue that boundary view is too coarse for consciousness.

Lookup tables and unfolded systems can match boundary behavior while lacking the insides. So the canonical structure must include internal workings and response profiles. They define a realization relation preserving building, state identity, transitions, and tests. The result is conditional: whatever realizes that structure has the same conscious traits. Substrate, biological or silicon, does not decide the question. To deny a simulation consciousness, critics must name the intrinsic structure it misses.
arxiv-2606-15448:
Lei and coauthors present EventConnector in a 2026 machine learning paper, a framework for finding hidden links between real-world events. Events that move together in time, an election rumor and a crypto price swing, may share no words or topic, so similarity search misses their connection. EventConnector builds a temporal graph whose edges encode local co-fluctuations and lead-lag patterns between event time series, such as prediction market prices.

An extension, EC-Fusion, blends the graph's retrieval scores with a Granger-causality signal, weighted by measured graph quality. Across two prediction market benchmarks and nine forecasting models, the fused retriever is the best non-oracle method in nearly every test cell. It cuts forecast error by about seven percent on average over the strongest rival. Temporally grounded retrieval like this can feed forecasters the events that actually move together, improving prediction of markets, elections, and public opinion.
arxiv-2606-15748:
Sun develops a method for estimating demand for a new product in 2026, where no sales history exists to learn from. Standard demand estimation starts from utility maximisation and observed purchases, neither available for products that have not launched. Sun instead takes willingness to pay as the primitive input and builds the demand function from it directly.

From the distribution of willingness to pay, he derives a general yet analytically simple demand function. An estimation procedure recovers the underlying demand consistently from such data, and Monte Carlo simulations show it identifies the true demand function well. The approach complements existing methods rather than replacing them. Uses range from teaching economics and pricing a product launch to non-market valuation, such as estimating demand for carbon emission reductions so policymakers can weigh welfare effects. Willingness-to-pay surveys, often treated as rough guides, become a rigorous basis for demand curves.
arxiv-2606-16148:
Zhao and colleagues report results in 2026 for a multicore chip that accelerates approximate inference for probabilistic models. Such models let machines reason and decide under uncertainty. Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampling performs the inference, but it is compute-intensive and hard to parallelize on ordinary processors. Their accelerator, AIA, was built to run this workload directly in silicon at the edge.

AIA combines a RISC-V host with a 4 by 4 mesh of customized RISC-V cores in a 16 nanometer process. Each core features a non-normalized Knuth-Yao sampler, which draws discrete samples efficiently, and an interpolation unit. Cores also access each other's register files directly, speeding data sharing. A custom compiler chain maps and schedules sampling algorithms across the mesh. The chip generates 1277 million samples per second at 0.9 volts and reaches 20 billion samples per watt at 0.7 volts in the reported measurements, up to twice the speed of prior implementations.
arxiv-2606-16248:
Mishra benchmarks three ways of fitting cosmic expansion data in 2026, asking whether faster methods match the exact one for late-time cosmology. Exact Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampling is the trusted but slow route. The rivals are Monte Carlo aided by a Gaussian process emulator, and neural simulation-based inference.

All three methods fit the same data: cosmic chronometers, DESI DR2 baryon acoustic oscillation measures, and the Pantheon+ supernova set. On the smaller data pairing, both fast methods match the exact posterior limits on the Hubble constant and matter density to better than 0.3 sigma. Adding the supernovae brings small method-dependent shifts, at most about 1.5 sigma in one parameter. All three still recover nearly the same expansion history, agreeing at the percent level. Fast inference, Mishra concludes, is now a practical stand-in for exact sampling in much late-time work.
arxiv-2606-16548:
Wu and co-authors prepare fractional quantum Hall states on quantum computers in 2026 with direct circuits that escape the one-dimensional corner earlier methods were stuck in. These states carry fractional charge and intrinsic topological order, making them prized targets and hard preparations. Adiabatic methods must evolve complex parent Hamiltonians, while prior circuit methods worked only near the thin cylinder or torus limit, effectively one-dimensional. The new scheme constructs circuits directly for arbitrary geometries.

The showcase is the Laughlin state at filling fraction one third, prepared precisely on the sphere geometry. Compared with variational quantum circuits, the construction needs significantly fewer two-qubit gates and shallower depth. The team also uses optimal control techniques to design the driving pulses for two hardware families, superconducting circuits and Rydberg atom platforms, identifying experimentally feasible protocols. Configurations with richer inter-qubit control reach the target fidelity in fewer layers.
arxiv-2606-16648:
Marazzato and colleagues present a 2026 design study, published in Acta Astronautica, for space-based sunshades. A sunshade near the Sun-Earth L1 point would cut sunlight reaching Earth and cool the planet slightly. The hard limit is mass: a shade must block enough light while sunlight pressure pushes it, so heavy designs cannot stay in place.

Their deflective design tilts reflective surfaces so sunlight is redirected rather than simply blocked. Shaping the surface geometry controls both shade and pressure, allowing ordinary aluminium films instead of exotic materials. Conical, pyramidal and louvered shapes are compared, with the cone studied in depth. A constellation of smaller units plus a Miura-Ori flat-folding pattern improves packing and launch scaling. The work gives engineers a lighter, more practical route for judging whether orbital sunshades could ever be feasible.
arxiv-2606-16748:
Lawrence Jang and colleagues introduce MyPCBench in a 2026 benchmark paper on computer-use agents. Existing tests place agents in impersonal setups, but real personal assistants must work across a user's logged-in accounts, history and files. Live web tests cannot safely exercise sites that need personal logins, which is exactly where assistants are most needed.

MyPCBench builds a Linux desktop with seventeen simulated web applications plus a full office stack, all seeded for one fictional persona. Its task set, drawn from real community requests, asks agents to act as that person's assistant across apps and long workflows. Six leading closed and open models are tested with the same tool access. The best model fully solves just over half the tasks, and it is the only one above that mark. Failures cluster on cross-application tasks and long trajectories, where personal context stresses an assistant most.
arxiv-2606-16948:
Grootveld and colleagues prove an optimality result for quantum state tomography in a 2026 quantum information paper. Tomography estimates an unknown quantum state from measurements on many copies. Protocols are compared by a rate function, which sets how fast the chance of a wrong estimate decays as copies accumulate.

The rate function acts like a quantum relative entropy between the true state and its estimate. It depends on the measurement scheme and never exceeds the plain quantum relative entropy. The authors first show that bound is sharp: some protocol family always approaches it. They then settle a conjecture of Keyl about covariant protocols, the basis-independent schemes that assume no prior knowledge of the state. Keyl's Schur-sampling protocol, they prove, has the largest possible rate function among all covariant schemes. Its rate is an annealed form of relative entropy, the gap reflecting the cost of learning the state's eigenbasis.
arxiv-2606-17048:
Mammadov and colleagues derive the exact posterior score for image restoration in a 2026 machine learning paper. Diffusion models learn a strong prior over images by training a denoiser. Solving an inverse problem, like deblurring, needs posterior samples given measurements, but the prior supplies only the unconditional score.

Existing fixes steer a frozen denoiser with approximate corrections, or train a separate conditional model. The authors compute the posterior score in closed form for linear Gaussian problems. Posterior sampling, they show, is just denoising at an operator-dependent shifted point with anisotropic noise. That identity becomes a training objective, EPS, shaped like ordinary pretraining, so models can be trained or fine-tuned. At test time it reuses the standard sampler, with no likelihood gradients. On five inverse problems it beats training-free and training-based rivals while using far fewer denoiser calls.
arxiv-2606-17748:
Tambača and Truhar present a 2026 arXiv paper on where to put a handful of dampers on a vibrating string, and how stiff each should be, to calm it fastest. Point dampers are cheap and local, but choosing their positions and viscosities is a stubbornly non-convex design problem. Working from a finite-element model recast in phase-space form, the authors build a Lyapunov-based framework in which three natural goals share the same machinery. The goals are average energy, average displacement, and energy from one fixed start.

For each goal, gradient formulas come from one primal and one dual Lyapunov solve, keeping the search cheap. A heuristic seeded from an exact single-damper formula supplies strong starting guesses against the non-convexity. Numerical examples show how spectral choices and grid refinement move the optimal layout. The result is a design tool for a classic vibration problem.
arxiv-2606-17948:
Berest and colleagues present a smarter filter for spotting overlapping signals in rare-event detectors, in a 2026 instrumentation paper. When two particle signals land nearly on top of each other, the pile-up can fake the very events physicists hunt and blur energy readings. The work is driven by CUPID, an experiment searching for neutrinoless double beta decay in cryogenic molybdate crystals, where pile-up from ordinary decays is expected to be the leading background.

Given a detector's known signal shape and steady noise spectrum, the authors derive the digital filter that best separates genuine single pulses from merged ones. Their approach optimizes the filter for discrimination rather than borrowing a generic shape.
