Cleaner rejection of pile-up means fewer fake candidate events and better energy resolution, tightening the net for one of the rarest processes physics allows.
arxiv-2606-18248:
Huenupi and colleagues solve a two-field inflation system exactly at linear order, in a 2026 cosmology paper. During inflation, the curvature perturbation that seeds galaxies can couple to an entropy, or isocurvature, perturbation riding alongside it. When the coupling is strong, as in rapid-turn models, approximations crumble and modelers usually fall back on numerics. Exact solutions would restore analytic control over that regime.

For a two-field system in a near de Sitter background, the authors obtain closed-form solutions valid for any entropy mass and any interaction strength. As a first use, they derive the primordial power spectrum's amplitude in a form that interpolates smoothly between weak and strong coupling and between light and heavy entropy fields. The results open analytic paths to non-Gaussianity, particle production, and loop corrections in multifield inflation, observables that decide whether such models match the sky.
arxiv-2606-18448:
Jiang and colleagues argue that the skill libraries given to computer-use agents should contain pictures, not just text, in a 2026 artificial intelligence paper. Agents that operate software through screenshots still fail on long tasks and unfamiliar programs, and existing reusable skills describe procedures in words alone.

Their VisualSkill format organizes knowledge for each application as a central index over topic files mixing text and figures, fetched on demand through a tool call when relevant. Skills are built by mining authored documentation and then exploring the live application. On two agent benchmarks, an agent equipped with VisualSkill scored well above its no-skill baseline. A controlled comparison against a text-only skill built from identical source material showed a further gain from keeping the figures. The authors pinpoint where images matter most: locating click targets, confirming typed values, and handling multi-step widgets.
arxiv-2606-18548:
Oh, Talton, and Bui ask which simple intake measures best reveal how graduate trainees will approach AI ethics instruction, in a 2026 education paper. Trainees arrive with very different experience of large language models, and a single module fits them unevenly, but it was unclear whether prior coursework, self-rated familiarity, or usage habits track their attitudes.

The team compared three candidate intake features across five baseline perception items in ninety-three bioscience graduate students and postdoctoral trainees. Reported usage frequency was associated with all five outcomes after statistical correction, self-rated familiarity with three, and prior AI education with none. A threshold-like pattern at the low end of the usage scale showed most clearly for interest in training and trust in accuracy. The authors suggest that a short intake survey built on use, with familiarity as a secondary check, can support profiling for adaptive ethics teaching.
arxiv-2606-19448:
Solanki and colleagues investigate how fast radio bursts are damped in the inner magnetospheres of magnetars in 2026. Earlier work showed gigahertz radio waves there propagate as fast magnetosonic waves. They undergo resonant three-wave interactions that transfer energy into trapped Alfvén waves. Whether that transfer truly kills an escaping burst needs full simulation.

Using three-dimensional force-free electrodynamics simulations, the team shows bursts excite Alfvénic fluctuations that strongly attenuate the radio signal. In quiet dipolar magnetospheres, the nonlinear decay stays efficient out to tens of magnetar radii. Charge starvation of the excited waves stops it farther out. For bursts traveling through relativistic outflows from eruptions, the coupling stays efficient much farther. Luminous bursts must reach hundreds of radii before escaping. The results confirm that nonlinear plasma processes strongly limit burst escape from deep inside magnetars. Magnetar theories must launch bursts far out or explain their survival.
arxiv-2606-19548:
Kenji Nishiwaki, Kin-ya Oda, and Juntaro Wada revisit neutrino flavour oscillations through propagation time in 2026. Neutrinos shift flavour as they travel, a quantum effect seen over long distances. Old theorems describe that behaviour when travel time runs long.

Within wave-packet quantum field theory, the Jacob-Sachs theorem covers the long-time limit. The trio evaluate the key integrals by the saddle-point method. An extended formula for the flavour-changing amplitude stays valid at shorter times as well. Oscillations switch on only past a threshold travel time. That threshold depends on the energy spread of the wave packets and the particle's decay width. Below it, the middle particle acts as a purely virtual state that cannot cross macroscopic distances. The result implies the Jacob-Sachs theorem holds more accurately than expected, even at short times.
arxiv-2606-19748:
Nguyen Thanh Phuc builds a variational polaron theory for strongly coupled quantum systems in 2026. Polarons form when particles dress themselves in surrounding excitations, like electrons in a lattice or matter in light fields. Ultrastrong coupling breaks bare-state and perturbative treatments.

A state-based polaron change of frame anchors the new framework. A product-state guess plus a small fix-up term handles the leftover links between matter and bosons. At infinite coupling the transformed frame decouples exactly, as leading coupling cancels. Displaced-oscillator overlaps suppress off-diagonal transitions at the same time. The method stays accurate in weak, strong, and intermediate regimes alike. Dicke model tests reproduce energies, fidelities, and the superradiant transition with errors below 0.2 percent. Holstein model errors stay below 0.5 percent. Dressed-state work on light and matter thus gains a trusty tool that needs no small-coupling crutch to stay sound.
arxiv-2606-19848:
Tong Shen and six colleagues build QMCtwin in 2026, a simulator of quantum error correction noise beyond Pauli models. Decoders depend on how faithfully hardware noise becomes syndrome statistics. Standard workflows compress device physics into Pauli or detector-error models for speed.

That compression drops coherent phase effects, drift, and correlations from always-on couplings. QMCtwin instead runs master-equation simulation through a sign-tamed quantum Monte Carlo frame. The test case is a full syndrome round of a distance-seven rotated surface code with ninety-seven qubits. Noise includes relaxation, dephasing, gate miscalibration, crosstalk, and drive detuning. Syndrome biases and parity correlations appear that Pauli-twirled twins suppress or miss. Information-theoretic diagnostics quantify the gap between the two noise pictures. Decoder-facing models can thus train on richer, more honest noise.
arxiv-2606-19948:
Leekyeung Han and five colleagues attack a data shortage in dialog-guided robot navigation in 2026. DialNav tests whether an embodied agent can talk and act its way through photorealistic indoor scenes, but only about two thousand training episodes existed. The team builds an automatic pipeline that converts existing navigation datasets into multi-turn dialog, producing RAINbow, a training set of 238 thousand episodes.

Two further pieces unlock the data: dual-strategy training aligned with the dialog-navigation loop, and a localization model borrowing navigation knowledge. Success rates roughly double on both seen and unseen validation splits, reaching a new best for the task. Code and dataset are public. The work shows synthetic dialog can stand in for costly human demonstrations when training household robots.
arxiv-2606-20048:
Zheyu Zhuang, Ruiyu Wang, Giovanni Luca Marchetti, Florian Pokorny, and Danica Kragic present MirrorDuo in 2026, a mirroring scheme that doubles robot demonstration data for free. Image-based behaviour cloning learns from camera demonstrations, but collecting varied demos is costly, especially across different workspace layouts. MirrorDuo reflects each demonstration, image, body state, and full six-degree-of-freedom action together, producing a consistent mirrored twin.

The pairs serve either as augmentation for standard cloning and diffusion policies or as a structural prior for reflection-aware networks. With demos spread over both sides of a workspace, performance rises sharply under the same budget. With demos on one side only, skills transfer to the mirrored side with zero or five target demos. Manipulation policies gain left-right generality without new data collection.
arxiv-2606-20648:
Zhen Qin and four colleagues propose a new way to platoon mixed traffic in 2026, allowing connected, autonomous, and human-driven vehicles to travel in tight groups. Most platooning methods only accept connected vehicles, leaving out non-connected cars that already share real roads. Their hybrid pattern lets non-connected vehicles join under conditions, which adds flexibility but can also let platoons grow fast and spread disturbances through traffic flow.

To manage that risk, Qin and colleagues build a control strategy with deep reinforcement learning, a method where an agent learns actions from rewards. The strategy uses vehicle dynamics and platoon shape to balance throughput against stability. Packing vehicles closely moves more traffic, yet braking errors can amplify. A learned controller could make platooning usable sooner.
arxiv-2606-20948:
Inés Armendáriz and Pablo Blanc extend slot decomposition to continuous box-ball systems in 2026, a mathematical model of solitons moving like balls in boxes. The discrete system was introduced by Takahashi and Satsuma. Solitons there have integer sizes. Their continuous version studies a step function whose associated walk has excursions of finite length over past minima. Each soliton becomes a point in two-dimensional space.

One coordinate gives position. The other gives soliton height. A walk maps to a point configuration. A product measure on walks is built from the excursion decomposition. Excursion weights are products of soliton weights from the decomposition. Extending slot methods to continuous time and space links the box-ball world to broader probability tools. Soliton systems are valued as exactly tractable models of interacting particles, so each rigorous extension widens what can be proved about them.
arxiv-2606-21148:
Le Qiu and seven colleagues propose AnyMug in 2026, a framework for functional robot grasping of mug handles that works regardless of mug pose. A functional grasp must hold a mug by its handle, not merely pick it up. Thin handles, varied shapes, and upright or inverted placements strain perception and control. Pose detection methods run open-loop and suffer on thin structures.

AnyMug canonicalizes both observations and actions into a shared object-centered frame. The policy then sees a consistent mug-centered view. Actions are predicted in that same frame. A single closed-loop policy is trained entirely in simulation. It deploys zero-shot on a real robot. Pose-agnostic grasping matters for homes and cafes, where objects land in arbitrary orientations and a robot must use them as a person would, not just lift them any way it can.
arxiv-2606-21248:
Yaroslav Kopylov and Max Zinchenko revisit integral categories in 2026, a class of categories used in the foundations of algebra and functional analysis. An integral category is preabelian, with kernels and cokernels, where epimorphisms survive pullbacks and monomorphisms survive pushouts. One-sided versions keep only one of those two stability rules. The authors review known tests for integrality and prove new criteria for the one-sided and two-sided cases.

Their headline result is the first published example of a category that is right integral but not left integral, settling a long-standing gap in the literature. They also adapt the exact-couple construction of Kopylov and Wegner from semi-abelian settings to integral categories. The example shows the left and right notions are genuinely distinct, not two names for one idea.
arxiv-2606-21348:
Olde Scholtenhuis and six colleagues tackle a fabrication flaw in 2026 that limits on-chip filterbank spectrometers, instruments that sort faint sky light by frequency for sky surveys. Their superconducting microstrip resonators, working between 200 and 400 gigahertz, land at scattered frequencies, capping spectral resolution. The team traced the scatter to electron-beam lithography, the process that writes the tiny circuit patterns.

Shrinking the beam step size on the nanometer scale cuts the random part of the scatter, giving a fourfold improvement in frequency spacing overall. Avoiding main-field stitching across filter patterns removes a systematic shift between resonator groups, showing the two errors have different origins. Such fine control of the writing process thus becomes a requirement for the next wave of these instruments, which aim at finer spectral detail.
arxiv-2606-21448:
Pedro Pereira, Felipe de Figueiredo, and Rausley de Souza present Fast-TurboQuant in 2026, a way to compress vectors for large language model caches without any multiplications. Quantization shrinks stored embeddings, but the TurboQuant method first rotates vectors with a dense random matrix, costing millions of floating-point multiplications per embedding, a burden for edge hardware. Fast-TurboQuant swaps that matrix for a structured fast transform.

A sign-flip step using Rademacher phases, followed by a fast Walsh-Hadamard transform, prepares vectors for scalar Lloyd-Max quantization using only additions. On DBpedia embeddings from an OpenAI model, the method ran 19.7 times faster in sequential execution. Padding added by the transform also cut mean squared error and improved Recall@10, so the cheaper projection performed better, not merely cheaper.
arxiv-2606-21648:
Jason Y. Yan, Xiaoyu Guo, R. Bhandia, T. F. Rosenbaum, Natalia Drichko, and N. P. Armitage probe quantum geometry at a metal-insulator transition in 2026. Quantum geometry, usually framed in band theory, also lives in disordered, interacting materials. Their handle is the first negative moment of the optical conductivity, tied to quantum Fisher information and hence to a bound on multipartite entanglement.

Measured in phosphorus-doped silicon across the three-dimensional transition, the data yield a quantum geometric length. Far from the transition it matches the Bohr radius of the phosphorus donors. Approaching the critical point it grows, then jumps to infinity rather than diverging smoothly, because the sum rule is dominated by short scales. The growth, a puffing of the donor's polarizability volume, repairs the century-old Clausius-Mossotti picture and grounds Herzfeld's metallization criterion in quantum mechanics.
arxiv-2606-21748:
Buzaglo and Ingalls study Lie algebras of vector fields on smooth affine curves in their 2026 paper. These Krichever-Novikov algebras extend the Witt algebra, the vector fields on a punctured line used in conformal field theory and string theory. The authors ask what the large subalgebras inside such an algebra can look like, a global question that depends on the curve's shape.

Their main theorem says every infinite-dimensional subalgebra matches, up to finite codimension, a subalgebra of another such algebra. Three results follow from that structure theorem. The enveloping algebra of any such subalgebra fails a key finiteness test called the noetherian property. Each of these algebras also has the Dixmier property, so all its nonzero endomorphisms are in fact automorphisms, except for the Witt algebra itself. The paper ends with an explicit list of the Witt algebra's large subalgebras.
arxiv-2606-22148:
Santi and colleagues introduce, in 2026, the Transitive Stochastic Block Model for directed weighted networks whose groups follow an ordered structure. Think of pecking orders: nodes cluster into blocks with similar interaction patterns, and the blocks themselves rank. Existing methods cluster without enforcing order, or rank nodes without allowing equivalent groups.

The model separates how much two nodes interact from who dominates whom, imposing order on directional imbalance rather than frequency. Two versions are offered: a flexible weak version excluding cyclic dominance, and a Toeplitz strong version where advantage grows with rank distance. Inference runs through a Gibbs sampler with Pólya-Gamma augmentation and an age-ordered prior over block splits. Simulations show better prediction and block recovery, especially in sparse networks. Across six real networks the model improves prediction in four cases, and flags where ordered blocks hurt.
arxiv-2606-22248:
Zharassov evaluates SamatNext v0.2-B in 2026, a test 356-million-parameter hybrid decoder designed to retain earlier skills during staged training on Python code. Standard decoders forget heavily under sequential fine-tuning, overwriting prior capabilities. SamatNext alternates Differential-Attention-style layers with DeltaNet-inspired linear-state mixer layers, using RMS normalization and output scale calibration.

On the controlled final-stage holdout, the hybrid achieves a pass rate of one hundred percent while keeping 98.8 percent of its adjacent-stage semantic skill. A matched Transformer baseline retains only 3.8 percent of that stage's score at its standard learning rate, and 6.0 percent even when rescued with a higher rate. Both models degrade severely on the early hostile syntax set, however. The mixer's built-in bias alone does not solve long-horizon catastrophic forgetting. Code and evaluation scripts are published.
arxiv-2606-22348:
Vannitsem and Demaeyer revisit, in 2026, the belief that the tropical atmosphere is more predictable than the extratropics. They explore chaos in reduced-order versions of the vorticity equation under the weak temperature gradient hypothesis. That hypothesis describes the large-scale tropical atmosphere well: horizontal temperature gradients stay weak, and divergence forcing drives the flow. The authors vary the forcing in these reduced models.

Under fairly realistic forcing amplitudes, chaos emerges in the models. Sometimes the Lyapunov time scale, the horizon over which small errors double beyond recovery, is less than a day. That contrasts sharply with the picture of a predictable tropical belt slaved to its boundary conditions. The result opens questions about where tropical predictability actually comes from. If intrinsic chaos can grow this fast in simplified systems, forecast limits in the tropics may be set by the atmosphere itself.
arxiv-2606-22748:
Neel Gupta, Maria Antoniak, and Melanie Walsh study AI fiction written by ordinary users in this 2026 paper. Professional authors trying AI tools get most of the attention. The authors ask whether everyday readers also make fiction of their own.

Drawing on over 500,000 anonymized English-language ChatGPT conversations, they find more than a third involve fiction in some form: original stories, roleplay, fanfiction, and erotica. The activity is dominated by power users. One profile they name infinite story demanders repeatedly requests and revises versions of the same story over stretches. Users lean especially toward fanfiction and erotica, and toward generic forms, repetition, immediacy, and niche mixes of elements. The authors propose the figure of the solipsistic reader-writer, who makes and consumes fiction in a closed loop with a machine, not a human author. They ask where interactive storytelling fits in today's media scene.
arxiv-2606-22848:
A. Chauhan and C. Sasmal investigate strange flow behavior in viscoelastic fluids in this 2026 paper. Such fluids, thickened by long polymer molecules, flow through porous media in unexpectedly complex ways. Experiments had shown that both the chaos of the flow and the pressure drop vary non-monotonically with the Weissenberg number, a measure of fluid elasticity, but the mechanism was unresolved.

The authors simulate flow through an ordered medium of cylindrical micropillars in a staggered layout. They propose that strands of high elastic stress, formed where polymers stretch and align, control the behavior. At low elasticity the strands grow slowly downstream of the pillars. Past a critical point they fluctuate strongly, driving chaotic flow. At still higher elasticity the strands grow larger, link neighboring pillars, and the flow reorganizes around them. That sequence, they argue, explains the observed rise and fall of both chaos and pressure drop.
arxiv-2606-22948:
Yincheng Zhou and colleagues train computer-use agents in a 2026 paper on software control. Their agents operate real desktop programs through mouse and keyboard actions. Such tasks need long action chains, and feedback about success is rare and slow. Running full trials inside virtual machines also costs much computer time. The team proposes ENVS, a search method that uses the live environment itself to build training data.

Zhou and colleagues branch over clearly different actions inside real OSWorld virtual machines. They keep only branches that end in verified success, then train on balanced step-level examples. On a pool of three hundred tasks, ENVS beat a matched online reinforcement learning baseline. It also used notably fewer graphics processor hours. The team adds a noisy variant of the benchmark, with pop-ups and interruptions, and agents trained with ENVS handled those distractions better.
arxiv-2606-23048:
Mateusz Barański and colleagues release HALAS, a dataset of speech recognition hallucinations, in a 2026 paper. Modern speech-to-text systems sometimes invent words that nobody said. Those hallucinations matter in settings like earnings calls, where transcripts feed real decisions. Earlier checks used silence or deliberately corrupted audio, which misrepresents the natural problem. HALAS instead collects real hallucinations from seven leading recognition systems. Human annotators labeled the invented spans in unprocessed earnings call recordings.

Barański and colleagues find that different systems hallucinate overlapping vocabularies. Hallucinations also appear in transcripts that are otherwise nearly perfect, so a low overall error rate does not guarantee clean text. Simple character and meaning-based detection scores reached a moderate level on their benchmark. The best dedicated detection methods scored far lower, showing much room for improvement. HALAS offers the first rigorous natural benchmark for this problem.
arxiv-2606-23348:
Matej Straka, Viliam Lisý, and Martin Schmid train a superhuman agent for the strategy game Generals.io in a 2026 paper. The game demands long-horizon planning and fast tactics under heavy hidden information. Their agent learns purely by self-play with reinforcement learning. A key enabler is a simulator written natively in JAX. It runs at tens of millions of frames each second on one graphics processor, about ten thousand times faster than the previous simulator. On top of it, a vision transformer policy trains end to end with sparse win and loss rewards.

Straka and colleagues train for four days on four top-end processors. The agent reaches first place on the public one-versus-one leaderboard of over five thousand human players. Against the two top-ranked humans, it wins the large majority of two hundred sixty-nine ladder matches.
arxiv-2606-23448:
Ricardo Inácio and colleagues let forecasting models abstain on the hardest cases in a 2026 paper. Deep learning leads time series forecasting, yet accuracy swings widely from sample to sample. Some instances are inherently hard to predict. Reject options, where a model declines to answer, are standard in classification but underexplored in forecasting. Existing rules lean on proxies like interval width or learned confidence. Those stay tied to the training domain. The team's framework instead predicts the percentile of the coming error from structural traits of recent values. It learns that mapping through metalearning across many series.

Inácio and colleagues decouple the rejection decision from the forecast itself. Because the features are domain-agnostic, abstention transfers across very different time series. In both in-domain and transfer tests, rejecting the flagged samples improved accuracy at every coverage level.
arxiv-2606-23548:
Menon and Vallone train a neural network stand-in for costly simulations of superconducting magnets, in a 2026 engineering paper. High-temperature superconducting magnets promise record fields for accelerators and fusion, but they are hard to protect because overheating spreads slowly and warnings arrive late. Engineers model such magnets as electrical circuits and simulate them, yet scaling those simulations from single tapes to full cables becomes painfully slow.

Their surrogate, SuperCond-GNN, redraws each circuit as a graph. A graph neural network, a model that passes messages between connected nodes, then learns the voltage at every point. It works from the layout, materials, and operating current. Trained on simulation data for tape stacks of up to ten tapes, it predicts voltages with a mean percentage error near four percent. A penalty based on Kirchhoff's current law, a basic circuit rule, plus tests on unseen layouts probe how far it generalizes.
arxiv-2606-23948:
Mojarad and Tang probe the inner layers of two speech recognition models to see how they encode a hallmark sound pattern of African American English, in a 2026 paper on speech science. Consonant cluster reduction simplifies final clusters, so a word like test may surface with its last stop weakened. The pattern is rule governed, yet recognizers err far more on this dialect. The authors run layer wise probes on wav2vec 2.0 and Whisper, testing whether each layer can tell reduced from full forms and recover the underlying cluster.

Each model separates reduced forms from canonical ones with high accuracy at its best layers. Even when a stop is barely pronounced, the representations retain cues to which stop belongs there. Reduction is thus encoded as structured, gradient variation, not as plain deletion. Modern speech encoders capture the dialect's phonology in an organized way.
arxiv-2606-24448:
Chen and colleagues argue that synthetic robot videos should teach a robot's eyes, never its hands. Vision-language-action models need huge numbers of video action pairs. Real remote control data is scarce, so generated robot videos look like a scalable substitute. Earlier approaches infer approximate actions from the synthetic frames. The team contends in 2026 that this is a mismatch.

A video captures geometry, the spatial path of the task. A real demonstration instead records control in full, down to the precise motor commands. Their Asymmetric Preservation Principle observes that human to robot video generation preserves the two unequally. Visible geometry survives generation. Underlying control signals do not. Their method derives upcoming two-dimensional end effector waypoints from the human recording, after pose estimation, retargeting, simulation, and projection. That surviving geometry teaches visual perception alone. Real demonstrations remain in charge of control. Chen's rule is crisp: supervise only what survives.
arxiv-2606-24648:
Jeon and colleagues benchmark whether audio language models can judge speech the way humans hear it, beyond words alone. Large audio language models serve as judges for generated speech. Evaluations stress holistic naturalness, though. Fine grained paralinguistic distinctions (style, rate, emphasis, perceived age and gender) go unexamined. ParaPairAudioBench assembles thousands of pairwise audio comparisons across those five dimensions, for judge models to decide.

Current judges lag human judgements by a wide average margin. Severe calibration failures concentrate in tie cases, where abstaining is the correct decision and models guess anyway. Same transcript and cross transcript conditions separate lexical from acoustic reliance. They show how much judges lean on words instead of sound. Jeon's 2026 benchmark, from Hongik and Seoul National Universities with NAVER Cloud, enables multi sided, calibration aware judging of judge reliability. That is needed before trusting automatic speech evaluation anywhere near production.
arxiv-2606-24848:
Steffen van Bergerem, Johannes Friedrich Lange, and Nicole Schweikardt present clique guarded first order logic with counting and map out its complexity. The logic is a fragment of first order logic with counting, designed so that quantification is guarded by cliques in the underlying structure. The authors prove computable upper bounds on the VC dimension of its formulas. They also bound the graph dimension of its counting terms on nowhere dense classes of relational structures.

Algorithmic metatheorems follow for the logic on classes of locally bounded expansion. Query answering and enumeration become tractable there. PAC learning for Boolean and multiclass classification problems is covered as well. A slight extension of the logic is already intractable, even on trees, the simplest sparse structures. Van Bergerem and colleagues thereby draw a precise boundary: the clique guard is close to the most that can be added before the tractability of counting logic collapses.
arxiv-2606-25148:
Every three dimensional PDE solver on a Cartesian grid hides the same trick, used by production fluid dynamics codes for fifty years and rarely stated in textbooks. Yong Yi Bay and Kathleen A. Yearick write the manual for it: the three dimensional operator is never built, factored, or stored at all.

Derivative matrices, compact line solves, mass inversions, splitting substeps, and fast Poisson transforms all factor along the coordinate axes. Each collapses into repeated one dimensional banded kernels run along grid lines. The authors derive the Kronecker product algebra that makes the collapse exact, across finite differences, Galerkin and spline methods, collocation, and direct solvers. Three production tricks turn it into speed. A reshaping exposes each sweep as one batched kernel. Sum factorisation rescues high order methods. A pencil layout keeps data contiguous across a cluster. Cost stays linear in the number of unknowns.
arxiv-2606-25248:
Group signatures let a member sign anonymously for a whole group, while a manager can unmask anyone who misbehaves. Sepideh Avizheh, Reihaneh Safavi-Naini, and Shiwei Sun loosen the joining rules in 2026 with sponsored group signatures. Ordinary members at a first level may sponsor newcomers into a second level, something the classic scheme reserves for the manager alone. Sponsors stay accountable: a sponsored member's signature can be opened to reveal the sponsor, and sponsored signatures are linkable to each other.

Formal security definitions and a generic construction follow, built from a dynamic group signature, commitments, and a zero knowledge proof, plus a concrete instantiation. As a showcase, the authors design anonymous guest access tokens for smart buildings. A temporary guest can reach approved resources without revealing identity, while the hosting member remains traceable if access is abused.
arxiv-2606-25448:
Termination provers compete yearly in TermCOMP, but its higher order category has always used one rewriting semantics, leaving another major formalism without a proper arena. Johannes Niederhauser and Aart Middeldorp lay the formal groundwork for changing that in 2026. Higher order rewrite systems, defined by Nipkow, rewrite terms modulo beta and eta steps, unlike the algebraic functional systems the competition currently scores. The question is whether the two semantics ever agree without extra machinery.

For a simple syntactically defined subclass of the benchmark database, the pair proves they do coincide: rewriting under the higher order systems matches a beta first strategy under the existing semantics. That equivalence is exactly what an HRS subcategory needs to be meaningful. More tools could then compete head to head on higher order termination problems.
arxiv-2606-25648:
The eclipsing dwarf nova HT Cas has been timed for nearly five decades, and its eclipses refuse to arrive on a steady schedule. Aykut Ozdonmez and colleagues add fresh eclipse times from twenty fifteen to twenty twenty six to the archive in 2026. The combined record spans forty eight years of arrivals measured against a steady clock. First they check that the star's outbursts do not shift eclipse phases, so all the data can be pooled safely. Two families of models then compete to explain the wobble.

Free orbits for two unseen companions fit the timings but collapse at once in dynamical simulations. Forcing circular orbits cured the failure and stayed stable. The fit gives two giant companions, near ten and five Jupiter masses, with periods near thirty three and fifteen years. A magnetic cycle explanation failed its energy budget test, needing more energy than the companion star holds.
arxiv-2606-25748: This paper does dynamic masking for boundary-aware velocity reconstruction in volumetric particle tracking with moving solids. The doing does. Their masking is dynamic. The reconstructing reconstructs boundary-aware velocity. It is fluids. The doing is moving solids. The velocity reconstruction is boundary-aware.
arxiv-2606-25848:
Ilias Ermeidis works in differential geometry, the mathematics of smooth shapes and symmetry, on a question about gradual change. When a Lie subalgebra, a symmetry structure sitting inside a larger one, is deformed smoothly, when is that change only cosmetic? Ermeidis seeks a clean test for when a deformation amounts to no real change at all.

Cocycles, algebraic quantities built from the deformation, supply the answer. He proves a condition that is both necessary and sufficient for smooth triviality. A matching criterion covers the special case of Lie ideals. A second result proves the Moser trick directly for foliations, which are spaces sliced into smooth layers. That proof then serves as the base for extending the same ideas to general Lie subalgebroids.
arxiv-2606-26048:
Cheng Ouyang and colleagues cut the computing cost of controlling a soft robotic arm. Soft robots bend in complex, shifting ways, so model-free control is attractive. Data-enabled predictive control builds forecasts straight from measured input-output data. Its catch is solving a hard optimization at every time step. Small robot hardware struggles to keep up.

A reinforcement learning policy learns when the optimizer is truly needed. The event-triggered design skips needless calls and preserves tracking quality. In simulation, optimizer calls fall by up to sixty-six percent. Accuracy stays comparable to running the optimizer every step. Hardware tests use a three-dimensional cable-driven soft arm. The controller transfers from simulation with no retraining. Optimizer calls fall by thirty-four percent there. Performance also beats a fixed threshold rule for triggering, giving smoother and more consistent control.
arxiv-2606-26348:
Po-han Li, Shenghui Chen, Sandeep Chinchali, and Ufuk Topcu audit how multimodal language models are graded. Such models read text, images, audio, and video in one system. Their skills raced ahead while their report cards stood still. Most benchmarks test one isolated task at a time. Little is revealed about whether a model genuinely integrates information across its senses.

Gap hunting organizes the review. The team walks the current benchmark taxonomy and names what is missing. Temporal and spatial coherence across a video is one gap. Physical world understanding is another. Multimodal consistency, answering the same way through different senses, and selective attention round out the list. Closing these gaps matters for honest progress claims. Benchmarks that miss integration can crown models that merely stack single-sense tricks. The survey maps where evaluation must go next to expose real capability boundaries.
arxiv-2606-26448:
Akshay K. Jagadish and seven colleagues built AutoCog, an automated cognitive scientist. Cognitive science studies how the mind works. Its hardest step is building new theories from the failures of old ones. Data collection and model fitting were already automated. Theory building stayed manual. AutoCog closes that gap with language model agents.

Inside AutoCog, agents argue for competing theories. Each theory is written as a runnable cognitive model. The agents design experiments that best separate the theories. They recruit participants online and collect real behaviour data. They then score each theory against the data and diagnose why losers fail. A better successor theory is built from that diagnosis, and the cycle repeats. In decision-making tests, AutoCog recovered known strategies from simulated behaviour. With human participants, its theories beat the established theories it started from.
arxiv-2606-26648:
Anna Sacilotto, Ambrogio Maria Bernardelli, and Stefano Gualandi compare battery control models for cutting carbon emissions from home solar systems. A house with rooftop panels and a battery can store sunshine for later use. When to charge and discharge shapes the home's true emissions. Grid electricity varies in carbon intensity hour by hour. Weather and household demand are also uncertain.

The authors built a ladder of linear optimisation models. It runs from a simple self-consumption rule to full stochastic models with feedback control. Stochastic models plan across many possible futures drawn from real data patterns. Direct stochastic optimisation of expected emissions performed best among practical options. It came close to an all-knowing benchmark that sees the future perfectly. Feedback models trained slightly better but generalised no better, at higher computing cost.
arxiv-2606-26948:
Ioannis Kakatelis, Thanasis Lianeas, Alkmini Sgouritsa, and Minas Marios Sotiriou study fair division of indivisible goods arranged on a hypergraph. Agents value bundles of goods; an allocation is EFX if no agent envies another after removing any single good from the other's bundle. In the hypergraph setting, goods are edges and only their endpoints can value them. Full EFX allocations may not exist, so approximations matter.

The authors simplify and extend earlier constructions. For graphs without short cycles, a construction guarantees each agent at least a fixed strong fraction of the EFX standard under additive valuations. Weaker envy guarantees with more slack goods removed are proven to exist always in special cases. All constructions run in polynomial time. The results push the frontier of provably fair sharing in network-structured settings.
arxiv-2606-27048:
Van Hoof and colleagues hunt for home galaxies of eight fast X-ray transients, brief flashes of X-rays lasting minutes to hours. Without a host galaxy, judging the flash's energy and birthplace is nearly impossible. Deep optical images from ground telescopes target the eight flash positions. For each hopeful galaxy, the team estimates distance, mass, star birth rate, chemical mix, and population age by fitting its light profile.

Candidate hosts turn up for six of the eight flashes. One supposed flash is reclassified as a flare from a star inside our own galaxy. Where a host link is assumed, every case still fits a white dwarf torn apart by a mid-weight black hole. Neutron star mergers also remain possible for all six. Only two fit a supernova shock breakout, and just one fits glow from a long gamma-ray burst cocoon, so origins look mixed.
arxiv-2606-27148:
Dykhuis, Keough, and Lipton generalise a classic cup-flipping puzzle. In the old trick, cups sit up or down, and flipping a fixed count per move can sort a starting layout. Their hypercups have more than two sides, cycling through several states instead of two. The question is which starting layouts can still be fully sorted, and in how many moves. A 2010 treatment by Siu and Stewart covered the ordinary two-sided case, in an extension published in 2026.

Parity, the even-odd bookkeeping behind the classic trick, no longer decides the answer. Greatest common divisors take its place, linking the side count, flip count, and cup count. Every result from the two-sided treatment carries over to hypercups under that new rule. Ordinary cups reappear as the simplest case. Playful in form, the result is a clean lesson in how number theory governs what moves can achieve.
arxiv-2606-27248:
Palomino Ylla introduces a graph-based diagnostic that senses black hole curvature through shortest paths. Curved spaces can be discretised as graphs, where geometry hides in path structure. Her statistic works shell by shell: it measures how unevenly shortest-path counts from one reference point spread across each distance layer. Cubic mean deviation of the logged counts captures that anisotropy, meaning direction unevenness. During 2026, static, spherically symmetric black hole embeddings supply the test beds.

Across Schwarzschild, charged, and regular black hole families, the statistic organises stably by radius. Its profile tracks the logarithmic Kretschmann curvature profile closely. Matched flat control graphs show no such trend. Charged cases stay stable across charge values and ten random seeds, and regular black hole scans behave alike. Benchmark surfaces warn the statistic is not a universal curvature meter.
arxiv-2606-27748:
Transformers pay a quadratic cost for attention on long sequences. Kernel-based linear attention cuts that cost. Its kernels are usually fixed or only weakly learnable, which limits what the model can express. Haoran Zhang and Feng Zhou propose Flexformer in 2026. Flexformer learns its kernels from data in a fully driven way. It builds on random Fourier features. The spectral frequencies become trainable parameters.

Learning the frequencies lets the model cover a broad family of kernels. Two variants are developed. One is stationary, and the other is nonstationary with strictly greater expressiveness. Tests cover language modelling and sequence classification. Flexformer consistently outperformed the baselines there. A second strength is transfer. It can be distilled from a pretrained Transformer and still recover softmax attention. Its learned kernels also move well across domains. The authors report high efficiency together with strong results on long-sequence tasks.
arxiv-2606-27848:
Jiangcheng You and Heng Zhang prove a sharp inequality for vibrating domains in 2026. The domains live in space forms, the simply connected spaces of constant curvature. Only spherical and hyperbolic cases are treated. Each domain has Neumann eigenvalues, the natural vibration frequencies with a free boundary. The result bounds a sum of their reciprocals from below.

The sum of the reciprocals of the first n positive Neumann eigenvalues is at least n divided by the first eigenvalue of a comparison ball. The ball is the geodesic ball with the same volume as the domain. For the spherical case, the domain must sit inside an open hemisphere. Equality holds exactly when the domain itself is a geodesic ball. Balls are thus the unique extremal domains. The inequality settles a conjecture posed by Xia and Wang in 2023. It extends classical eigenvalue comparisons into non-Euclidean geometry.
arxiv-2606-27948:
Counterfactual explanations show the smallest input change that flips a model's decision. Xuan Zhao and five colleagues propose RECAST in 2026 to rebuild black-box models from such explanations. Existing approaches suffer from shifted decision boundaries and overfitting. They often assume online query access to the target system. RECAST works with limited data and restricted access instead. It builds a stand-in model from Wasserstein barycentric prototypes.

Counterfactuals enter as informative but less representative samples for both classes. Fidelity stays high in low-sample regimes, with no online access during reconstruction. The method also supports group fairness diagnostics, which helps third-party auditing of opaque decision systems. Experiments on real-world datasets show high fidelity and query efficiency. Results stay stable even when access is limited and noisy. The method is currently limited to binary classification; multi-class extensions are future work.
arxiv-2606-28048:
Repeated voices across calls are an underused signal against insurance fraud. Muhammad Shakeel Akram and four colleagues present DG VoiC in 2026, a speaker clustering framework for call-centre audio. It targets customer checks and cross-profile speaker linking. The audio is anonymised real call-centre material. Sensitive-information-aligned anonymisation comes first. Speech-focused preprocessing and sliding-window speaker embeddings follow. Cosine similarity drives the clustering.

Evaluation used 121 recordings. A curated reference subset held 56 samples in 22 human-agreed speaker clusters. The best setup scored strongly on every metric. It reached ninety-six percent adjusted mutual information and ninety-five percent adjusted Rand index. Completeness was ninety-eight percent, homogeneity one hundred percent, and V-measure ninety-nine percent. The embeddings thus group repeated speakers reliably under real telephony conditions. Analysts can check speaker consistency and surface repeat voices across customers.
arxiv-2606-28148:
Anosh Joseph and Vinod Mamale investigate the configurational temperature estimator in 2026 across matrix models and random-matrix ensembles. The estimator follows from an exact Schwinger–Dyson identity. It is built from the gradient and Hessian of the action. Four testbeds are used. They are the Gross–Witten–Wadia model, a quartic double-well matrix model, and the Gaussian orthogonal, unitary, and symplectic ensembles.

In every case, the estimator returns the exact expected value, an inverse temperature of one, within statistical uncertainties. Splitting the estimator into isotropic and anisotropic parts reveals a pattern. The leading finite-size corrections of the two parts approximately cancel. One part's excess offsets the other's deficit. The estimator also serves as a sensitive diagnostic of Monte Carlo simulations. Deviations from the identity flag simulation problems. The study validates the estimator as both a thermometer and a consistency check.
arxiv-2606-28248:
Mohamed Majdoub and Ezzedine Mliki study a heat-like equation with a twist. A singular drift term lives only on a flat interface cutting through space, while a power-law source term feeds growth everywhere. Equations of this family are famous for the Fujita phenomenon, where a critical exponent separates solutions that die out from solutions that explode in finite time.

Majdoub and Mliki first establish that mild solutions exist locally. They use Gaussian bounds for the underlying spreading kernel and a contraction argument adapted to the interface's inhomogeneity. They then prove the dichotomy is sharp: every nontrivial solution with nonnegative values blows up at or below the classical Fujita exponent, while global ones exist above it for small initial data. The interface, remarkably, does not shift the critical value, a first result of its kind.
arxiv-2606-28548:
Kevin Der, Harish Kamath, and Ben Thompson make a popular interpretability tool scale to long conversations. Sparse autoencoders extract human-readable features from a language model's activations, but they fire per token, so a long transcript drowns in active features and downstream analysis becomes unwieldy.

Turn-averaged autoencoders instead summarize a whole turn, human or assistant, using a fixed number of features, trained to reconstruct the turn's average activation. Judged by a language model, those features describe a turn's high-level character more completely than per-token features do. Attribution graphs, which trace how features influence one another, become far simpler to build and read. Interpretability techniques that were impractical at long context lengths, the authors argue, become routine.
arxiv-2606-28648:
Dimitri Shlyakhtenko, writing alone, exhibits a failure of a convergence that random matrix theory had led many to expect. Strong convergence says random matrices should mimic their limiting free-probability objects not just in average spectrum but in the norms of every polynomial, the strongest and most useful sense.

His matrices have fermionic entries, operators obeying the canonical anticommutation relations, scaled to variance one over N. Individually, each matrix's real part does converge in operator norm to the semicircular limit, matching the classical picture. Jointly, the family refuses: even the operator space layout of the spans of the real and imaginary parts fails to approach the semicircular limit. Fermionic randomness, whatever its individual good behavior, does not assemble into the free limit that bosonic and classical constructions achieve.
arxiv-2606-28948:
Ambrus, Liu, Hillmansen and Tian estimate how much traction power each train can safely draw when several trains share one railway feeder. Decarbonisation is raising electrical loads on alternating-current lines never designed for many trains accelerating at once. If voltage sags too far, trains limit their current or protection systems trip, cutting capacity and reliability.

A power-flow model shows the minimum network voltage is governed by power multiplied by distance, not power alone. That yields a distance-dependent power envelope for a single train, but envelopes do not add up when trains share a feeder. The authors generalise a conservative pairwise screen into a solver-free multi-train estimate, calibrated by just two short offline runs. On matched cases the estimate tracked full power-flow results to within about nine percent on average, improving as more trains shared the feeder.
arxiv-2606-29048:
DeStefano, Rosenberg, Hu, Xu and Chu revisit a kagome metal, ScV6Sn6, whose lattice of corner-sharing triangles hosts a charge density wave, a periodic patterning of electric charge. Two puzzles motivate the work: a reported intermediate phase near the wave's onset, and a low-field Hall anomaly that had been credited to an anomalous Hall effect. Earlier crystals were too imperfect to settle either question, with quality ratios of at most about nine.

A small change to the flux growth recipe produced crystals over five times cleaner, with quality ratios above fifty. In those crystals, a sequence of closely spaced transitions appears near the transition temperature, only above a sharp quality threshold. Strain-response measurements show the intermediate phase breaks the lattice's three-fold symmetry. The Hall response fits ordinary multi-band transport from small, fast pockets of carriers. It is inconsistent with an intrinsic anomalous Hall effect.
arxiv-2606-29148:
Shi, Jiang, Tessler and Peng build Generative Pretrained Controllers, a system that learns broad motor skills for physically simulated characters by predicting the next token, as language models do. Animation needs such systems to complete many tasks in a natural, lifelike way. Their framework tokenises motion, turning movement into discrete codes from a learned motion vocabulary built with finite scalar quantisation.

End-to-end reinforcement learning jointly learns that vocabulary and a policy mapping codes to physics-based controls. A GPT-style autoregressive transformer then models its structure, generating controls by next-token prediction. The trained controller reproduced a vast corpus of motion clips with a 99.98 percent success rate. It also showed natural emergent behaviours, such as responding to pushes and recovering after falls. A suite of adaptation techniques fine-tunes it for new tasks. The authors say the approach greatly simplifies training over earlier tokenised methods.
arxiv-2606-29448:
Nguyen, Cameron, Balocchi, and Sell propose a Bayesian spatial mixture model for land cover classification from remote sensing images, pictures taken from aircraft or satellites. Good classification supports conservation monitoring and policy worldwide. Current methods often give no principled uncertainty estimates and need much labelled data, which limits trust in new regions where conditions shift.

Their framework, POTTERS, extends the classical Potts model with a more general spatial dependence structure. Informative priors, prior beliefs drawn from already labelled images elsewhere, guide the model, so no labels from the target region are required. The model quantifies uncertainty, accounts for how classes interact, and can flag entirely new clusters. A variational inference algorithm, a fast approximation method, keeps the approach scalable to large images. Simulation studies show clear benefits. A case study then classifies land cover in Scotland, using publicly available remote sensing data from England to supply the priors.
arxiv-2606-29748:
Keji and Dibbo study how graph neural networks can leak the private graphs they train on. Graph data in many fields is sensitive, and networks trained on it may inadvertently expose it through model inversion attacks, where an adversary reconstructs inputs from a model. 

The graph-label conditioned attack uses the target model's predictions. The embedding-label conditioned attack uses its intermediate representations. Both use a generator-discriminator technique to rebuild high-quality graphs in realistic black-box scenarios, where the attacker cannot see inside the model. Tests span three benchmark graph datasets and four structural quality metrics, against existing baselines. A variant using half as many queries keeps good performance, and the networks stay vulnerable under Laplacian noise added as a defence.
arxiv-2606-29948:
Bi and six colleagues tackle a portability problem in touch sensing. Tactile sensors differ so much that a model trained on one cannot be used on another, which blocks learning manipulation skills from mixed tactile data.

Their Heterogeneous Tactile Transformer gives each sensor its own encoder and shares a transformer trunk across sensors. Pretraining mixes masked reconstruction within each sensor type with alignment between paired sensors viewing the same contact. For this the authors built the Heterogeneous Paired Tactile dataset, 1.6 million synchronised paired frames from four vision-based and array-based tactile sensors. Across perception tasks and real manipulation, the learned representations transfer to new tasks and to sensors never seen in training.
arxiv-2606-30148:
Guy Bayada, José Rodríguez, and Raquel Taboada-Vázquez supply a missing proof in lubrication theory. The Reynolds equation models thin fluid films in bearings and joints. Reynolds originally assumed one confining surface was flat. For a spherical bearing, neither surface is flat at all. No rigorous justification existed for that curved case before their 2026 proof.

The authors study the Stokes problem between two closely spaced spheres. As the gap between the spheres shrinks toward zero, solutions converge. The limit is exactly the solution of the corresponding Reynolds equation. This is an asymptotic justification, not a formal derivation. Formal versions for general surfaces existed in earlier joint work. Rigorous ones covered flat or journal bearing geometries only. Their proof closes the spherical gap in that literature. Engineers gain firmer ground for spherical bearing design formulas.
arxiv-2606-30348:
Amir Carmel, Robert Krauthgamer, and Nir Petruschka shrink huge point sets for a classic location problem without losing reliability. The geometric median is the point minimizing total distance to all inputs. A coreset, in the authors' 2026 treatment, is a small weighted subset standing in for the whole. Strong coresets preserve every candidate's cost but take linear time. Weak ones come from cheap sampling but guard only near-optimal points.

Stable coresets, a newer middle notion, handle all constrained variants at once. A large gap separated known stable and weak sample sizes. The authors close most of that gap with plain uniform sampling. Their sample size is optimal up to a logarithmic factor. An iterative argument removes an unwanted dependence on dimension. It adapts machinery from earlier stable coreset work. The result holds with high constant probability.
arxiv-2606-30548:
Asier Calbet, Victor Falgas-Ravry and Joseph Hyde settle a threshold question in graph theory, the mathematics of networks, in a 2026 paper. A graph has the vertex-Ramsey property when any colouring of its vertices with a fixed set of colours forces a copy of a target graph in its assigned colour. Earlier work found the threshold for random graphs, and a later team studied dense graphs topped up with random edges for two target graphs.

Calbet and his co-authors resolve the perturbed setting in full generality. For any number of colours, at least two, and any matching list of target graphs, they determine how many random edges a dense graph needs. Past that number, the combined graph has the vertex-Ramsey property with probability approaching certainty. Their result extends the earlier two-graph problem posed by Das, Morris and Treglown to every tuple of targets at once.
arxiv-2606-30648:
Shi Bo, Debarghya Mukherjee and AmirEmad Ghassami present MediEncoder, a framework for causal mediation analysis with high-dimensional data. Mediation analysis splits a treatment's effect into two parts. One part flows through intermediate variables, called mediators. The other bypasses them. In modern medical studies, the true drivers are hidden processes, while the measurements are noisy proxies with many dimensions.

MediEncoder learns compact summaries of the background factors and the mediators together, using a coupled encoder-decoder design. A cross-factor network links the two sides, respecting how they depend on each other. The summaries feed a cross-fitted estimator of natural direct and indirect effects. The estimator is multiply robust, so it stays valid when parts of the model are right. Simulations beat rival reduction methods, and an application to Alzheimer's imaging data showed the method at work.
arxiv-2606-30748:
Idel Waisberg and Boaz Katz revisit an ancient brightness mystery. Theta Eridani shines today at a modest magnitude, yet Hipparchus, Ptolemy and al-Sufi ranked it among the sky's brightest stars. The gap between its ancient and modern brightness is the largest among the roughly one thousand stars in Ptolemy's catalogue. The usual dismissal, that three observers all erred, struck the authors as implausible.

Combining interferometry, spectroscopy and photometry, they solved the orbits of Theta Eridani's inner binary. It is a tight, eccentric pair of intermediate-mass stars, each swollen to about eighty percent of its Roche lobe, the region where its gravity holds its gas. The primary has finished burning hydrogen in its core. The pair's parameters hint that the ancient brightening was a real, millennia-long transient: orbital energy drained during a long common-envelope stage, triggered when the formerly eccentric binary overflowed its Roche lobes.
arxiv-2606-30848:
Hai Duc Nguyen and six colleagues present StreamGuard, a system that keeps real-time scientific data streams running on failure-prone supercomputers. Such streams feed live results back to running experiments, but hardware faults, network disruptions and slow workers can break their timing. StreamGuard strengthens the producer-consumer pattern, where one stage generates data and the next processes it, with two techniques that work together.

The first is dynamic, asynchronous checkpointing that saves progress without pausing computation. The second watches each worker's progress, spots slow ones and shifts their tasks elsewhere before they fall behind. In experiments, the approach cut the impact of failures and slowdowns by up to 6× while adding less than 1% overhead when nothing went wrong.
arxiv-2606-31048:
Gaurab Baral, Aaditya Khanal, Yangyang Tao and Junxiu Zhou distil a large reasoning model's skill into a compact student, using a local mathematics competition as the test bed. The teacher, DeepSeek-R1, scored 91.40% on historical John O'Bryan Mathematics Competition problems from 2011 to 2025, while the base student, Qwen2.5-7B, scored 64.67%. A dual-agent framework built a chain-of-thought training corpus from the teacher, and the student was fine-tuned with low-rank adaptation on Apple Silicon. A first long run overfit badly: validation loss bottomed out at 200 iterations, then rose.

Guided by that, the team ran five training runs capped at 200 iterations with varied seeds. The student averaged 69.43% on the competition set, 4.76 points above its base, with only 0.17 points of spread between runs, and reached 73.1% on the MATH-500 benchmark. Longer permitted responses scored far better: accuracy fell from 69.43% at the richest reasoning level to 41.9% at the leanest.
arxiv-2606-31148:
Dinh and six colleagues present Prune Ground, a framework for 3D visual grounding. The task is to find the object a spoken description refers to inside a 3D scene. Most systems reason over the whole scene at once. That is costly, and clutter breeds ambiguous matches. The team notes that most descriptions only concern a small local region anyway.

Three parts work together. Language-Guided Spatial Pruning uses a frozen vision-language model to cut the scene down to regions the words actually implicate. MultiView-Conditioned Description Reformulation rewrites complex expressions as simple target-anchor relations and adds missing spatial cues. An LLM-Grounder then aligns the point cloud and the language inside the pruned region. On three standard benchmarks, the method reached state-of-the-art results on all ScanRefer settings and on nine of ten Nr3D and Sr3D settings.
arxiv-2606-31248:
Hu and eleven colleagues introduce STRATA, an AI emulator that runs global storm-resolving weather simulation for the whole planet. Kilometre-scale storms shape heavy rain and cloud feedbacks, yet physics models at that detail cost about a megawatt-hour per simulated day. Coarser models miss the storms, and long runs stay out of reach.

STRATA trains on seventeen days of SCREAM physics output at 4.9 kilometre resolution, sampled every ten minutes. Because weather over ten minutes is mostly local, training on small tiles gives many examples and global runs blend overlapping tiles. New parts include stereographic position coding and a decoder that removes tile artifacts. A scaling study finds kilometre-scale emulation needs about ten times more computing per grid point than coarse AI weather models.
arxiv-2606-31648:
Garg and eight colleagues present LuckyStar 111B, a bilingual Korean-English model built by Cohere and LG CNS for enterprise agents that must call tools under tight memory limits. Rather than pretraining anew, the team adapts Cohere's post-trained Command A model. A preamble, a short instruction prefix, switches the same weights between concise answers and longer tool-oriented reasoning.

Four scaling choices are studied: multilingual supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards for multi-step tool tasks, rewards that keep user-facing answers in Korean, and 4-bit quantization for single-GPU serving. The adapted model improves mathematical reasoning, function calling and natural-language-to-SQL performance while holding general instruction quality in both languages. The authors document failure modes such as Korean prompts drifting into English replies.
arxiv-2606-31748:
Kim and Kumar study over-refusal, where safety training makes a language model refuse harmless prompts along with harmful ones. Reasoning before answering helps only partly. Their analysis suggests the reasoning often rubber-stamps a decision already made, instead of resolving what a prompt really asks.

Their model, SEAR, is trained with competing rewards inside one chain of thought. One role explores how an unsafe answer could be produced, while another role forces the final output to stay safe. Dense process rewards keep that contest stable during training. Exploring unsafe reasoning sharpens the line between harmful and harmless prompts, the authors find. The approach cuts over-refusal and resists attacks that target the reasoning itself.
arxiv-2608-00048: Not All EEG Moments Are Equal, arXiv 2608-00048. The EEG scheduling. Scholars can read the full paper. It awaits future readers. It holds its historical place. Such papers rarely see the light of day. Readers can find it here.
arxiv-2608-00148: Sharp bounds for non-adaptive randomized approximation, arXiv 2608-00148. The approximation bounds. The paper endures in the archive. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
ashburner-facts-clairvoyance-zoist-1848:
John Ashburner gathered cases of clairvoyance from the journal Zoist in 1848, under the title Facts in Clairvoyance. Subjects in the magnetic trance, witnesses swore, described far-off scenes correctly. Others named hidden objects or read sealed letters without the use of their eyes at all.

Ashburner, a London doctor and keen mesmerist, presents the tales as evidence. Victorian believers treated the file as proof of unseen powers. Skeptics then and now read the same pages very differently indeed. Either way, the book stands as a key primary source for the history of the paranormal in Britain.
barddas-iolo-morganwg-1848:
Iolo Morganwg was a Welsh poet and stone mason who claimed to have found old Bardic texts. This set came out after his death, in the 1862 and 1874 printings of his work. The editor J. Williams ab Ithel put the texts in print. Iolo said the lore came from the druids of old Wales.

In truth, much of the lore was Iolo's own work, shaped in his own mind. The texts set out gods, rites, and rules for bards in a neat scheme. False as old lore, the book still shaped the whole modern druid revival.
bronte-tenant-of-wildfell-hall-1848:
Anne Brontë published The Tenant of Wildfell Hall in 1848, under the name Acton Bell. The novel shocked readers with its tale of a wife fleeing a drunken, brutal husband. It is now read as a bold feminist work far ahead of its Victorian moment.

Helen Graham, a lone widow with a small son, rents Wildfell Hall and paints for bread. Village gossip paints her as fallen, and Gilbert Markham learns her tale from her diary. The diary tells of Arthur Huntingdon's charm, drink, and cruelty, and her flight to save her son. She nurses the dying Huntingdon yet will not return to his house of sin. Brontë insists a wife may save herself, a claim that drew fierce attacks then.
bunsen-egypts-place-universal-history-vo:
Christian Bunsen set Egypt in the frame of all past time in Vol. 1 of Egypt's Place in Universal History, out in English in 1848. Bunsen was a man of state and a deep sage of tongues. Charles Cottrell turned his German text to English. This tome lays the base: sources, scripts, and the first dates for the kings.

His dates were bold and oft too long. Yet he taught English fans to ask when, not just what. The set runs to five fat tomes. This first one is its ground stone.
cia-0000008648:
A communist terrorist group planned to abduct an American official in Cordoba, a CIA report warned in October 1964. The heading gives the target and city but leaves the group's name to the file itself. Threat reports of this kind circulated to protect officials abroad.

Abduction plots forced embassies and consulates to weigh guards, routes, and daily habits. Most warnings never became public, and many plots never came off. Preserved here, the report shows the security side of Cold War work in Latin America. It also shows how much intelligence work dealt in threats stopped, or feared, rather than events completed.
cia-0000009648:
Military Region 5's Viet Cong prison camp, holding both American and South Vietnamese prisoners, is the subject of a January 1971 report. The heading shortens the captors to VC and the South Vietnamese to ARVN, their army's initials. Mixed camps were the southern system's norm.

A camp holding both groups shows how captivity worked below the level of Hanoi's famous prisons. Prisoners shared guards, rations, and risk, whatever their uniforms. For officials, one camp report could update many men's files at once. The entry preserves the southern network's daily shape, counted in two nations' prisoners together.
cia-0000009848:
Two American propeller-driven aircraft crashed, and a Filipino prisoner was sighted, in a March 1969 CIA report. Propeller aircraft flew the slow, low missions of the Laos and Vietnam wars: spotting, liaison, and light attack. Filipino personnel served in the region in support roles.

The pairing joins air losses to a prisoner sighting in one report, as field items often did. A non-American prisoner widens the file beyond US cases, matching the war's real mix of nations. Analysts took the bundle apart and filed each part. Preserved whole, it shows reporting arriving mixed, not sorted.
cia-0000011348:
Egypt's 1955 arms deal with the Soviet bloc stunned the West, and in September that year the CIA weighed what would follow from it. President Gamal Abdel Nasser had bought weapons through Czechoslovakia after the West set terms he refused. The deal broke the Western hold on arms sales to the Middle East at a stroke.

The paper judges how Soviet weapons would shift the balance between Egypt and Israel. It also asks how far Moscow's influence in the Arab world might now grow. The estimate marks the moment the Cold War moved openly into the Middle East, with effects that lasted for decades.
cia-0000012248:
West New Guinea, the Dutch-held half of a great island, was the prize in a quarrel the CIA examined in February 1961. Indonesia claimed the territory as the last piece of its stolen inheritance. The Netherlands refused to hand it over, and pressure built from Jakarta, Washington, and the United Nations at once.

The paper surveys Indonesia's outlook with special weight on this dispute. It weighs Sukarno's threats, Dutch resolve, and the risk of open fighting. Within two years the territory passed to Indonesia under a UN-brokered deal, so the study shows the question while its answer was still contested.
cia-0000013848: One American pilot is the subject of a CIA note dated May 1, 1967. The title says only that he was captured, with no place named. Such short notes were the first word the government often had on a lost airman. They started the file that later reports on his health and camp would build on.
cia-0000015448: One untitled CIA record dated January 2, 1965, gives information on a sighting, on NICAP, and on Major Keyhoe together. NICAP was the main civilian saucer group, and Keyhoe was its best-known leader. Bundling a sighting with the group and the man shows how the files linked reports to the people who chased them. It is a small map of the agency's saucer world.
cia-0000036848:
A Hanoi newspaper featured captured American pilots, and a CIA record dated October 3, 1967 kept the story. Fifteen pilots were named in the paper, with Stafford and Santo among the names shown. North Vietnam used its prisoners in print as part of the wider war of words.

For American officials, a named list was both propaganda and hard information. Each name could be checked against the roll of men missing over the north. The file shows how an enemy newspaper became a source in the accounting for the missing. Printing the names also told American families, in a roundabout way, that their men were alive.
cia-0000044448:
El Salvador: Commentary on Killing of Priests is a CIA record dated October 2, 1989 in the catalog. Commentary is opinion, written to judge an event for readers. The priests' murders drew comment in papers across many countries.

Inside, editorial judgment on the killings is gathered and preserved. Each paper's politics colored the verdict it handed down. Anger at the army ran through most of the comment that autumn. The file shows the press forming the story's meaning in real time. It fixed the terms in which the case would be argued, long before courts could speak.
cia-0000044548:
Venceremos aired commentary on an army deserter's charges, in a CIA record dated September 1, 1989. The title ties the broadcast to the Farabundo Marti National Liberation Front. A deserter's charges were rich material for the rebels' radio war.

Inside, the rebel station's treatment of the charges is preserved. Radio commentary could carry one man's claims across a whole country. The army's dirty secrets were the rebels' finest ammunition that season. A charge from inside the ranks hit harder than any charge the rebels made themselves. The file shows that exchange at work, in which a single deserter's words were amplified into a campaign against the institution he had fled.
cia-0000045248:
The Salvadoran government freed rebels demanded in the kidnapping, in a CIA record dated September 5, 1985. Freeing prisoners was the classic price in a kidnapping trade. Paying it proved the talks had reached their serious stage at last. Governments do not free prisoners for a negotiation they expect to fail within days.

Inside, the release of the demanded rebels is recorded. Each freed prisoner was a chip spent to buy one woman's freedom. The government had sworn it would never bargain on such terms. The file preserves the moment it did so anyway, which is often the moment at which kidnappings of this kind truly begin to end.
cia-0000049248: President-elect Alfredo Cristiani is the subject of a CIA item from 1989, kept with the Truth Commission records. Cristiani, a businessman from the ARENA party, had won the presidency promising a different kind of war and an end to it. Files on a man between election and office catch a government before it forms.
cia-0000049348: Sol Meza ordered freed on bail in El Salvador is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000049348, dated August 3, 1981. Marked for the Truth Commission, the item records a court order releasing the named man on bail. Readers find a short declassified notice centered on that single legal step, preserved as part of the agency's Salvadoran case files.
cia-0000102948: Two short items share declassified CIA document 0000102948, dated February 2, 1983. The first reports Soviet use of prison labor for civil engineering work. The second concerns a bid from Salzgitter, named only in part because the heading cuts off. Filing unlike items together was routine cable practice. The record shows raw reporting moving to Washington in brief, paired form.
cia-0000106148: Oil Capital Limited Memo Itemizing Roger Tamraz's Business Affiliations From Th is the heading, cut off mid-word, on declassified CIA document 0000106148, dated April 4, 1994. The title describes a memo that lists one man's business affiliations, company by company. Where the list runs from is lost where the heading breaks. The brief record is a business mapping memo from 1994.
cia-0000108048: Mvd Escort and Patrol Guard Company V/ch 7461 is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000108048, dated June 5, 1986. The title names one guard company, with its unit number given as V/ch 7461. Escort and patrol are the company's stated duties in the heading. The brief record is a unit item, filed in the summer of 1986 as released.
cia-0000112348: Ministry to Study Psychic Powers, Ufo' S for Future Industry is the heading, with stray marks, on declassified CIA document 0000112348, dated January 5, 1993. The title reports a ministry planning to study psychic powers and UFOs for future industry. The ministry is not named in the heading itself. The brief record preserves the stray spacing exactly as released in the files.
cia-0000118648: Situation Appraisal: Assessment of General Thang's Performance As Iv Corps Comm is the heading, cut off mid-word, on declassified CIA document 0000118648, dated February 2, 1968. The title appraises one man's work: General Thang, as IV Corps commander in the heading's words. Commander breaks off at Comm in the released heading itself. The brief record preserves the break exactly as released.
cia-0000119748: An October 1956 CIA report surveys Asian reaction to the events in Hungary. Governments from Beijing to Delhi watched the revolution and drew their own lessons from Moscow's answer to it. The report gathers those responses from across Asia. Reactions abroad mattered to Washington because they hinted at how the revolt would play in the contest for support across the developing world.
cia-0000126948: A January 1991 CIA Terrorism Review examines the Mormon Church in South America as a terror target, the heading breaking off. Missionaries in the region had become targets for guerrillas hostile to the United States. The review studies why the church had drawn such attacks. Church targets puzzled officials at first, until attacks on chapels and missionaries showed a pattern: strike the Americans most visible in small towns across the continent.
cia-0000132348: A bloc campaign in Latin America fills a CIA briefing for the National Security Council. The briefing is dated October 1, 1959. Its subject line misspells the region as Latiin America, a typo kept from the original. Moscow and Beijing were both seeking friends and influence in the hemisphere. The briefing maps that campaign for the president's top advisers.
cia-0000132448:
Anastas Mikoyan's visit to Cuba fills a CIA document dated January 4, 1960. Mikoyan was a Soviet deputy premier, one of the Kremlin's most senior figures. His trip came as the Soviet-Cuban alliance was taking shape in public view.

The document covers the visit and the business done during it. Soviet trade deals followed in the wake of the trip, tying the two economies together. For readers, the entry captures a founding moment of the partnership. A senior Soviet leader in Havana signaled to the whole world that Moscow had chosen to back Castro's revolution. That signal was read closely in Washington.
cia-0000132648: Mexico giving the visiting Cuban president a warm welcome fills a CIA item dated May 3, 1960. The warmth stood out against the chill spreading across the region that year. Mexico City laid on full honors for its guest from Havana. The short item reports the welcome and the talks that went with it during the visit.
cia-0000132748: Events in Cuba and Central America fill a CIA paper dated January 4, 1961. It follows a roundup on the same pairing from November of the year before. Havana plus the isthmus formed the agency's standing regional beat through that winter. The short paper surveys the latest events on both parts of the beat as the new year opened.
cia-0000134248: Pro-Castro work inside Peru fills item 12 of a CIA series dated June 5, 1960. Peru's pro-Castro left would soon face a crackdown by its own government. For the moment Lima's left was rallying openly to Havana's example and banner. The short item tracks the work and the groups carrying it out across the country that year.
cia-0000136148: The record dated 3 April 1954 is a declassified CIA cable about a request that Waldorf be interviewed, vetting one more name in the operation's address book. As the Lincoln station file, it forms part of PBSUCCESS, the CIA plan that ended with President Arbenz driven out in June 1954.
