The acting secretary of state sent instructions to John Winant, the American ambassador in London, on 16 July 1945. That was the day before the Potsdam Conference, where Truman, Churchill, and Stalin met outside Berlin in July and August 1945 formally opened. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

London was Washington's closest partner and its first sounding board in 1945. Instructions sent on the eve of a summit set the line an ambassador should hold with the host government. Readers can use this message to see what Washington wanted London to know. To do. As Truman and Byrnes set out for Germany and the talks with Stalin began.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-148: An editorial note placed after document 710 in the second Potsdam volume adds the editors' guidance at a packed point in the files. Such notes in Foreign Relations volumes cite sources and tie papers together. They may also admit where the record is silent. This one helps readers judge the strength of the evidence around it.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-48:
A United States delegation memorandum sets the agenda for the foreign ministers' meeting of July 21, 1945, at noon. It is an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. Five items of business are listed in order.

First came the date for formally setting up the new Council of Foreign Ministers. The Big Three had left that choice to the ministers the day before. German economic questions came second, on the subcommittee's first report after days of work. Poland came third, on the liquidation of the London government and the carrying out of the Yalta agreement. Fourth came the same Yalta declaration as applied to liberated Europe and the satellite states. The U.S. was presenting a new paper spelling out the steps it believed should be taken there. Italy and the other satellites closed the list.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d748:
Document 748 is a proposal the United States delegation tabled at Potsdam on July 21, 1945. It dates from the conference's fifth day. By then each side knew the others' opening lines. New texts were drafted to probe and to trade. The proposal was printed in the second Potsdam volume.

Mid-conference proposals carry the marks of contact. They answer points made across the table. Readers can line this text up with rival drafts of the same week. The comparison shows bargaining as a written duel. The document adds one dated step to the path from first claims to the final protocol.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d848:
Document 848 is a working paper of the United States delegation dated July 16, 1945. It was drafted before the conference formally opened. Teams arrived in Germany with paper ready for the first sessions. This draft was kept in the delegation files and printed in the second Potsdam volume.

A pre-opening draft shows the summit before the summit. Staff had war-gamed the talks and written for them. Readers can measure the plan against the event. The document honors the foresight, and the misses, of the planners. It opens the working-paper run at its true start: in the quiet days when everything was still expected to go as written.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d948: Seymour Rubin wrote to his deputy Covey Oliver on July 29, 1945, about a British worry over Soviet republics filing separate reparation claims. Rubin had read the Department's telegram passing the idea to Pauley. He reports it has not happened so far. The Soviet Union seems set on treating its claims as a whole. In any case, Rubin argues, the zonal plan now taking shape makes the question moot. Soviet and Polish claims would be met from the eastern zone, plus a set amount from the west.
frus-1948v02-d548: A 1948 FRUS editorial note from the Germany and Austria volume on the Clay-Sokolovsky exchange. The Berlin crisis was brewing. This note preserves that context. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years.
frus-1950v01-d148: Another 1950 FRUS document on national security and foreign economic policy. The Cold War's economic front mattered. This document holds that record. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
frus-1977-80v06-d248: A 1977-1980 FRUS editorial note on the Carter-Brezhnev relationship. The two leaders. This note provides that context. It holds its historical place. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
gao-gaoreports-b-298248: Triple H Services doubled its August 2006 protest — two case numbers, one service fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer. Two dockets, one fair verdict.
gao-gaoreports-b-306748: Customs and Border Protection's moving expenses got a fiscal ruling in this July 2006 GAO call, which tests the relocation spending. The decision reads the money law. The ruling decides whether the moving dollars were legal. The law had the final word.
gao-gaoreports-b-310548: This 2007 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Cornell Companies, Inc. The December 3, 2007 ruling examines how the agency evaluated the bids. The ruling sets ground rules for future federal contract contests. Its full text is kept in the library next to this description.
gao-gaoreports-b-316048: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Applicability of the Congressional Review Act to Letter on State Children's Health Insurance Program. Decided April 17, 2008, it reviews whether the agency ran a fair competition. Agencies almost always follow these rulings, which build the case law for federal contracts.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-248: The Ticket to Work program needed better planning in 2005, and GAO's report says the disability employment effort could be more effective. The review writes the roadmap. The disabled workers deserved the real chance. The planning had to improve. The disabled workers deserved the real chance.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-348: Troops' money troubles needed more Pentagon action in 2005, and GAO's report says further steps were required on personal finances. The review pushes for the follow-through. The young soldiers deserved the financial shield. The actions had to come. The young soldiers deserved the financial shield.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-548: Joint military training transformation needed enhancing in 2005, and GAO's report says actions were required for the program. The findings demand the upgrades. The report warns that the warfighters deserved good training. The actions had to be taken. The warfighters deserved good training.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-748: Medicaid financing games got a GAO review in 2005, and the report says states' use of contingency-fee consultants highlighted oversight needs. The findings demand the watch. The report warns that the federal dollars deserved guarding. The need had to be addressed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-148: Lead in drinking water needed stronger action in 2006, and GAO's report says EPA should strengthen efforts to protect consumers. The findings demand the vigilance. The report warns that the tap water should not poison. The efforts had to be strengthened.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-348: The Battle Monuments Commission's books got audited for 2005 and 2004, and GAO's 2006 report delivers the financial opinion. The findings grade the statements. The report shows the war memorials' money got counted. The audit kept the books honest. The memorials' books stayed open.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-648: VA hospital credentialing mostly passed in 2006, and GAO's report says selected requirements were met at seven facilities, though one privileging aspect lagged. The findings balance credit and caution. The report warns that the veterans deserved fully vetted doctors. The privileging had to be complete.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-248: The land-border ID system was struggling in 2007, and GAO's report says the US-VISIT program faced strategic, operational, and tech troubles at the crossings. The findings list the woes. The report warns that the digital eye at the border was half-blind. The gates needed better glasses.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-48: Military families outside the managed-care fold needed access in 2007, and GAO's report examines care for those who skipped TRICARE Prime. The findings target the gaps. The report warns that the uniformed deserved care however they enrolled. The access had to follow the family.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-448: The Government Accountability Office dug into defense Acquisitions: Progress Made in Fielding Missile Defense, but Program Is Short of Meeting Goals in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-548: GAO published its findings on employment and Training: Most One-Stop Career Centers Are Taking Multiple Actions to Link Employers and Older Workers in 2008. GAO digs into federal programs at Congress's request and reports back what it learns. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-748: This 2008 report from the Government Accountability Office looks at financial Audit: Material Weaknesses in Internal Control over the Processes Used to Prepare the Consolidated Financial Statements of the US Government. Working for Congress, GAO checks how federal programs spend money and whether they deliver results. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
hume-enquiry-human-understanding-1748:
David Hume published An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding in 1748 in London. Hume, a Scottish philosopher, recast the hard arguments of his earlier Treatise in a clearer, shorter form. The Enquiry became his most read statement of empiricism, the view that knowledge rests on experience.

Hume argued that we never see causes, only events following each other, yet the mind expects the pattern to hold. He tested miracles, free will, and belief in God against that standard and found them wanting. His calm, polite style carried radical doubts. The book still sets the terms for debates on reason, belief, and what the mind can know.
in-the-fire-of-the-forge-a-romance-of-ol:
Georg Ebers turns to a servant's loyalty in Volume 6 of In the Fire of the Forge, his romance of old Nuremberg. Ebers lets Biberli, the faithful attendant of Heinz Schorlin, argue against his master's newest plan. A friar has just left, and Heinz is again drawn toward entering a monastery, a step Biberli fears more than any battlefield danger in this volume.

Chapter V gives the servant a blunt, funny case for marriage instead. Even a wife far below Heinz in rank, he argues, would keep his master in the world where he belongs. He recalls the knight dancing with Eva Ortlieb while onlookers praised the pair. Then his tone hardens: respectable people now point at the Ortlieb sisters and repeat a scoundrel's slander. Honor, love, and gossip pull the knight three ways.
israeli-declaration-independence-1948:
Israel's Declaration of Independence was proclaimed in Tel Aviv on May 14, 1948, and the hosted text is the declaration in full. It opens with the Jewish people's bond to the land. There they were born as a nation, and there their faith and culture took shape. Exiled by force, they kept faith with the land through long centuries abroad.

In modern times they returned in growing numbers. Pioneers revived the Hebrew tongue and built towns, farms, and a working economy. The text grounds the new state in the United Nations vote of November 1947 calling for a Jewish state. It declares Israel open to Jewish return and promises full equality to all who live there. It also calls on Arab neighbors to choose peace. War began the next day.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lowenstamm-saul:
Saul Löwenstamm, rabbi of Amsterdam, is the subject of a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906. Born at Rzeszow in 1717, he wrote under a name drawn from his book Binyan Ariel. He served as rabbi in Hungary and then at Dubno, following his father-in-law. In 1755 he moved to Amsterdam after his father's death. He died there in 1790.

The article describes Binyan Ariel as a three-part work of notes on the Pentateuch, the Five Scrolls, and Talmud passages. He also wrote notes on the Shulhan Aruk, the Mishnah, and many poems and approbations. Much of his energy went to the study house his father had founded, which gained a new home in 1778. The entry ends with his son Jacob Moses succeeding him, a picture of rabbinic Amsterdam in the eighteenth century.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-machpelah-10248:
Machpelah, the field and cave Abraham bought for a family burial place, is described in a 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia article. The name's meaning is unclear, though the old translations render it the double. The field lay near Mamre, or Hebron, and belonged to Ephron the Hittite. Abraham paid four hundred silver shekels for it.

The article lists who was buried in the cave. Sarah came first, then Abraham, Isaac, Rebekah, Leah, and Jacob. Josephus mentions the tombs without using the name Machpelah. From the twelfth century, travelers began visiting the cave. Benjamin of Tudela describes six sepulchers shown to visitors for a fee. He tells of an iron door, lit candles, and two empty caves before the tombs. Samuel ben Samson counted twenty-four steps down a narrow passage in 1210. The entry blends Bible, Josephus, and pilgrims' reports into one site history.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-manchester-1034:
Manchester, the Lancashire manufacturing city, receives a Jewish community history in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. About 25,000 of its 543,969 people were Jews. That made it the second largest Jewish community in the British empire. Jews began settling near Shudehill and Long Millgate about 1780.

The article starts with two brothers from Liverpool, Lemon and Jacob Nathan. They founded the first synagogue in the upper room of a house. Lemon Nathan became its first president, and a cemetery opened at Pendleton in 1794. A charity for winter relief followed in 1804. The congregation moved to Halliwell Street in 1824 and built its own synagogue. A schism in 1856, after Rabbi Schiller-Szinessy's appointment, produced a Reform congregation. Gustav Gottheil then led the old congregation for thirteen years before leaving for New York. The entry traces a community built, split, and reunited within three generations.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-marx-adolf-bern:
Adolf Bernhard Marx, a German writer on music, is profiled in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 by Isidore Singer and Joseph Sohn. Born at Halle on May 15, 1799, he was meant for the law but gave up a legal post to study music in Berlin under Zelter. He died at Berlin on May 17, 1866, after decades of teaching and editing.

Marx helped found a leading Berlin music journal in 1824 and, with Kullak and Stern, the Berlin music school of 1850 that became the Stern Conservatory. His own compositions faded, and a quarrel over them ended his close friendship with Mendelssohn. His books lasted better: a four-volume treatise on composition, a life of Beethoven, and a study of Gluck and the opera.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-medini-hayyim-h:
Hayyim Hezekiah Medini was a Palestinian rabbi who built an encyclopedia of Jewish law. Isidore Singer and M. Franco profile him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Jerusalem in 1833, son of Rabbi Raphael Eliahu Medini, and took his rabbinical diploma at nineteen. He spent thirteen years on a rabbinical court at Constantinople and was called in 1866 as chief rabbi to Kara-Su-Bazar in the Crimea. He returned to Palestine in 1889, and from 1891 acted as chief rabbi of Hebron.

His books of responsa and Talmudic studies appeared steadily. But the entry crowns one work, “Sede Hemed,” an encyclopedic collection of laws and decisions arranged in alphabetical order. Twelve volumes of it had appeared at Warsaw since 1890. It is the kind of lifetime reference work that makes the name of a scholar permanent. The entry treats it as the center of his career.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-menahem-ben-zeb:
Menahem ben Zebi was a German rabbi. He died, probably at Posen, in 1724. The Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 enters him through the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and A. S. Waldstein. He had studied under two noted teachers. One was R. Heschel. The other was Aaron Samuel Kaidanover. Kaidanover wrote the "Birkat ha-Zebah." The entry lists three books by Menahem. All three carry his name worked into their titles.

The "Zinzenet Menahem" was printed at Berlin in 1719. It explains difficult passages of the Haggadah. The "Lehem Menahem," Bread of Menahem, collects his responsa. It also explains Talmudic passages. The "Ta'ame Menahem" comments on Rashi's Pentateuch commentary. No incident of his life survives in the notice. The notice rests on two sources. One is Steinschneider's Bodleian catalogue. The other is Azulai's "Shem ha-Gedolim." A bibliography and a shelf of books stand in for a biography.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meyer-albert-10:
Albert Meyer, a Danish tenor born at Sorö in Zealand on October 29, 1839, is profiled in a Jewish Encyclopedia entry by Isidore Singer and Frank Cramer, published in 1906. He began in the chorus of Copenhagen's Royal Theater in 1860, studying under H. Rung, before war service in 1864 interrupted his start.

A concert on his return paid for a year of study under Lamperti in Milan, and from 1866 he sang as soloist at the Folketheatret. In 1873 he turned to teaching, publishing a singing method grounded in the physiology of the voice and opening his own Copenhagen school. He also conducted the synagogue chorus from 1882 and compiled its Sabbath melodies in 1892.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-minden-lob-b-mo:
Löb ben Moses Minden, born Judah of Selichow in Lesser Poland in the seventeenth century, was a cantor and poet who took his name from the town where he sang. Herman Rosenthal and Meyer Kayserling wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906. He served as ḥazzan at Minden-on-the-Weser and died, very old, at Altona or Hamburg in 1751.

His Shire Yehudah set Hebrew songs beside German translations with music, opening with drinking-song lines addressed to dear brothers and companions. An epilogue printed at Amsterdam in 1696 scolds rabbis who let people chatter through services, a cantor's complaint from inside the pulpit. A second songbook, Zemer wa-Shir, was printed at Frankfurt in 1714 by Solomon London.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-monis-judah-109:
Judah Monis was Harvard's Hebrew instructor for thirty-seven years — and a convert who kept the Jewish Sabbath all his life, as Crawford Howell Toy and Frederick T. Haneman write in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Algiers about 1683 and educated, it is said, in Italy, he reached Boston early in the eighteenth century. His first firm record is his baptism, in College Hall at Cambridge, in 1722.

At the baptism Monis preached and printed his own confession of faith, then threw himself into his new religion's cause — while never giving up Sabbath observance. Harvard appointed him in 1722; he resigned in 1759, on his wife's death, and withdrew to Northborough, where he died a few years later. The entry weighs Hannah Adams against Harvard's historian Quincy for his dates.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moser-moses-110:
Moses Moser was a German merchant best remembered as the closest friend of the poet Heinrich Heine. Isidore Singer and Joseph Jacobs wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. Born in 1796, he trained for business in Berlin and worked as assistant to the banker Moses Friedländer. He later served as confidential cashier to Moritz Robert.

Moser had real talent for mathematics and also studied philology. With Gans and Zunz he helped found the Society for the Culture and Science of Judaism. Heine valued his ability and character, called him a living appendix to Nathan the Wise, and sent him many intimate letters. Their closeness lasted until 1830, and the entry preserves a figure known mainly through his famous friend.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-silas-mey:
Silas Meyer Moses was a Bombay banker who rose to president of the Bank of Bombay. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. Born in Bombay on November 23, 1845, he was educated there and was related to the Sassoon family. As a young man he went to China for David Sassoon and Company.

In 1880 Moses returned to Bombay and became manager of the bank. When his uncle Solomon Sassoon died in 1894, he took his place as a director and on the Port Trust. In 1897 he was elected president of the bank, the first member of the Jewish community to reach that post. He also sat on the legislative council of the Bombay presidency.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-myers-asher-isa:
Asher Isaac Myers was an English journalist born in London in 1848 and dead there in 1902. Joseph Jacobs wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. Trained in the clothing business, he became joint proprietor of The Jewish Record in 1868. A year later he joined The Jewish Chronicle, the paper that made his career.

Under Dr. Benisch, Myers managed the Chronicle's business, and at Benisch's death in 1878 he inherited a share of it. As joint owner and acting editor he raised the paper to the first rank of Jewish journalism. He also helped found the Jewish Workingmen's Club in 1872. His house became a center of Jewish intellectual life in London.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nesvizh-11448:
Nesvizh was a small town in the government of Minsk. Herman Rosenthal and S. Janovsky wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The town stood already in the thirteenth century. The census of 1897 counted 8,446 people there. Of those, 4,764 were Jews, well over half.

Market gardening was a common trade among its Jews. The town held 650 Jewish artisans in that count. Day laborers among them numbered 110 more. A Talmud Torah taught 120 pupils there. Day schools served forty-three boys and fifty-eight girls. Charities ran a dispensary and free-loan funds for the poor. Eight synagogues served the town's Jewish life. Fire struck Nesvizh hard in that census year, 1897.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nimrod-11548:
Nimrod was a son of Cush and a mighty hunter. Emil G. Hirsch, M. Seligsohn, Wilhelm Bacher, and the Editorial Board wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His kingdom held Babel, Erech, Accad, and Calneh. Those cities stood in the land of Shinar. His name became a proverb for hunting skill.

Rabbinic lore makes him the first great rebel. His name is read as, he who made all rebel. He first taught men to eat meat, tales say. Adam's skin coats, stolen down the line, empowered him. Beasts crouched before him in those coats. He is blamed for urging the Tower of Babel. He threw Abraham into a furnace, says tradition. Esau slew him at last, two hunters made jealous. Critics match him with Gilgamesh or with Marduk.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-obed-edom-11648:
Obed-edom was a Gittite in whose house the Ark rested. Jacob Zallel Lauterbach, Schulim Ochser, and the board wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The Ark had been kept at the house of Abinadab. It stayed with Obed-edom for three months in all. Then it was borne to the City of David.

God blessed Obed-edom and all his house, the Bible says. Rabbis taught that he lit a candle by the Ark. He lit it twice each day, at dawn and at dusk. They said his blessing took the form of many children. His wife and eight wives of his sons bore young. Other men of this name kept the Temple gates. One played the harp as the Ark was moved.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-orabuena-11748:
Orabuena was a Spanish family of Navarre, in Spain. Gotthard Deutsch and Meyer Kayserling wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It thrived in the thirteen and fourteen hundreds there. Many of its men were rabbis or tax farmers. A like named family, Buenahora, may have been kin.

Juze Orabuena stands first in the line, a chief rabbi. He was doctor and aide to the king of Navarre. He was born at Tudela in the mid thirteen hundreds. The king set him a wage and a grant for life. His son Judah took his place as rabbi in 1408. Judah rode oft with King Charles the Third himself. He drew a grant of gold from the king each year. A third Judah served as rabbi at Tudela in 1348.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pagay-josephine:
Josephine Pagay was an Austrian actress born at Vienna. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote her entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. She died at Berlin on November 18, 1892. At the age of fourteen she first took the stage. Her first part was Cupido in a famed light opera.

That first work was Orpheus in the Underworld, a hit piece. Her brisk speech, her wit, and her gifts won all hearts. She scored great wins in the works of Offenbach. She won in works by Suppé, Millöcker, and Strauss too. She shone in the farces of Kaiser and of Costa. She stood at the height of her fame for two decades. In the mid eighties she left the stage all at once. She then lived in quiet at Berlin till her death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-patto-pato-benj:
Benjamin Dias Patto was a Spanish preacher and teacher in Amsterdam. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Patto studied under Saul Levi Morteira, a leading rabbi of the city. He was killed in April 1664.

Patto helped edit Morteira's sermons for print in 1645. He became the first teacher at Abi Yetomim. That school served orphans and opened in Amsterdam in 1648. A colleague's epitaph for him confirms that he was murdered. He also wrote a Spanish poem for a martyr named Bernal. The poem was printed in a memorial volume.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pilegesh-hebrew:
A pilegesh was a concubine known to ancient Hebrew law. Emil G. Hirsch, Schulim Ochser, and the Executive Committee wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. In the house she held a wife's standing. Her person was held as sacred as a wife's.

Barren wives gave their maids to their husbands. Sarah, Leah, and Rachel all did this in Genesis. Her sons ranked equal with the wife's sons. The outrage at Gibeah cost Benjamin thousands of men. Later kings kept concubines out of sheer luxury. Solomon alone is said to have kept three hundred.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pollak-kaim-122:
Kaim Pollak was a Hungarian writer born at Liptó-Szent-Miklós in 1835. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He learned Talmud in his home town, Presburg, and Sátoralja Ujhely. In 1858 he went to Prague and heard Rapoport lecture. He then taught at Jewish schools in three towns.

Pollak kept his last school post until a pension in 1902. He wrote school books of many kinds. His geometry book for public schools reached eight editions. In 1880 he brought out a full Hebrew-Hungarian dictionary. He turned works of Gabirol into Hungarian. He also gave Hungarian readers a book on Israel's past.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-presbyter-12348:
Presbyter is a Greek title for an elder in a community. Richard Gottheil and Samuel Krauss wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. From Moses to Talmudic times, elders formed a standing body. In Greek they were called the Gerusia. The word presbyter itself shows up late, though. It is not found before the first Christian years.

Still, the title must have been in use before then. The Christian office of presbyter was taken straight from Judaism, they say. A list of officers of a Jewish town in Cilicia proves the point. It names synagogue heads, priests, and presbyters side by side. The article sorts out who these elders were and what they did.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-purim-12448:
Purim is the Jewish feast of lots, kept each year in Adar. Kaufmann Kohler and Henry Malter wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It falls on the fourteenth day of the month. In Shushan it was kept on the fifteenth as well. It marks the rescue of Persia's Jews from Haman's plot. That plot sought to wipe them out in one blow.

The Book of Esther tells how the feast was founded. Mordecai and Esther set it as a national feast, it says. The writers leave the book's own tale to a sister article. Here they treat the feast as it grew after its founding. Customs, foods, gifts, and noise fill the later account.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ramah-ramath-or:
Ramah is a Hebrew word meaning height. Emil G. Hirsch and Immanuel Benzinger wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The word forms part of many place names in Palestine. Several different towns were also called simply Ramah.

The article works through those towns one by one. It places one Ramah in Asher and one in Naphtali. A third lay in Benjamin, north of Jerusalem. King Baasha fortified that town, and King Asa tore the works down. A fourth Ramah is linked to Samuel's home. The entry helps readers keep same-named Bible places apart. It matches old names to sites known in 1906.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rehumai-i-rab-1:
Rab Rehumai was a Babylonian amora of the fifth generation. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He studied under Raba b. Joseph b. Hama. He also put questions to Abaye.

The article is best known for the tale of his death. He always went home on the eve of the Day of Atonement. One year study at Mahoza held him too long. His wife waited, then wept at his failure to come. Legend says heaven punished his neglect with death. The roof where he sat fell in and killed him. He died on that same holy eve. The entry joins Talmud teaching to a warning tale.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rieger-paul-127:
Paul Rieger was a German rabbi and historian born on July 4, 1870. Isidore Singer and Hermann Vogelstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Dresden. He studied at Breslau and Berlin universities.

The article says he also studied at Jewish seminaries in both cities. His Breslau thesis treated crafts in the Mishnah. Its title asks about their technology and terminology. He served as rabbi at Potsdam from 1896 to 1902. Hamburg's Temple congregation then called him as rabbi. With H. Vogelstein he wrote a history of Rome's Jews. That work filled two volumes in 1895 and 1896. He also wrote a small pamphlet, Hillel und Jesus, in 1904.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosenfeld-leopo:
Leopold Rosenfeld was a Danish composer born in Copenhagen on July 21, 1849. Isidore Singer and Frank Cramer wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He spent six years in a counting-house before his father let him study music.

At the Copenhagen Conservatory from 1872 to 1875, Rosenfeld focused on composition. A scholarship in 1881 let him travel abroad, and in 1889 he became a professor. He wrote many piano pieces and more than thirty booklets of songs. His orchestral piece Henrik og Else won great favor in 1885. He also wrote a guide to teaching singing, Om Textsang.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ruth-rabbah-cal:
Ruth Rabbah, also called Midrash Rut, is a homiletic commentary on the Book of Ruth. Wilhelm Bacher and M. Seligsohn wrote its entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. It belongs to the Midrash Rabbot, covering all five scrolls.

Eight sections carry the reader through Ruth verse by verse. Some verses get a literal reading, others an allegorical one instead. A long introduction of separate proems stands before the commentary proper. Its spirit is that of the Palestinian teachers of legend and sermon. Its main sources include the Jerusalem Talmud and Bereshit Rabbah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-salvador-franci:
Francis Salvador was a patriot of the American Revolution who died on August 1, 1776. Cyrus Adler and L. Hühner wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He came of the wealthy London Salvador family, once Jessurum Rodriguez.

Salvador inherited great wealth, increased by his marriage dowry in London. Then the Lisbon earthquake and the Dutch East India failure swept it away. About 1773 he emigrated to South Carolina, leaving wife and children in England. Within a year he had bought considerable lands in the colony. He threw himself heart and soul into the American cause there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-ben-solo:
Isaac Broydé wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, issued with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board in 1906. It profiles Samuel ben Solomon of Falaise, a tosafist of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. In French he was called Sir Morel. Rabbinic books often cite him by that name. He studied under Judah Sir Leon of Paris and Isaac ben Abraham of Sens.

In 1240 Samuel took part in the famous Paris dispute. The baptized Jew Nicholas Donin had stirred up that attack on the Talmud. Samuel also wrote tosafot, or notes, on several Talmudic tracts. His notes on Abodah Zarah were printed with the text. He wrote rulings on points of ritual law as well. Meïr of Rothenburg and other leading rabbis cite those rulings often.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schapira-herman:
Herman Rosenthal and Isidore Singer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Hermann Schapira. He was a Russian mathematician. Schapira was born in 1840 at Erswilken, a small town in Lithuania. He died at Cologne on May 8, 1898. Trained for the rabbinate, he held a rabbinical post at twenty-four. Then he turned the rest of his life to secular science.

Schapira studied at Odessa and at Berlin's Gewerbeakademie. After years in trade, he returned to study at Heidelberg. He took his doctorate in 1883 and taught mathematics there. He still loved Hebrew literature all his life. He edited the Mishnat ha-Middot from a Munich manuscript in 1880. He was also an ardent Zionist from the start. On a Zionist lecture tour he caught pneumonia at Cologne and died.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schwerin-gotz-1:
Gotthard Deutsch and Eduard Neumann wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Götz Schwerin. He was a Hungarian rabbi and Talmudist. Schwerin was born in 1760 at Schwerin-on-the-Warthe. He died on January 15, 1845. He studied at the yeshibot of Presburg and Prague. In 1796 he settled in Hungary as a private scholar at Baja.

In 1812 Schwerin became rabbi of Szabadka, and in 1815 of Baja. His house became the district's center of learning. In 1827 Hungary's communities elected him chief rabbi of the country. He could summon parties and compel their appearance. No ritual official could be appointed without his consent. Thousands of disputes passed through his hands. He used his power with unbending justice. He also gave the sermon its due place in worship. His grandson Samuel Kohn wrote his life in Hungarian.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shema-13548:
Shema is the first word of the verse Jews recite as their confession of faith. Kaufmann Kohler and Judah David Eisenstein wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. Hear, O Israel: the Lord our God is one Lord. At first the Shema was that single verse from Deuteronomy.

In the liturgy it grew to three full portions. The first commands love of God and teaching children. It also commands words on arm, head, and doorposts. The second promises reward for obedience and warns of punishment. The third gives the law of fringes as a reminder. The entry shows how one short verse became the center of Jewish prayer, morning and night, across the centuries.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sifre-zuta-the-:
Sifre Zuta, the Small Sifre, is a distinctive midrash on the book of Numbers. Wilhelm Bacher and S. Horovitz wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. It holds special interest for the study of Jewish law. Weiss questioned its authenticity, but wrongly, the entry argues.

Medieval authors knew it under two other titles as well. To separate it, one work calls the big Sifre Rabbati instead. The small Sifre itself has not survived whole. A later writer notes it was already lost in his day. Earlier authors still quoted it in their books. Samson of Sens used it on Mishnah orders. Many fragments live inside the Yalkut Shim'oni on Numbers. Brüll gathered and compared those fragments for scholars. The entry tells how a lost book is rebuilt from quotations.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simon-moritz-al:
Moritz Alexander Simon was a German banker and philanthropist born at Hanover in 1837. Isidore Singer and Frederick T Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He worked in his home town with the banking house of Ezechiel Simon. After some years in New York he founded his own bank. In New York he saw the misery of poor Jewish immigrants.

Simon came to see the Jewish question as a social one in part. In 1893 he opened a school at Ahlem near Hanover. It trained boys in farming and in handicrafts. By 1905 it had trained about 170 pupils. He left the school 750,000 dollars in his will when he died.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-spektor-isaac-e:
Isaac Elhanan Spektor was a Russian rabbi and author born in 1817. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Peter Wiernik wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Rosh, in the government of Grodno. His father, a rabbi with Hasidic leanings, first taught him. The boy soon won fame as a prodigy, an ilui.

At thirteen he married and settled with his wife's parents. He studied under Benjamin Diskin, who ordained him as rabbi. When his wife's dowry was lost, he had to earn a living. In 1837 he became rabbi of tiny Sabelin in poverty. His pay was five Polish gulden a week there. He died at Kovno on March 6, 1896.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-stieglitz-juliu:
Julius Oscar Stieglitz was an American chemist born at Hoboken on May 26, 1867. Cyrus Adler and I. George Dobsevage wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He went to public schools in New York City. He then studied in Carlsruhe, Berlin, and Göttingen. His training spanned both sides of the Atlantic.

After returning home, Stieglitz joined the University of Chicago. He served there as instructor, then assistant and associate professor. He published often in chemical journals of two countries. His articles ran in American and German periodicals from 1892 to 1903. The brief entry tracks a chemist rising through one young university. It also shows the close ties between American and German chemistry then. Readers get his posts and publication record in compact form.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-targum-14248:
A targum is the Aramaic translation of the Hebrew Bible. Wilhelm Bacher wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about it in 1906. It forms part of Jewish traditional literature. Its roots reach back to Second Temple times. The word itself appears in Ezra for an Aramaic document.

In Mishnaic speech the verb could mean any translation. Aquila's Greek version is called targum in places. By itself, though, Targum meant the Aramaic Bible alone. Aramaic passages inside scripture also bore the name. The Hebrew text beside them was called Mikra. Targum served both synagogue worship and Bible study. Public reading paired the text with its translation. That pairing was already an ancient institution. The entry traces a translation that became tradition itself.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tordesillas-144: Tordesillas is a Spanish city near Valladolid with an old Jewish community. Joseph Jacobs and Meyer Kayserling wrote this brief Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. Vicente Ferrer visited the town late in 1411. His aim was to win Jews to Christianity. He urged them to move into Valladolid's narrow ghetto. The community disregarded his advice and stayed. In 1474 its Jews still paid 900 maravedis in taxes. That sum shows the community remained sizable. Tordesillas was also the birthplace of Moses ha-Kohen.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-vashti-14648:
Vashti was the first wife of King Ahasuerus in the Book of Esther. Her refusal and punishment open that story. Emil G. Hirsch, the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board, and Judah David Eisenstein wrote this entry. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Her name may come from an Elamite goddess.

The entry gives both the Bible account and later rabbinic tales. In the rabbinic telling, Vashti held a feast for women. The king ordered her to appear before his guests wearing only her crown. She refused, and the rabbis gave varied reasons. Some said she had fallen ill with leprosy. These added tales fill out her brief Bible role.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wahb-ibn-munabb:
Wahb ibn Munabbih was a Muslim traditionist of Yemen. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He came from Dhimar, near Sanaa. He died at age ninety, in a year given as 725 to 737. His father had Persian knightly roots. His mother was a Himyarite.

Some claimed Wahb had converted from Judaism. Most biographers do not call him a Jew. He knew Jewish traditions deeply and wrote much on them. He was said to have read over seventy books on the prophets. Muslims trusted his tales of Muhammad and Bible figures. Others, like Ibn Khaldun, charged that he invented freely. His story collections shaped later Islamic lore.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-weiss-markus-ni:
Markus Nissa Weiss was a Hungarian advocate of Reform. Isidore Singer and Alexander Büchler wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was also called Mardokai Ungvar. In 1792 he kept a small business at Pesth. In 1794 he leased an estate near Munkacs. Complaints rose against his rule there.

In 1802 Weiss published a plea for Reform ideas. Hungarian Jews attacked the pamphlet bitterly. He answered with a second pamphlet in 1803. The attacks did not stop, so he converted to Christianity. He later wrote on accounting methods and Bible texts. He also commented on the great Paris Sanhedrin. The entry traces a reformer's losing fight.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yadayim-hands-1:
Yadayim, which means hands, is a tract on the clean state of hands. Joseph Jacobs and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It stands in the Mishnah and in the Tosefta. It is the eleventh tract in the order on purity.

The tract has four parts with twenty-two short rules. Part one treats the water used to wash the hands. It tells how much water and what jars will serve. It tells what water may not be used at all. Part two treats how the water is poured out. Part three treats things that make the hands unclean. One odd rule says holy books make the hands unclean. That rule kept the books apart from priest food gifts. Mice had harmed both when they were stored as one.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zadok-gaon-call:
Zadok Gaon, also called Isaac ben Ashi, led the Sura school briefly. Isidore Singer and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He held that post from 820 to 821 of this era. One court reply of his lives on in a law book.

That reply shows how he judged the men brought to him. When a man was found at fault but could not be fined, Zadok spoke. He charged that man to beg grace from the man he wronged. He could pay cash to that man in place of grace. If the man said no, he was cast out of the group. Zadok was one of the first school heads to doubt old rules. Yet his doubt led him to more stern use, not less.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zerffi-gustav-r:
Gustav Zerffi, born Hirsch, was a Hungarian news man and rebel. Isidore Singer and Newell Dunbar wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in Hungary at a date near 1820. His first book came out at Vienna in the year 1848.

That book held twelve droll cuts at men of the day. As chief of Der Ungar he lashed the Germans in print. He lashed the royal house of Austria in like terms. With five peers he set the tone for the rebel cause. In 1848 he served as a chief aide in the honved host. When the revolt fell, he fled to Belgrade in 1849. There he served the French consul in a staff role. In 1850 he turned the works of Kossuth into German. Two years on he went to Paris and then to London.
kingsborough-mexico-vol-8-1848:
Book Eight of the Antiquities of Mexico came out in 1848. Lord Kingsborough had died in debt in 1837, and the set had stalled for years. The full work runs to nine books in all. This book takes the long run of plates toward its close.

Texts and plates on the towns, gods, and past of old Mexico fill the book. The copies in the set save the look of books now lost or worn. Kingsborough's wild claim on the roots of the Mexicans drove the whole work. The set stands as a great store in spite of that claim.
kingsborough-mexico-vol-9-1848:
Book Nine ends Lord Kingsborough's Antiquities of Mexico. The last book came out in 1848, long past his death in 1837. The full set runs to nine books of plates and text. Kingsborough had spent his whole fortune on the work and died in a debt jail.

The last plates round out the store of codices and town views. Text in the set backs his claim that Mexico's folk came from the lost tribes. That claim has few friends now, but the plates endure. The set is a chief source for the art of old Mexico.
lowell-biglow-papers-1848:
James Russell Lowell published the first series of The Biglow Papers in 1848, during the Mexican-American War. Lowell, a young Massachusetts poet and abolitionist, wrote them as newspaper pieces in Yankee dialect. His farmer-poet Hosea Biglow speaks, while the learned Parson Wilbur adds mock-serious introductions.

Biglow's verses attack the war as a slaveholders' land grab and mock the politicians who sold it. A recruiting officer gets a famous dressing-down in rough, funny, perfectly rhymed dialect. Lowell based the speech on real New England talk, then sharpened it into a weapon. The papers became the masterpiece of American comic verse and the ancestor of all later dialect poetry in the United States.
lowell-fable-for-critics-1848:
James Russell Lowell published A Fable for Critics in 1848, the same year as The Biglow Papers made his name. Lowell was twenty-nine, brilliant, and unafraid of judging his elders. He cast the poem as a tour: the god Phoebus brings a visiting critic to meet America's living writers one by one.

Poe, Emerson, Hawthorne, Longfellow, Whittier, and Lowell himself each get a galloping verse portrait, praise and puncture mixed. Phoebus complains that American letters are all promise and brag. The judgments are so apt that many stuck to their subjects for life. The poem is the founding document of American critical reputation-making, and still the liveliest survey of the era's literature.
lowell-vision-sir-launfal-1848:
James Russell Lowell published The Vision of Sir Launfal in 1848, his telling of the Grail quest as a moral allegory. Lowell was in his great early burst, issuing the Biglow Papers and A Fable for Critics the same year. The poem's prelude, The Present Crisis, outgrew the poem itself in fame.

Sir Launfal rides out from his castle in pride, searching the world for the Holy Grail. He returns old and broken, and finds the Grail's lesson at his own gate, in sharing his last crust with a beggar. The Present Crisis, written against slavery's expansion, gave abolitionism a battle cry: truth forever on the scaffold, wrong forever on the throne. Generations of reformers quoted it, and Launfal's winter and summer landscapes remain lovely.
macaulay-history-england-vol-1-1848:
Thomas Babington Macaulay published Volume 1 of his History of England in 1848. The History became the best-selling work of history of the 1800s. Volume 1 opens with a survey of England from Roman times to the Restoration. It then focuses on the reign of Charles II and the accession of James II.

Macaulay writes Whig history: the story of liberty advancing through Parliament against kings. His famous third chapter paints the state of England in 1685 in rich detail. Markets, roads, alehouses, and clergy all come alive. The narrative art is brilliant and confident. Macaulay aimed to replace the novel in the reader's hands, and often succeeded.
macaulay-history-england-vol-2-1848:
Thomas Babington Macaulay published Volume 2 of his History of England in 1848, alongside the first. This volume covers the reign of James II in depth. James's push for Catholic power and standing armies alarms the nation. The trial of the Seven Bishops and the birth of a royal son spark crisis.

William of Orange lands in 1688, and James flees to France. Macaulay tells the road to revolution with narrative art at full power. His sympathies are clear: he honors those who defended law and Protestant liberty. Critics fault his partisanship, yet few deny his skill. The volume ends with William and Mary on the throne.
marx-manifesto-1848:
Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels wrote The Communist Manifesto in 1848. The text here is the English edition of 1888, edited by Engels. Its four parts move from class war to the stance of the party.

The famous first line says a spectre haunts Europe, the spectre of communism. Part one calls all past history a tale of class fights. Slave and free, lord and serf, boss and hand stand in its long line of foes. Later parts sort rival kinds of socialism and mock weak plans. The pamphlet ends by placing the party among the foes of the old order.
mill-principles-political-economy-vol-1-:
John Stuart Mill published Principles of Political Economy, Volume 1, in 1848. For fifty years the Principles served as the dominant textbook of economics in English. Volume 1 treats production: labor, capital, land, and the laws that govern their cooperation. Mill restates classical economics in a clear, final synthesis.

He studies large and small farming, cooperation, and the limits of growth in output. Mill writes with unusual care for the human side of industry. His sympathy for workers and for reform sets the book apart from colder texts. The stationary state, treated later, already casts its shadow. Volume 1 lays the base for the whole system.
mill-principles-political-economy-vol-2-:
John Stuart Mill completed Principles of Political Economy with Volume 2 in 1848. This volume treats distribution and exchange: wages, profits, rent, money, credit, and trade between nations. Mill argues that the laws of distribution are human-made and can be reformed. That claim opened economics to social reform.

He also develops the theory of value and of international trade in classic form. Chapters on the functions of government weigh taxes, education, and poor relief. Mill's hope for a stationary state of capital, paired with rising human culture, closes the work. The two volumes formed generations of economic thought. They remain readable and humane.
montezuma-s-daughter-pg1848:
H. Rider Haggard's historical novel follows Thomas Wingfield from England to Aztec Mexico. The contents open with why Thomas tells his tale, and the coming of the Spaniard. He swears an oath of vengeance and says good-bye to his sweetheart. Shipwreck and the stone of sacrifice carry him into Montezuma's world.

Thomas saves Guatemoc, enters Montezuma's court, and is treated as a god. He marries Otomie, the emperor's daughter, in the naming of the brides. Later chapters bury Montezuma's treasure and record the fall of Tenoctitlan. The book closes with Otomie's farewell and Thomas back from the dead, across forty chapters.
needham-observations-generation-1748:
John Turberville Needham, an English priest and man of science, read this paper to the Royal Society in 1748. He claimed to have seen life spring up where none had been. His claim dealt with the birth, make up, and break down of living stuffs. The theme drew heat, since it bore on how life first came to be on earth.

Needham boiled broth, sealed it, and found tiny forms in it days later. He took this as proof that dead stuff holds a force that makes new life. Pasteur and Spallanzani spent the next age of work to show where his trials went wrong.
openalex-w1586227748:
Perianayagam Arokiasamy and many co-authors wrote this global health study. It appeared in BMC Medicine in the year 2015. Multimorbidity means living with two or more chronic diseases. Such illness adds a large burden in poorer nations, they note. Little research had tested its effects in those settings.

The team used the WHO SAGE survey of adult health. It covered more than forty thousand adults in six nations. Those nations were China, Ghana, India, Mexico, Russia, and South Africa. Having many diseases linked to worse daily function and mood. It also linked to poorer self-rated health and life quality. Russia showed the highest rates in the sample.
openalex-w1800605248:
Nelson Avonce, Gabriel Iturriaga, and two co-authors wrote this study. It appeared in BMC Evolutionary Biology in December 2006. Trehalose is a sugar that shields cells from stress. It builds up under heat, cold, or dry conditions. Many thought it lived only in extreme-loving organisms.

The team showed the making pathway is far more widespread. It appears in bacteria, archaea, plants, fungi, and animals. Bacteria hold five distinct routes to make the sugar. Other kingdoms hold only one route, they report. In bacteria the key genes sit clustered together. In eukaryotes they are fused into one protein. Vertebrates cannot make trehalose but can break it down.
openalex-w1971699048:
María Guzmán, Eva Harris, and co-authors tested dengue diagnostics. Their study appeared in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2010. Early dengue diagnosis helps sort and treat patients well. Blood tests for the NS1 virus protein promise speed. Two commercial test kits were ready for checking.

The team ran a multi-country evaluation of both kits. They measured sensitivity, meaning true cases caught. They also measured specificity, meaning false alarms avoided. Clinics in Asia and Latin America supplied patient samples. Fair scores tell programs where rapid tests help most. The study guides dengue care in endemic regions.
openalex-w2004015348:
Anna Vassall, Sanne van Kampen, Hojoon Sohn and colleagues studied the costs of a fast tuberculosis test. Their paper appeared in PLoS Medicine in 2011. The Xpert test finds tuberculosis quickly. It costs more than the older microscope method. Programme leaders worried about the price.

The team used a decision model for three countries. The countries were India, South Africa and Uganda. They compared Xpert with microscope checks and clinical judgement. Adding Xpert found more true cases in all three settings. Testing costs per case found also rose. The cost for each year of healthy life gained stayed modest. The authors judged Xpert good value in these settings.
openalex-w2102203148:
Ted Feldpausch, Jon Lloyd, Simon Lewis and colleagues tested what tree height adds to forest biomass estimates. Their paper appeared in Biogeosciences in 2012. Tropical forests store huge amounts of carbon. Estimates usually rely on trunk width alone. Height is often ignored, which can bias totals.

The team gathered paired height and width measurements. They covered hundreds of plots across the tropics. Harvested trees provided ground-truth weights. Adding height changed biomass estimates notably. Regional height patterns differed between continents. Taller forests stored more carbon than width alone suggested. Climate and soil shaped tree height patterns. Carbon accounting should include height, they conclude.
openalex-w2132582148:
Paul Reiter, Sarah Lathrop, Michel Bunning, and colleagues published this study in Emerging Infectious Diseases in 2003. They investigated a 1999 dengue outbreak on the Texas-Mexico border. The twin cities of Laredo, Texas, and Nuevo Laredo, Mexico, sit side by side, yet dengue stayed rare on the United States side.

Blood surveys showed more recent dengue cases in Nuevo Laredo than in Laredo. Oddly, the mosquito that spreads dengue was more abundant in Laredo. The authors point to daily life differences that cut contact with mosquitoes. Air conditioning and time spent indoors in Texas help explain why the virus spread less there despite more mosquitoes.
openalex-w2140941348:
Philippe Truc, Philippe Büscher, Gérard Cuny, and colleagues published this review in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2013. They collect human infections caused by trypanosomes that normally infect animals. The classic human forms are sleeping sickness and Chagas disease, but other Trypanosoma species sometimes infect people too.

The review covers cases tied to six animal species or subspecies. Some infections passed on their own, while others needed treatment, which worked in most cases, though two patients died. Nineteen patients are reviewed, with eight cases confirmed between 1974 and 2010 as molecular tests improved. The authors note the true count of such infections is likely underestimated.
openalex-w2308892148:
Kathryn Lafond, Harish Nair, Mohammad Rasooly, and colleagues published this analysis in PLoS Medicine in 2016. They estimated how much childhood respiratory hospitalization worldwide is caused by influenza. Testing of hospitalized children has expanded over a decade, yet most data never fed a global burden estimate.

The team pooled a systematic review and surveillance platforms spanning three decades. About one in ten respiratory hospitalizations in children tested positive for influenza. The share ranged from about one in twenty in young infants to about one in six in older children. Applied to global totals, influenza sends roughly three hundred seventy-four thousand infants to hospital yearly. For all children under five, the estimate reaches about eight hundred seventy thousand admissions.
openalex-w2511044748:
Juan Carlos Jiménez-Muñoz, Cristian Mattar, and Jonathan Barichivich, with colleagues, wrote this 2016 Scientific Reports study of the Amazon rainforest. They examined the El Niño event of 2015 and 2016, a Pacific warming pattern that drives climate extremes across the tropics. Forecasters expected it to rival the huge 1997 to 1998 event. The team asked what it actually did to Amazon heat and rainfall.

They found record warming and a wider spread of extreme drought than in earlier strong El Niño events. The pattern split the basin: the east dried as expected, while the west turned unusually wet. They link that split to where the Pacific warming peaked, in its central part. The basin had already warmed since 1980, adding to the stress. Effects on the forest itself, they note, still need documenting.
openalex-w2804430248:
Sergei Dubovsky, V. Gorbenko, and Guzmán Hernández-Chifflet wrote this 2018 theory paper in the Journal of High Energy Physics. It studies the TT-bar deformation, a way of modifying two-dimensional theories that stays exactly solvable. Such deformed theories behave like theories of gravity. Scattering results were already known from coupling the original theory to Jackiw-Teitelboim gravity.

The authors show the gravity description also works in finite volume, not just for scattering. They compute the torus partition function of any matter theory coupled to this gravity. Their first-order formulation supplies natural clocks and rods inside the theory. The resulting partition function is exact at one loop. It reproduces the known deformed energy spectrum in finite volume. The result strengthens a rare case where a gravity problem can be solved completely.
openalex-w2889449548:
Sharon Huws, Christopher J. Creevey, and Linda Boniface Oyama lead this 2018 review in Frontiers in Microbiology, on the rumen microbiome. The rumen, a cow's first stomach, hosts bacteria, protozoa, fungi, methane-making archaea, and viruses. Together they digest plant material humans cannot, powering the animal. Ruminants thus convert grass into meat and milk rich in protein and vitamins.

The same archaea vent methane, a potent greenhouse gas, as a by-product. That makes the rumen central to global farming challenges: food security and climate impact pull opposite directions. The review traces understanding of this microbiome from past methods to present sequencing power. It looks ahead to manipulating the community for efficiency and lower emissions. Knowing which microbes do what is the prerequisite for any intervention. The authors frame rumen science as a lever on agriculture's footprint.
openalex-w3112186348:
Pablo Tittonell, Gervasio Piñeiro, Lucas Garibaldi, and colleagues published this research agenda in Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems in 2020. It asks how agroecology, farming in tune with nature, can work on large-scale farms. Big export farms in regions such as the South American Pampas are the test case.

High output per hectare is often praised as efficiency, and even as green, under land-sparing arguments. The authors note the catch: output bought with heavy outside inputs carries a high environmental cost per hectare. More farmers, governments, and green groups now see agroecology as a way to cut nitrogen pollution and wildlife loss while holding yields. The paper sets the research agenda for proving that at scale.
openalex-w3195130348:
Paul Bastard, Adrian Gervais, Tom Le Voyer, and colleagues report on harmful autoantibodies in COVID-19, in Science Immunology in 2021. Autoantibodies are immune proteins that attack the body's own defences. Here they block type I interferons, signals that help fight viruses early in infection. Earlier work had linked these blockers to life-threatening COVID-19 pneumonia in some patients.

The team reports that about four in a hundred uninfected people over seventy carry these autoantibodies. As the title states, they account for about a fifth of COVID-19 deaths. Their share rises steeply with age, which helps explain why older people face far greater risk. Testing for them could flag patients who need early, close care.
openalex-w4317716348:
Dann Turner, Andrey Shkoporov, Cédric Lood, and colleagues summarise the 2022 taxonomy update for bacterial viruses, in Archives of Virology in 2023. The update comes from a subcommittee of the ICTV, the world body that classifies viruses. It covers proposals made in 2021 and ratified by vote in 2022. Virus classification had long grouped many bacterial viruses, called phages, by their shape under the microscope.

That shape-based scheme now ends. The old families Podoviridae, Siphoviridae, and Myoviridae, and the order Caudovirales, were abolished as misleading. A two-part naming system for species was established in their place. The update also created or moved hundreds of genera and species, aligning phage names with their true family relations.
openalex-w4366482848:
Hans-Otto Pörtner, Robert Scholes, Almut Arneth, and colleagues review the linked climate and biodiversity crises in Science in 2023. Pollution, overuse of resources, habitat loss, and inequality strain both nature and society. Climate change sharpens nearly every one of those pressures. The authors set out a roadmap that treats the two crises as one problem with shared solutions.

Their roadmap calls for holding warming to one and a half degrees. It also calls for conserving and restoring working ecosystems across a third to a half of land, fresh water, and ocean. Protected and shared spaces would form one connected mosaic. Reaching that future, they argue, needs bold, joined-up policy from local councils to global bodies, and it is urgently overdue.
openalex-w4392193048:
Dave Van Veen, Cara Van Uden, Louis Blankemeier, and colleagues test whether language models can summarise clinical text better than doctors. Their study appeared in Nature Medicine in 2024. Clinicians spend huge shares of their day writing summaries, reports, and notes. Documentation can take two hours for every hour spent with patients, feeding burnout. The team adapted several large language models, open and commercial, to summarisation tasks in medicine.

Adaptation means extra training on clinical material so the models learn the style and content. As the title states, the adapted models outperformed medical experts in the study's comparisons of clinical summaries. The reference summaries came from practising clinicians. If such tools prove safe at scale, they could return hours of the working day to patient care.
openalex-w588204548:
H. Abramowicz, I. Abt, L. Adamczyk, and the H1 and ZEUS collaborations combine all their deep inelastic scattering data. Their paper appeared in the European Physical Journal C in 2015. The data come from the HERA electron-proton collider. Scattering electrons off protons probes the proton's inner structure.

Each collaboration had published many cross-section measurements separately. Combining them cancels some errors and sharpens the result. The merged dataset spans neutral and charged current reactions. The authors then run a quantum chromodynamics analysis on it. Such fits pin down how quarks and gluons share the proton's momentum. Precise parton distributions feed predictions for every other collider experiment, including the Large Hadron Collider.
openalex-w7128707048:
Mariko Fukui, Kenji Suzuki, Yoshihiro Itagaki, and colleagues review robot-assisted thoracic surgery for lung cancer at Juntendo University. Their article appeared in the Juntendo Medical Journal in 2026. Robotic operations were rare in lung surgery before 2018. Insurance coverage then opened the door in Japan.

Robotic procedures now exceed fifteen percent of lung cancer operations there. Juntendo began its programme in 2017. It now performs about two hundred fifty robotic surgeries a year. The authors assess the programme's safety and benefits. Their experience helps other hospitals judge the costs and gains of robotic surgery. It also shows how a new surgical platform matures into routine care.
openalex-w7204260448:
Emilly de Azevedo Leite led a Portuguese-language integrative review, published in Brazil in 2026, on what energy drinks do to the central nervous system. Searching three databases for studies from 2021 to mid-2026, the team screened thirty-two papers down to a final sample of nine. The question matters because consumption is heavy among young people, who often drink these products while short on sleep.

The drinks produced narrow cognitive gains, mainly in attention, alertness, and reaction time, especially under fatigue, but the benefits were not uniform across mental abilities. Frequent or excessive use, by contrast, was associated with disturbed sleep, anxiety, irritability, and other behavioral effects. The stimulation is temporary, the authors warn, and habitual or heavy consumption calls for caution.
openalex-w7204448948:
Ana Erica Batista Silva and Wágner Bruno Silva Coelho published a Portuguese-language review in Brazil in 2026 on artificial intelligence in the teaching of biological sciences. AI tools are entering classrooms fast, widening what teachers can do while raising teaching, ethical, and school problems. Searching two sources for work from 2020 to August 2026, the team assessed the potential and the problems for teaching and learning processes.

AI can personalize learning, give feedback, diversify materials, clarify complex content, support data analysis, and help teachers plan, the review finds. But unreliable information, technological dependence, school integrity, authorship, privacy, unequal access, and teacher training all pose risks. AI helps, they conclude, only as a complement under clear teaching goals and teacher mediation, preserving students' critical thinking.
openalex-w7204987148:
Kayky de Menezes Marsicano Leite led a Portuguese-language epidemiological study, published in Brazil in 2026, profiling drug poisonings in the state of Paraíba in 2025. Of more than seven thousand exogenous poisonings recorded in the state that year, just over half were caused by medications, an incidence near ninety per hundred thousand inhabitants. The descriptive, retrospective, quantitative study reads the notification data for who was poisoned, how, and why.

Suicide attempts caused the largest share, nearly two thirds of the drug poisoning cases. Accidents, abuse, and self-medication together made up most of the remainder. Drug poisonings are multifactorial problems, the authors conclude, tied to irrational medicine use, self-medication, and social and mental health factors. They call for stronger health education and wider public policies on mental health and suicide prevention.
openalex-w7204991548:
Felipe Yoschio Moreira Saijo led a Portuguese-language review, published in Brazil in 2026, on low blood pressure during surgery and acute kidney injury. Drops in blood pressure are among the most frequent disturbances during operations, and reduced pressure can starve the kidneys of blood flow, mainly in patients with little functional reserve. Searching five sources for mainly 2020 to 2026 studies, the team asked how the intensity and duration of intraoperative hypotension shape kidney outcomes.

Episodes of reduced mean arterial pressure were linked to higher risk of acute kidney injury, mainly when pressure stayed below a key threshold for prolonged periods. The effect looked dose-dependent in both depth and accumulated time. Age, hypertension, prior kidney disease, diabetes, surgical complexity, and vasopressor need modified the risk. Judging hypotension, the authors conclude, requires intensity, duration, and individual vulnerability together.
openalex-w7205000548:
Geovanna Aguiar Mota led a Portuguese-language review, in Brazil in 2026, on university students misusing the stimulants lisdexamfetamine and methylphenidate. Entering higher education brings heavy cognitive and emotional demands, and many students take these ADHD drugs without a diagnosis hoping to perform better. Using standard review method across three sources for 2020 to 2025 publications, the team selected fifteen studies.

Careless use was linked to higher risk of dependence and tolerance, cardiovascular changes, sleep problems, anxiety, irritability, and other physical and mental harms, the review finds. There is no consistent evidence that the drugs improve school results in people without ADHD. Unsupervised use is a real public health problem, the authors conclude, requiring education, prescription oversight, and mental health plans.
openalex-w7208785448:
Jose Roberto Coelho, Niceas Arcoverde Gusmao Neto, and Leonardo David Quintiliano read what the growth of base rights means for Brazil's courts. The list of rights the law guards keeps its spread. New claims now join it: rights of the wild world, of the web, and of small groups. The team read law lore, laws, and court calls, framed round the rights' past, the courts' part, and the walls courts hit.

Judges hold a core part in keep rights safe, they close. But courts alone cannot hand them out. Deep change of the frame, joint work of state arms, and a share for the folk must walk with court acts. A court house that is open and swift keeps man's worth at the core of the free state. Fair checks on courts, and strong state plans, do the rest.
openalex-w7208822448:
Giovanna Azevedo Rodrigues leads two colleagues in a plan to take the mad mind's false tales apart, bit by bit. The mad ills shift much from soul to soul, which foils plain frames. Their sweep of the last five years' work, run by set rules, spans the sides of the ill and its prime signs of old lore. It spans drug use, ties with autism, and broke sleep.

From that stock the team builds a read grid. In their frame the ill runs on a scale, not in a box. Its core weak spot sits in what they call the next self. That is the part that keeps touch with the real, holds one's life tale in one piece, and soaks up swings of mood. When that part is frail, the false tale finds its foot. The sweep gives staff a map, not a lone root.
openalex-w7213224648:
Naidelyn Mishelle Merelo Solorzano leads a team that grades the Chone River in Manabi, Ecuador. The river serves farms and towns, and its health is in doubt. The team took tests at five spots in the basin, at two depths. They fed nine signs into a known score for stream health: air in the water, germ counts, sour rank, rot load, and salt and silt loads.

The scores ran from poor to fair, with most spots in the low bands. One spot near the top of the basin stood best. A mid spot stood worst, weighed down by rich salts, rot load, murk, and germs. Depth made scant odds: the harm ran through the whole stream. The river, the team holds, sits under strain from waste and farm wash. Towns that drink or wash from it need watch, curbs, and care of the basin as a whole.
openalex-w7214311248:
Taiki Kajiwara and colleagues at Tohoku University in Japan studied hernias that form at the old stoma site after ileostomy reversal, in a 2026 surgical article. An ileostomy diverts the bowel through the abdominal wall; after it is closed, the weakened spot can bulge into a hernia. The team reviewed 194 patients treated for bowel growths between 2010 and 2023.

About one in ten patients developed such a hernia, found on scans at a median of roughly nine months, and a few needed repair surgery. Higher body mass index was a consistent risk factor. Braided absorbable stitches used to close the muscle layer were also linked to hernia, though the link weakened when the treatment period was considered. The authors say stitch choice deserves more study.
openalex-w7214343448:
Rennan Gleyson Sousa de Sá and colleagues used network analysis to track dengue spread across Rio Grande do Norte, Brazil, in a 2026 study. Dengue is a mosquito-borne disease tied to climate, cities, and local sanitation. The team combined weekly disease reports with temperature and rainfall records from 2010 to 2023, linking towns into a network based on how their outbreaks lined up in time.

Transmission followed a repeating seasonal pattern, rising at the end of summer and during autumn. Some years, notably 2016 and 2022, broke the pattern with much stronger epidemics. The network view also revealed critical weeks when outbreaks synchronize across towns. The authors argue health services can use such signals to act earlier, focusing prevention before peaks arrive rather than after hospitals fill.
openalex-w7214507048:
Amábile Jorge da Silva led a large 2026 review team examining mitapivat, a new oral drug for anemia in thalassemia. Thalassemia is an inherited blood disorder in which red blood cells break down too fast and the body makes blood poorly. Care long rested on regular transfusions, drugs that remove excess iron, and, for some, stem cell transplant.

Mitapivat works differently: it activates an enzyme in red blood cells so they produce more energy, which reduces oxidative stress and helps the cells survive longer. Drawing on two large phase three trials, the review reports higher hemoglobin and reduced transfusion need compared with placebo after the drug's 2025 approval in the United States. Liver monitoring is required because of a risk of liver cell injury, and long-term data are still needed.
openalex-w7218524048:
Lorena Silva Boiko led a nine-author 2026 review on right ventricular remodeling after repaired tetralogy of Fallot, the most common cyanotic congenital heart defect. Surgery now lets most patients reach adult life, but repair does not end cardiovascular risk. Chronic leakage of the pulmonary valve, often from the repair patch, overloads the right ventricle with volume, driving dilation, shape change, progressive dysfunction, and tissue that can trigger dangerous rhythms.

Simple volume measures alone predict risk poorly, the review finds. Readings of heart muscle deformation and of scarring, from echocardiography and cardiac magnetic resonance, add real prognostic value. Current risk assessment should join volume, function, deformation, and fibrosis data with electrical measures, the authors conclude. Done so, it can time pulmonary valve replacement better and reduce arrhythmia and sudden death in this growing adult population.
owen-archetype-homologies-1848:
Richard Owen, Britain's leading anatomist, published his study of the vertebrate skeleton in 1848. Owen compared bones across fish, reptiles, birds, and mammals. He saw one hidden pattern beneath their many shapes.

Owen calls that pattern the archetype, an ideal plan of the backbone and skull. Bones that match across species, he names homologies, a term science still uses. His scheme came before Darwin and pointed to a rival cause, yet it framed the debate. Darwin later used Owen's own facts to argue for descent with change. His terms let anatomists compare skeletons across the whole animal kingdom.
plos-pbio-0020248:
Robert L. Hammond and Laurent Keller reviewed a conflict inside insect societies in PLOS Biology in 2004. In ant, bee, and wasp colonies, workers are often related more to some males than to others. That skew creates conflict over which males get raised and whose sons the queen's mates produce.

Theory predicts workers should favor their closest kin, yet colonies mostly run smoothly. The authors weigh how workers police each other and how queens limit strife. Their review sorts strong evidence from neat but untested ideas. Social insects are a test bed for the whole theory of cooperation. A clear account of their one big conflict sharpens that theory.
plos-pone-0000048:
Matthias Nahrendorf, Ralph Weissleder, and Georg Ertl asked in 2006 whether a clotting factor is needed for the heart to heal. After a myocardial infarction, a heart attack, the dead muscle is replaced by scar tissue. Factor XIII helps stabilize blood clots, and the team tested whether lacking it impairs wound healing in the heart.

The question links bleeding biology to recovery: a repair process that starts with a clot may falter if the clot is weak. Their title poses the question plainly, and the study answers it in the injured heart. For patients born without factor XIII, or treated in ways that lower it, the answer bears on how well the heart can mend.
plos-pone-0000148:
Chunyi Li, Jo-Ann L. Stanton, Tracy M. Robertson, and colleagues published this deer biology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Red deer regrow their antlers every year, one of the fastest examples of organ regeneration in mammals. The authors measured nerve growth factor messages in the regenerating antler tip of Cervus elaphus.

Nerves must regrow along with bone and skin for a new antler to form. Tracking where and when nerve growth factor is expressed shows how that regrowth is guided. Antlers are a prized natural model of regeneration, so findings here interest biologists who study how tissues rebuild themselves.
plos-pone-0000248:
Jonathan S. Friedlaender, Françoise R. Friedlaender, Jason A. Hodgson, and colleagues published this population genetics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It studies the mitochondrial DNA of Melanesian peoples, the populations of the Pacific islands northeast of Australia. The title flags the theme: their mtDNA shows striking complexity.

Melanesia was settled in layers over tens of thousands of years, and its DNA carries that history. The authors untangle patterns of maternal lineages across the region. The work helps reconstruct how humans spread through the Pacific, one of the last great chapters of human migration.
plos-pone-0000348:
David Lusseau published this dolphin behavior paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. In the bottlenose dolphin population of Doubtful Sound, New Zealand, male social relationships are unusually complex. The author asks why, examining the social network of males in this isolated fjord population.

Male dolphins elsewhere form alliances with clear tiers; Doubtful Sound's pattern differs. Working out what drives that difference tests general theories of animal society.
