Byproduct compounds built up steadily during storage, fastest in warmer rooms. Each strain kept a distinct profile, the starch type standing apart on amino acids. Cold rooms instead piled up simple sugars in the tubers. Heat plus long storage lifted bitter plant toxins, a shift that matters for safety.
pmc-13241648:
Jenny Ahlborn and co-authors present a 2026 chemical analysis of a garlic-scented mushroom. The species grows across central Europe and is prized as a seasoning. Its flavor chemistry had never been profiled in this depth.

Freeze-dried mushrooms grown in the lab were examined with sensitive gas-based instruments plus a smelling port. Nine sulfur compounds were identified, and one of them had never been reported in this mushroom group before. A solvent extract held only four aroma compounds, which the team measured precisely. Comparisons with a garlic-scented plant pointed to a shared aroma precursor in the fungus. The work explains the mushroom scent and may inform future culinary use.
pmc-13242448:
Farzana Sabir and colleagues gave cork oak its first detailed map of aquaporins, the channel proteins that move water through plant cells. Their paper appeared in Plant Cell Reports in 2026. Cork oak woodlands face deepening drought as the climate warms, yet the tree's water plumbing was largely unstudied. The team tested four aquaporins in yeast, located them in young stems, and tracked their gene activity under mild drought.

Three of the four channels carried water in the yeast tests, and the NIP members also passed glycerol and other small molecules, including boron and arsenic. One channel was oddly switched on by mercury, an effect traced to a single amino acid. In stems, the channels spread across many tissue layers. Under drought, leaf and stem genes for two families rose while root levels fell, a pattern that may limit water leaking back into dry soil.
pmc-13242748:
Michel Kalongo Ilumbulumbu and a large team present a 2026 case of a rare nerve sheath tumor in a six-year-old girl that mimicked a kidney tumor. The malignant Triton tumor is an aggressive variant with muscle-type differentiation. It is seldom seen in the belly cavity of children.

The girl arrived with a painful right flank mass and trouble using her leg. Ultrasound suggested Wilms tumor, the common childhood kidney cancer. Surgery found the mass stuck to the spine, and tissue testing after removal gave the true diagnosis. Gentle chemotherapy followed, but the tumor returned quickly and she died within weeks. The authors stress early tissue confirmation and team-based care, especially where advanced testing is scarce.
pmc-13244248:
Kanav Gupta and colleagues report a spine infection that wore the mask of tuberculosis until surgery exposed a killer fungus. Their case report appeared in Case Reports in Infectious Diseases in 2026. A fifty-four-year-old man with liver cirrhosis, diabetes, and thyroid failure arrived with a week of worsening back pain and leg weakness. MRI showed infected spinal discs with an abscess, read as Pott's spine, and tuberculosis drugs were started.

When his neurology crashed, surgeons drained the abscess, and the microscope changed everything: broad, ribbon-like fungal threads of a Mucorales species filled the tissue. Three antifungals were thrown at it, but organ damage forced repeated dose cuts. He developed liver failure with sepsis and died after surgery. The authors count his as the twelfth case, and the first blamed on end-stage liver disease. In TB-endemic regions, they warn, do not anchor on tuberculosis.
pmc-13244648:
Xuepeng Gong and co-authors tested Calculus Bovis, a traditional medicine made from cattle gallstones, against a scarring liver disease in mice. Their study appeared in Chinese Medicine in 2026. Primary sclerosing cholangitis destroys the bile ducts and has no approved drug therapy. Mice fed a toxin diet that mimics the disease received the medicine at three doses. The standard bile acid drug served as comparison, and liver, gut, and blood measures were tracked.

Treatment eased liver injury and fibrosis and repaired the leaking intestinal barrier. Bile acid patterns settled across blood and liver while excretion through feces rose, and disturbed blood lipids improved. Gene and network analyses pointed to a dual mechanism: switching on a SIRT1 energy-sensing pathway and activating bile acid receptors. The authors present the gallstone preparation as a multi-target candidate working along the gut-liver axis. Animal success is a beginning, not an answer.
pmc-13244848:
Shadi Bagherzadeh and colleagues asked a simple question: when cardiologists say a heart pressure changed, how big a change do they mean? Their study appeared in Echo Research and Practice in 2026. Right ventricular systolic pressure, estimated from ultrasound, tracks pulmonary hypertension, yet no guideline defines a meaningful shift. Using a Stanford registry, the team extracted more than thirty-two thousand paired scans from nearly six thousand patients and used language processing to sort the reports.

Almost half the pairs were described as stable, the rest split between rises, falls, and no direct comment. A decision-tree analysis recovered the cut-offs doctors apply when choosing those words. A duplicate-reading experiment, in healthy volunteers and pulmonary hypertension patients, measured how much two expert readers differ on the same scan. That measurement noise sets a floor under any claimed change. The authors offer their numbers as groundwork for reporting standards.
pmc-13245748:
Abdelrehim, Qi, and Tran validated an ultrasound method for measuring gum-disease bone loss, in this 2026 PLOS One proof-of-concept study. The bone holding teeth erodes in periodontitis, and tracking tiny changes usually means repeated X-rays. The team used forty-megahertz ultrasound, fine enough for sub-millimeter work, on an outside-the-body model where they created controlled bone-loss steps and checked readings against calibrated photographs.

Automated ultrasound measurements erred by well under a tenth of a millimeter and could reliably detect changes of roughly a seventh of a millimeter, matching photographs closely with excellent repeatability. Detection sensitivity ranged from about four fifths to perfect depending on method and step size. The authors say the radiation-free method suits following bone loss over time, the monitoring task dentists actually face.
pmc-13246548:
de Chiusole, Epifania, and Anselmi introduce a new computerized intelligence test in this 2026 Behavior Research Methods paper. MatriKS measures fluid intelligence, the ability to solve fresh problems, using Raven-style pattern matrices. Unusually, it was built on knowledge structure theory, a mathematical framework from personalized learning, making it the first large-scale use of that theory for intelligence testing.

The authors validated the test on five hundred sixty-eight Italian children aged four to eleven, analyzing results three ways: classical test theory, item response theory, and knowledge structure theory. Each method exposed different structural features, and all three supported that the test works adequately. The authors close by weighing what the knowledge-structure approach adds for building tests and profiling individual minds.
pmc-13246848:
Kodi, Nandakumar, Kishore, and co-authors review the dialogue between two cellular systems in this 2026 Molecular Neurobiology article. One is the NLRP3 inflammasome, a protein machine that fires inflammation and is implicated in diseases from Alzheimer's to heart and lung disorders. The other is AMPK, the cell's fuel gauge, which senses low energy and restores balance.

The review explains how AMPK restrains the inflammasome through several routes: ramping up cellular cleanup, protecting mitochondria, easing endoplasmic reticulum stress, and preserving lysosome integrity. It then walks through brain disease models, including stroke, Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and multiple sclerosis, where this brake seems to fail. The authors close with drug strategies aimed at strengthening the AMPK side of the partnership.
pmc-13248448:
Hanan S Khalefa and co-authors characterize E. coli from hidden udder infections in Egyptian dairy cows in a 2026 study. Subclinical mastitis drains milk yield without clear signs, and E. coli is a frequent cause. Slime layers called biofilms help the germs resist drugs and cleaning.

The team sampled 254 milk specimens from five farms. E. coli turned up in about a quarter of samples, with rates varying by region. Every isolate carried a biofilm gene, and most formed moderate or strong biofilms in dishes. Over half resisted several drug families at once. All isolates still fell to one modern drug, which gives vets a fallback.
pmc-13248848:
Rizu and co-authors built a room-temperature gas sensor from butterfly-shaped crystals, reported in 2026. Their material is tungsten diselenide, grown without hydrogen in a vapor process. The crystals mix two atomic arrangements: a stable semiconducting phase and a smaller share of a metallic phase, and their open shape exposes many reactive edges.

The sensor answered strongly to nitrogen dioxide at levels below one part per million, with a calculated detection limit in the single-digit parts per billion. It stayed stable over forty weeks without heating or light boosts. Computer simulations, tuned by Bayesian methods, confirmed the gas sticks weakly to the surface, matching the fast response seen in tests.
pmc-13249648:
Dimitra Sigala and co-authors wrote this 2026 systematic review of digital health tools for women before, during, and after pregnancy. Apps, telehealth, and chatbots can prompt healthy habits, but how well they work across the whole maternal period was not well summed up.

Following standard review guidelines, the team searched four databases for trials from 2020 to May 2025. They included 31 trials with 7,153 women. Reminders, self-tracking, and goal setting were the most common features. Tools helped with diet, activity, and sleep during pregnancy, and cut weight gain in women with overweight. Effects before pregnancy and after birth were weaker and less steady.
pmc-13249748:
Müller and co-authors show that a benchtop centrifuge can concentrate lentiviruses, in a 2026 methods paper. Labs use these viruses to deliver genes, but first they must be spun down and collected. The standard tools, ultracentrifuges and chemical precipitation, are expensive, slow, or missing in high-containment labs where they are needed most.

Spinning samples in an ordinary tabletop centrifuge gave higher virus yields and better infection rates than the chemical method. Shortening the spin to fifteen minutes kept the enrichment strong. The authors offer the shortcut as a cheap, fast alternative for gene delivery work, antiviral screening, and infection studies, especially where specialized equipment is scarce.
pmc-13250248:
Wang and co-authors build a smart gel system to regrow jawbone lost to gum disease in diabetes. Their 2026 International Journal of Nanomedicine paper tackles a hostile repair site: high sugar, low oxygen, infection, and inflammation all block healing. The material packs manganese dioxide nanoflowers, tannic acid, and strontium inside a sugar-responsive hydrogel.

Once placed, an enzyme in the gel consumes local glucose, while the nanoflowers split peroxide and release oxygen. That sequence lowers sugar, eases oxygen shortage, mops up harmful reactive molecules, and fights bacteria. Tannic acid and strontium then release on schedule, steering immune cells toward a healing mode and speeding bone cell growth. In cell and animal tests, damaged bone repaired faster and with better quality.
pmc-13250948:
Han Yin and colleagues report a 2026 study of a gel designed to heal bone defects weakened by osteoporosis. Bone lost to the disease heals poorly because new bone growth and new blood vessel growth both falter. The team built the gel from the natural matrix produced by stem cells, after treating those cells with a drug called Yoda1 that switches on a pressure-sensing channel named Piezo1.

In laboratory tests, the gel pushed mouse bone precursor cells to multiply, move, and mature into bone-forming cells. It also encouraged human vessel-lining cells to multiply and form new vessel networks. In animals with osteoporotic bone defects, the gel produced more new bone and more blood vessels than untreated defects. The authors argue that coupling bone growth with vessel growth is the key to restoring balance in fragile bone.
pmc-13251348:
Bartoli and colleagues pooled the evidence in 2026 on what marks out people with bipolar disorder who take their medicines poorly, a pattern that feeds relapse. Their systematic review searched major databases to March 2025 and combined results across studies with random-effects models, expressing links as odds ratios or standardized differences.

Nineteen studies qualified. Poor adherence tracked with younger age, less schooling, not being in a relationship, and earlier illness onset. Psychotic features, past suicide attempts, more manic and mixed episodes, and more hospital stays also raised the odds. Cannabis and alcohol use disorders, added anxiety and personality disorders, lower insight, and worse overall functioning all clustered in the poorly adherent group. The authors caution that effects were small and the evidence uneven, yet say the profile can help clinics spot patients who need adherence support most.
pmc-13253648:
Annika Kasprzak and colleagues weigh iron as a warning sign in bone marrow disease in this 2026 study. Myelodysplastic syndromes are marrow disorders where blood making falters, and iron often piles up in the marrow even before transfusions begin.

The team analysed 3,748 patients at first diagnosis. About half already had raised marrow iron, which tracked with worse anaemia and higher blood ferritin, a stored-iron marker. Extra marrow iron shortened survival mainly in the subgroup with more immature cells, where it was the strongest single survival predictor after adjustment. Age and disease subtype dominated overall, with ferritin also independent. The authors back checking iron at diagnosis.
pmc-13254148:
Emad Shalaby and colleagues test grapefruit peel extract against liver cancer cells in a 2026 study. Peels were dried and soaked in 70 percent ethanol, and the extract was screened for plant compounds. Its effect on HepG2 liver cancer cells was measured, and computer docking tested how compounds fit a target protein.

Naringenin was the most abundant compound found. The extract killed cancer cells with an IC50, the dose halving cell survival, stated in the paper. In docking, ellagic acid bound most strongly, followed by rutin and quercetin. The authors name these as lead molecules, while noting more work on safety is needed.
pmc-13254848:
Ryan Yao and colleagues build a living model of glioblastoma's surroundings to learn what makes radiation succeed or fail in a 2026 paper. Glioblastoma, the commonest malignant brain tumor in adults, nearly always returns after treatment. Response to radiation varies, and the tumor's microenvironment, its stiffness, oxygen level, and neighboring neurons, is suspected to pull the strings.

Their organotypic platform grows tumor tissue in an engineered setting where those surroundings can be watched and adjusted at the same time. The highlights report that mechanical cues and oxygen availability regulate how cells respond to radiation. Neuronal networks woven into the model also altered the tumor's metabolic activity, an influence flat cell cultures cannot show. The authors position such biomimetic platforms as reproducible tools for brain tumor biology. Their stated aim is prediction: testing a patient's likely radiotherapeutic response in the model before committing the patient to a course.
pmc-13255348:
Kaiwen Tan and co-authors report a 2026 field study of how seabuckthorn tree canopies of different ages shape the light beneath them. Seabuckthorn plantations serve both ecological repair and fruit production in China, so light distribution affects growth and yield. The team measured stands aged 3, 4, 8, and 11 years at three heights in each canopy.

Stand age and height within the canopy significantly affected every light and structure measure taken. Statistical modeling showed gaps in the canopy let light through most directly, while dense leaf area reduced light mainly by closing those gaps. A random forest model could guess a stand's age from canopy traits with about eighty-five percent accuracy. The authors suggest pruning to keep a suitable gap fraction as a practical management lever.
pmc-13256248:
Beaumont and colleagues tested how e-cigarette aerosol damages the airway lining, focusing on the junction protein E-cadherin. They exposed human bronchial cells and mice to aerosols from a programmable puffing system, using a nicotine salt e-liquid. Barrier strength was measured electrically and by dye leakage, and the amounts of cleaved E-cadherin were tracked.

Aerosol exposure raised levels of three matrix metalloproteinases and increased soluble E-cadherin in cell supernatants and mouse lung washings. Barriers weakened and became leakier. Pretreatment with fisetin, a metalloproteinase inhibitor, preserved barrier function and cut soluble E-cadherin release, mainly by suppressing one enzyme. The authors name cleaved E-cadherin as an early injury biomarker.
pmc-13256448:
Pengyi Zhao and co-authors describe a 2026 smart wound dressing built from a self-healing hydrogel carrying a metal-organic framework loaded with two actives. Chronic wounds stall in unbalanced tissue environments, and plain dressings cannot respond or dose drugs. The framework particles held copper ions and curcumin together, a one-carrier, dual-function design, inside a gel stitched by reversible Schiff base bonds.

The gel was porous, injectable, and able to mend itself after damage, with comfortable mechanical behavior. It degraded faster in acidity like that of infected wounds and released its cargo steadily, about seventy percent over seven days. It killed both E. coli and Staphylococcus aureus while keeping cultured cells largely healthy. The authors offer the dressing as a responsive candidate for managing chronic wounds.
pmc-13256948:
Sara Isla Cainzos and co-authors describe a 2026 mouse study on recovery after ischemic stroke. Few medicines help long-term rehabilitation, so the team tested timing. They briefly removed microglia, the immune cells of the brain, during days three to seven after stroke.

Depletion used a drug that blocks a receptor microglia need to survive. Treated mice regained near-complete fine motor skill by day seven on a skilled reaching task. Recordings from both sides of the cortex showed stronger beta-band connections in motor areas, and stronger connections tracked better movement. When microglia returned, their shape and gene activity differed from before. The work suggests a short treatment window could help the brain rewire, a hypothesis that invites careful follow-up.
pmc-13257148:
Mustafa Sevindik leads a 2026 study that uses artificial intelligence to tune extraction from an edible mushroom. Amanita caesarea holds phenolic compounds with antioxidant and other useful actions. Extraction time, heat, and solvent mix decide how much of that value is recovered.

Two optimization routes were compared: a neural network paired with a genetic algorithm, and classic response surface methods. The best hands-on extract was also tested. Chemical profiling measured phenolics, while assays covered antioxidant, cell-growth, and enzyme effects. The network-guided extract performed best overall, with stronger antioxidant action and more gallic acid. Food and supplement developers get evidence that smart optimization beats trial and error. The mushroom itself emerges as a credible source for functional products.
pmc-13257548:
Xiaoyi Zeng and colleagues report a platinum catalyst that burns methane at low temperature in a 2026 study. Trapping methane emissions matters because the gas warms the climate strongly, and lean streams are hard to ignite. A half-percent platinum loading was confined inside a manganese oxide and porous alumina carrier.

Ninety percent conversion arrived at a notably low temperature, beating a cobalt-doped comparison catalyst. Platinum shrank the manganese oxide lattice and created oxygen vacancies that cycle oxygen quickly. The porous carrier spread platinum into particles under two nanometers and kept them stable. Continuous running held near-full conversion for three hundred hours with little structural drift. Emission control engineers gain a durable design for dilute methane streams, such as ventilation air from mines.
pmc-13258548:
Mehmet Sahap and colleagues analyze timing of lumbar spine surgery in a 2026 retrospective cohort study. Four hundred sixty patients were split between regular hours and after hours operations. The main question was which patients needed intensive care after surgery.

Intensive care admission was far more common after hours than during the day. Hospital stay length and events during surgery looked similar between groups. Patients operated after hours arrived with higher inflammation markers and lower albumin. Adjusted models still tied after hours timing to intensive care use. Hospital planners can weigh staffing and case selection for night spine work with these figures in hand.
pmc-13258748:
Lili Xu and colleagues isolate five new alkaloids from a medicinal plant in a 2026 natural products study. The plant, Daphniphyllum macropodum, has a folk history for sores, cough, and joint pain. Stems and leaves yielded compounds with cage like carbon frameworks.

One compound carries a ring system never seen before in this family plus a rare nitrogen group. A second shows a heavily rearranged fused skeleton. Two others belong to a known subgroup and were confirmed by crystal analysis. Those two also promoted cell cleanup activity in tests. A proposed formation pathway links the new structures to known relatives.
pmc-13260348:
Wenwen Guo and Kangjian Li reviewed in 2026 the whole-person care of asthma in children, from diagnosis through prevention and future tools. Childhood asthma inflames and narrows the airways and places heavy costs on families and health systems. Their review gathers recent progress in tests such as exhaled nitric oxide, blood eosinophil counts, and artificial intelligence aids.

Daily care in their account joins symptom tracking, steady use of prescribed medicine, active play, and sound sleep. Prevention adds allergy avoidance, protection from viral infections, cleaner air, and healthy daily habits. Outcomes also hinge on genes, surroundings, and family circumstances, so caregivers, schools, and care teams must work together. The authors highlight digital self-management tools and community programs as routes to fairer, better control of the disease.
pmc-13262148:
Jing Wang, Zhimin Xu, and Jun Ning re-analyze human egg development as a two-part duet. Each follicle pairs an oocyte with surrounding granulosa cells that must mature in loose step. Mining one hundred forty-eight public sequencing libraries, their 2026 study tracks both partners separately.

Which compartment a sample came from outweighed every other signal in the data. Eggs changed steadily from stage to stage, emphasizing RNA processing early. Granulosa cells saved their biggest reorganization for the final, pre-ovulatory leap, firing up energy production. A heat-shock gene, HSP90AA1, marked late remodeling in the shared architecture both compartments kept.
pmc-13262848:
Heejin Yoon and colleagues look for signs that predict vision recovery in a sudden optic nerve disease in a 2026 journal article. The disease, shortened to NAION, causes painless vision loss in middle-aged and older adults, and no treatment is proven to help. The team reviewed records of 38 patients, 41 eyes in total, checking eye tests and blood measures taken at the first visit.

Eleven eyes, or 26.8 percent, recovered meaningfully in side vision by three months. Recovering eyes started with better sharpness of vision, less severe field loss, and lower blood sugar marker levels. Starting field scores predicted recovery on their own in adjusted analysis. Nerve layer thickness on scans did not reliably predict who recovered, the team found.
pmc-13263748:
Lauren Wagner and colleagues scan babies' brains to see language taking shape before first words. About a tenth of children develop language delays, and their roots may lie in infancy's wiring. Their 2026 study uses resting brain scans from the Baby Connectome Project and follows development into toddlerhood.

A machine learning sort split infants into typical, advanced, and lagging language trajectories that assessments confirmed. Across the first year, the language network's regions synchronized and specialized broadly with age. The lagging group wired several connections distinctively, and those early differences predicted language scores at age two. Such markers could someday flag babies for early support.
pmc-13263948:
Louise Deshayes and colleagues wrote a 2026 article on triage, the sorting of patients by how urgent their care is. They tested a changed version of the South African Triage Scale for use before hospital, in one Swedish region. They also asked whether nurse experience changed the scores.

Thirty-four nurses each scored 30 written patient cases, giving 1,010 ratings in all. Agreement between nurses was poor, with full agreement in only three cases. Nurses often raised the urgency level by hand, in 25 of the 30 cases. Sex, years of service, and extra training showed no link to scores. The authors urge careful testing of changed triage tools.
pmc-13264248:
Yuki Takano and colleagues evaluate a motion-tolerant MRI method paired with deep learning cleanup for head and neck scans in a 2026 study. Thirty-four patients had imaging on a high-field scanner. A rotating method designed to cut swallowing and movement artifacts was compared with standard sequences. Two scan types were tested, one highlighting fluid with fat suppression and one tracking water movement in tissue. All images were rebuilt with the same learning algorithm.

Two radiologists scored quality, lesion clarity, anatomy and artifacts, while signal measures were taken in lesions and glands. The rotating method scored significantly higher on every judged feature for both scan types. Reader agreement ranged from moderate to good depending on sequence. Sharper, calmer images could improve tumor assessment in a region prone to motion.
pmc-13264348:
Chloe McCreery and colleagues report a hand artery aneurysm that imaging missed in a 2026 case report. Hypothenar hammer syndrome injures the ulnar artery where the palm heel strikes objects repeatedly. A fifty-four-year-old man had episodic pain and color change in three fingers of one hand. Scans showed reduced artery flow but no bulge, catheter imaging showed only mild waviness, and ultrasound signals were merely softer on the affected side of the hand.

Clinical suspicion stayed high despite the negative pictures. When conservative care failed, surgical exploration found a one centimeter aneurysm hidden in a short artery segment, which was removed and reconnected end to end. The case warns that clean angiography cannot rule out this syndrome.
pmc-13264548:
Tatsuya Kiuchi, Suk-Ling Wee, and Stefan Schulz wrote a 2026 study of scent signals in Bactrocera umbrosa, a fruit fly that attacks breadfruit relatives. Males eagerly eat methyl eugenol, a plant scent, but how they use it to signal was unclear. The team studied the chemicals in male glands.

Young males made four scent compounds, and mature males added six more, including two never before seen in insects. After eating methyl eugenol, males stored six changed forms of it. In tube choice tests, two gland compounds and two changed forms drew in virgin females. Three changed forms also drew males at dusk. The authors say these signals help males gather and court, which may aid pest control.
pmc-13264648:
Thércia Rocha Balbino and a large team wrote a 2026 study on making carotenoids, the pigments behind many red and orange foods, from farm waste. They fed a yeast with liquids made from corn, soybean, rice, and wheat bran, with no added nutrients. The aim was a cheap, greener route to a valued product.

The yeast grew and made pigment on all four brans. Rice bran gave the most pigment per litre and the richest pigment per cell mass. Soybean bran grew the most yeast. Checks with light and infrared tools confirmed the extract held carotenoid pigments. A life cycle review found the rice bran route had the lowest impacts, with power use in fermentation as the main hotspot. The authors back rice bran for greener production.
pmc-13264748:
Jeeyeon Lee and colleagues assess an injectable dermal fiber filler for breast shape after conservation surgery in a 2026 volumetric study. Twenty-five patients received the paste-like material to fill defects, with complications reviewed for all. Seven patients had MRI scans before surgery and a year later. The scans allowed three-dimensional measurement of volume change and symmetry between breasts over time. That goes beyond what photographs or surgeon impression alone can quantify for a subtle contour change.

Only one fluid collection needing a single drainage occurred. Total breast volume drifted down over the year, likely reflecting radiation effects and weight change, yet symmetry held or improved versus baseline in the imaged group. The filler gave stable contour support without major safety signals. Small imaging numbers limit certainty, so larger volumetric follow-up is needed.
pmc-13264848:
Alejandro Rodriguez and a large multinational team analyze road deaths and safety policy in Ecuador from 1990 to 2022 in a 2026 ecological study. Death certificates supplied fatality counts, converted into crude and age-standardized rates for the whole population and by sex, age, region and province. Safety policies over the same period were catalogued, and breakpoint analysis tested whether trend shifts lined up with policy timing across places and groups.

The national rate barely moved across three decades, starting and ending near twenty deaths per hundred thousand people. Flat national lines can hide regional improvement or deterioration, which the geographic breakdown exposes. Linking policy dates to local trends helps judge which measures coincided with real change. Persistent high rates argue for stronger enforcement and safer road design.
pmc-13264948:
Daisuke Miyamori and colleagues present a 2026 follow-up study from Japan on kidney failure risk after COVID-19. Using a nationwide claims database from six prefectures, they matched people who had COVID-19 with similar uninfected people. They then tracked who started kidney replacement therapy, meaning dialysis or transplant, over two years.

The matching built more than three million pairs. COVID-19 was linked to nearly triple the risk of reaching kidney failure, with a hazard ratio of 2.79. Risk was raised for both main dialysis types, while the transplant estimate was too wide to judge. The pattern held across age, sex, blood pressure, diabetes, and illness severity groups. The authors urge close kidney checks after COVID-19 and early risk sorting for high-risk patients.
pmc-13266148:
Seyeon Chang and colleagues replace fishmeal with black soldier fly larvae in pig diets, in a 2026 feeding study. Alternative protein sources are sought for sustainability. Thirty-six growing pigs received fishmeal or two larvae powder levels. Growth, nutrient use, blood, and gas output were tracked.

Growth and feed measures did not differ between diets. Protein digestibility was higher with the top larvae level at later checks. Amino acid digestibility broadly favoured larvae diets over fishmeal. The higher level beat the lower level for several amino acids. Blood profiles and gas emissions showed no differences, supporting larvae as a workable protein swap.
pmc-13266748:
Rebecca Boraz and colleagues report a 2026 survey on why patients often do not pick up naloxone. Naloxone is a drug that can reverse an opioid overdose. The survey went to members of Kaiser Permanente Northwest who had a naloxone order in one year that looked unfilled in pharmacy records.

Of 481 people who replied, about 58 percent said they never got the drug. The top reason, given by about 55 percent, was feeling they did not need it. Others had not known a doctor ordered it, were unsure what it was for, or worried about cost. The authors call for clear, nonjudgmental talk about overdose risk and what naloxone does.
pmc-13266848:
Ryaan EL-Andari, Maira Machhiwala, and Sabin J Bozso weigh in 2026 whether high-risk patients with heavy calcium on the mitral valve ring should undergo surgery. Calcium there can disturb heart rhythm, invite infection, and force larger replacement valves. The commentary discusses a case of an 82-year-old whose failed catheter repair led to surgical replacement despite severe calcium and high risk.

Options range from removing calcium and rebuilding the ring to placing a catheter valve inside the calcium through open surgery. New ultrasound tools can dissolve hard calcium while sparing nearby tissue, easing suture placement. Each route carries serious risks such as tearing or bleeding. Careful patient selection and team judgment decide whether operating helps.
pmc-13267548:
Manuela Montatore and colleagues present a 2026 case report on an abnormal passage between colon and bladder after surgery. Their patient was a 49-year-old man who had planned surgery to remove part of his sigmoid colon for repeated diverticulitis, an infection of small pouches in the bowel wall. Two weeks later he passed air and stool in his urine, classic signs of the passage.

Repeated contrast CT scans tracked the change from a pelvic abscess to a clear channel between colon and bladder. A contrast study through the rectum added proof. The scans also showed wide spread of infection into nearby soft tissue. Watching the images over time guided a careful, non-surgical plan. The authors highlight steady imaging in such complex after-surgery problems.
pmc-13269148:
Berat Dilek Demirel and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on surgery for babies born with a blocked back passage and an abnormal channel into the vagina. The operation rebuilds the passage while sparing a band of tissue between the openings. One surgeon did all the operations at one center.

Records covered 26 patients treated from 2018 to 2024, at a median age of 40 days. Sixteen had a one-stage repair, and ten first had a temporary bowel opening. Two patients got wound infections that cleared with local care. Among 18 children older than three years, 15 had voluntary bowel control, or 83.3 percent. Seven had constipation, and none had soiling.
pmc-13269648:
Naima Sultana and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 cataloging the E2F gene family in Brassica rapa, a leafy crop plant. These genes act as checkpoints that control when cells copy their DNA and divide. The team searched the plant's genome and compared its genes with those of five other species.

Fourteen family members were found, including six pairs copied in large genome blocks over evolution. Change rates suggested the copies kept similar jobs. Certain small RNA molecules that respond to stress targeted four of the genes most heavily. Switch regions in the genes pointed to roles in growth and in coping with living and non-living stresses. The authors present the catalog as a base for crop stress research.
pmc-13269948:
Alyssa C Bonnell and co-authors report in 2026 two cases where a hole formed in the center of the retina after vitrectomy surgery, then closed on its own without another operation. Both patients, a man of seventy-two and a woman of sixty-seven, had surgery to repair a detached retina. The authors pair the cases with a review of every similar report they could find.

Small and medium holes seemed most likely to seal themselves. Among published eyes with spontaneous closure, about two thirds closed within a month of diagnosis and four in five within three months. More than a third later reopened, some needing surgery after all. One patient's closure in this report lasted seven years, showing that watchful waiting can sometimes be the right call.
pmc-13270248: A correction notice from 2026 fixes one author's affiliation in a 2025 paper led by M S Mohamed on health workers' and students' views about raising public awareness of antimicrobial resistance. Author Mona Timan Idriss had been linked to the wrong institution, in the Department of Medical Sciences and Preparation Year at Northern College of Nursing in Arar, Saudi Arabia. Her correct affiliation is the Nursing Department at North Private College of Nursing, also in Arar. The notice apologizes for the error.
pmc-13270448:
Vincent J Leopold and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on ischiofemoral impingement, painful pinching between hip and pelvis bones, in young patients with non-arthritic hip pain. Imaging for 250 patients included MRI, CT, and standing and seated spine-pelvis X-rays. Pinching was confirmed by swelling or wasting of a deep hip muscle.

Impingement was found in 14 patients, 5.6 percent, all female. Their bone-to-bone spaces were far narrower: 24.8 millimeters against 34.9 in others. They also showed a larger ischial angle, more thigh bone twist, and smaller offsets at hip and socket. Standing posture differed too, with more pelvic tilt. Combined analysis singled out the narrow muscle space as the strongest independent predictor.
pmc-13271148:
Qin Lu is lead author of a 2026 journal article on using chest muscle size on scans to spot malnutrition in patients with sudden worsening of chronic lung disease, shortened to AECOPD. Such patients often lose muscle, and standard nutrition checks can miss that loss, so the team tested total pectoralis major area, the size of both main chest muscles.

Among 123 patients, 35 were malnourished, and their chest muscle area was clearly lower. Larger muscle area protected against malnutrition even after adjustment. Alone, the measure diagnosed malnutrition fairly well; combined with blood albumin or total protein it performed much better. Muscle area also rose with other good nutrition signs and fell as symptom burden rose.
pmc-13271348:
Aradhika Vijeev and colleagues review in 2026 how light from LEDs and ultraviolet lamps can keep fruits and vegetables fresh after harvest. Produce spoils quickly through natural aging, germs, and quality loss during storage and transport. Light treatment leaves no chemical residue, which makes it attractive for food storage.

The review compares results across the growing and storage stages, covering photosynthesis, antioxidant levels, germ control, and shelf life. Responses differ widely by crop type, growth stage, and light settings, which has blocked shared standards. By mapping those differences, the authors set out steps toward crop-specific light recipes that farms and warehouses could actually use.
pmc-13271948:
Li Zhuang and coauthors gather in 2026 recent studies on exercise, resilience, and mental health in teenagers. Adolescent mental health is a worldwide concern, and activity programs are a practical public tool. Resilience, the ability to recover from stress, may explain part of the benefit.

The review covered studies from 2022 to 2025 across five databases, focusing on youth aged about ten to nineteen. More active teenagers generally reported better mental health and stronger resilience. All ten studies that formally tested the pathway found resilience carried part of the exercise effect. Programs built on mastery and social connection looked most promising.
pmc-13272248:
Wulan Koagouw is lead author of a 2026 journal article profiling drug pollution along Jakarta's Ciliwung River, in Indonesia. Drug residues threaten water life and human health. Yet tropical city rivers are far less studied than temperate ones. So the team sampled along a gradient of urbanisation to test whether pollution builds up downstream.

They analysed 53 compounds at eight sites and detected thirteen. These spanned antibiotics, painkillers, heart drugs, and scan contrast agents. Combined levels rose clearly downstream. The nerve drug gabapentin showed the strongest build-up. Eleven compounds increased steadily, signalling cumulative loading with little breakdown. Local spikes for two drugs suggested point sources such as health facility discharge. Gabapentin is proposed as a watch-list indicator.
pmc-13272348:
Zibing Zhao and Zhuangzhuang Zheng review in 2026 how macrophage states help decide whether radiotherapy succeeds against cancer. Macrophages flip between an attack-oriented state that aids tumor control and a suppressive state that shields tumors. Radiation itself can push that flip in either direction.

High-dose and particle radiation tend to favor the attack state, while standard fractionated treatment often breeds the suppressive one, feeding resistance. Oxygen shortage, metabolic signals, and cytokines in the tumor surroundings steer the balance. The authors survey strategies that block macrophage recruitment, remove suppressive cells, or reprogram them to restore radiation sensitivity.
pmc-13272748:
Yoonsang Ra leads a 2026 review of wearable sensors that use triboelectric effects, where contact and motion generate electric charge. Such sensors can power themselves while sensing the body, which suits smart devices worn day to day. The review sets out principles, materials, device designs, and ways to make them.

The authors highlight artificial intelligence processing of sensor signals, plus artificial synapses and brain-like computing, as bridges to adaptive human-machine interfaces. Uses they organize include health care, gesture control, robotics, and smart transport. The review closes with future directions toward electronics centered on human comfort, motion, intention, and personal needs, rather than on devices alone.
pmc-13273148:
Shilei Li leads a 2026 study of single-atom iron catalysts for the oxygen reduction reaction, a key step in fuel cells and metal-air batteries. Each iron atom sits in a ring of five nitrogen atoms on porous carbon. The team used a dual-confinement strategy, joining a wood framework with iron binding, to shape the catalyst.

The wood-derived carbon had hollow, linked pores at several scales, and sulfur doping came from the plant material. Tests and theory showed this set-up lowered the energy bar for releasing a key intermediate, speeding the reaction. The catalyst reached a half-wave potential of 0.964 volts, and zinc-air batteries using it beat a platinum benchmark.
pmc-13273248:
Anuradha Kesharwani and co-authors targeted a DNA sensing pathway in Huntington disease in a 2026 mouse study. Huntington disease is inherited, damages the brain, and involves strong inflammation, with no treatment that slows it. The pathway, called cGAS-STING, switches on inflammatory genes when stray DNA appears in cells.

In a humanized knock-in mouse model, removing the cGAS gene calmed brain immune cells, saved neurons, and limited shrinkage of the striatum, a movement center. Motor function improved, and gene activity patterns moved toward normal. A drug that blocks the partner protein STING gave similar relief of behavior and tissue damage. The authors name this pathway a promising target for future Huntington treatments.
pmc-13273848:
Tang and colleagues build a bispecific antibody against liver cancer using chemical assembly. Their 2026 journal article targets glypican-3, a marker on liver tumor cells. The antibody also blocks SIRP-alpha, a brake on immune cells called macrophages.

Standard bispecific antibodies need complex genetic production. This team used a rapid one-pot, two-step chemical process. Peptide dimers were linked to a native anti-SIRP-alpha antibody. The product draws macrophages toward tumor cells and boosts engulfing. In cell tests, tumor cell clearance beat the plain antibody. In mice, tumor growth fell by 68 percent. Macrophage entry into tumors rose, with more M1-type cells. Antigen presentation also increased. No visible body-wide toxicity appeared.
pmc-13274248: The notice is a correction only, issued in 2026 for an article on the Know Your Number; Control Your Number screening campaign in Nigeria. It fixes the author order, printed wrongly: the Nigeria Health Commissioners' Forum belongs first, ahead of Ayotunde Oguntade and the other named authors. It also replaces Figures 1 through 10, charts of results for over one and a half million participants, which were unclear and hard to read. Higher resolution versions appear with the notice, and the original article has been updated.
pmc-13274548:
David Belada and a large team report 2026 results from the phase three PERSPECTIVE trial in follicular lymphoma, a slow-growing blood cancer. Patients were untreated and unfit for standard chemoimmunotherapy because of age or other illness. They received the antibody rituximab plus either the targeted pill ibrutinib or a placebo.

In total, 445 patients were randomized, three to one in favor of the drug combination, and followed a median of about fifty-four months. Time without disease worsening stretched to a median of 42.0 months with ibrutinib versus 32.8 months without. Response rates also favored the combination, at eighty-one versus sixty-eight percent. Overall survival did not differ significantly, and serious side effects were more common with ibrutinib.
pmc-13275248:
Zhihao Xiong and co-authors set out a trial protocol in 2026 to test acupuncture for post-stroke spasticity. That stiffness is common and disabling. Acupuncture may ease it, but earlier studies were weak, so benefit and safety stay uncertain.

Their randomized trial will enroll 180 patients and split them three ways: real acupuncture, sham acupuncture, or standard care alone. Treatment lasts four weeks, with four more weeks of follow-up. The main measure is a standard spasticity scale, backed by scores for movement, daily living, and nerve function, plus muscle recordings and ultrasound measures of stiffness. The authors also plan to explore how acupuncture might calm spastic muscle. Results should clarify whether the practice deserves a place in stroke rehabilitation.
pmc-13275748:
Patricia S Coffey and colleagues offer a 2026 practice note on preventing preeclampsia in five low- and middle-income countries. The countries covered are Burkina Faso, Ethiopia, Kenya, Nigeria, and Pakistan. Global guidance backs low-dose aspirin and calcium supplements, yet real-world rollout remains patchy.

The team reviewed policies and interviewed 59 informants at global and national levels during 2023 and 2024. Aspirin progress was slowed by uneven clinical practice, low awareness, late antenatal visits, and weak supply chains. Calcium faced a complex dosing schedule and unclear national plans. The authors recommend stronger primary antenatal care and a coordinated package of preeclampsia measures.
pmc-13276448:
Pei-Lin Lee and colleagues present a 2026 study of white matter injury that is too heavy for a person's age. Bright scan spots grow with normal ageing, so raw amounts can mislead doctors about hidden small-vessel disease. A normative model instead compares each brain with what is expected at that age.

People whose burden sat far above the age norm carried worse vascular risk profiles. Their thinking skills suffered across several domains, and grey matter shrinkage was greater. Severe deviation predicted notably higher long-term death rates, roughly double in the strongest group. The authors propose age-adjusted scoring to flag high-risk people earlier, before symptoms appear.
pmc-13276748:
Marcel Mietzner and co-authors present a 2026 case report on a new drug tried in a rare, deadly lung vessel disease. Pulmonary veno-occlusive disease blocks the lung's small veins. No drug has proven benefit, standard vessel-widening drugs can flood the lungs, and most patients once died within a year.

Two patients with the hereditary form received sotatercept, the newest approved drug for related lung hypertension, on top of standard therapy. The drug works unlike the others, trapping growth signals to rebalance vessel biology. Both patients stabilized in overall condition and in how their lungs take up oxygen. Two lung transfer measures improved slightly under treatment. Neither the drug's trials nor prior experience covered this disease. The authors suggest it may steady such patients and stretch the bridge to a lung transplant, the only lasting fix.
pmc-13277348:
Michelle Venâncio Hong leads a 2026 follow-up study of patients who developed pressure injuries, skin damage from sustained pressure, during a hospital stay. Little is known about how these patients fare after going home. The team tracked healing, return to hospital, and death after discharge.

By sixty days, about half of the injuries had improved and a third had fully healed. Yet twenty-two percent of patients had died after discharge, and some were readmitted. Having had a stroke made healing harder. Half of the patients got no care in the first week at home, a gap the authors flag. The findings argue for tighter follow-up plans at discharge.
pmc-13277448:
Xing Xu and colleagues build a phone-based three-dimensional scanning method for banana plants, in a 2026 paper. Measuring banana growth precisely matters for yield forecasting, yet laser scanners cost too much for wide farm use. Ordinary photo methods struggle with the plant's tangled canopy and weakly textured leaves.

Their framework, BN-NeRF, sharpens a fast neural rendering method with three fixes. Camera drift from handheld filming is corrected frame by frame, and sparse point clouds anchor true scale. A thin-leaf rule cleans up leaf surfaces that usually render poorly. Trials on ninety orchard plants gave high-quality reconstructions and trait values close to hand measurements. The study shows cheap phones can support serious field phenotyping.
pmc-13278448:
Zhiqiao Cheng and colleagues present a 2026 study of skid resistance in road asphalt made with steel slag, a steelmaking by-product. Skid resistance keeps vehicles from sliding, and it fades with wear and heat. The team ran accelerated wear tests at three steel slag levels and three temperatures, tracking two standard grip measures over time.

Both grip measures fell clearly as wear cycles rose, and high temperature sped the decline sharply. The two measures moved together overall, though their link differed across early, middle, and late wear stages. Those stages support segmented forecasts of how long grip will last in service. The results guide how much steel slag to use in different climates, the authors say.
pmc-13278748:
Martin Jacobsson and co-authors measure the error made when surgical blood pressure is stored too sparsely, in a 2026 study. Low blood pressure during surgery predicts complications, so researchers total its depth and duration. Records are often saved only every fifteen seconds to keep files manageable.

Data from 419 open-abdomen surgery patients at Karolinska University Hospital were compared against full waveform records. Fifteen-second sampling skewed event counts and total low-pressure time by roughly a quarter to a third. The area measure fared better but still missed by about a tenth. Attempts to correct the errors mostly failed to help. The authors insist on continuous data for trustworthy counts.
pmc-13279148:
Connor W. Smith and colleagues report a 2026 case of a very rare cause of low blood sugar. The cause is insulinomatosis, where many small tumours in the pancreas gland make too much insulin. Insulin is a hormone that lowers blood sugar. Their patient was a woman in her sixties with low sugar episodes through her life.

Blood tests fit the pattern of too much insulin from the body itself. Scans pointed to many tumours spread through the pancreas. Surgeons removed the whole pancreas, and lab checks of the tissue proved the diagnosis. Family members had past signs like hers, yet the gene basis stays unclear. The case shows why blood, scan, tissue and gene checks must line up.
pmc-13279748:
Mengtian Huang and colleagues give a 2026 review of tea proteins and interface design. Tea plant waste holds proteins that could serve as green food ingredients. Poor solubility and weak function hold them back. Interface engineering, which shapes how proteins act at oil water or air borders, is the key fix in their frame. The review links protein structure, interface acts and final function in one map.

Two sources lead: tea residue protein from leaf waste and tea seed protein. Change routes span physical, chemical, biological and mixed means. Uses hold food stabilizers, edible films, health peptide starts and particles for Pickering emulsions, which are drops armoured by solid grains. Scale up hurdles hold safety, taste, cost and legal rules. The authors chart routes to round, low waste food systems built on tea waste.
pmc-13280948:
Claudia G Aguirre and colleagues compared how male and female rats learn for rewards in a 2026 study. Most past work used males only, which can skew results. Rats tapped a screen to pick between options for food. In one task, the picture itself marked the better odds. In the other, the side of the screen did. Midway, the better choice flipped, and rats had to adapt.

Females learned and adapted just as well as males. Yet they claimed fewer rewards and skipped more trials in both tasks. Math models of each choice fit best when they allowed shifts in focus over time. Females lapsed more once a rule was learned, as if their interest dropped. The authors say drive, not skill, split the sexes here.
pmc-13281248:
Puthy Pat and colleagues studied mental health care inside Cambodian prisons in a 2026 report. Prisoners face high rates of mental strain, yet care in prisons is thin. The team held group talks in three prisons across the country. Fifteen people took part, most of them prison health staff, plus four officials. Talks probed what blocks care and what might help.

Staff said basic care, referrals for severe cases, and some preventive steps do happen. But mental health gets little focus, and staff give what emotional support they can. Workers felt devoted yet worn down by low skills and scarce supplies. They asked for more training, awareness drives, job training for prisoners, and stronger backing from leaders and outside groups.
pmc-13281948:
Li Ling and colleagues surveyed family doctors on lung disease skills in Shanghai in a 2026 study. The district was Pudong, a large city zone. COPD narrows airways for life and needs steady local care. Four hundred fifty-seven doctors answered, close to all who were asked. Most saw a modest flow of COPD patients each month. For nearly all, such patients filled under a third of their list. Yet hands-on lung testing was rare.

Four in five doctors ran the key breathing test ten times a year or fewer. Nearly half sent cough or breathless patients straight to specialists. Gaps showed in inhaler drugs, staging, symptom scales, test reading, and inhaler coaching. Confidence in managing the disease averaged under three of five. Training in residency and disease courses raised skill. So did age. The authors call for training that pairs facts with hands-on drills.
pmc-13282248:
Vanja Miljanić and co-authors describe a 2026 report of a new virus found inside a fungus that attacks hop plants. The fungus, Verticillium nonalfalfae, causes wilt disease in crops. The virus, given a tentative name shortened to VnaVM, carries its genes in six segments of double-stranded RNA, the chemical cousin of DNA. Segment lengths ran from about one thousand to about two thousand four hundred units.

Four segments code for known viral tools, including the enzyme that copies the virus genome. Two segments code for proteins with no known match, so their roles stay unknown. The known proteins differ enough from relatives to support a new species in an existing virus genus. Family tree analysis backed that placement. The authors say this is the first such virus reported in this fungus genus. Cataloguing fungal viruses matters because some may weaken the fungi that harm crops.
pmc-13282348: Qiaoping Qu and co-authors issued a 2026 correction to their study of cell-free mitochondrial DNA as a possible marker of hypoxic stress. That DNA comes from the cell's power plants and is found outside cells. Hypoxic stress means harm from low oxygen. Figure 7 of the original article had appeared incorrectly. The correction replaces it with the right version, showing exosome features from cells exposed to low oxygen, and displays both versions for transparency. No other content is changed.
pmc-13282548:
Daniele Omar Traini and co-authors report a 2026 case using a non-invasive skin imaging method to diagnose a rare skin disorder. The disorder, shortened to CRP, makes dark small bumps merge into plaques with a net-like edge, usually on the trunk. Their patient was a twenty-nine-year-old woman with a three-year history of mildly itchy dark bumps on her back, sides, belly, and groin. A magnified skin view showed a brain-like network pattern.

The imaging method, a form of optical coherence tomography that scans skin in vivo, showed a thickened, bright outer layer and a wavy boundary between skin layers. Tissue biopsy confirmed the classic features: thickened surface, extra basal pigment, and raised surface growth. The authors say the scan's features matched the biopsy criteria in this case, a first report for this disorder.
pmc-13282848:
Wei Chen and co-authors present a 2026 study on whether eating more live microbes in food links to lower death rates in middle-aged and older stroke survivors in the United States. Dietary live microbe intake reflects eating microbe-rich foods such as fermented products. Using national survey data from 2003 to 2018, the team followed one thousand three hundred thirteen stroke survivors for a median of six years.

Five hundred thirty-nine participants died, two hundred nine of them from cardiovascular causes. Those with high microbe intake had about a third lower risk of death from any cause than the low intake group, a link that held across several adjusted models. No significant link appeared for cardiovascular death specifically. Subgroup and sensitivity checks generally supported the main finding. The authors call the results exploratory, since diet was captured by a single day's recall and stroke type was self-reported.
pmc-13282948:
Early lung tumors that come back after surgery motivated Wangyu Chen and partners to hunt for a better risk marker in 2026. Many patients relapse after surgery meant to cure them. Current markers such as PD-L1 guide care poorly at this stage, so the team searched for a stronger signal.

Gene data from large cancer databases were screened with machine learning tools. A gene called ERO1A stood out as a marker of poor survival and relapse risk. Tumors with high ERO1A grew fast yet also drew in active immune cells. They showed higher mutation load and PD-L1 levels. Tests on patient tissue confirmed the pattern and support its use for risk grouping.
pmc-13283048:
Chaymae Cherrabi and colleagues presented in 2026 the case of a seven-year-old girl with two overlapping autoimmune liver diseases. She had lasting jaundice, strong signs of liver cell injury, and high levels of immune proteins in her blood. Scans showed bile duct changes, and a liver sample confirmed autoimmune hepatitis, where the immune system attacks the liver itself.

Doctors diagnosed overlap between that disease and primary sclerosing cholangitis, a scarring disease of the bile ducts. The pairing is rare in children and hard to pin down, since no standard test rules exist. Treatment with prednisone and azathioprine, two immune-calming drugs, brought clear gains in her symptoms and blood tests. The report stresses early suspicion and shared care across specialties.
pmc-13283948:
Plant-made silver particles capped with a sugar ring are tested against crop germs and a crop pest by Chellasamy Panneerselvam and colleagues in 2026. Fruit extract of Peganum harmala both formed and stabilized the particles. The coating is beta-cyclodextrin, meant to keep particles dispersed.

Microscopy showed round, well-spread particles in a small size range. The particles blocked growth of four plant pathogens in dose-linked fashion. Killing values were low, which signals strong germ and fungus action. Larvae of the beet armyworm died more with higher dose and longer exposure. Feeding dropped sharply, supporting dual crop protection use.
pmc-13284148:
LinXin You and colleagues tested electroacupuncture in 2026 in a rat model of sudden hives. Acute urticaria affects about one in five people across a lifetime, and the molecular action of electroacupuncture for it was unclear. The team triggered a local allergic skin reaction with egg protein, then treated two acupoints on the leg and arm for five days, tracking wheal size and scratching.

Treated rats showed smaller wheals, less scratching, and less leakiness of skin blood vessels. Protein and metabolite profiling of skin and blood pointed to shifts in fat and amino acid pathways. Levels of two complement alarm signals, C3a and C5a, and their receptors fell in skin, and blood levels of three inflammatory mediators dropped. The authors frame the results as exploratory.
pmc-13284548:
Dessie Tegegne and co-authors give a 2026 five-year record review of gut parasite infections among HIV patients in northwest Ethiopia. Parasites remain common where water and sanitation are poor, even for patients on HIV therapy. Records for 600 patients on antiretroviral therapy at Debre Tabor hospital from May 2020 to May 2025 were reviewed for parasites, CD4 counts, and social traits.

One third of patients had a gut parasite infection in the records reviewed for this study period. The team used standard tests to find linked social and clinical factors, though local data had been scarce before. Full local results can guide targeted screening, deworming, and hygiene work for HIV patients at this hospital and in like settings.
pmc-13284748:
Ying Zhang and co-authors report a 2026 method for reusing costly chips in two-dimensional materials research. Making test devices needs pricey patterned substrates and cleanroom access, which many labs lack. The team cleaned used chips in a warm ultrasonic bath of N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone to lift off old material without harming electrodes.

Electrical tests, Raman checks, and surface scans showed no trace of prior material after cleaning, with even surface charge and like device results after reuse. Reusing one chip many times could cut waste, lower costs, and speed early device trials. The authors frame the protocol as a practical step toward greener microfabrication for small research groups.
pmc-13285148:
Lemi Ushu Sime, Tilahun Yamane, and Wakjira Kebede report a 2026 school study on anemia among children in Metu town, southwest Ethiopia. Anemia harms growth and learning and is common in poorer regions, yet local data for this town were missing. The cross-sectional study enrolled children aged seven to fourteen at public primary schools in 2024, with blood tests for counts, malaria, and gut parasites.

About one in ten children had anemia, classed as a mild public health level in the authors findings, and most cases were mild in grade. Linked factors included a mother with no formal schooling, low family income, male sex, gut parasite infection, and drinking coffee or tea with meals. The team urges targeted school health action.
pmc-13285648:
A methyl tag on a ring RNA fuels bowel cancer growth through a growth switch, Jinhai Tian and co-authors show in a 2026 study. Bowel cancer kills widely and its drivers stay partly hid. The ring, circKPNA2, ran high in tumor tissue and cell lines, and the team traced how it acts with pull-down and protein reading tools.

The ring grabs a protein called RIN1 and lifts its level, switching on the Ras growth path and pushing cells to multiply, crawl, and invade. An enzyme that lays methyl tags, METTL3, controls how much of the ring gets made. Cutting the ring breaks the chain. The authors pitch circKPNA2 as both a drug target and a test mark.
pmc-13286148:
Thong Duc Hong and colleagues model the best ignition timing for a diesel engine running on methanol blends in a 2026 simulation study. Methanol can stand in for part of the fuel, but it burns slower and changes when the spark of compression should land. Software trials swept blend share, burn length, and load to find the timing that gives peak power and leanest fuel use.

The model matched bench data within a small margin, which lent trust to its timing maps. Burn length moved the ideal timing most, blend share came second, and engine load mattered least of the three. Simple straight-line formulas captured each link, for both the power goal and the fuel goal. Garages and test cells can now read timing straight from the formulas, skipping many costly trial runs on the bench.
pmc-13286448:
Ping Yu and Jin Xiao map how pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor cells change their energy habits as they develop, using single-cell data. Published in 2026, the study reanalyzed public gene-reading data cell by cell. Tumors commonly switch between burning fuel with oxygen and fermenting sugar, yet that switch had not been charted in this tumor type.

The analysis sorted cells into ten clusters and three energy states, from oxygen-leaning to sugar-leaning. Hundreds of genes separated the extremes, with energy machinery genes on one side and sugar-breaking enzymes on the other. A long non-coding RNA called MALAT1 best distinguished the states. Lab tests in two tumor cell lines confirmed the patterns at RNA and protein levels.
pmc-13286748:
Hyunjoo Na and colleagues trace a pathway from heavy smartphone use to cyberbullying among Korean teenagers, using six years of national panel data. Published in 2026, the study followed 2,242 adolescents. Problematic phone use has been linked with online aggression, yet the steps between them over time were unclear.

Statistical models found that troubled phone use predicted rising aggression, which in turn predicted more cyberbullying of others. Parenting that structures phone use did not soften the chain as expected; the link between phone problems and aggression ran stronger where such structuring was high. Prevention, the authors argue, needs school and community programs alongside family rules, with strategies matched to teenagers' stage of development.
pmc-13286948:
Tong Liu and colleagues examine whether vitamin D levels relate to overactive bladder in women, and whether inflammation explains part of any link. The 2026 study analyzes a United States health survey of about twenty-five thousand adults plus a hospital cohort of roughly twenty-four hundred patients. Overactive bladder brings urgency and frequent urination that erode quality of life.

Among women, higher vitamin D tracked with lower odds of the condition, with the top quarter showing about a quarter less risk than the bottom quarter. No such pattern appeared in men. Two inflammation measures weakened the association when accounted for, suggesting they carry part of it. Genetic analysis pointed the same way. The authors read the combined evidence as a possible protective role.
pmc-13287048:
Rachana Verma and a large team report a working system for regenerating and gene-editing pigeonpea, a drought-tolerant legume that feeds many people in India's dry zones. Published in 2026, the work attacks a longstanding problem: pigeonpea tissue culture resists the callus growth and shooting that plant editing pipelines need, which has stalled improvement of the crop.

Adjusted growth regulators plus silver nitrate in the shoot medium lifted regeneration to roughly eighty-six percent and transformation success to nearly half of attempts. A gene gun delivered editing machinery aimed at a pigment gene, and sequencing confirmed mutations in about a tenth of cases. The platform, the authors say, can produce marker-free edited plants that ease biosafety concerns.
pmc-13287148:
Natalia Avila Soares led a 2026 grazing trial comparing two Urochloa pastures for crossbred Holstein and Gyr dairy cows under rotational grazing in rainy seasons. One pasture used Paiaguás grass and the other used the hybrid Ipyporã, each grazed down by half from a set starting height.

Paiaguás produced more herbage overall and carried more animals per hectare. Ipyporã offered a higher share of leaf and denser herbage. Milk output per hectare did not differ between the two swards. Intake differed only in one phase, favouring Ipyporã. The authors conclude that both cultivars can sustain good production when grazing heights are matched to each grass.
pmc-13287248:
Merve Erdoğan Soysal and co-authors surveyed 99 people in 2026 with systemic sclerosis, a hardening illness, to learn what drives mouth-related difficulty in daily life. Patients completed scales covering mouth handicap, worry about appearance, mood, resilience, and quality of life, alongside clinical measures of skin and organ involvement.

Mouth handicap ran higher with thicker facial skin, gut involvement, calcium deposits, small vessel marks, and finger ulcers. It also rose with anxiety, low mood, and appearance worry, and fell as quality of life scores rose. In combined models, skin score, gut involvement, and anxiety each kept an independent link. The authors frame mouth problems as both physical and emotional in this illness.
pmc-13287748:
Yi-Ping Wu and co-authors profiled proteins and their phosphate tags in 2026 in nasopharyngeal cancer. That tumour of the upper throat is common in parts of Asia. Cancer tissue was compared with healthy tissue from the same region. Patterns split the cancers into two molecular subtypes with different clinical behaviour.

The second subtype showed stronger signs of immune suppression. Marker panels for diagnosis and outlook were built from the protein data. A drug hunt flagged panobinostat, a broad gene-switch drug, which shrank tumours in cell and animal tests by cutting a growth gene and weakening DNA repair. Pairing it with radiation worked better still. Subtype-specific drug leads were also tested.
pmc-13288548:
David J Cangemi and co-authors review how to assess and treat patients whose constipation comes with prominent bloating, in a 2026 clinical article. Because the two complaints often arrive together yet can stem from different causes, the authors stress sorting out the underlying condition before choosing treatment.

Their walk-through separates chronic idiopathic constipation from the constipation form of irritable bowel syndrome, among other causes, and lays out a stepwise workup. Options covered range from diet changes and pelvic floor biofeedback to laxatives bought without prescription, secretagogues such as plecanatide, linaclotide, lubiprostone, and tenapanor, plus neuromodulators and antibiotics. Fixing constipation alone does not always settle bloating, they note, so care should match each patient's own pattern.
pmc-13289248:
Jiawen Xu and coauthors report a 2026 field and lab study on carbon washed from rotting bamboo wood in southern China. The forest was a subtropical moso bamboo stand, and the species studied was Phyllostachys edulis. They ask how added manganese, a metal that affects decay, changes dissolved organic carbon in water passing through dead wood.

Four wood parts were tested: culm base, rhizome, culm root, and culm stem. After 360 days outdoors with manganese added, leached water generally held more dissolved carbon, with larger and more aromatic molecules. At the same time, microbes could use that carbon less easily, so bioavailability fell overall. Higher aromatic share, larger size, and phosphorus ratios tracked with lower use, linking wood decay chemistry to carbon and nutrient flow in soils.
pmc-13289348:
Aghil Rostami, Haleh Ashraf, and Ali Hosseininasab carried out a 2026 umbrella review on whether blood pressure drugs protect the heart during chemotherapy. Heart damage from cancer drugs drives later illness in survivors. Drugs that block angiotensin or slow the heart have been proposed as shields, but proof strength across reviews was murky.

The team gathered meta-analyses of randomized trials through May 2025 and reanalyzed their data with standard grading of certainty. A total of 35 reviews with 108 links entered the synthesis. Angiotensin blockers and beta blockers each preserved pumping fraction to a degree, though certainty grades stayed low or very low for those outcomes. One filling measure improved with beta blockers at moderate certainty, urging caution in claims.
pmc-13289648:
Qing Xia and coauthors present a 2026 cell study on how platelets and immune cells release granules, tiny storage sacs, in different ways. Granule release drives clotting in platelets and defense in immune cells, yet shared versus distinct controls were unclear. Mouse platelets, neutrophils, and mast cells grown from marrow were compared side by side under the same chemical triggers.

Two activators alone and together sparked distinct patterns by cell type and granule type. Platelets dumped one granule class strongly, neutrophils surged only with both triggers, and mast cells ignored one trigger yet answered the other strongly. Blocker tests then mapped which signal paths each cell needs. Thrombin-driven platelet release relied on just two paths, showing tight, cell-specific wiring.
pmc-13289948:
Giulia Iacono and colleagues run a 2026 prospective cohort hunting early warning signs of chronic lung transplant failure, called CLAD. That failure is diagnosed only after lasting lung decline, when damage is already fixed, so earlier signals are badly needed. Lung wash samples were tracked for microbes, metabolites, fats, and gene activity up to thirty months after transplant in recipients still free of failure.

Fifty-six recipients gave longitudinal samples, and wash profiles from thirteen who stayed free were compared with thirteen who developed failure. Early months after transplant showed low microbe diversity, more Staphylococcus and Candida, strong immune activation, and raised nitric oxide chemistry in the data. Repair and T-cell return followed as immune drugs tapered.
pmc-13290448:
A three-month detour through traditional healing left a teenage footballer's knee stiff and weak, in a 2026 case report from rural Cameroon by Ibrahim Npochinto Moumeni and Fred Dikongue Dikongue. The 17-year-old from Foumbot hurt his left knee in a neighborhood match.

Money worries and cultural beliefs led the family to massage sessions and therapeutic scarification instead of a hospital. He reached the rehabilitation unit in Bafoussam only after his coach noticed his play declining. Examination found limited motion, pain, disuse bone loss on X-ray, and fear of movement; his Lysholm knee score sat at 41 of 100. A seven-week, three-phase program that trained his parents as co-therapists lifted the score to 87 and returned him toward sport. The authors use the case to argue for culturally aligned, family-based rehabilitation where delays are common.
pmc-13290648:
Kexin Yu and co-authors review how loneliness and social isolation may drive cognitive decline, in a 2026 synthesis. Both states raise dementia risk, but the pathways between feeling alone and losing memory stay murky. The team gathered thirty-eight articles that tested mechanisms directly. Physiological studies qualified when they used mediation tests or measured brain disease changes. Behavior pathway studies all needed formal mediation analysis.

Body pathways under study included Alzheimer's pathology, brain structure, inflammation, and heart risk factors. Stress hormone function, growth factors, and gene activity also appeared, with mixed findings across reports. Behavior pathways looked steadier, led by depressive symptoms and low sense of control. Poor sleep, neuroticism, and withdrawal from social or leisure activity also carried part of the link. The authors list these mechanisms as targets for programs that fight isolation. Trials can now test whether easing loneliness moves those same pathways.
pmc-13290748:
Thyroid hormones trace who survives heart-attack shock, Priyanka Boettger and colleagues report in a 2026 prospective cohort study. In cardiogenic shock after myocardial infarction, hormone levels shift with critical illness, and the team asked whether their paths predict death in hospital.

From a shock registry, 41 patients had TSH, free T3, and free T4 measured at admission and four times over the following 96 hours after stenting. Survivors kept higher TSH over time while non-survivors' levels sank. Free T3 fell in everyone early on but dropped steeper in those who died, and lower values tracked with worse illness and higher mortality. Free T4 drifted down in both groups without separating them. The authors suggest serial thyroid checks could sharpen risk sorting in the cardiac ICU, pending larger studies.
pmc-13290848:
The liquid pooling at the bottom of baijiu fermentation pits works as a flavor crossroads, Wei Cheng and colleagues show in a regional survey from 2026. Huangshui, long treated as a byproduct, links microbes in the fermented grains and pit mud during strong-aroma baijiu making, and the team asked how place shapes its chemistry and ecology.

Samples from nine production regions differed sharply in acidity, nitrogen, minerals, and organic acids, proof of distinct fermentation microenvironments. Lactic acid dominated everywhere, while fatty acids swung widely. Bacteria leaned on Lactobacillus, methane-making archaea, and chain-elongating Caproiciproducens; yeasts such as Pichia and Saccharomyces led the fungi. Among 162 volatile compounds, esters ruled the aroma profile, again with regional fingerprints. Cheng and colleagues conclude local chemistry filters which microbes thrive, making huangshui a tool for origin testing and tighter fermentation control.
pmc-13290948:
Drones with lasers can watch rice grow day by day and expose its growth genes, Weicheng Xu and colleagues show in a study from 2026. Early height gain predicts canopy build and yield, but hand measuring cannot track it often or gently. So the team flew UAV-LiDAR over 211 rice accessions at ten time points in the 40 days after transplanting.

Reconstructed height curves yielded each line's growth-rate peak and timing, separating early vigor patterns cleanly. Genome-wide association across the panel found 604 significant markers, 33 of them stable across environments, pointing to five candidate genes tied to cell elongation, hormone signaling, and photosynthesis. Xu and colleagues present the pairing of dynamic sensing and genetics as a breeding framework for fast-establishing, high-vigor rice.
pmc-13291148:
Ashraf Hassan Abd El Mobdy heads a 2026 study of vitamin D and artery health in dialysis patients. People on hemodialysis face high heart risk. Thick neck arteries can warn of hidden disease. The team asked if blood vitamin D levels track with that warning sign.
