Ninety patients on regular dialysis took part. Neck ultrasound split them into normal and thick artery groups. Blood tests covered vitamin D, calcium, fats, and inflammation marks. Vitamin D showed no clear link to artery thickness. Calcium levels did differ between the two groups. Body weight stood out as a predictor of low vitamin D. The findings warn against assuming vitamin D alone explains artery change here.
pmc-13291548:
Nerve and immune timing can rescue diabetic bone healing. Xuanyu Qi leads a 2026 study of jaw bone defects in diabetes. Poor healing stems from inflammation gone off track. Weak sensory nerves may share the blame.

In diabetic defects, nerve fibers ran thin. White blood cells arrived late yet lingered too long. Cleanup cells failed to clear the spent fighters. A cookie-like scaffold was built to fix the timing. Its chips burst out a cell lure first. Its base then leaked nerve growth factor slowly. Fresh nerves guided fighter cells to a calmer form. Diabetic rat jaws regrew bone far better with the scaffold.
pmc-13292048:
Zhengzheng Li's team reports a 2026 study naming PARK2 as the enzyme that tags the glycolysis protein PGK1 for destruction in triple-negative breast cancer. PGK1 helps these tumors spread, but what controls its stability was unclear. The team analyzed clinical datasets and 50 tumor samples, then ran binding and ubiquitin assays in cells and a mouse lung spread model.

Tumors showed high PGK1 and low PARK2, and high PGK1 tracked with worse survival. PARK2 gripped PGK1 through its RING2 domain and attached K48-linked ubiquitin chains, sending PGK1 to the proteasome. Raising PARK2 cut mesenchymal markers, migration, invasion, and lung metastases, while extra PGK1 reversed those gains. The authors suggest boosting PARK2 activity as a strategy against metastatic disease.
pmc-13292248:
Liang Song and co-authors engineer a 2026 treatment platform of core-shell microgels meant to heal the immune imbalance after a heart attack. Infarction leaves regulatory T cells scarce and weak near the damage. The microgel surface carries an antibody that neutralizes CCL17, a signal that misdirects those cells, while the core holds a prodrug that releases propionic acid when enzymes cleave it.

In lab tests, the platform drew in 4.2 times more regulatory T cells and raised their Foxp3 expression by 1.8 times over baseline measures. In mouse heart attack models, cell infiltration into the injured region rose 2.4 times while Th17 cells fell in the treated hearts. Heart function improved and scarring shrank. The authors pitch the system as local immune repair for infarcted tissue.
pmc-13292448:
Huanhuan Song and a large team decode a 2026 imaging puzzle: what cells actually produce the TSPO signal used to picture brain inflammation on PET scans. They swapped the usual tracer for a fluorescent cousin, Cy5-PEG3-DPA714, that works under microscopes and cell sorters as well as in living animals. Several mouse models of acute and chronic neuroinflammation carried the test.

Tissue checks confirmed the signal comes mainly from activated microglia marked by Iba1. Sorting by brightness isolated a microglial subgroup glowing strongly for the probe. Those cells resembled disease-associated microglia, with fierce inflammatory behavior and rewired metabolism. They also leaned heavily on CSF1R signaling, and wiping them out with the inhibitor PLX3397 calmed brain inflammation. The authors offer the framework for aiming future treatments at the exact cells lighting up scans.
pmc-13292848:
Min Gu leads a ten-year review, published in 2026, of bloodstream Candida infections at a large hospital in eastern China. Cases rose over time, and the team tracked which yeast types caused illness and which patients died in hospital.

Records covered 387 patients from 2015 to 2024, with just over half treated in intensive care. Candida albicans stayed the most common type, followed by three other Candida types that varied by ward. Many tropicalis strains resisted azole drugs, while albicans mostly stayed drug-sensitive. Older age, intensive care stay, and kidney failure raised death risk, while prompt antifungal treatment linked to lower risk.
pmc-13293348:
Yuji Hidaka and co-authors report colon surgery in a woman born without a left kidney, in a case published in 2026. The fifty-four-year-old patient had a blocking tumor in her sigmoid colon, and scans taken after decompression showed no spread of disease. Missing organs can shift the usual landmarks surgeons rely on, so the team planned the keyhole operation with that altered anatomy in mind.

Finding the tissue plane behind the abdomen proved easier than feared, since it connected smoothly with familiar layers. Freeing the splenic flexure was the hard part, because the colon had drifted into the empty kidney space, stretching instrument reach. Adjusting ports and stance let the team finish safely without open surgery. The tumor was stage II, she received chemotherapy, and she stayed free of recurrence for nine and a half years.
pmc-13293448:
Jafar Keighobadi and Farnaz Imani present, in a 2026 study, a way to calibrate an atomic gyroscope that measures rotation with high precision. Exact tuning matters for navigation, yet testing with real hardware is costly and slow.

Road data from GPS-aided inertial units fed a software model of the sensor, with laser beams as the input signal. A two-stage filter estimated bias and tuning values at once, without a physical device. Bias uncertainty fell sharply, and pointing accuracy rose by 35% over the untuned case, a gain the authors report. Tuned values also sharpened a rubidium light test, lifting peak strength by 20% in their tests.
pmc-13293648:
Prachi Saluja and co-authors tell of a blood test that pointed the wrong way in a 2026 case report. Scans showed many small cysts in both lungs, and a blood marker called VEGF-D came back high, which usually supports a diagnosis of lymphangioleiomyomatosis, a cystic lung disease of women.

Closer reading of the cyst shapes instead suggested Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome, an inherited condition. Genetic testing found a harmful change in the folliculin gene, confirming that second diagnosis. A lung biopsy taken later during planned surgery showed no trace of the first disease. The case warns clinicians that this marker can mislead and that careful review of imaging remains central in cystic lung disease.
pmc-13293948:
Jiayu Liu and a large team survey drive and anxiety among college students in a 2026 one-time survey in Jining, China. In September 2025, students at Jining Medical University answered questions on background, achievement motivation, and anxiety with the GAD-7 scale. Of 3,173 questionnaires sent out, 2,827 valid replies came back, an 89.09% rate.

Mild anxiety was reported by 28.76% of students, with smaller shares at moderate and severe levels. High motivation appeared in 59.43%, while 35.58% showed low motivation. Anxiety severity tied to being left behind in childhood, family income, parent health, chronic illness, and study satisfaction. Motivation and anxiety were also linked, though direction needs longer follow-up.
pmc-13294148:
Karen Dyreborg and colleagues report a 2026 case series on infected ankle fracture repairs with skin breakdown. No set care exists when infection follows outer ankle bone fixation. Their unit used long drug cover until the bone healed. Then came one late operation with hardware removal, deep cleaning, and deep sampling. Local drugs plus a calf muscle flap and skin graft closed the wound.

Eleven patients treated from 2020 to 2023 had median age 58 years. Six had drug cover for a median of 147 days. Infection was controlled in all 10 patients who could be checked. One person died of other causes soon after surgery. Part flap loss hit 36% and graft loss 55%, mostly handled without more surgery.
pmc-13294648:
Ece Yalçındağ and co-authors set cutoff values for a gentle dry eye test, in a 2026 study. Dry eye disease harms the tear film that shields the eye surface, and one key sign is how fast that film breaks up after a blink. Newer tools time the breakup with no touch and no dye. The team tested forty-six patients and thirty-five healthy people with the new tool plus older checks.

First and average breakup times split patients from healthy people with high accuracy. Cutoffs near eleven seconds for the first breakup and twelve for the average flagged disease best. The new readings tracked the older tests closely, matching dye timing almost exactly. The authors back the test as a keen, touch-free aid for diagnosis.
pmc-13294948:
Igor José dos Santos Nascimento and colleagues create and test new malaria drug candidates in a 2026 study. Malaria still kills many people worldwide, while current treatments suffer side effects and growing parasite resistance. Quinazoline based compounds offer a fresh chemical starting point for new medicines.

The team made 36 related compounds and checked each one carefully. Four stood out against the malaria parasite in lab tests, killing it at low doses without harming human cells in the same tests. None worked against two other parasites tested, hinting at malaria-specific action. Computer modelling pointed to a parasite enzyme called N-myristoyltransferase as the likely target and explained the selectivity.
pmc-13295348:
Fares Boudjouan and co-authors review how microbes make fermented foods better at fighting oxidation, in a 2026 survey. Foods from yogurt to pickles earn health praise partly for antioxidant power, and much of that power is built during fermentation itself. The review sorts the microbial toolkit into three routes and traces how each one raises the content or force of the finished food.

First, microbes secrete exopolysaccharides, long sugar chains that can quench radicals and grab metal ions that would spark harm. Second, microbial enzymes free phenolics, peptides, and other guard compounds locked inside the food matrix. Third, fermentation shifts the whole system's chemistry toward a reducing state. The authors frame the three routes as a design guide for fermented foods with planned antioxidant profiles.
pmc-13295848:
Mariana Noboa-Salgado and Fabricio González-Andrade analyse, in 2026, deaths among very sick newborns in a large neonatal unit in Quito, Ecuador. Local evidence of this kind is scarce in lower-income settings, so they built and tested a risk model from unit records.

Among 220 babies admitted during 2022, 87 died in hospital. Babies small for their stage of pregnancy faced higher odds of death even after other factors were counted, while very low birth weight alone did not predict death. Early instability, acid buildup and poor oxygen measures marked those who died. The model sorted risk well after internal checking.
pmc-13296448:
Melanie Spears and colleagues report the randomised SIGNAL trial on radiation dose schedules before breast cancer surgery, published in 2026. Patients had early-stage, low-risk tumours and received radiation ahead of their operation. The open question was which schedule best wakes up immune activity inside the tumour.

Sixty-one patients received either one large dose or the dose split across three sessions. Both schedules were tolerated without significant side effects. Tumour samples from forty-seven patients showed stronger immune pathway activation after the three-session schedule, across several immune cell types. The authors advise future immune-priming trials to favour three fractions, such as ten gray per session, over a single dose.
pmc-13296648:
Laura-Mihaela Ion and colleagues profile, in 2026, children with long-running gut symptoms, testing whether food-related IgG antibodies gain meaning inside a wider inflammation picture. Guidelines warn against using such antibodies alone for diagnosis, so the team combine them with gut markers, microbes and ultrasound in over five hundred children.

One group showed the full pattern together: broad IgG reactions, raised inflammation and leak markers, and bowel changes on scans. Their antibody burden tracked with bowel wall thickening, and reactions centred on gluten grains and dairy. The authors present the combined profile as exploratory, not diagnostic.
pmc-13296948:
Liliana Bobirică and colleagues test mineral-based photocatalysts that break down humic acids in water under ultraviolet light in a 2026 study. Humic substances resist ordinary treatment and can form harmful by-products during disinfection. Their catalyst couples titanium dioxide with a natural zeolite scaffold, with one version doped with silver.

Breakdown proceeded in stages, with colour fading first, ring structures next, and full mineralisation last. Acidic water sped the process by improving contact and reactive species production, though activity persisted near natural acidity levels. The silver version performed fastest on several measures. The system mimics natural self-purification in sunlit waters, offering insight for treatment design.
pmc-13297048:
Wenyan Yuan and colleagues rank three candidate enzymes that may explain lauric acid richness in Litsea cubeba seed oil in a 2026 computational study. Seed oil composition shifts during development from longer-chain fats toward lauric acid dominance. The candidates came from a freshly assembled seed gene catalogue.

Sequence family trees, shared motifs, and structural models favoured two candidates over the third. Docking a twelve-carbon stand-in molecule gave cleaner binding poses for those two. Long simulations then separated them further, with the leading candidate holding the molecule in a steadier, more compact pose. The authors stress the ranking is a structural clue for laboratory testing, not proof of enzyme function.
pmc-13297348:
Sabina Caciolli and a large team chart heart problems in adults who received stem cell transplants for blood diseases, in a 2026 study. Transplant can cure such diseases, yet it can also strain the heart, and today's patients are often older with more prior illness. The team reviewed one centre's large cohort for both clear heart events and hidden muscle weakness shown by strain imaging, a fine measure of heart squeeze.

Most clear events were rhythm faults, fluid or rubbing around the heart, or weak pumping, while heart attacks and strokes stayed rare. Hidden muscle weakness showed up more often than clear events, above all after gentler preparation regimens. Routine heart checks and joint heart-cancer care are the authors' plea.
pmc-13297848:
Upper second premolars hide more anatomical variety than their usually single root suggests, warn Michał Głąbski and colleagues in a 2026 narrative review. Missing an extra canal can sink root canal treatment, so the authors gathered population studies of this tooth's internal shape.

From 358 papers found in PubMed, 27 studies using cone beam imaging qualified. Single roots appeared in over 70% of teeth, two roots came next, and three roots stayed under 2%, with men showing two roots more often. All eight Vertucci canal patterns occurred, Type I leading at over 50%, though some populations showed many complex forms. The review urges imaging-guided caution before assuming simple anatomy.
pmc-13298448:
Zeyu Wu and a large team examine whether intense exercise changes the machinery that builds microRNAs in human muscle, in a 2026 secondary analysis. Muscle biopsies came from two earlier studies: one single interval cycling bout, and six weeks of interval training against a control group. Gene messages and proteins for four biogenesis components were measured.

The single bout lowered one component's message, with a near-significant dip in another. Six weeks of training changed none of the measured proteins, and a representative muscle microRNA stayed flat at both early and mature stages. The authors highlight how complex microRNA control remains and ask for closer timing studies.
pmc-13298648:
Chatbots play the prisoner's dilemma in surprisingly cooperative ways, report Saptarshi Pal and colleagues in a 2026 study of five leading language models. The team probed how the models cooperate or defect across repeated rounds, varying payoffs, stopping chances, and whether the final round was known.

The models generally behaved generously, often landing on strategies that evolutionary theory deems robust, and they adjusted sensibly to many parameter changes. Yet none stayed fully consistent across every task, and some responses broke with both theory and human experimental patterns. Tournaments between the inferred strategies added further evidence. The authors frame the results as a check on trusting AI advice in social decisions.
pmc-13298948:
A drug-resistant E. coli strain hiding in a market fish's gills carries its resistance in its chromosome, report Amit Kumar and co-authors in a 2026 genome study. The isolate came from rohu carp bought at a retail fish market in Punjab, India, and resisted several antibiotic classes.

Sequencing produced a 3.70 Mb draft genome with 3,814 genes and 39 resistance determinants, including beta-lactam resistance and efflux pumps, plus virulence traits for iron capture, biofilm building, and host colonization. No plasmids turned up in the assembly. Prediction tools judged the strain, typed as ST8020, likely pathogenic to humans. The authors frame farmed fish as a possible resistance reservoir under a One Health lens.
pmc-13299048:
Genes guarding cells against oxidative stress and aging also shape who develops COPD, report Yanina Timasheva and colleagues in a 2026 genetic association study. They tested thirty-three variants in 747 patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and 703 controls, and built polygenic risk scores from the hits.

Signals landed in antioxidant genes such as NFE2L2 and HMOX1, in growth signaling genes, and in the mitochondrial gene TOMM40, among others. The strongest single variant, in PIK3R1, carried an odds ratio of 2.31. A weighted score alone discriminated moderately, and adding age, sex, and smoking lifted accuracy to an AUC of 88.1%. The authors tie the loci to stress adaptation and cell aging pathways.
pmc-13299148:
Emily M. Melnick and co-authors study whether letting WIC households buy frozen or canned produce improves benefit use, in a 2026 nutrition study within an Arizona tribal organisation. The programme grants monthly cash-value benefits for fruits and vegetables. Administrative data covered thousands of households, joined by a participant survey.

Households that bought frozen or canned items alongside fresh produce redeemed more of their benefit value, and heavier frozen purchasing predicted higher redemption. Families with several enrolled members used the option more, and longer shelf life was the most cited reason. The authors suggest programme policies should allow and promote preserved produce for American Indian families.
pmc-13299348:
Fresh-made compounds made rays hit one brain tumor line hard and left a next line near whole. Dorota Natorska-Chomicka and her team report that split in a 2026 study. They built two new hydrazide-hydrazone agents from a bromo-iodo benzoic acid and paired each with X-rays on glioblastoma cells.

In LN-229 cells, agent 3 at 164 μM plus 2 Gy cut cell life by 65%. It also pushed more cells toward death. Agent 4 at 242 μM halved cell life across 2 to 5 Gy. It stalled the cell cycle and drove cell death. In U-87MG cells, the same agents did scant work or even sped growth. The team stress that each tumor's own make-up sets whether a sensitizer helps.
pmc-13300948:
A Sikorska and co-authors probe the acute heart safety of cardioneuroablation in a 2026 prospective study. The procedure burns nerve inputs to slow a vagal brake that works too hard in people with fainting or functional slow rhythms. Critics worry that taking away parasympathetic restraint could invite dangerous ventricular rhythms. Eighty patients had programmed ventricular stimulation and timing measurements before ablation, after it, and again after atropine and a stimulant drug pushed denervation further.

Ventricular tachycardia could be set off in only two patients, one before and one after the procedure. Both had earlier heart disease. The action potential grew shorter after ablation. The refractory period barely moved, except under the stimulant, and one QT formula showed lengthening only in the fully drugged state. Dispersion of repolarization never changed. The authors conclude acute proarrhythmia looks rare and tied to underlying disease, while long term course stays unknown.
pmc-13301448:
V Probst and co-authors test how faithfully a Brugada syndrome gene predicts the disease inside large families in a 2026 genetics study. The team enrolled 463 people from forty-five families, each built around a patient carrying a pathogenic variant in SCN5A, the main gene tied to this fainting and sudden death condition. Relatives were checked for the family variant and challenged with a drug test that unmasks the heart tracing.

The mismatches ran both ways. Of 258 carriers, seventy-five, about thirty percent, never showed the syndrome even after provocation, an incomplete penetrance. Meanwhile thirty-two people diagnosed with Brugada did not carry their family's variant at all. About twenty-four percent of individuals were genotype phenotype mismatches. The authors conclude the SCN5A variant is neither necessary nor sufficient, and they now hunt the background factors that tip carriers toward or away from illness.
pmc-13302648:
Chenyujun Hu and co-authors review, in a 2026 paper, hydrogel materials designed to grow blood vessels and bone together during repair. Bone healing fails when vessel growth lags, a coupling that weakens with age, poor circulation, and chronic inflammation. The gel, called GelMA, mimics natural tissue matrix and can be shaped by three-dimensional printing.

Strategies are sorted into three families: building guidance into the material itself, delivering active cargo such as growth factors and cells, and making gels that respond to local signals. Delivery systems hold the strongest early evidence, while built-in designs may prove easier to manufacture consistently. Responsive systems remain mostly small-animal experiments. The authors urge simpler, reproducible designs over added complexity.
pmc-13303148:
Christos G. Nikolaidis and co-authors review, in a 2026 narrative review, how gut microbe imbalance may feed the complications of type 2 diabetes. Organ damage keeps rising even as glucose control improves, hinting at other drivers. The authors gather microbial patterns linked to kidney, eye, nerve, and vessel complications.

Shared routes include a leakier gut barrier, toxin seepage into blood, and smouldering inflammation that ages tissues faster. Some microbial signatures repeat across organs, while others appear specific to one complication. Microbe-based tests and treatments, plus machine learning over microbiome data, are discussed as add-ons to standard care. The authors stress that most proof is still associative and needs long-term mechanistic studies.
pmc-13303448:
Sally Fuchs and co-authors report a 2026 mouse study mapping protein kinase A parts in healthy and diabetic kidneys. Diabetic kidney disease can end in dialysis or transplant, and signals driven by cyclic nucleotides may help drive the damage.

Kidney tissue was stained to locate the catalytic subunits called Cα and Cβ. Diabetes was triggered with streptozotocin in normal mice and in mice lacking endothelial nitric oxide synthase. Cα appeared in all kidney cell types, while Cβ was strong mainly in proximal tubules and weak elsewhere. Neither subunit changed clearly in diabetic or knockout kidneys compared with controls.
pmc-13303848:
Andrea Migliorelli and co-authors scope, in a 2026 review, whether simple blood inflammation ratios can forecast outcomes in cancers of the nose and sinuses. These rare tumours are often found late and recur often, so cheap prognostic clues are welcome. Six studies covering just over a thousand patients met the criteria.

The neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio was the most studied marker and the one most often tied to worse survival, later stage, and higher recurrence. Composite scores mixing platelets, albumin, and inflammation counts may add extra signal, early evidence suggests. Every included study was retrospective and single-centre, with inconsistent cut-off values between them. The authors call for prospective multicentre work before these ratios guide real treatment decisions.
pmc-13304148:
Shuyang Li and colleagues test road base mixes that swap in steel slag, a steelmaking leftover often stockpiled in huge piles, in a 2026 engineering study. Cement dose and slag share were varied to find a strong, greener blend.

Crushing, stiffness, and splitting tests tracked strength as mixes changed. More cement raised every strength measure, though gains slowed at high doses. Strength rose with slag share up to a point, then eased, while stiffness kept climbing. At the best slag level, key strengths peaked well above the plain control mix. Microscope views showed denser internal structure behind the gains.
pmc-13306848:
Xuelei Jia improved flexible pressure sensors by spreading copper particles evenly with ultrasound in a 2026 study. Clumped filler inside soft PDMS layers destabilises electrical response, so sound-wave mixing was used during layer making.

Models and simulations showed even spread steadies permittivity and calms local electric field spikes. Finished sensors beat standard builds on sensitivity, stability and working range in reported tests, reaching 0.157 kPa−1 in the low range of 0 to 1 kPa in the given units. Performance held across 1000 loading cycles, supporting wearable and robot touch uses. Soft touch skins for health wear and robot hands are named as prime uses.
pmc-13307048:
Jon Stewart Dy and colleagues map research in 2026 on neuroarts, the study of how creative experiences affect brain, body, and well-being. Their scoping review gathered studies from 2000 to late 2025 across five databases, screening more than nine thousand records. Sixty-seven studies met the inclusion rules.

Music, dance, literature, visual arts, and wider cultural engagement all appeared as interventions in healthy and clinical groups. Reported gains covered mental well-being, cognitive function, and quality of life. Study categories followed World Health Organization groupings of art forms. The authors present neuroarts as a framework linking artistic practice to health mechanisms. They support bringing arts-based activity into therapy and health promotion, while noting the field is still defining its foundations.
pmc-13308648:
Chengsong Yue and colleagues analyse in 2026 whether minutes spent inside the artery during clot removal predict recovery after large-core stroke. Records covered 490 patients at thirty-eight centres who had thrombectomy for major vessel blockage with already large infarcts. Outcomes were scored ninety days later for function, death, and brain bleeding.

Every extra ten minutes of procedure time lowered the odds of a reasonable functional outcome and raised mortality odds. Modelled chances of moderate recovery fell from about forty-five percent at one hour to about twenty-eight percent at two and a half hours. Curve analysis found no safe threshold where extra time stopped mattering. Bleeding complications showed no consistent link with duration. The authors propose procedure time as a live risk gauge, prompting teams to reassess strategy as minutes accumulate.
pmc-13308948:
Kewei Jia, Xin Li, and Bin Liao report in 2026 a near fatal aortic hole torn during a neck vein line try for dialysis in a man aged 61 years. He had stage 5 kidney disease at the time. The line had crossed an artery and the brachiocephalic trunk, with its tip outside the aorta and blood pooled around the heart.

Surgeons took the line out under direct sight, with hand pressure and a heart lung bypass rig on standby for control. He healed with no snags after that high risk rescue in theatre. Blind pulling of a suspect line can kill, the team warns, so fast scans, surgical calls, and live ultrasound for each try are key.
pmc-13309448:
Cornelia Hildegard Oberrauter and colleagues report a 2026 surgical study on a simpler way to reattach bone in reverse shoulder replacement after a bad upper arm break. The usual method uses four or five stitches to fix the bone knob that anchors key muscles. The team tested a two-stitch method meant to shorten surgery without hurting healing.

Seventy-three patients were followed for two years after surgery, and most were older women with weak bone. Shoulder scores at two years were high, and scans tracked whether the bone knob healed in place. A side comparison looked at cemented versus uncemented stems. The authors present the simpler stitch method as workable in this frail group.
pmc-13309848:
Deeksha Singh and co-authors profile the genes at work in a medicinal pepper plant in a 2026 study. Piper chaba, a relative of black pepper, makes the pungent compound piperine, valued for drug-like effects. Which genes build piperine, and where the plant stores most of it, were unknown.

Gene reads from spike, leaf, and root tissue yielded 228,481 transcripts, trimmed to 184,574 unique genes for analysis in the study. Chemical assay found piperine richest by far in the spike, at 331.3 mg/g in the reported measure, with root and leaf far lower. Thirteen candidate genes tied to piperine building were flagged from pathway maps. The authors offer the gene set as a base for breeding and biotech work.
pmc-13310648:
Nikoleta Papanikolaou and co-authors image testicle blood vessels at super-fine detail in a 2026 study. Male infertility and low hormone output are rising, and current tests capture vessel health poorly. Tiny vessel flow underpins testicle function, and a new ultrasound method maps vessels far below standard resolution.

Men with a hormone-driven low-output condition were compared with healthy men, then tracked across treatments including testosterone, hormone therapy, and fertility care over twelve months. A rodent model of blocked puberty joined the design. Vessel density, width, and winding separated patients from controls and tracked hormone levels in the reported results. Azoospermia, the absence of sperm, showed reduced vessel measures. The authors propose vessel mapping as a diagnostic aid.
pmc-13310948:
Rafael Yoshida and co-authors compare growing and fixed rods for brittle bone disease in children in a 2026 review. Osteogenesis imperfecta weakens collagen, so bones bend and break with ease. Rods placed inside long bones give support, and telescopic rods extend as a child grows, which may cut repeat surgery.

Past studies totaled 36 in number, covering 1,711 patients and 2,459 treated bones. Telescopic rods linked to far lower revision rates than fixed rods. Overall complication rates did not differ clearly between rod types. Longer implant life supports favoring growing rods in clinic practice, with care matched to each child.
pmc-13311148:
Hanvit Lee reports a 2026 case of a tunneled vein catheter placed through one skin cut in a newborn. A preterm boy needed long term vein feeding after gut concerns and hard vein access. Standard tunneling uses two skin cuts, and the exit near the diaper zone raises germ risk, so a single cut method was tried.

Guided by imaging, the line entered through one small thigh cut and tunneled under skin into the thigh vein, placing the exit away from the diaper area. The line worked steadily for 14 days with no infection or slipping. One case proves feasibility only, not lower infection rates.
pmc-13311248:
Beata Huszcza and colleagues, in 2026, give a narrative review of enteroscopy, the set of scope methods used to inspect and treat the small bowel. The bowel's length and folds make it hard to reach with standard scopes.

The review, drawn from MEDLINE papers from 2001 to 2025, covers capsule scopes and device-assisted scopes. Main uses include finding bleeding sources, checking Crohn's disease and celiac disease, and finding tumors. Assisted scopes also allow biopsies, stopping bleeding, widening narrow spots, and removing polyps or stuck objects. Reported risk stays low, and the methods can cut the need for surgery.
pmc-13311648:
Anne Sophie Mathiesen and co-authors report the 2026 randomized trial of guided self-determination, a talk-based method that supports patient autonomy, for adults with type 2 diabetes. The rival was an attention control program.

The two-center trial stopped early after 150 of 224 planned patients were enrolled, with 74 in the method group and 76 in the control group. Sessions ran face-to-face, by phone, or by video. The main outcome was diabetes distress at twelve months, with mood, quality of life, and side effects also tracked. Early results favored the method on distress. The trial shows both promise and the cost of early stopping.
pmc-13311748:
Bolin Jin and co-authors hunt blood protein markers that warn of coming carotid plaque in a 2026 nested case-control study. Plaque in the neck artery is an early sign of the vessel disease behind heart attacks and strokes.

The ChinaHEART cohort supplied 145 people who developed plaque and 147 matched controls without it at the start. Eleven proteins stood out, among them thrombomodulin, growth differentiation factor-15, adiponectin, and IL-10. The team then checked how the findings travel to the UK Biobank, a far larger British cohort. A blood panel of this kind could one day flag risk years before symptoms.
pmc-13311948:
Naomi Kemps and colleagues present a 2026 multi-country study on whether low blood pressure helps spot serious illness in children at acute care sites in poorer countries. Routine pressure checks in children have been questioned.

Data came from three sites in The Gambia and Suriname, covering more than twenty-two thousand visits in all. Low pressure by age-based cutoffs appeared in 8.3 to 17.3 percent of visits across sites. Serious illness, defined by admission or referral upward, was the outcome tested. The study weighs whether a cheap cuff reading earns its place in first assessment where illness runs high.
pmc-13312248:
Matthew Smith and colleagues ask, in a 2026 study, whether an epidural changes the risk of surgical site infection after open colorectal surgery. Epidurals bring several known gains for these patients, but infections remain common after colorectal operations, and any link between the two had barely been studied.

The team analyzed 2022 and 2023 data from the American College of Surgeons quality registry, with 6,343 patients, of whom 1,495, about 24 percent, got an epidural. Across all models, epidurals showed no clear link to infection overall, to infection at the wound, or to deep organ-space infection within 30 days. A second analysis using propensity weighting agreed. Patients having stoma-forming procedures fared worse on all three infection outcomes than those having surgery without a stoma.
pmc-13312448:
Ioulia Exapicheidou and a large chemistry team report a 2026 hit-to-lead study of compounds that block energy-coupling factor transporters in bacteria. These membrane proteins ferry needed vitamins into many Gram-positive bacteria. They are absent from human cells, making them an attractive antibiotic target as resistance spreads. Starting from an earlier inhibitor, the researchers varied one end of the molecule using click chemistry. They optimized several drug-like properties at once.

The refined compounds gained stability and dissolved more readily. They kept strong activity against the transporters and against a panel of Gram-positive bacteria. Against Enterococcus faecium, killing was rapid. The best leads then proved themselves in living infection models, working in wax moth larvae and in zebrafish. Confirming efficacy in animals moves this compound class from an interesting lab finding toward a credible drug development path.
pmc-13312548:
David T. Hogan and co-authors report, in a 2026 chemistry study, a small fluorescent molecule with an unusually wide gap between the light it absorbs and the light it emits. Most dye families absorb and emit at close wavelengths, causing self-reabsorption and blocking multi-color sensing from one excitation light, and the usual fix is donor-acceptor charge transfer design.

The team instead placed permanently charged donor and acceptor groups in meta positions on a single benzene ring, a neglected geometry. The resulting zwitterion absorbs ultraviolet light at 375 nanometers and emits yellow-orange at 605 nanometers, a Stokes shift above 10,000 wavenumbers, the largest recorded for such a compound. Calculations credit stronger charge transfer and extra energy shed through structural reshaping after excitation, tied to excited-state antiaromaticity. Extended versions kept the wide shift, suggesting a general design rule.
pmc-13312748:
Stina Engelheart and Lisa Spang explore, in a 2026 case study, where older immigrants with dementia want to live as the disease advances. They also ask how their families weigh home against residential care. Ageing populations grow more diverse, yet how immigrants experience dementia inside a foreign culture, and what care they wish for, remains little studied.

The team interviewed people with dementia and their relatives in two households where a husband had the disease. One couple fought to preserve togetherness as abilities faded; in the other, acting-out symptoms pushed safety ahead of staying together. Both saw moving into residential care as a deep threshold, shadowed by rigid routines, doubt about staff skill, and cultural and language mismatches. The authors ask officials to design services that protect identity and meaningful daily habits for this group.
pmc-13313148:
Alice Moura Martins and co-authors chart, in a 2026 micro-CT study, the hidden side canals inside baby upper molars. Children's root canal treatment fails when accessory canals, tiny branches off the main root canal, shelter bacteria from cleaning, yet the anatomy of these canals in primary teeth was poorly mapped.

Seventeen primary maxillary molars from donors aged 2 to 8, together holding 47 roots, were scanned and reconstructed in three dimensions. Over two thirds of roots, 68.08 percent in the reported count, held at least one accessory canal, and 96 canals were found in all. The tip third of the root was the most crowded, carrying 42.71 percent of the canals, ahead of the middle and neck thirds. The authors say the survey proves these teeth are anatomically trickier than they look and demands thorough disinfection in treatment.
pmc-13313748:
Alejandro Montenegro-Avila and co-workers pool trial data in a 2026 review of whether GLP-1 drugs cut heart risk in type 2 diabetes. Heart outcome trials hint these drugs lower major adverse cardiovascular events in people who also have artery disease, but the size of the gain, with new trials and pill forms, was unsettled.

The team searched five databases on 6 May 2025 under set review rules, registered as CRD420251034652. Seven trials with 56 191 participants in total were pooled, with a mean follow-up of 3.5 years, per the report. The drugs cut major events, such as heart attack, stroke, and heart death, against placebo or usual care, with landmark trials like SOUL included. The pooled numbers give doctors a firmer sense of how much heart protection these drugs add.
pmc-13313948:
Asma Abdlhusen Shrshoh and Nafea Sabih Jasim report, in a 2026 study, the design and trial of a multi-epitope mRNA vaccine against Newcastle disease, a scourge of poultry farming. Rather than using whole virus, the vaccine stitches together predicted immune-triggering fragments from the virus's two proteins. They were selected for binding strength, antigenicity, safety, and conservation across strains. Two hundred eighty chickens were randomized into eight groups, including the vaccine, six commercial vaccines, and an unvaccinated control, then challenged with a virulent strain.

Birds receiving the mRNA vaccine mounted higher antibody titers than controls, with stronger lymphocyte proliferation and more interferon-producing cells. After challenge, that group showed the best protection, with the fewest and mildest clinical signs and the lowest mortality. It edged out rival products. The authors claim a first for this vaccine architecture against Newcastle disease. They argue such mRNA designs could modernize poultry vaccination.
pmc-13314148:
Marina Louza Palmeira de Carvalho and colleagues synthesize, in a 2026 review and meta-analysis, how often hormone diseases appear in Brazilian dogs and cats treated at hospitals and referral centers. Local evidence was fragmented, with no population-wide registry like the British VetCompass system to anchor estimates. Searching seven sources for studies from 2005 to 2025, the team screened 2,501 records. They kept thirteen that met their criteria, appraising quality and pooling proportions where the designs allowed.

Frequencies swung widely with setting, exactly the referral bias the authors suspected. Hormone disorders looked uncommon in broad hospital caseloads but far more frequent inside specialist cohorts. Hyperparathyroidism stayed consistently rare, between 0.01 and 0.07 percent across studies. One multicenter cohort put hypoadrenocorticism at 0.09 percent of its dogs. The authors insist Brazilian numbers be read as setting-specific caseload shares, never as population prevalence. They use British primary-care figures only as a benchmark for contrast.
pmc-13314348:
Hanan Waleed Kasim Agwaan compares, in a 2026 feeding trial, three supplement strategies for Awassi rams enduring heat stress in arid conditions. Heat degrades growth, blood health, and hormone balance in sheep, and feeds are a proposed countermeasure. Twenty-four rams were randomized for ninety days to plain feed, beta-glucan, a vitamin C and zinc pairing, or all three supplements together. Productivity, blood, biochemical, stress, and hormone measures were tracked.

Every supplemented group beat the control, but the full combination dominated. It produced the heaviest final weight at 72.5 kilograms. It also produced the fastest growth rate at 26.97 percent, and the best feed conversion, alongside stronger red and white blood cell counts. Blood chemistry improved, with sugars, cholesterol, and liver enzymes down and protein and antioxidant status up. Stress cortisol fell and hormones rose. Agwaan concludes the trio acts and recommends it as a heat-season ration strategy.
pmc-13314748:
Ketum Ateh Stanislas and a large team compare what young women think their heart risk is with what scores say, in a 2026 study. Heart disease is the top killer of women, yet awareness among women of childbearing age has fallen, and low risk sense can blunt prevention.

The study drew 139 women from the Baltimore and Washington DC area, aged 18 to 50 years, with a mean age of 32.0 years as stated in the report. Each woman rated her own heart and stroke risk against peers on a seven-point scale. True heart health was graded by the Life Essential 8 set of measures. Crossing the two sorted women into matched or mismatched groups, and models hunted traits that predict underrating risk. The gap matters: women who feel safe may skip the checks that catch risk early.
pmc-13315648:
Shabnam Anjum and co-authors built in 2026 a fiber system that releases two agents at different times to heal bone defects weakened by osteoporosis. Healing needs strong early bone building plus steady restraint of bone loss across the whole repair period, a timing match that current methods miss.

Core-shell fibers made by coaxial spinning held the drug alendronate in the core and carried stem cell exosomes on the surface, fixed with a chemical coating. Tests confirmed the build, with tensile strength of 22.77 megapascals and a very low water contact angle showing a wettable surface. The timed release aims to coordinate bone-forming and bone-resorbing cells.
pmc-13316748:
Zuhui Zhang and colleagues, in a 2026 prospective study, test whether large language models can help train eye specialists in China. Shortages of ophthalmologists are unevenly spread, and training support is one proposed use for these systems. Eleven leading models were compared with ten resident doctors from a tertiary eye hospital.

Models first sat a national ophthalmology examination in Chinese and English. Several Chinese models scored very highly, and the best outperformed every resident on the Chinese paper. Giving residents that model for help raised their average text examination score markedly, and all ten passed. Help with classifying images of corneal inflammation, however, brought no gain. Trainee feedback matched that split, warm for text and much cooler for images.
pmc-13317448:
Chunyan Chi writes, in 2026, about new work toward pure red light from organic displays. Ultra-high-definition screens need narrowband red emitters, yet red versions of a much-watched material class still emit across too wide a spectrum. Broadening comes largely from shaking and settling inside the material, which grow worse at longer wavelengths.

Chi discusses a study that rebuilt a globally aromatic molecule, ovalene, into related structures with varied fusion patterns. Work using chemical shift analysis showed that fusion choices change aromatic character and how the material emits. Structures with more local aromaticity cut the shaking link and sharpened the spectrum. The piece frames electron spread as a design lever for meeting strict display colour standards in future devices.
pmc-13317548:
Jiaying Wu, Xiaorong Peng, Yunan Chang, and Hongmei Xu build a 2026 prediction model for serious liver injury in children with chronic hepatitis B who have never been treated. A biopsy can prove injury but is too invasive for routine use in children, so they sought answers in ordinary clinical data.

Records held 246 children who had biopsies, and 59.8 percent of them showed serious injury. A feature-picking method chose five predictors, and among nine learning models a plain logistic model proved steadiest, scoring 0.799 in training checks and 0.707 on a held-out test group. The chart form beat the standard single enzyme test across most decision thresholds, though the gain stayed modest.
pmc-13318548:
Abdullahi Hassan Elmi and Fahma Hussein Ibrahim recount a 2026 case of necrotising fasciitis, a fast-moving flesh-destroying infection, in an eight-year-old girl who had been healthy before. She arrived with high fever, severe pain, and spreading dead tissue on her right leg and buttock, two months after chickenpox.

Blood tests showed strong signs of serious infection, and her risk score of 10 pointed to high danger in this presentation. Wound cultures grew Proteus mirabilis, an unusual culprit, and treatment followed the sensitivity results. Urgent surgery to cut away dead tissue, intravenous antibiotics, and ongoing wound care brought improvement. Because chickenpox had ended long before, the authors warn against assuming it directly caused the infection.
pmc-13318648:
Rui Wu and Gaiqi Yao present a 2026 cross-sectional study linking routine blood count inflammation markers to thickened heart muscle in people with diabetic kidney disease. Their sample held 419 patients treated at Peking University Third Hospital between January 2020 and September 2025.

Heart scans split the group into 106 patients with thickening and the rest without. Higher neutrophil counts and a combined immune-inflammation index each tracked with thickening, as did uric acid and urea, while male sex and calcium pointed the other way. Adding the two blood markers to basic factors lifted prediction accuracy to an AUC of 0.816 in their model. Kidney stage did not change those links in the analysis.
pmc-13318848:
Antoine Christiaens and colleagues test, in 2026, whether a trial result on reducing blood pressure medicines in very old adults holds in routine English primary care. The OPTiMISE trial found that stopping one such drug did not worsen short-term control in people aged 80 and over. Trial participants, however, are usually fitter than typical patients.

The team rebuilt a target population from records of practices in England, covering nearly eight hundred thousand eligible adults. This real-world group was frailer and carried more illness than trial participants. Statistical weighting aligned the groups on likely trial entry. After calibration, reducing medication was not linked to higher risk of hospital stay or death, matching the trial's long-term findings. The authors judge the result transferable, with somewhat wider uncertainty.
pmc-13319048:
Weihan Kong and colleagues present a 2026 multi-omics study of polysaccharide build-up in the medicinal fungus Ganoderma tsugae. Fruiting bodies were grown on oak logs in a nature-mimicking setup. Five growth stages ran from early primordia to the end of spore release. Gene activity and metabolite profiles were measured together.

Crude polysaccharide content rose through the first three stages. It peaked at stage three, reaching 0.90 g per 100 g in their measurements, then declined. Analysis found 5,676 genes and 911 metabolites changing across stages. Starch and sucrose metabolism formed the core pathway for accumulation. Galactose metabolism played a supporting role in supplying building blocks. The authors name stage three as the key turning point for harvest timing research.
pmc-13319248:
Yuki Yoshida and colleagues evaluate, in 2026, a modified examination position for spotting early throat cancers during stomach endoscopy in high-risk patients. People treated for food pipe or throat cancer face raised risk of new cancers low in the throat. That area is hard to see because of its anatomy.

Forty-five patients were examined by the conventional method and then by the modified Killian method during the same session. Visibility scores for the lowest throat area rose with the modified method, and rose further when a straining manoeuvre was added. Viewing of neighbouring areas did not suffer. The method took longer, yet it found three early cancers the conventional pass had missed. No adverse events occurred, supporting wider use in this high-risk group.
pmc-13319948:
Ibrahim Ragab Eissa and co-authors study a collagen grip protein that keeps killer immune cells out of pancreas tumors in a 2026 article. This cancer wraps itself in dense scar like tissue that aids growth and blocks immune entry. The grip protein helps tumor cells cling to collagen, and the team asked whether it also shapes the immune scene around the tumor.

Tumors held far more of the protein than healthy pancreas tissue. When the protein was removed, tumor cells clung less, tumors grew slower, and far more killer cells moved in, while wiping out those cells restored growth. Loss of the protein also raised a signal that calls killer cells in and loosened collagen layout. A blocking drug copied those gains, which marks the protein as a care target.
pmc-13320348:
Stefanos Mastrotheodoros and co-authors follow teens into young adulthood in a 2026 study of social stress, body swelling, and low mood. Stress with parents and peers in the teen years lifts later low mood risk, and lasting low grade swelling may be the bridge. Gene tag scores for a swelling marker in spit were used to test that bridge over time.

Data came from 434 teens in a Dutch study, with stress drawn from rows with parents and from peer harm, tracked to age 27. Stress showed no link to the swelling scores at age 17 or 25 and no link to low mood at 27 in the main models. One side check hinted that harsh parenting, not peer harm, may touch one swelling score in mid teens only.
pmc-13320448:
Grace Marley and co-authors pilot a pharmacist led help service for addiction drug dispensing in a 2026 study from North Carolina. A key drug for opioid addiction is stocked unevenly at drug stores, held back by stigma and poor links with prescribers. Five community pharmacists took an online course plus about six one to one help meets with a peer coach and acted out patient visits before and after.

The pharmacists rated the coaching as fitting and useful because it bent to each store own snags, from staff talks and buyer limits to red flag checks and bridge scripts. A first in person visit plus short video follow ups was the favored shape. Talks with acted patients got better after coaching, though some stigmatizing words lingered.
pmc-13320548:
Heydar Ghiasi and Navid Ghavi Hossein-Zadeh run a 2026 computer simulation on breeding dairy cattle for both milk yield and fertility. Selecting hard for milk alone often harms fertility, since some gene markers push the two traits in opposite ways. The simulation used the direction of marker effects from genome wide studies to test smarter selection plans.

Markers with opposing effects created trade-offs and negative links between the traits, and single trait selection gave the most gain in that trait while hurting the other. Markers that favoured both traits allowed more balanced progress. The results stress that marker direction and shared gene action should guide breeding choices when two valued traits pull apart.
pmc-13321148:
Bernard Benichou and colleagues issue a 2026 correction to a first-in-human phase I study of VTX-PID, an enzyme made to clear antibodies that block gene therapy. The NAVIgATE study tested the IdeS enzyme in people with neutralising antibodies to an AAV vector. The correction fixes Figure 4 and an omission in the acknowledgments.

Panel 4C now shows the correct negativity threshold, set at below 1 to 5, and the legend now names that threshold. The figure tracks total and neutralising antibody levels up to day 90 after dosing, with early detail to day 13. The acknowledgments now credit writing assistance from Nicolisha Narainpersad of Parexel, which had been left out.
pmc-13322948:
Ruming Liu and co-authors mine United States safety reports for two cancer immune drugs, in a 2026 pharmacovigilance study of ipilimumab and nivolumab. They drew on the FDA adverse event system from 2004 to the end of 2024, covering each drug alone and the pair together.

Among more than 21 million reports in the database, the three groups held thousands linked to these drugs in the authors' counts. Harm timing mostly showed an early peak plus a long tail of risk, and patterns varied with age. Signals stood out for colitis, adrenal failure, cancer progression and death reports. Age and weight also shaped reporting, and the authors urge close watch during combined treatment.
pmc-13323148:
Yulong Li and co-authors model how childhood events relate to teen mental health, in a 2026 study of 700 adolescents. They measured adverse and positive childhood events. They also scored rumination, resilience and mental health with standard scales.

Adverse events linked to poorer mental health in their models. Rumination and resilience each carried part of that link. Together they formed a chain from adversity through rumination and resilience to mental health. Positive events softened several of those links, acting as a buffer. The authors suggest that schools and families watch for rumination. They also advise building resilience and adding positive events when spotting teens at risk.
pmc-13323248:
Huichao Zhang and co-authors pool how often delirium strikes hospital patients with heart failure, in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. Reports in single studies varied widely, so they searched ten databases to May 2026 and screened work with two independent reviewers.

Seventeen studies with 17,944 patients qualified, and the pooled incidence came to 18.5 percent of hospitalised heart failure patients in their random-effects model, with very high variation between studies. Subgroup checks pointed to year, country, age, sex, screening tool, sedative use, ventilation, disease class and past stroke or dementia as possible influences, yet no source explained the spread. The authors call for standard screening in heart failure wards.
pmc-13324448:
Mª Pilar González-Navarro and colleagues characterize drug-resistant Campylobacter coli from broiler chickens in a 2026 study from northeastern Spain. Campylobacter infection is the most reported zoonosis in the European Union, and poultry is the main source for people.

The team tested 40 strains from chicken gut and liver with broth dilution and whole genome sequencing. Every strain resisted ciprofloxacin, 95 percent resisted tetracycline, and 70 percent resisted several drugs. Gene findings matched the lab results closely, including the gyrA change behind fluoroquinolone resistance. Liver and gut strains looked alike, which flags chicken liver itself as a route of risk for resistant infections in consumers.
pmc-13325148:
Chanikan Sonklin and colleagues put freeze-dried cowpea fiber through lab digestion to test its health effects in a 2026 food study. Cowpea is an underused legume, and the fiber from low-grade pods is barely studied.

The cowpea powder held water at 4.27 g per g and oil at 3.90 g per g, showing strong binding power. Its insoluble fiber fraction was rich in pectic sugars. After mock stomach and gut digestion, antioxidant action rose as phenolic compounds were freed. The fiber itself was not fermented by test bacteria, yet the liquids left after fermentation calmed inflammation in immune cells. The team sees prebiotic and blood sugar promise worth deeper checks.
pmc-13325748:
Ghada AlSwayied, Rachael Frost, and Fiona L. Hamilton co-built a culturally fitted mobile health intervention to promote movement among midlife women going through menopause in Saudi Arabia. Their 2026 interview-based study, guided by a creative co-design plan for new healthcare ideas, brought partners jointly online to make and rank usable advice. Movement benefits during this change are well established, yet adherence stays low worldwide and especially in conservative settings.

The process proved feasible and acceptable. It yielded locally grounded guidance on program content, design features, and rollout, including digital skills and inclusion, linking with current health systems, clinician backing, and cross-sector links for uptake and lasting use. The authors present the work as one of the first structured joint co-design efforts for digital health in Saudi Arabia, offering a foundation for a population left out of research. Prototype development and feasibility testing come next.
pmc-13326948:
Yirong Wang and colleagues link brain waste clearance with sugar use in chronic disorders of consciousness in a 2026 imaging study. The glymphatic system flushes metabolic waste, but its state in these patients was unknown.

Combined PET and MRI scans covered 41 patients and 26 healthy controls. A diffusion index of perivascular flow, DTI-ALPS, ran far lower in patients. Within the patient group, the index tracked sugar uptake in frontal and parietal cortex, thalamus, brainstem, and striatum. The brainstem link was strongest, at r of 0.665 on the reported scale. Older age and lower parietal or brainstem uptake each predicted weaker clearance. Behavior scores showed no such tie.
pmc-13327248:
Tobias Walther and team built tiny gel beads made from DNA, with stiffness set by code design. Their 2026 paper fills a tool gap for studying cells in 3D growth and animal models. Gel beads are strong tools, but tuning their traits precisely has been hard. The beads form when two DNA star shapes and a linking DNA strand are packed by channels into oil-water drops. That gives control over size, stiffness, stretch response, and surface signals.

Shifting star arm counts tuned stiffness a thousandfold, from 30 pascals to 6.5 kilopascals, with distinct stretch response. A click-chemistry link of a fibronectin ring peptide let beads join fibroblast balls, where they held for days and were reshaped, showing live cell-bead interplay. The team puts the DNA beads forward as a flexible, body-friendly tool for probing and shaping tissue in 3D growth, with easy add-on functions and stimulus response.
pmc-13327848:
Leehyun Yoon and team tested how low mood signs and people troubles shape each other in teen girls over time. Their 2026 study trailed 543 girls from the Pittsburgh Girls Study across four rounds, mean ages 16.5 to 19.3 years, with self-reports of low mood signs and eight kinds of people troubles. Past work mostly weighed gaps between people, leaving within-person paths murky, so the team asked if links ran one way or both ways.

Within-person rises in low mood signs foretold later rises in over-caring and socially shy troubles, but those troubles did not foretell later low mood signs back. Low mood signs and bossy troubles, by contrast, foretold each other over time. The team flags bossy troubles as a possible fix target for breaking joint backing with low mood. Treating low mood signs may bring social gains by cutting later over-caring and shy troubles.
pmc-13328448:
Paul R Schreiber and Aladin El-Mafaalani reframe relations between public administrations in a 2026 conceptual article. Drawing on Luhmann's social systems theory, they use second-order observation, watching how analysts themselves watch, to ask what inter-administrative relations really are. Two traditions are placed side by side.

In actor-centered institutionalism, such relations appear through a success-or-failure lens, mostly as coordination problems or fixes for policy delivery. Through systems theory, administration becomes a decision system, and cross-boundary links are forms that keep separate decision worlds connectable amid complexity. The object changes with the lens, the authors show, so diagnoses and reforms follow from choices observers may not notice they made.
pmc-13329148:
Sanjay Arvind Krishna and colleagues describe long-term care of a rare eye socket disorder in a 2026 case report. The patient was a 58-year-old man who first had a blocked nose, then developed disease in the orbit. Tissue tests confirmed Rosai-Dorfman disease, a rare growth of immune cells that can mimic cancer or swelling from other causes.

Steroid treatment helped only in part. Guided radiation of 36 Gy in 20 sessions cleared the disease for five years. When it returned with a bulging eye and pressure on the optic nerve, a second course of 24 Gy in 12 sessions was given. Vision improved and scans stayed stable at two years, with no late radiation harm reported. The case supports repeat radiation when drugs fail.
pmc-13329948:
Elisa Bertulla and Edoardo Raposio assessed the online landscape of Brazilian Butt Lift information. Their 2026 study notes that the Brazilian Butt Lift has grown popular yet remains among the highest-risk aesthetic procedures, making clear information vital since patients often research online. Using Startpage to reduce bias, the team reviewed the first ten eligible English-language websites with readability indices, understandability scoring, JAMA quality criteria, and visibility estimates.

Readability for all websites passed the sixth-grade level, with a mean score of 21.68 on the scale used. Sixty percent of sites scored 83% on understandability, held back by long sentences and unexplained terms, while 40% met all criteria. Few sites gave references, author credentials, or publication dates, and readability linked only weakly with traffic. The team concludes that online Brazilian Butt Lift information is mostly hard to grasp and lacks vital quality markers.
pmc-13330248:
Hwasook Cho and colleagues test a stress reduction programme for middle-aged nurses in a 2026 pilot study. Lasting job stress harms nurse health and patient care, and may speed cell ageing. The 12-week programme mixed biofeedback, thought and behaviour teaching, mindfulness, and exercise. Sixty nurses aged 45 to 60 years from two large hospitals took part.

Groups held 31 nurses in the programme and 29 in control care. Felt stress fell more in the programme group, with clear group by time effects for stress and cortisol in the reported results. A protective enzyme marker rose, and telomere length differed between groups after care. Two markers showed no change. The authors read the signs as early protection worth larger trials.
pmc-13330548:
Aurore Ughetto and a large group study age effects in cardiogenic shock treated with small axial flow pumps in a 2026 report. Older patients are often missing from trials of temporary heart support. Records covered 1,043 patients across 11 European centres from 2010 to 2023, split into four age bands.

The oldest group held more women, more illness burden, and less intensive support than the youngest in the reported data. Death risk at 30 days and at 1 year rose for the two older bands after adjustment. Each added year of age raised 30-day risk by a small share in those models. Heart strength recovery fell with age. Age should shape support choices, the authors argue.
pmc-13330648:
Natalie J. Adamyk studies gender and emotional work at a Michigan regional burn in a 2026 article. Lakes of Fire is a yearly Burning Man style gathering where participants, called Burners, run the event as a community. Adamyk draws on 42 one-to-one interviews with men and women participants.

Women often took empowered mothering and caretaking roles that demanded heavy emotional work to hold the community together. Men rejected harsh macho styles and took softer identities, yet their emotional work leaned toward leading and managing. The two styles thus reinforced each other as separate domains. Such events can both challenge and copy wider gender patterns, Adamyk argues.
pmc-13330848:
Imane Maimoune and colleagues report the synthesis and crystal structure of a lidocaine-like compound in a 2026 article. Lidocaine numbs tissue by blocking sodium channels in excitable cells. The analogue swaps in a morpholine ring on an acetamide frame and was made by an alkylation reaction under reflux in toluene.

The phenyl ring tilts against the amide unit, with a measured angle of 66.59 degrees in the reported structure and a close second tilt nearby. Nitrogen to oxygen hydrogen bonds plus ring contacts link molecules into chains along one axis. Surface analysis showed hydrogen to hydrogen contacts made up nearly 70 percent of all close contacts in the crystal.
pmc-13331348:
Iain Armstrong and Peter Winter argue in a 2026 essay that artificial intelligence in digital health can misrecognise patients. Systems tend to know people through what is easiest to measure, while missing lived details that resist coding. Patient and caregiver accounts are often treated as lower-grade knowledge in calls on burden and benefit.

The risk takes differing forms in narrow prediction tools versus text-generating systems, the authors note. Reliance on cost, use, and adherence proxies can harden thin views of illness into software. Pulmonary hypertension serves as the case, with a patient-led outcome measure showing that measurement is never neutral. The core test is what experience stays visible, they argue.
pmc-13332848:
Soufyane Elkadiri and colleagues report a 2026 case of a giant scalp skin cancer that demanded wide surgery and staged rebuilding. Giant cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma of the scalp is rare and hard to treat, given its size, nearness to key nerves and vessels, and complex rebuilding needs. The patient was a 68-year-old woman with a 20-centimetre outward-growing occipito-parietal tumor that had evolved over one year. Biopsy confirmed a well-differentiated cancer, and imaging showed a mixed mass touching the skull without spread to nodes or distant sites.

Treatment was wide surgical removal, including the skull covering layer and scraping of the outer bone table, followed by staged rebuilding. Rebuilding used pedicled transposition flaps plus split-thickness skin grafts. Pathology confirmed a well-differentiated invasive cancer at stage III with clear margins. Outcomes were satisfactory in both function and appearance.
pmc-13333148:
Hajar Fahli and colleagues report a 2026 case of a chronic spine inflammation disease presenting as severe spinal curvature without pain, plus a literature review. The disease is a chronic condition that inflames the spine and pelvic joints mainly. Progressive structural change can form bony bridges, fuse the spine, and produce the classic bamboo spine look. The patient was a 32-year-old man with progressive spinal curvature and cosmetic concern but no significant current pain.

The deformity had grown since adolescence, starting at age fifteen with alternating hip pain. Examination showed marked upper-back hunching, front-back imbalance, left shoulder elevation, and right pelvic tilt, with severely limited spinal movement. Imaging showed a bamboo spine with fusion of back spine bones. The case shows that advanced disease can present through curvature alone, and it reviews how such painless, severe curvature should be assessed.
pmc-13333348:
Thurston Lacalli returns to what consciousness is for in a 2026 theory paper. He tests his ideas against a model in which conscious feelings are made by local brain modules, acting locally. Vision is his test case: any theory must explain how a flat display of the world arises.

For the model to work, what you see must depend on where each module sits in the body. The layout of sight itself then carries meaning. Controlled gaze becomes a tool for logging key facts no unconscious process can match. It also helps give experience its sense of knowing. He backs Merker's view linking gaze control to the work of consciousness. He ties the months babies spend sharpening sight to the learning of agency. His model credits attention control plus memory writing for why consciousness pays off. Species that barely use sight may still carry a position-based sense through other channels.
pmc-13333448:
Alexandra Lianou and a large team systematically review extracellular vesicles in newborn health in a 2026 synthesis. These tiny membrane-wrapped parcels shuttle proteins and genetic material between cells, and researchers have begun finding them at work in the first days of life.

Searching PubMed and Scopus between August and November 2025 under a registered protocol, the team included 43 mostly observational studies of term and preterm babies. The studies were generally small to moderate in size and varied in setting. Vesicles were drawn most often from umbilical cord or peripheral blood, sampled at birth or soon after. Across many newborn conditions, the vesicles were consistently present and biologically active, supporting roles both as drivers of disease processes and as candidate markers for diagnosis and outlook. The authors caution that methods differ too much between studies to settle clinical use, and they call for larger, standardized work.
pmc-13333648:
How well do birth-care providers keep what training taught them? Beatrice Erastus Mwilike and co-authors checked in a 2026 mixed-methods follow-up study in Tanzania, focusing on the Helping Mothers Survive and Helping Babies Survive modules.

The training reached providers through the 50,000 Happy Birthdays project, run from 2018 to 2020 by the Tanzanian Midwives Association with partners. Researchers compared earlier post-test scores with follow-up scores for 210 providers in the Tanga, Geita, and Katavi regions. Written tests covered four knowledge areas and checklists covered five skill areas, while interviews probed what helps or hinders retention. The largest knowledge drop appeared in pre-eclampsia care, a finding that can shape refresher training.
pmc-13333748:
Yuanxin Shao and co-authors paired machine learning with resting-state functional MRI in a 2026 imaging study of post-stroke depression. Depression after stroke is common, but its brain activity pattern is still only partly mapped.

Fifty patients with post-stroke depression and fifty matched healthy controls had resting-state scans. The team took four kinds of measures covering local activity, link strength, and network links across brain regions. LASSO screening narrowed the differing traits, and nine classifiers were trained and set against each other, with SHAP values showing which traits drove the best model. Patients showed spread differences involving cingulate, thalamic, prefrontal, insular, and visual areas. Such readable models could in time support earlier spotting of depression after stroke.
pmc-13334848:
Yufan Sun and co-authors tested a chicken-origin probiotic strain, Ligilactobacillus agilis R22, in a 2026 study hunting for antibiotic options in poultry. The strain was put through lab tests, genome and metabolite mapping, and live bird trials.

R22 grew strongly, tolerated lab-made gut conditions, and showed strong germ-killing activity. Its genome carried multiple probiotic-linked genes, no virulence genes, and machinery to synthesize nutrients the host can use. Fed to broilers, it boosted growth and gut structure while shifting gut microbes and metabolites. A chick infection model with Salmonella Pullorum and a fecal transplant test in mice probed how protection works. The joint evidence presents R22 as a candidate feed additive that could cut antibiotic reliance in chicken farming.
pmc-13336448:
Amin Hajarian, Jiwoo Seo, and SungWoo Nam measured how phonon polaritons in hexagonal boron nitride shift with layer count in a 2026 near-field spectroscopy study. These hybrid light-matter waves are tightly confined, but their resonance energies versus thickness had never been mapped directly.

Using photo-induced force microscopy on flakes from about 10 to 60 layers, the team recorded the first systematic spectra. The two main Reststrahlen bands moved in opposite directions: the in-plane resonance blue-shifted as layers added, while the out-of-plane resonance red-shifted and grew stronger, even as the in-plane peak weakened and broadened. Knowing exactly where resonances sit at each thickness helps engineers design infrared nanophotonic devices from this van der Waals material.
pmc-13336748:
Jin Hyeok Yang and co-authors review how lithium-ion batteries fail and how to make them safer in a 2026 article. These batteries pack much energy but can catch fire or explode when heat runs away. The review follows that cascade step by step, from surface breakdown to separator shrinkage, fluid breakdown, and oxygen release from the cathode.

Safety fixes are sorted by scale. Material tweaks include coated cathodes, ceramic separators, and flame-resistant additives. Cell, pack, and system designs add structure and smarter controls, including AI tools and digital twin models that predict trouble. The authors propose matching stage-specific warning signs to fixes at each level, so high-energy batteries can be safer by design.
pmc-13337748:
Daniel Huth leads a 2026 online experiment testing a video meant to raise COVID-19 vaccine acceptance. Worry and low risk awareness were common during the pandemic, even among people with mental disorders who faced higher risk. The video aimed to inform that group in particular.

A total of 639 adults in Germany were assigned at random to watch the video or receive nothing. The video raised awareness of why vaccination matters for people with mental disorders and raised perceived severity in the reported results. It also prompted more careful decision making. Willingness to vaccinate and vaccine beliefs did not shift, though people reporting a mental disorder felt more susceptible afterward.
pmc-13339148:
Isobelle F. McClements, Megan E. Driscoll, and Brett P. Fors start controlled polymer growth from amine groups in a 2026 study. Light-controlled atom transfer polymerization normally needs alkyl halide starters, limiting grafts and conjugates. Amines are common on surfaces and biomolecules, so starting there widens use.

An iridium light catalyst stripped nitrogen from activated primary amines to launch chains, with an added bromide source. Products showed narrow size spread near 1.2 to 1.3 and chain-end fidelity above 99 percent in the reported measures. Masses matched targets closely. The route opens advanced polymer shapes built directly from everyday functional groups.
pmc-13339948:
Jan Boeckhaus and colleagues test urine protein ratios as predictors of kidney decline in Alport syndrome in a 2026 study. This inherited disease scars kidneys at very different speeds, and early warning helps time treatment. Records for 127 patients from two centers were modeled.

Follow-up averaged 42 months, and 24 percent lost kidney function rapidly in the reported grouping. Albumin-to-creatinine ratio correlated most strongly with yearly function loss at minus 0.435 in the reported value and stayed predictive after adjustment. Urinary IgG was most sensitive for spotting decliners. Simple urine tests may flag patients needing closer care.
pmc-13340148:
Wes Baumgartner leads a 2026 reference chapter on lesions of fish special senses for toxicology pathologists. Part of the INHAND standardization series, it covers eye, inner ear labyrinth, lateral line, smell, and taste organs in teleost fish. Anatomy differences across species complicate reading tissue harm.

Introductory material compares fish senses with those of rodents and humans, then lists microscopic findings in a standard format. The fish eye, for example, uses a spherical lens unlike higher vertebrates as detailed. Standard names and criteria help labs worldwide describe the same change the same way in safety studies.
pmc-13340248:
Full genome sequencing of 24 gram-negative bloodstream isolates from Lebanon anchors a 2026 study led by Carni Boujanian. Six species showed, among them E. coli and Klebsiella, and testing showed broad resistance to beta-lactam and other drug classes.

Extended-spectrum beta-lactamase output showed up in 62.5% of isolates, while 37.5% counted as carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales. In E. coli and K. pneumoniae, resistance rode mainly on plasmids carrying ESBL and carbapenemase genes, whereas Citrobacter relied more on chromosome-based routes. One colistin-resistant isolate carried a frameshift change in mgrB rather than mcr genes. The findings give Lebanon rare gene-level detail on hard-to-treat invasive bacteria.
pmc-13340648:
Reza Hosseinpour and colleagues reported a penetrating neck injury case in 2026 with delayed oesophageal perforation, a major cause of late death after such injuries. Neck wounds carry high morbidity because vital structures crowd the cervical region, and oesophageal injuries are often missed at first. A previously healthy 17 year old boy arrived three hours after a Zone II gunshot wound to the right neck.

He was haemodynamically stable and initial imaging showed no abnormality, yet fever and related signs twelve hours later revealed perforation. The case stresses repeat assessment and a low threshold for oesophageal investigation after neck gunshot wounds, even when the first evaluation looks reassuring.
pmc-13341048:
Güven Soner and colleagues asked non religious patients in Türkiye in 2026 about care and mental health. How belief, or lack of it, shapes care matters for fair, open health services. The study talked in depth, face to face, with 17 people in Samsun from June to August 2025, and grouped their words by theme.

Five themes came out: whole person health views, identity and invisibility, mixed care experiences, fragile mental health in context, and hopes for a fair, professional system.
