Many hid their non religious identity, and those who shared it often met judgement or unasked religious advice. Such care eroded trust and at times led people to shun care.
pmc-13342048:
Foot angle timing separates strong water polo treading, in a 2026 biomechanics study by Eisuke Kawai and colleagues. Twenty-two male university players kept up continuous eggbeater kicking as underwater cameras and pressure sensors recorded foot motion and force distribution.

Players were split into upper and lower groups by propulsive force norms from an independent dataset. Time-series statistics found group differences in dynamic pressure and foot angles concentrated in the out-kick phase, while foot speed and acceleration did not differ. How the foot is oriented, and exactly when, may matter more than how fast it moves, a coaching cue for a skill that keeps players upright.
pmc-13345648:
Guopeng Han and co-authors report a new crystal form of a lithium solid electrolyte in 2026. The triclinic variant of Li7Si2S7I carries a touch of chlorine and reshuffles its silicon building blocks into alternating silicon-free and silicon-rich layers, raising the question of whether lithium still races through it.

Simulations on the measured structure predict conductivity of 0.019 siemens per centimeter with a low activation energy near 0.16 electronvolts, matching the known monoclinic form within error. Sixteen lithium sites create many redundant low-energy paths. The skeleton of sulfur and iodine, it seems, protects fast ion travel even when cation order scrambles, a resilience useful for solid-state battery design.
pmc-13346848:
Rasha Sayed Asaad and Marwa Beleidy compare three ways to anchor a three-unit zirconia bridge, in a lab study from 2026. Full-coverage retainers were set against two endocrown designs on premolar and molar abutments, each bridge was copied onto resin models. Gaps at the edges were measured before and after heat and load cycling.

Every design showed wider gaps after aging, yet the plain butt-joint endocrown kept the smallest gap both before and after the cycling treatment. Full-coverage bridges resisted breaking best, while the butt-joint design broke at the lowest loads, and cracks clustered at the connectors. Fit and strength thus pull in opposite directions for these designs.
pmc-13347348:
Zouwei Liu and colleagues review how fine metal masks for OLED screens are made, in a technology review from 2026. Masks pattern pixels during vacuum coating, yet making millions of tiny clean holes in Invar alloy foil stays a bottleneck for sharp displays. So three routes are weighed, covering chemical etching, electroforming, and laser cutting.

Etching alone is mature and fast but wastes material through missed or half-cut holes, electroforming promises finer shapes yet struggles with alloy control and cost. Lasers have reached 3000 PPI detail but cut too slowly for whole masks. The authors propose etching first, then laser repair of bad holes, with four technical hurdles named for that hybrid route.
pmc-13347948:
Nathan K. Schaefer, Bryan J. Pavlovic, Matthew T. Schmitz, and Alex A. Pollen release CellBouncer, a toolkit for untangling pooled single-cell data, in a study from 2026. Pooling cells from many donors or species saves time and cuts batch noise. Yet software must sort cells back to sources, spot stray RNA, and count doublets before any biology can be read.

The toolkit sorts mixed species and donors, finds unknown mitochondrial types, reads treatment or guide barcodes, and beats rival tools on those jobs in the reported tests. Stray RNA shares per cell and per donor are also estimated, and fused human-chimp cells then revealed a growth edge for human mitochondria plus signs of cross-species mismatch.
pmc-13348648:
Ozkan Aba and co-authors tracked in 2026 brain pressure signs and brain oxygen during keyhole belly surgery. They asked whether these signs forecast early thinking problems after surgery. Carbon dioxide inflation of the belly can raise brain pressure. Thinking problems after general anaesthesia remain a worry.

Fifty patients aged 20 to 60 had keyhole belly surgery under general anaesthesia. Optic nerve sheath width and regional brain oxygen were read at five points, from pre-induction to post-deflation. Belly pressure was read too. Thinking was tested with the Mini-Mental State Exam pre-surgery and one day later. Linking noninvasive brain reads to thinking change could help anaesthetists spot at-risk patients while surgery is still under way.
pmc-13348948:
Rohit S Deshpande and colleagues report robotic removal of a rare kidney renin tumour that, unusually, caused no symptoms, in a case report from 2026. A 56-year-old woman with thyroid underactivity had a 2.7 by 2.5 cm right kidney mass found on a routine check. Robot-assisted partial removal kept the rest of the kidney while tissue and stain tests confirmed a juxtaglomerular cell tumour.

Such tumours usually strike young patients with high blood pressure, low potassium, and high renin from hormone spill, none of which appeared in this older, quiet case. Clean margins and a classic stain pattern settled the call, and sparing surgery is backed where the lump allows it.
pmc-13349748:
Xiyin Guan and co-authors model brain injury risk after a second carbon-ion course for returned throat cancer, in a study issued in 2026. Records for 89 patients retreated from 2016 to 2020 were split into training and validation groups. First-course dose maps were warped onto new scans. That step built single-course and combined dose risk models for temporal lobe injury.

Injury appeared in 27 patients, a share of 30.3 percent, mostly on one side and often silent on scans alone. Both lead models sorted risk well, with AUC values of 0.8450 and 0.8225 in the reported fits. Carbon tolerance ran about 20 percent above photon values, guiding safer retreatment caps.
pmc-13349848:
Alia Al-Mohtaseb and co-authors built a deep learning system in 2026 to spot intestinal metaplasia, a precancerous stomach change, in biopsy images. Their model, called CNXTGeM, was trained on 1,037 stained samples from a hospital in Elazığ, split by patient to avoid leakage.

The design mixes a ConvNeXt-Tiny backbone with pooling and attention parts meant to sharpen pattern reading. It was also tested on a public set of 33,284 image patches, and three explanation methods showed which tissue areas drove its calls. Reliable automatic screening could help pathologists catch a step on the road to stomach cancer earlier and more evenly.
pmc-13349948:
Kexin Niu and co-authors tested low-dose CT scanning for colorectal cancer in a 2026 prospective study. Long abdominal scans help stage the disease, but patients needing repeat imaging absorb large amounts of radiation.

Each of 203 patients with proven cancer received a normal-dose scan and a scan at one tenth of the exposure settings. A new AI-based rebuilding method was applied to the low-dose images and compared with standard rebuilding. Readers judged image quality and accuracy for judging spread through the bowel wall and into nearby lymph nodes. If low-dose images stay reliable, patients could be scanned more safely and more often.
pmc-13350148:
Eisuke Hosoya and a team of chemists isolated a new plant alkaloid in a 2026 study of Yunnan Kopsia arborea, a tree in the dogbane family. The compound, kopsiyunnanine N, joins three building blocks from different alkaloid families into one molecule, a combination never reported before.

Its three parts come from eburnan, vinylquinoline, and aspidosperman units, linked in part by a rare ring containing oxygen and nitrogen. Spectra revealed the layout, and X-ray crystallography settled the full three-dimensional arrangement. Such intricate natural molecules stretch chemists' understanding of how plants assemble complex structures and can hint at new drug scaffolds.
pmc-13350248:
Sasho Stoleski and fellow editors introduced a 2026 research collection on environmental hazards in the modern workplace, gathering 46 manuscripts from 264 researchers. Classic workplace health focused on injuries and toxic exposures in heavy industry.

Today's workers face layered risks at once: physical, chemical, mental, ergonomic, organisational, and digital. Contributions range from data-driven safety methods to whole-body vibration and chronic back pain among transport and heavy equipment workers. The editors argue these combined pressures shape health, wellbeing, productivity, and long-term quality of life, so safety work must widen beyond the factory floor hazards of the past century.
pmc-13351148:
Ross Jones and David Nay weighed in 2026 outcomes from eras before and after one surgeon adopted muscle signal checks as an objective end point for spinal decompression. Adequacy of decompression is most often judged by sight and touch, leaving no physiologic proof that nerves are truly freed.

In a look-back era-based cohort of 600 consecutive adult decompression patients, 300 before adoption and 300 after stable full muscle signal use, the post-adoption era used threshold-guided decompression aimed at 2.0 milliamperes or less. The main end point was unplanned return to surgery within ninety days, with incidental dural tear and three-month pain as confirmatory end points, adjusted for life and procedural traits. The weigh-up tests whether objective muscle signals lift surgery completeness.
pmc-13351248:
Dan Lu and co-authors issued a correction in 2026 to their study of rosuvastatin protecting the blood-brain barrier after experimental stroke. One panel of a key figure, an iron staining image in Figure 2G, had been assembled wrongly during preparation, and the correction supplies the fixed figure.

They also measured two biomarkers: lipopolysaccharide, a bacterial wall fragment, and nerve growth factor, a signal at the gut-brain border. Earlier work had left these links in heavier adults unclear.
pmc-13397648:
Satishkumar Singh and co-authors hunt for blood-vessel growth receptors that could serve as drug targets in mantle cell lymphoma. The gene pattern behind its vessel growth had stayed poorly mapped.

Four code for surface receptors (FGFR1, VEGFR1, VEGFR2 and PDGFRB) that receive growth signals and sit within drug reach. The team then checked those targets across four lab models, including tumour material taken from patients, to judge real treatment promise.
pmc-13397748:
Deeptima Jaiswar and Manjusha Dixit review molecular convergence in gallbladder cancer in a 2026 paper. This highly aggressive cancer shows up late with few options and grim survival, and prior studies chased lone genetic or epigenetic events rather than joined mechanisms.

Genes often altered — TP53, KRAS, ERBB2, CDKN2A — hit Ras, PI3K, Wnt, and p53 cascades, with aberrant ERK firing as a pivotal driver. Epigenetic shifts, non-coding RNAs, and immune microenvironment factors add complexity. The review folds genomic, epigenomic, and immunologic data into one landscape to speed biomarker and therapy discovery.
pmc-13399448:
Carina F. Mugal and Marie Sémon introduce a PLOS Biology study on how the male and female germlines evolve at different speeds, in a 2026 primer. The study they discuss, by Hariyani and colleagues, built single-nucleus atlases of ovaries and testes from two strains of Drosophila melanogaster and one of its close relative D. simulans. In the ovary it rose in early germarium stages and in late follicle cells. Expression changed faster in male than in female gamete formation. pmc-13399848:
Joshua T. Bram and colleagues, with senior author Peter D. Fabricant, describe a biological middle path for treating osteochondritis dissecans of the elbow's capitellum in adolescent athletes, in a 2026 technique article. Their method spreads a scaffold of extracellular matrix mixed with the patient's own concentrated bone marrow over the lesion.

The example case is an 11-year-old right-handed pitcher with a loose body visible on imaging. Lesions that are larger, uncontained, or deeply bony still go to plug transfer instead. Promising early clinical results are reported for the scaffold approach. The authors frame it as a favorable compromise: more biological potential than marrow stimulation alone, less collateral damage than grafting.
pmc-13400448:
Jiyeon Oh and co-authors map, in 2026, the global burden of melanoma skin cancer tied to ultraviolet radiation across 185 countries. Sun exposure is a proven, changeable cause of melanoma, yet worldwide estimates of its share were dated. The team also projected the burden forward to 2050.

Drawing on cancer registries and death records, they estimated about 330,000 new melanoma cases in 2022. Roughly 88 percent could be tied to ultraviolet exposure under their reference method. Rates were highest in wealthy countries, notably in Oceania and Northern Europe, while death relative to cases was worst in poorer settings. By 2050, sun-linked cases are set to climb fastest where development levels are low or middle.
pmc-13400948:
Yuxin Liu and a large team set out, in 2026, the protocol for a phase two trial in advanced liver cancer combining several treatments in sequence. Stage C disease with tumor growth into the portal vein or limited spread elsewhere is often inoperable and hard to treat, even with modern immunotherapy combinations.

Patients with preserved liver function will receive chemotherapy infused directly into the liver artery, followed in each cycle by two antibody drugs and a vessel-blocking antibody. After up to four cycles, those without progression get focused high-dose radiotherapy to remaining targets. Patients reaching complete response continue systemic therapy alone. The single-center, single-arm study will characterize safety, feasibility and efficacy of the sequence.
pmc-13401748:
Barbara Freire and colleagues report a 2026 case of Waugh's syndrome in an adult, the rare pairing of intestinal malrotation with one segment of bowel telescoping into another. Malrotation is a birth defect of gut positioning usually found in infancy, and adult telescoping, called intussusception, usually signals an underlying lesion.

Their patient was a 76-year-old man with two weeks of intermittent abdominal pain, more frequent bowel movements, and weight loss, plus a palpable abdominal mass. Ultrasound and contrast CT showed ileocolic intussusception together with malrotation. Surgery confirmed both, finding abnormally positioned bowel and a telescoped segment that could not be undone. He underwent removal of the right colon with its mesentery and a new join between small bowel and colon. Tissue study found an inflammatory fibroid polyp acting as the lead point that dragged the bowel inward.
pmc-13401848:
Xiao Yang and co-authors propose a new computational method for spatial transcriptomics in a 2026 paper. It blends deep learning with Bayesian statistics to estimate which cell types occupy each spot in a tissue sample. Mainstream spatial techniques measure gene activity with location intact, but rarely say how uncertain those estimates are.

It uses sparse shortcut points and standard spatial kernels, optionally joined with a Matern kernel. That learned pattern becomes an informed prior for spot-by-spot cell proportions, which are then estimated by a negative-binomial sampling routine with automatic tuning and convergence checks. The authors benchmarked the method against existing approaches on datasets including pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma tissue, arguing that explicit uncertainty makes deconvolution results safer to interpret.
pmc-13402348:
Al Mejamai and co-authors probe, in 2026, the metal-insulator transition in five-layer platinum diselenide, a flat semiconductor whose bandgap of 0.1 electron volts places it near the semimetal edge. Whether such changes are driven by electron interactions or by disorder is debated. Scaling supported interaction-dominated transport in that regime. Below 50 kelvin, a disorder-related energy scale emerged, matching flow through puddles. The authors conclude that in high-mobility devices, disorder stays relevant at the lowest carrier levels, challenging a purely interaction-driven picture.
pmc-13402648:
Arman Norouzi-Ghalehbala and colleagues test whether D-limonene, a citrus compound, adds protection after surgery for undescended testes in young rats. Surgery, called orchiopexy, is the standard fix, yet it often fails to restore full testicular function. Twenty-four male rats were split into a sham group, a surgery-only group, and two surgery groups given D-limonene at 50 or 100 milligrams per kilogram.

Treated rats showed stronger antioxidant defenses, including higher total antioxidant capacity, and the higher dose cut the damage marker malondialdehyde more and lifted superoxide dismutase activity further. Testis size measures, sperm-making scores, and tubule structure all improved, cell death markers fell, and testosterone and sperm quality rose. Recovery stayed partial: no measure fully normalized. The authors back D-limonene as a supporting add-on after surgery, not a cure by itself.
pmc-13402848:
Yansong Liu and colleagues test patient-specific 3D-printed guides for cutting out sacral tumors and rebuilding the pelvis, among the hardest operations in bone oncology. The sacrum sits deep, wrapped in nerves and vessels, and freehand cuts often miss margins or bleed heavily. Their review covered 19 patients with tumors spanning the upper sacrum, ten guided by printed templates and nine done freehand, between 2006 and 2020.

Guided operations ran shorter by roughly two hours on average, lost about a liter less blood, and needed fewer than half the fluoroscopy shots. Cut angle error dropped from 6.79 to 3.33 degrees on average, and hospital stay fell from about 18 days to under 11 days. Complication rates stayed similar between groups. The authors back printed guides as a precision and safety upgrade for sacral surgery.
pmc-13403048:
Ayalew Sirbemo Degebo and co-authors review the role of pharmacists in the mpox response, from vaccine fridges to community trust. Pharmacists anchor supportive care, infection prevention, and supply of vaccines, disinfectants, reagents, and protective gear. They also watch for drug harms, a duty teams call pharmacovigilance. In Africa, mpox vaccines still fail to reach 1.2 billion people, so that equity work is front-line public health.

Their thematic synthesis of database literature and technical reports maps both reach and limits: uneven clinical authority, thin outbreak training, and exclusion from planning tables blunt pharmacist impact. The authors propose fuller joining into response teams, stronger training in infectious disease and safety monitoring, and larger roles in surveillance and cost evidence. Supply chains strengthened by inventory discipline, local production, and digital tools feature throughout.
pmc-13403148:
Holly Coffey, Kshitij Arora, and Matthew J Giefer report a 12-year-old boy with juvenile polyposis syndrome. A routine surveillance colonoscopy turned up a colonic ganglioneuroma in him, a benign nerve-cell tumor almost never seen in this condition. Such tumors in children usually ride with named syndromes like MEN2B or neurofibromatosis type 1. His testing and examination showed no trace of those. He had already lost a colon segment to heavy polyp burden.

The lone ascending colon polyp retrieved proved to be the ganglioneuroma. Genetic testing found several variants of uncertain significance in the boy, two shared with his mother. None explained the picture cleanly. The authors argue juvenile polyposis is more varied than its label suggests and may spawn unusual polyp types. So the standard three-year scope interval may be too loose when genetics stay unexplained.
pmc-13403448:
Ellen K. K. Jepsen led a 2026 pilot study of a skills program for adults with complex dissociative disorders. Thirty patients spent three months in hospital care built around the program. They then kept working through its topics for nine months in local outpatient care.

The program holds 30 topics, each with a short video, a script, and written plus hands-on tasks. Patients finished 19 topics on average over the year. Scores for coping skills, trauma stress, and self-kindness rose a lot, while dissociation scores rose only a little in the good direction. People who finished more topics tended to gain the most.
pmc-13404248:
Yuto Kaneda and a multicenter team looked back in 2026 at seven leukemia patients who share a rare splice variant in the ABL1 gene. The variant drops a chunk of the gene yet keeps its reading frame. It turned up during routine checks in patients whose response to treatment ran oddly slow.

All seven patients reached normal blood counts on standard blocker drugs. Deeper gene-level responses came, though often late. None moved to an advanced phase during a median follow-up of 39 months. The variant seems inactive as an enzyme, so its presence alone should not be read as drug resistance. Bigger shared studies with finer measures are needed.
pmc-13404348:
Bevily Nukeri, Velibanti Sukati, and Pheagane Motsime William Nkoana charted sight faults in 2026 among adults at three private eye practices in Witbank, South Africa. Records for 1,245 patients were picked at even steps from clinic files. Ages ran from 18 to 101 years, with a mean near 44.6 years in the group.

About 66 percent of patients had a focusing fault of some kind. Astigmatism led the list at 43 percent, ahead of short sight and long sight. Most patients with weak unaided sight had astigmatism as well. Over 70 percent of those aged 35 and up needed reading help. Sex and ethnic group showed no firm links.
pmc-13405548:
Yuwei Ren and colleagues combine genome and gene-activity data to find heart-related selection marks in Wuzhishan pigs, in 2026 work. The Hainan minipig is prized for meat quality and used as a model for human heart disease. Knowing which genes breeding has shaped could serve both farming and medicine.

Whole-genome resequencing was paired with heart RNA data from five growth stages. Three screening pipelines together nominated 236 distinct genes. Of these, 52 were highly active in the heart and 44 changed between growth stages in the reported analysis. Enrichment in known pathways supports the list, which the authors offer as targets for breeding and model development.
pmc-13406748:
Yingxin Zhou, Leilei Shi and Weichen Wang engineer miniature antibodies against interleukin-33, an alarm signal in inflammation, in a 2026 study. Nanobodies are small binding proteins drawn here from a synthetic display library. Joining two different binders into one molecule can grip the target more firmly.

Five single nanobodies bound the target at low concentrations in instrument measurements. The paired construct Nb1-Nb2 held on longest, thanks to a much slower release rate. The two partners bind mostly separate patches, tests suggested, so they do not block each other. In a scratch healing test with colon cancer cells, the pair blunted the closure that interleukin-33 normally speeds.
pmc-13406848:
Alessandra Telesca and colleagues pooled trial results in 2026 on brain stimulation for chronic primary pain. These are long-lasting pain conditions with no clear tissue cause. They gathered randomised trials published up to February 2025 that measured pain, emotional distress, and daily disability.

Fifty-four studies qualified, covering 1,371 people given real stimulation and 1,103 given a sham version. Real stimulation eased all three core problems right after treatment, with gains still present a month later. Benefits faded when pain had lasted longer, a pattern seen across outcomes at follow-up. The authors call for shared treatment protocols and more consistent follow-up timing in future trials.
pmc-13407848:
Mohammad Matin Behzadi and co-authors simulate, in 2026, diamond-shaped pores with effectively no depth, a geometry meant to free DNA sequencing sensors from ultrathin membranes. The pores form where triangular microchannels cross, and the team modelled electrical transport through them with finite-element software, checking the model against experiments to within a few percent.

Beyond a critical channel length, conductance scaled in a predictable, linear way with pore diameter, corner angle, and salt concentration, yielding a formula to estimate pore size without microscopy. Electric fields peaked at defined critical points on the pore's mid-plane, growing stronger with wider angles and narrower pores. Equations for maximum field and effective pore length follow from voltage and geometry. The authors frame the results as design groundwork for future sensing devices.
pmc-13408048:

Lenvatinib, a targeted pill, plus pembrolizumab, a checkpoint antibody, showed activity in a prior phase II trial. Median time before progression was 4.0 months and median survival 9.6 months. Side effects were generally manageable, with one severe gut inflammation case. Small and retrospective, the series supports feasibility and argues for prospective trials.
pmc-13408148:
Claire Stokes and Phillip Good argue, in 2026, that the future of cancer trials for the frailest patients is local. Decentralised trials and teletrials move study activities into homes and local communities instead.

Their experience suggests mitigations work: careful trial selection, rigorous screening and support, and close liaison with treating oncologists and palliative teams. Round-the-clock clinical phone support helps too, along with accessible IT help in working hours and local coordinators where available. Reach can grow, they contend, without surrendering rigour or safety.
pmc-13408848:

Temperature becomes the dial that switches its personality.

Run hot, it answers a one-percent hydrogen challenge with a response in the thousands and stays nearly linear up to two and a half percent. pmc-13409148:

pmc-13410548:

pmc-13410848:

pmc-13410948:

pmc-13411148:

pmc-13412548:

pmc-13412648:

pmc-13413948:

pmc-13414248:

pmc-13414648:

The map gives new researchers a quick view of active fronts.
pmc-13415748:

Genetic testing still guides family screening best.
pmc-13415848:

pmc-13416648:

Decision support, not replacement, is the fair current role.
pmc-13417248:

pmc-13417448:

pmc-13417648:

pmc-13417848:

pmc-13418048:

pmc-13418148:

These measures may sharpen follow up planning.
pmc-13418748:

pmc-13419948:

pmc-13420348:

The review portion of the paper gathers the traps that delay this diagnosis in young patients. Persistent pain that outlasts a fracture timeline deserves a second look, the authors argue. Their management summary gives hand surgeons a checklist for the next puzzling case.
pmc-13420648:

pmc-13420848:
Rui Zhou and colleagues prove that a common fungus, Alternaria alternata, causes black spot on roses, then screen rose collections for resistance. Black spot strips leaves and weakens plants worldwide, worst in humid weather. The team recovered the fungus from three rose cultivars and confirmed its identity by shape and gene sequencing.

Re-inoculation reproduced the disease, closing the proof loop for causation. Field scoring of 48 rose accessions split them into 8 resistant types, 19 in the middle band, and 21 highly susceptible types in the counts reported. Leaf wax and lignin, the plant's structural defenses, were examined for their part in holding the fungus back. Breeders gain both a confirmed enemy and a ranked shelf of planting stock to cross from.
pmc-13421448:
Sandeep and colleagues tested in 2026 how much short carbon fiber strengthens a nylon and Teflon blend used for engineering parts. An 80-20 blend served as the base, with fiber loadings of 10, 20, and 30 percent molded by twin-screw extrusion and injection molding, then pulled, bent, and struck in lab tests.

Strength rose with fiber content up to 20 percent, which beat the neat blend by 10 percent in tension, 25 percent in flexure, and 41 percent in impact. Loadings above 30 percent weakened the material and melt flow kept falling. Designers gain a sweet spot for strong, heat-resistant parts without overloading the blend.
pmc-13422848:
Budnik and colleagues test in 2026 whether proteins in urine can flag early disease across many conditions at once. Urine is cheap and painless to collect, yet most protein studies chase one disease at a time.

The case-control study analyzed 264 samples from a Ukrainian biobank. They covered patients with seven cancers, multiple sclerosis, or a metabolic liver disease, plus 66 healthy controls. All were profiled on a platform measuring thousands of proteins at once, by staff blinded to diagnosis. Panels of five to seven proteins beat any single protein. Accuracy was high for most diseases, with the best panels separating ovarian cancer patients from controls almost perfectly and the weakest result, still solid, coming for multiple sclerosis. The authors stress that these accuracies are upper-bound estimates from an exploratory study and demand prospective testing.
pmc-13422948:
Allan Wilson and seven colleagues present a 2026 model-based evaluation of AI-assisted digital cytology for the NHS cervical screening programmes in England and Scotland. Cytology there serves as a triage step after a positive HPV test. The team compares the Genius digital system against manual microscopy for the time needed to review and report slides.

A decision-tree model, built from published evidence and expert input, costed the work. Handling 479,125 slides a year in England would take 31,842 staff hours with digital help, against 103,151 hours by microscope. Mean review time fell from 12.9 minutes per slide to 4.0 minutes. The authors note the model covers slide review only, not training or new equipment.
pmc-13423048:
Mapaseka Seheri and five co-authors set out a protocol for a scoping review of efforts to widen access to health care for people living with rare diseases in Africa. Patients there, they note, face late diagnoses, few treatment options, and fragmented services, yet the interventions tried so far have never been mapped as a whole.

Following the Arksey and O'Malley framework with later refinements, the reviewers will search PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science, plus grey sources such as conference proceedings and institutional reports. Eligible work must come from Africa, date from 2004 to 2024, and target access to care. Two reviewers will screen records independently, chart the data, and consult stakeholders before reporting.
pmc-13423148:
Kaddas and colleagues studied in 2026 whether a simple blood ratio can flag severe gut disease in preterm babies. Necrotising enterocolitis is a dangerous bowel disease of premature infants that can worsen fast. The team reviewed 47 preterm infants treated at an Indonesian hospital in 2023 and 2024.

Severe cases had clearly higher procalcitonin and clearly lower platelet counts than milder cases. The combined ratio was also much higher in severe disease. In accuracy testing, the ratio scored higher than either measure alone, correctly sorting most babies. It identified about 86 in 100 severe cases while clearing about 83 in 100 milder ones at the chosen cutoff. The authors argue the ratio is practical because both tests are routine and cheap.
pmc-13423748:
Ji-Woo Woo and five colleagues test whether drinking habits predict primary malignant brain tumours in Korean adults, using a national health insurance sample cohort. Records covered 240,948 adults who completed health screening between 2006 and 2008, with drinking amount, frequency, and heavy episodic drinking captured by standard questionnaires.

Over an average twelve years of follow-up, 209 malignant brain tumours appeared. Daily amount of alcohol and heavy episodic drinking showed no link with tumour risk. Frequency told a different story: people who drank almost daily carried over twice the risk of non-drinkers, with a hazard ratio of 2.61, and risk rose with frequency. Checks excluding early cases and limiting the group to over-forties gave similar answers.
pmc-13424448:
Kaapangelwa and colleagues chart in 2026 nearly three decades of kidney disease found by biopsy in people living with HIV at Tygerberg Hospital in South Africa. Kidney damage is a common complication of the infection.

The retrospective study covered 554 patients biopsied between 1992 and 2020, split at the 2004 rollout of antiretroviral therapy, the drugs that control HIV. HIV-associated nephropathy, a kidney pattern directly tied to the virus, accounted for just under half of all cases. Its share fell from three fifths before the rollout to a lower share afterward. After the rollout, more than half of patients showed only other patterns, most often immune-complex glomerulonephritis and disease of the kidney tubules and surrounding tissue.
pmc-13424548:
Brandon A. Güell and Nathan J. Dorn test whether a native Florida crayfish recognises the Asian swamp eel, an invader blamed for the collapse of crayfish in Everglades sloughs and, with them, food for nesting wading birds. In laboratory trials, slough crayfish met either the eel or a common native predator, the warmouth fish.

Against the warmouth the crayfish did everything right: they moved less, kept their distance, and fed less. Against the eel they barely reacted at all. Crayfish from invaded and uninvaded wetlands behaved the same, so more than ten generations of exposure have not taught recognition. Direct observations suggest a cruel trade-off, since the stillness that fools fish may leave crayfish open to eels.
pmc-13424748:
He and colleagues traced a molecular chain in 2026 that weakens skin cell grip in pemphigus vulgaris, a life-threatening blistering disease where the immune system attacks the skin. A small RNA called miR-125b-5p is raised in patients, and it was known to target a gene called P63. The team tested how that chain affects desmosomes, the rivet-like links that hold skin cells together.

Lab tests confirmed the small RNA binds the P63 message directly and lowers the protein. A second protein under P63 control, called PERP, fell as well. In mouse tongue tissue treated with a disease-causing antibody, extra small RNA widened the gap between desmosome halves, thinned the fibers anchoring them, and left the links visibly damaged. The authors conclude the RNA drives blistering by cutting P63 and PERP, and name it as a possible treatment target.
pmc-13426048:
James Melrose reviews keratan sulfate, a sugar chain molecule found in cartilage, cornea, and other tissues, as an electrical conductor involved in nerve signalling. His 2026 narrative review argues that this glycosaminoglycan does more than provide structure and hydration.

According to the review, keratan sulfate helps stabilise ion flows and electrical gradients at cell surfaces, which set the membrane states that trigger neurons. It also interacts with kinases, growth factors, and guidance proteins that steer growing nerve fibres and wire up neural networks. Its ability to capture and shuttle protons is presented as an ultrasensitive signalling system supporting sensory perception. Melrose highlights several keratan sulfate carrying proteins and calls for more work on these roles in sensation and tissue function.
pmc-13426348:
Yifan Hou and colleagues surveyed primary care teams in Beijing about vaccination teamwork for lung disease patients in a 2026 multicenter cross-sectional study. Family doctor teams answered a structured questionnaire from October to December 2025, yielding 209 valid responses at a response rate above ninety-two percent. While 57.9 percent endorsed shared responsibility for vaccination, only 24.9 percent reported frequent team discussion and 9.1 percent reported none in three months.

Questions covered collaboration behavior, influencing factors, guideline awareness, and vaccination practice for people with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. The gap between shared responsibility in principle and discussion in practice highlights where team routines need strengthening. Teams that talk more tend to act more, and the poll lays bare how rare such talks still are in the day to day work of care.
pmc-13426448:
Joseph Etah Oben reviews the linked effects of climate change, migration, and health for older migrants in Africa in a 2026 article. Resource-poor settings already face humanitarian strain and rising chronic disease, and older people who move under climate pressure carry compounded risks. His review searched Google Scholar, Google, and Web of Science for studies and documents addressing the three-way connection, with special attention to elderly outcomes.

Guidance offered to governments covers folding climate mitigation into health system planning so older migrants can cope and age healthily. The synthesis argues elderly migrants deserve explicit place in both climate policy and health planning.
pmc-13427048:
Frank Marino and Alexander Marino explore the physiology of survival through the third man, the sensed companion reported by people in extreme danger. Ernest Shackleton described such a presence during his 1916 crossing of South Georgia, when three men each felt a fourth beside them.

The authors argue the sensed presence is not madness but a normal, helpful response to isolation, monotony, cold, low oxygen, and threat. They link it to the body's forward-looking controls, which adjust effort, pacing, and perception before hard limits are reached. A felt companion can hold off despair and keep a person moving, which itself protects body function. Marino asks whether belief and expectation, like a placebo escape hatch, can shift survival odds.
pmc-13427148:
Mustapha Hamdaoui and colleagues make hydrogen from seawater and silicon waste with no metal catalyst at all. Silane hydrolysis, splitting silicon-hydrogen bonds with water, was little explored without noble metals, though hydrogen is prized as fuel and feedstock.

Simple bases served as catalyst with dimethyl sulfoxide as promoter, backed by mechanism and computer studies. Phenylsilane reacted at 202 turnovers per minute, far above other metal-free systems at 8 or fewer and above noble-metal systems at 170 or fewer. The method also ran fast on seawater with a silicon-industry waste, turning two discards into fuel.
pmc-13427448:
Shuo Wei and coauthors show that lacking a fat-processing enzyme makes chicken liver cells vulnerable to ferroptosis in a 2026 study. Ferroptosis is iron-dependent cell death driven by lipid peroxidation and increasingly tied to liver injury. Stearoyl-CoA desaturase 1, the rate-limiting enzyme for making monounsaturated fatty acids, helps maintain lipid balance in embryonic chicken liver cells.

Knocking the enzyme down shrank lipid droplets and lowered triglyceride and total cholesterol levels significantly, while shifts in oxidative stress and iron handling raised death susceptibility. Poultry researchers gain a lipid pathway lever over a newly recognized injury mechanism.
pmc-13427648:
Roland Muhindo Muyisa and colleagues survey, in 2026, what market vendors in Butembo, in the Democratic Republic of Congo, believe about type 2 diabetes. Markets gather much of daily life there, yet health knowledge in such settings is rarely measured. Interviewers questioned 433 adults across seven big markets in French or Swahili during March and April 2025. Most had heard of diabetes, and their answers were analyzed in detail.

Weight loss and constant tiredness were the signs named most often. Many linked the illness to high blood pressure and knew that healthy food and exercise help prevent it. Prayer and poisoning beliefs also appeared alongside medical explanations, held by sizable minorities. Just over half said they would see a doctor first if diabetes seemed likely. Health educators gain a clear picture of where teaching should start.
pmc-13427748: Engineering research impact exceeds citation counts. This piece argued for broader measures. The perspective reframes evaluation. Impact is more than numbers. Research evaluation needs broader metrics. Numbers alone miss engineering impact. Impact assessment needs qualitative insight. Engineering impact needs narrative evidence.
pmc-13427948:
Adéla Bubeníková and colleagues test Emotrics, a computer-vision tool that scores faces objectively after surgery for vestibular schwannoma, a balance-nerve tumour. Face weakness is common after removal, but standard grades rely on human judgment and often disagree.

Thirty-six patients, averaging 51.2 years, had standard front photos before surgery, at discharge, and at three months. Emotrics scored symmetry and movement for still faces, moving faces, and unwanted linked movements, then composite scores were set beside clinical grades. Dynamic function rose from 0.41 at discharge to 0.56 at three months, showing recovery that eyes alone might miss.
pmc-13428048:
U. M. G. Sanketha Francis and co-authors tally, in a 2026 systematic review, what preventable dental emergencies cost health systems. Tooth problems that routine care could have caught still send crowds to emergency departments and hospital wards. The team screened about 2,600 studies and kept 25 that reported costs, most from the United States. Charges were converted to 2024 United States dollars for fair comparison.

Average charges per emergency visit ran from roughly 410 dollars to about 2,741 dollars. Hospital admissions cost far more, with charges reaching above 62,000 dollars in the costliest group, infections spreading from teeth. Tooth decay was the commonest reason for emergency visits. Uninsured patients, public insurance holders, and low-income neighborhoods appeared most often. The authors push for cheaper routine dental access and better links between medical and dental care.
pmc-13428248:
Guang-Lin Li, Ming-Tai An, and colleagues describe, in a 2026 paper, a new plant species from the limestone hills of Guizhou, China. The plant, named Ophiorrhiza saxatilis, belongs to a genus famed as a natural source of a cancer drug compound. It grows in karst country, the rugged limestone terrain of the region. At first glance it resembles a known relative, Ophiorrhiza lignosa, so the team compared the two trait by trait.

Seven stable differences separate them, including hair patterns on stems and leaves, longer bracts, shorter leaf stalks, and where the stamens sit inside the flower. The new species also carries two flower forms, while its relative has one. A full description and comparison table back the claim of a distinct species. Karst floras keep yielding novelties to patient field botany.
pmc-13428448:
Kawata and colleagues compared two knee replacement operations in 2026 using a nationwide Japanese database covering 2010 to 2022. Partial knee replacement treats one compartment, while total replacement rebuilds the whole joint. Their cohort held 36,235 partial and 322,424 total replacements. The main outcome combined in-hospital death and major body-wide complications needing further treatment, balanced statistically between groups.

Partial replacement carried about a third lower risk of the combined outcome overall, and its transfusion risk was about a tenth of the total replacement risk. Age changed the picture. In patients aged seventy-nine and under, partial replacement roughly halved the complication risk. In patients eighty and over, the two operations did not differ significantly, though transfusions stayed lower with partial replacement in both age bands. The authors urge the same careful risk checks for very old patients whichever operation is chosen.
pmc-13428548:
Panfeng Xu and Shan Lu report, in a 2026 case review, an aggressive lung tumor that shrank on a targeted drug. Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumors are rare growths that usually behave mildly, though some invade and spread. Their patient was a 39-year-old woman with two weeks of fever, cough, and breathlessness. Scans showed a large mass in her right upper lung reaching into the chest center, plus nodules across the lung lining and fluid around the lung.

Biopsy confirmed the tumor type, and staining showed it carried the ALK marker, a growth switch that certain drugs block. After three weeks on brigatinib, a drug from that class, scans showed the lung mass and spread sites much smaller and the fluid reduced. Her symptoms eased in step. The authors offer brigatinib as an option worth testing for similar ALK-positive cases.
pmc-13429248:
Ogbu and colleagues published a 2026 study on bowel leakage as a warning sign in adults. Fecal incontinence, the accidental leaking of stool, affects about one in twelve adults. The team asked whether it flags wider disease in the heart, lungs, and kidneys. They used a national survey of 14,731 adults linked to death records.

Adults with leakage carried far more disease across all three body systems. They were also about a decade older and reported more low mood. Death rates ran higher, driven mainly by the pile-up of other diseases. Even after full adjustments, leakage still tracked with kidney disease markers. The authors urge full body checks when patients disclose bowel leakage. Routine questions about leakage are rarely asked, so cases stay hidden for years.
pmc-13433748:
Tyler Schneider and co-authors stress-tested a Canadian hospital record system in 2026 for drug study worth, using heart-stretch drugs and grave heart events as the probe case. A map of links across more than twenty thousand tables came first. Machine checks faced two outside banks, while hand chart reads checked a second slice.

Forty-three tables held the core drug study fields. Most plain fields matched at near-total rates: age, sex, ward, drug gives, lab reads, and time stamps. Grave heart events past death matched poorly, as did some past illness fields. Both weak spots healed once charts linked to a hand-coded national bank. The authors warn that even a top paid system holds fields too thin for drug work alone.
pmc-13434448:
Md Azree Othuman Mydin and colleagues test cement kiln dust variants as partial cement replacements in lightweight foamed concrete. Cement production drives nearly 8 percent of global carbon dioxide emissions, and foamed concrete, prized for insulation and light weight, still leans heavily on ordinary Portland cement.

Three kiln-dust variants, alkaline-rich, calcium-rich, and iron-rich, replaced 40 percent of cement in foamed concrete targeted at 1000 kilograms per cubic metre. Fresh tests covered flow, setting, and density, while hardened tests spanned compressive, flexural, and tensile strength at ages from 7 to 180 days, plus elasticity, water transport, thermal properties, and microstructure. Builders get a waste-valorising route to lighter, greener concrete.
pmc-13434648:
Shanshan Zhang and coauthors rewrite plant enzymes so gut bacteria can make them well in 2026. Plant sugar adding enzymes often fold badly in bacteria, which stalls green factories for natural products. A design program reshaped two such enzymes while keeping their key parts intact.

The rebuilt enzymes dissolved far better and worked faster than the wild forms. Dish tests and whole cell runs agree, beating the usual tack on fixes. Tank growth reached 2.11 grams per liter for one product and 4.05 for another. Computer views credit a better balance of water loving and water shy surfaces. Factories gain a general fix.
pmc-13435648:
Rui Jing and coauthors test an old mood drug against a fatal cat virus in 2026. Feline infectious peritonitis has no vaccine and few cures. Imipramine blocked the virus in dishes with a wide safety margin, acting at entry and at copying stages.

The drug grips a host protein that moves cholesterol, which jams virus entry. Swelling signals from infection also fell, without use of the usual interferon path. Treated cats carried less virus and showed milder signs. An approved human drug may cross over to cat care fast. Dose and safety work in cats comes next.
pmc-13435748:
Guigang Zhao's team built the first single-cell atlas of hawthorn leaves in 2026, a plant prized for food and traditional medicine. Hawthorn leaves gather flavonoids and other valued compounds, yet which cells make them, and how leaves develop cell by cell, was unmapped despite genome data. Combining two single-cell methods across two species, the team profiled over thirty-two thousand cells into sixteen clusters and nine cell types.

Developmental paths converged on mesophyll dominance late in growth, species differed in photosynthesis, volatile, and low-oxygen genes, and flavonoid-making enzymes were split across cell groups rather than housed in one. Plant scientists get a cell map for breeding and harvesting leaves with richer chemistry. The atlas should guide work on yield and medicinal quality.
pmc-13435948:
Tommaso Barlattani's team tracked psychiatric admission ages in 2026 at the sole ward serving L'Aquila, Italy, over seventeen years from 2006 to 2022. National inpatient numbers fell after psychiatric reform, but whether admission age shifted by diagnosis, sex, and voluntary versus compulsory status was unclear. Over five thousand adult admission episodes were grouped into schizophrenia spectrum, major depression, bipolar disorder, and alcohol or substance use disorders.

Admission age fell sharply for major depression and moderately for bipolar disorder, driven by men in depression and women in bipolar disorder, while other patterns varied by admission type. Service planners get a long, local trend that may reflect earlier help-seeking, changing thresholds, or both. The single-catchment design limits how far the pattern travels.
pmc-13436648:
Zahra Ridha and coauthors scope the literature on emergency department closures in 2026. Searches across three databases since 2000 yielded 1,725 papers, of which twenty two fit. Those papers cover 147 single closures plus national scale United States counts.

Findings sort into four themes: patient outcomes, care access, equity, and system strain. Most studies watch outcomes after the fact rather than testing closure plans. Staff shortages and crowding drive most closures in the reports. Rural and poor areas bear the sharpest access losses. Planners need closure impact checks before doors shut, the review argues.
pmc-13437448:
Alex Agundez-Moreno and a large team checked whether switching a multiple sclerosis drug from vein drip to skin injection keeps the body in the same state. Natalizumab is a strong therapy for the relapsing-remitting form, and patients increasingly move to the easier injection. Their 2026 study followed forty-eight patients at many centers on the drip at least six months, half on a four-week cycle and the rest on a stretched six-week cycle.

The drug's grip on its target receptor stayed level on every immune cell type tracked, across both dosing plans. Levels of a nerve damage marker also stayed flat, with no gap between groups. No patient showed new scan activity or worsening disability during follow-up. They read the results as support for the injection as a stand-in for the drip, even on the stretched schedule, in stable patients.
pmc-13437648:
Adnan Kisa and Sezer Kisa mapped the world literature on social prescribing, where health workers link patients to community help beside medicine: choirs, gardens, debt advice, walking groups. The approach targets the social roots of poor health, yet reports vary wildly in model and setting. Their 2026 scoping review screened 7,602 records and kept 115 studies from sixteen countries, about sixty-four percent from the United Kingdom alone.

Reported gains clustered on the human side: better mental well-being, less loneliness, more confidence, and stronger social ties. Hard clinical and cost outcomes swung more. Working parts seemed to include a steady link worker, personal tailoring, and meaningful activities. Barriers repeated too: poverty, shaky funding, stretched community groups, and staff pressure. Migrants, minority groups, and young people were barely studied, and cost evidence was thin. Their map gives planners a shared picture and a frank list of what remains unproven.
pmc-13438548:
Marcia McNutt and Ellen Stofan, leaders of two of America's oldest science institutions, use the nation's two-hundred-fiftieth year to argue for the next era of discovery. Their 2026 essay recalls how curiosity built the transistor, the GPS constellation, and modern medicine, often from questions that looked impractical at the time. A June gathering under the America250 banner, joining scientists, engineers, historians, and leaders, frames their message.

Progress is not automatic, they warn. Each generation must rebuild the conditions that let discovery thrive: funded people, strong institutions, and room for odd ideas. Quantum theory, a century-old abstraction, became semiconductors, lasers, MRI scanners, and the phone in every pocket. The authors ask what bold questions this era should dare to fund. Their piece is both a celebration and a charge, addressed to a country deciding how much of its future to stake on science.
pmc-13438748:
Lingfeng Chen and colleagues trace a vicious circle in keloid scars, where collagen building the lump also shields it from the immune system. Keloids are firm, growing scars that return after removal, and no reliable prevention exists. Comparing keloid and normal skin, their 2026 study found collagen piled up and builder cells multiplying. The immune crowd was tilted: fewer killer T cells, more regulatory ones, and more of a checkpoint shield called PD-L1 on the builder cells.

The team then showed the mechanism in lab-grown keloid cells. Extra collagen grips a handle called CD44, which wakes a growth switch named YAP1, ordering more PD-L1. That shield tells immune cells to stand down, so collagen is never cleared and builders keep multiplying. The authors argue the circle offers several places to cut in: block the handle, mute the switch, or strip the shield.
pmc-13439248:
Liying Zhang and co-authors track how trauma symptom networks settle over time in young earthquake survivors, reporting in 2026. Network temperature is a new gauge of how stable a web of linked symptoms is: high values mean symptoms shift easily. The team built eight follow-up groups after three Chinese earthquakes, Wenchuan, Yaan, and Jiuzhaigou. Together the groups held 5,794 children and adolescents, each checked two to four times across up to ten years.

Network temperature fell in every group, meaning symptom webs grew steadier and harder to shift with time. Speed of settling differed by age group, quake, and years since the event. Younger children settled faster than adolescents early after Wenchuan, for instance. The authors argue for help that starts early while symptoms stay movable, tuned to age and setting.
pmc-13439948:
Carballar-Lejarazú and colleagues built malaria-blocking mosquito strains in 2026 that carry stacked anti-parasite genes meant to spread through wild populations by gene drive. The approach, called population modification, aims to make African malaria mosquitoes unable to pass on Plasmodium falciparum rather than killing the insects. Effector genes include antimicrobial peptides and engineered single-chain antibodies aimed at parasite stages.

The team created four lines across two Anopheles species, pairing effector cargoes in two combinations. Used a swapping method that can insert large DNA pieces and expand the cargo at the landing site. Parasite challenge tests with blood meals at low and high parasite doses showed cuts in infection prevalence, with the size of the cut depending on exposure dose, a key realism check. The authors weigh these compound strains against the modeled thresholds for blocking transmission and discuss fitness and drive resilience.
pmc-13440948:
Yu-hang Chen, Xue Zhou, and Jun-shan Chen pool randomised trials comparing two seizure-based depression treatments, publishing a 2026 meta-analysis. Magnetic seizure therapy induces a seizure with magnetic pulses, aiming for electroconvulsive therapy's punch with gentler side effects. Trials up to March 2026 across seven databases yielded six studies with 429 patients with major depressive disorder.

Depression scores after treatment ran slightly worse for the magnetic method, suggesting a small efficacy edge for electric therapy. Thinking tests told the reverse story. Magnetic therapy preserved word fluency, immediate memory, delayed memory, and verbal learning significantly better across the pooled trials. The authors frame the trade plainly: a little less antidepressant force in exchange for clearer cognition. Larger trials are their stated requirement before practice should shift on this evidence.
pmc-13441348:
Appel, Mattes, and Gerlach tested whether intolerance of uncertainty drives indecisiveness. Intolerance of uncertainty is a deep-seated dread of the unknown. The test ran in people with anxiety and obsessive-compulsive disorders. In a study listed in advance, 154 diagnosed patients were split by chance into tasks meant to raise or lower their intolerance. They then rated two decisions that mattered to them.

The shift produced no direct main effect on indecisiveness in the patient sample studied. It did shift in-the-moment intolerance of uncertainty. Those levels rose with how undecided patients felt about their decisions at that moment. A path check found a clear indirect path. The assigned group moved indecisiveness through the intolerance it induced. Effect sizes were small against earlier non-clinical work. The authors suggest stronger treatments may be needed in clinical groups. They cautiously stretch the causal account to mental disorders.
pmc-13442048:
Lang and Sato extend a family of quantum chemistry methods for simulating mixed fermion systems in this 2026 theoretical paper. Coupled-cluster methods model how electrons and other fermions move and interact over time, but they can suffer numerical instability and overparameterization when approximations are truncated. Their earlier work used a bivariational principle to build stable methods; this paper develops eighteen non-bivariational variants with more flexible equations of motion.

The new methods keep the constraints that prevent overcounting and preserve convergence to the exact active-space limit as the approximation grows. They can be aimed at electron dynamics or at vibrational dynamics, depending on the system under study. One notable result separates them from the older family. All eighteen violate the Ehrenfest theorem, a consistency law for average motion. They do so even when they respect gauge invariance.
pmc-13442448:
Ying Wang and colleagues chart herpes brain illness in 56 children treated in Zhengzhou from 2018 to 2023 in a 2026 study. Herpes simplex virus can inflame the brain, and young age may change both signs and lasting harm. Children split into three age bands, under three years, three to six years, and six to eighteen years, for side-by-side checks.

Half the group was under three, since 60.7 percent of cases fell in the youngest band. Face or mouth twitching showed in 33.9 percent of cases, all of them under age five, and it peaked at 70.0 percent in the middle band. That sign tracked with harm to front brain zones and with severe lasting speech loss. Long follow-up, a median span of 62.5 months in this cohort, let the team weigh which early signs warn of poor outcomes.
pmc-13442848:
Ruijie Liu and coauthors report a 2026 laboratory study of apatinib, a drug that blocks a blood-vessel growth signal, as a treatment for synovial sarcoma. This rare and aggressive soft-tissue cancer strikes mainly adolescents and young adults. The team tested the drug in two sarcoma cell lines and in mice carrying human tumor grafts. The tests traced how it acts on two signaling routes inside tumor cells and on the vessel-lining cells that feed tumors.

In the cell tests, apatinib lowered cell survival, halted growth at an early cycle stage, and triggered cell death and self-digestion, while curbing migration, invasion, and vessel-tube formation. In mice, it slowed graft growth and shifted the same signaling routes. The work supports testing this vessel-signal blocker in people with advanced sarcoma, though clinical trials must still confirm safety and benefit in patients.
pmc-13443048:
Ivanka Simić Stanojević and colleagues ask what builds staff faith in LGBTQ-affirming care for people with learning and growth disabilities in a 2026 study. Workers who doubt their skill may dodge talks on sexual identity, which leaves needs unmet. The survey covered 114 support staff, from teachers and nurses to therapists and social workers.

Staff filled scales on know-how, views, and past work with LGBTQ+ people, plus a faith scale for affirming care. Ties among facts, views, life contact, and faith were weighed in staged models. Faith theory from Bandura framed the checks. The authors argue that training must build facts and warm views together, since facts alone may not lift faith. Care that affirms both disability and identity takes staff who feel able, not just willing.
pmc-13443148:
Liu and a large team review the Warburg effect in stomach cancer in this 2026 article. The Warburg effect is the tendency of cancer cells to burn sugar rapidly even when oxygen is plentiful, producing lactate. In gastric cancer, low oxygen, oncogenic signaling, non-coding RNAs, and gene-control rewiring all converge on sugar transporters and core glycolytic enzymes such as HK2 and LDHA, the review explains.

Lactate is not mere waste. It acidifies the tumor's surroundings. It weakens killer T and natural killer cells, and favors suppressive immune cells. It also helps tumors resist chemotherapy, targeted drugs, and immunotherapy. The authors survey biomarkers from imaging and blood tests to gene signatures, grading each by readiness for clinical use. They argue future treatment should pair metabolic targeting with standard therapy, guided by biomarkers, rather than blocking glycolysis alone.
pmc-13443748:
Xue Fei and colleagues solve the structure of a degrader drug locked onto its target in a 2026 paper. The drug, KT-474, drags a kinase called IRAK4 to the cell's shredder, and trials test it for skin and sweat gland ills. Ice-cold microscope views caught the drug bridging IRAK4 and the CRBN shredder arm.

The bridge forms a fresh contact face that neither protein shows alone. A phenylalanine at spot 150 on CRBN anchors the grip among mixed polar and greasy contacts. Oddly, the parts bind with negative teamwork, since snug contacts fight the drug's flex. That flex helps explain why the drug picks IRAK4 over kin. The authors say such structures can steer degrader design with eyes open.
pmc-13444748:
Xue Li and colleagues study reality shock among new nurses, the jolt felt when ward life falls short of what training promised, in a 2026 survey. That jolt may erode how strongly young nurses see nursing as their own profession. The survey ran at one large hospital in Sichuan Province in late 2025.

Replies from 238 nurses with three years of service or less fell into two groups. About three in five felt low shock, while the rest felt high shock tied to overtime, contract type, and weak job satisfaction. Nurses in the high shock group held a weaker sense of professional identity, so the authors urge lighter loads and stronger support during the first years.
pmc-13445148:

pmc-13445748:

pmc-13446148:

pmc-13446548:

pmc-13446648:

pmc-13446748:

pmc-13447048:

pmc-13447248:

pmc-13448548:

pmc-13449848:

pmc-13450048:

pmc-13450748:

Cancer cells are known to react to the stiffness of what holds them, so a tunable stand-in helps labs probe that link. The piece places the gel in a fast-growing line of synthetic tissue models for health research.
pmc-13452148:
Alberto Herrero Babiloni and a large team chart in 2026 sleep complaints in survivors of head and neck cancers near the airway, after radiation care. pmc-13452348:
Miguel Lopez-Moreno, Gonzalo Quesada-Fernandez, and Jose Francisco Lopez-Gil argue in 2026 that nutrition science keeps weak claims alive through set reasoning slips. pmc-13453948:

pmc-13454148:

pmc-13455148:

pmc-13455248:

pmc-13455348:

pmc-13457148:

pmc-13457248:

pmc-13457548:

pmc-13457748:

pmc-13457848:

pmc-13458048:

pmc-13458348:

pmc-13459548:

pmc-13459948:

pmc-13461948:

pmc-13463048:

pmc-13463648:

pmc-13465248:

pmc-13465548:

pmc-13465648:

pmc-13466748:

pmc-13467648:

pmc-13467948:

pmc-13468348:
